# **Abstract**
---
***Abstract*-Floating multimodal electrochemical sensors report the glucose concentration and cell density inside bioreactors to the process control loop, readings that an adversary may seek to intercept or forge. The secure delta-sigma modulator (S-DSM) of Yasar *et al.* [1] protects such readings inside the analog-to-digital converter: each 1-bit modulator output is XORed with the keystream of a 16-bit linear-feedback shift register (LFSR), for a reported 1.8 % power overhead and up to 2.67× lower wireless energy than a decimate-then-encrypt design. We propose deriving the key from a physically unclonable function (PUF), so that no key is held in on-chip non-volatile memory (NVM): a 128-bit key is regenerated at every power-up from the start-up state of 600 static random-access memory (SRAM) cells, corrected by a fuzzy extractor with a Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) code and hashed, and is held only in volatile registers while the chip is powered. The key drives the Grain-128a stream cipher, which also authenticates every frame: it computes over the frame a 32-bit message authentication code (MAC), a tag that only the key holder can produce, so the receiver rejects an altered or forged frame except with probability 2<sup>−32</sup> per attempt. Each frame also carries a frame counter, so that a replayed old frame is rejected, and the cipher is initialised from two nonces, that is, values never repeated under the same key: a session nonce sent by the receiver at the start of each session and a chip nonce derived from the chip's noisy power-up state, so that the keystream is not reused as long as either nonce is fresh. The analog front end and the bit-level XOR of [1] are unchanged. To evaluate both designs, this notebook builds a bit-exact model of the link and checks it before use for consistency with the measured bit-flip probabilities and energy table of [1] (48.2 % and 50.0 % of bits differ against 49.8 % and 50.05 % measured; the ratios of transmitted bits match the energy ratios of [1] within 0.18 %). The principal result is the security evaluation: of 15 attacks, the original design fails 11 in the model; with a simplified representation of the dither of [1], it withstands the cryptanalyses of [1] only as [1] carries them out, and fails once its 16-bit key is brute-forced, a few keystream bits leak, a session nonce is replayed, or the attacker holds the chip or transmits on the link (six of the 11, beyond the eavesdropper evaluated in [1]); in the same model the proposal withstands all 15 (9 verdicts simulated, 2 analytic, 4 assumed). At block level, the model's circuit parameters are then taken from the SkyWater SKY130 open process design kit: the noise and offset of the modulator's StrongARM comparator and the power-up statistics of a six-transistor (6T) SRAM cell, simulated in ngspice from extracted layouts (post-layout, tt: comparator noise 0.58 mV and offset σ 4.4 mV at 27 °C; PUF noise-to-mismatch ratio 0.0225 at 25 °C). Sized from the simulated error rates of 1,000 Monte Carlo chips (a cell model fitted to the post-layout SPICE Monte Carlo of the cell), no BCH code for 600 cells enrolled at 25 °C meets both the 10⁻⁶ key-failure target from 0 to 85 °C, which needs t ≥ 39 at the 99th percentile, and the secrecy budget of a 128-bit key, which allows at most t = 35; an enrolment at two temperatures resolves this (below); the system simulations use t = 45 (94–137 secret bits) as a working setting. At system level, across 45 process, voltage and temperature (PVT) conditions, each effect is first predicted by a first-order theory and then simulated: the simulated sensor (behavioural model with the SKY130 parameters) keeps a signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR) of 60.3–60.4 dB with a margin of about 90× in comparator noise and needs only about 40 dB of integrator amplifier gain; against an attacker who scans the whole capture, with the model's dither, comparator noise protects the original design only from 197× its largest PVT value, at a cost of 7.5 dB of SNDR, and neither comparator offset nor integrator capacitor mismatch protects it at any value tested; and at the fast-nMOS corners some simulated SRAM cells reverse their preferred state with temperature, so the key generator must be sized and enrolled for its worst corner; an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C meets the 10⁻⁶ target at every corner for at least 99.7 % of the Monte Carlo chips with t = 17 and 284–352 secret bits. Yosys synthesis of register-transfer-level (RTL) descriptions, verified against published test vectors, onto the sky130_fd_sc_hd cell library, with every design given the same low-power techniques (a radix-16 parallel state update and clock gating), gives 869, 2,931 and 9,869 gate equivalents (GE) for the S-DSM, the Trivium stream cipher and the proposal's keystream block. The block is placed and routed with OpenROAD (no design-rule violations, layout matching the netlist, timing met at 10 MHz with extracted wires; 16 antenna violations remain), and gate-level simulation under the same conditions for every design gives 64.3 µW for the placed block at 1.8 V and 10 MHz (wire loads estimated on the placement; 73.4 µW with the extracted wires), 6.5× less than as written for one bit per clock and 3.6× the S-DSM in the same flow, a ratio taken within one process, so no process scaling enters it. Without scaling any number between processes, a figure of merit built only from reported results and published process facts, the energy per bit over L<sub>min</sub>V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> of each design's own process, per bit of security level and per security property provided, gives 29.1 aJ/(nm·V²) for the proposal (gate-level simulation) against 1,603 for the S-DSM measured in [1]. For the same information at an oversampling ratio of 50, the proposal sends 1.44–1.60× fewer bits than the decimate-then-Trivium design of [1], but 3.1× more than a design that decimates on the sensor and sends 16-bit words; no radio is designed, so no radio energy is claimed. A key-generator compiler turns the reliability and secrecy specification into a generated decoder, verified in RTL simulation bit for bit against the model, synthesised and placed and routed: with a 25 °C enrolment no code meets the target at all five corners, while an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C with a repetition-3 and BCH t = 4 code meets it with 1,395 cells and 194 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy, the same 192-bit budget; with a synthesised SHA-256 core, the designed parts of the key generator and keystream block total 38,638 GE. Finally, a mixed-level simulation of the complete sensor, with the SRAM array and the comparator at transistor level and the key decoder and cipher in RTL, regenerates the key from transistor-level cells and finds the comparator model in agreement decision by decision over 2,000 decisions at tt and 37 °C. Every result is computed by running this notebook in one Colab session or shown from a recorded run of the same code, which a switch re-runs.**

***Index Terms*-Delta-sigma modulator, physical-layer security, physically unclonable function (PUF), SRAM PUF, fuzzy extractor, BCH code, Grain-128a, message authentication, stream cipher, Berlekamp-Massey, SKY130, mixed-level simulation, open-source EDA.**

**Structure of the notebook.** The notebook is organised as a journal paper, with numbered sections, captioned figures and tables, and references, in the order given in the Overview above. Each section opens with the question it answers, why it matters and what it takes from earlier sections, and ends with a summary of its findings. Within a section, each study is a chain of short, labelled steps: Goal (what is determined and why), Theory (the principle, its symbols and the prediction to be tested), Setup (the level of simulation, the parameters and where each comes from, the sweeps and the metric), Next cell (what the code cell below does, step by step), the cell and its figure or table with a caption, Result (the numbers of this run, compared with the prediction) and Interpretation (what the result means for accuracy, security, power or cost). The notebook can be read from beginning to end without execution, since all outputs are saved, or executed with modified settings.

DISPLAY_PX = 1000      # display width of every plot: at least GitHub's notebook column, so there (no styles) each viewer
                       # scales the centred canvas to the column; wider Jupyter and Colab columns keep this size and the
                       # style above centres it (a full-width 2000 px made every plot 1.6x larger on wide screens)
def _journal_case(fig):
    """Journal style: axis labels and panel titles start with a capital letter ('(a) noise' -> '(a) Noise'), unless they
    start with a symbol, a number or math. Applied to every figure in show(), so each cell need not do it."""
    import re
    # only an English word is capitalised: not a Greek letter (σ, θ), a one-letter variable (q, k) or math ($...$)
    nets = {"dp", "dn", "outp", "outn", "qb", "clk", "tail", "vdd", "vss",          # net names and process corners stay
            "tt", "ss", "ff", "sf", "fs"}                                           # as written
    word = lambda s: (m := re.match(r"([a-z][a-z]+)(?![_$^{a-zA-Z0-9])", s)) and m.group(1) not in nets
    cap = lambda s: s[0].upper() + s[1:] if s and word(s) else s
    # only the text is changed (Text.set_text): set_ylabel/set_title would also reset the alignment (a row label drawn with
    # rotation=0, ha="right" would be centred on the axis and overlap the plot) and the title's font size and weight
    for a in fig.axes:
        for lab in (a.xaxis.label, a.yaxis.label):
            lab.set_text(cap(lab.get_text()))
        for t in (a.title, a._left_title, a._right_title):
            s = t.get_text()
            m = re.match(r"^(\([a-z]\)\s+)(.*)$", s, re.S)
            new = (m.group(1) + cap(m.group(2))) if m else cap(s)
            if new != s:
                t.set_text(new)

def show(*args, **kwargs):
    """Replaces plt.show(): every open figure is displayed as one PNG, then closed. The figure is drawn in the middle of a
    white canvas of the two-column width (wider figures keep their width), so that it is centred in every viewer, and the
    PNG carries a display width (DISPLAY_PX) of about GitHub's notebook column: GitHub (which strips styles) scales it to
    the column, so the figure is centred there without a style, and in wider Jupyter and Colab columns the style printed
    before it centres it at this size; a plain PNG output is rendered by every notebook viewer (GitHub strips
    images embedded in HTML outputs). With show.capture set to a list, the PNGs are collected instead of displayed (static copies of widgets)."""
    import io
    from IPython.display import Image
    from PIL import Image as PILImage
    for num in plt.get_fignums():
        fig = plt.figure(num)
        _journal_case(fig)
        dpi = 110 if show.plain else 170
        buf = io.BytesIO(); fig.savefig(buf, format="png", dpi=dpi, facecolor="white")
        # every figure on one canvas of the two-column width, centred on it: the figure is centred in every viewer, also
        # where the centring style below is stripped (GitHub), and all figures share one display scale
        canvas_in = max(W2, fig.get_figwidth())
        im = PILImage.open(io.BytesIO(buf.getvalue()))
        wpx = int(round(canvas_in * dpi))
        if im.width < wpx:
            page = PILImage.new("RGB", (wpx, im.height), "white")
            page.paste(im.convert("RGB"), ((wpx - im.width) // 2, 0))
            buf = io.BytesIO(); page.save(buf, format="png", optimize=True)
        if show.capture is not None:
            show.capture.append(buf.getvalue())
        else:
            display(HTML(_CENTER))                       # centres the canvas in Jupyter and Colab
            display(Image(data=buf.getvalue(), width=DISPLAY_PX))
        plt.close(fig)
show.plain, show.capture = False, None
plt.show = show

def display_widget(w, png=None):
    """Displays an ipywidget together with a static PNG of its initial view (png: bytes): a live notebook shows the widget,
    a viewer without a kernel (GitHub, a saved copy) shows the PNG instead of an empty output."""
    import base64
    bundle = w._repr_mimebundle_() if hasattr(w, "_repr_mimebundle_") else None
    if bundle is None or png is None:
        display(w); return
    import io
    from PIL import Image as PILImage
    im = PILImage.open(io.BytesIO(png))                 # centred on the canvas of show(), like every plot
    wpx = int(round(W2 * 170))
    if im.width < wpx:
        page = PILImage.new("RGB", (wpx, im.height), "white")
        page.paste(im.convert("RGB"), ((wpx - im.width) // 2, 0))
        buf = io.BytesIO(); page.save(buf, format="png", optimize=True); png = buf.getvalue()
    data = dict(bundle[0] if isinstance(bundle, tuple) else bundle)
    data["image/png"] = base64.b64encode(png).decode()
    display(HTML(_CENTER))
    display(data, raw=True, metadata={"image/png": {"width": DISPLAY_PX}})   # spans the column, like the plots of show()

def panel(ax, label, text=""):
    """IEEE-style panel caption, '(a) text', above the axes at the left."""
    ax.set_title(f"({label}) {text}".strip(), loc="left", fontsize=10.5, pad=5)

# ---------- result cards: the cells report their results as small tables instead of plain prints
_CARD = ("font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;"
         "border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid {c};padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px")
def card(title, rows=(), note=None, tone="ok"):
    """A compact result panel: a title line, then label | value rows, then an optional note.
    tone: 'ok' (blue: a check that passed / the proposal), 'bad' (orange: a weakness), 'info' (grey)."""
    c = {"ok": COL["ok"], "bad": COL["bad"], "info": COL["faint"]}[tone]
    body = "".join(f'<tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">{k}</td>'
                   f'<td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">{v}</td></tr>' for k, v in rows)
    display(HTML(f'<div style="{_CARD.format(c=c)}"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">{title}</div>'
                 + (f'<table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px">{body}</table>' if rows else "")
                 + (f'<div style="margin-top:4px;opacity:.85">{note}</div>' if note else "") + "</div>"))

def table(header, rows, caption=None, align=None):
    """A booktabs-style table (top and bottom rules, no vertical lines), IEEE caption above it."""
    al = align or ["left"] + ["right"] * (len(header) - 1)
    th = "".join(f'<th style="text-align:{a};padding:4px 12px;border-bottom:1px solid currentColor;font-weight:bold">{h}</th>'
                 for h, a in zip(header, al))
    tr = "".join("<tr>" + "".join(f'<td style="text-align:{a};padding:3px 12px">{v}</td>' for v, a in zip(r, al)) + "</tr>" for r in rows)
    cap = (f'<div style="text-align:center;font-variant:small-caps;letter-spacing:.04em;margin-bottom:4px">{caption}</div>'
           if caption else "")
    display(HTML(f'<div style="font-family:\'STIX Two Text\',\'Times New Roman\',Times,serif;font-size:15px;margin:10px auto;max-width:900px;width:fit-content">{cap}'
                 f'<table style="border-collapse:collapse;margin:0 auto;border-top:1.6px solid currentColor;border-bottom:1.6px solid currentColor">'
                 f'<thead><tr>{th}</tr></thead><tbody>{tr}</tbody></table></div>'))

# icons, animations and the explorer page live in a small public companion repository (nothing secret)
ASSETS = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chennakeshavadasa/secure-sensor-figures/main"
LAB_N = 30000                            # modulator clocks used by the attack experiments and sweeps

try:
    _ip = get_ipython()
    for _ev, _f in (("pre_run_cell", _cell_start), ("post_run_cell", _cell_end)):
        for _old in [g for g in _ip.events.callbacks[_ev] if getattr(g, "__name__", "") == _f.__name__]:
            _ip.events.unregister(_ev, _old)  # re-running this cell replaces the timer instead of adding a second one
        _ip.events.register(_ev, _f)
except NameError:                        # not in IPython
    pass

# **I. Introduction**
---
### A. Secure sensing for biomanufacturing

Biomanufacturing produces plastic components, food ingredients and active pharmaceutical ingredients with living cells, cultivated in large bioreactors whose conditions must be tightly regulated: control of the culture determines the accuracy, efficiency and yield of the process [1]. The culture is currently monitored by extracting samples for offline analysis or by large fixed probes, which risk contamination and observe a single location at a time. Yasar *et al.* [1] instead place a **multimodal electrochemical sensor in a capsule that floats inside the bioreactor** and reports wirelessly, so that a closed control loop observes the entire vessel in real time. The chip (65 nm CMOS, 1.2 V) is a potentiostat front end with three measurement modes:

* cyclic voltammetry (CV), to find the redox potential of a reaction;
* amperometry, to measure the glucose concentration (demonstrated from 1.5 to 5.6 mM, R² = 0.9981), the nutrient the culture consumes;
* electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS, up to 100 kHz), to measure the *E. coli* cell density (4.0 × 10⁷ to 2.4 × 10⁹ cells/mL), the growth of the culture.

The same three techniques underlie electrochemical sensing well beyond bioreactors, wherever a current or an impedance at an electrode must be read at low power:

* *Medical monitoring.* Amperometric enzyme electrodes are the sensing principle of blood-glucose meters and of the continuous glucose monitors worn by people with diabetes; amperometric and voltammetric electrodes also measure lactate, oxygen and pH in blood and sweat, and fast-scan cyclic voltammetry measures neurotransmitters such as dopamine in the brain.
* *Implants and wearables.* Impedance spectroscopy monitors implanted electrodes and the tissue around them, and wearable patches combine the three techniques to track metabolites and electrolytes in sweat.
* *Diagnostics, food and water.* Impedance and voltammetric biosensors detect bacteria, viruses and proteins at the point of care, and voltammetry detects heavy metals and other contaminants in water and food.
* *Energy and industry.* Impedance spectroscopy estimates the state of health of batteries and fuel cells, and voltammetry and amperometry monitor corrosion and electroplating baths.

In the medical cases the readings are personal health data, and in continuous monitors and implants they can drive therapy, such as an insulin dose, so the requirements of confidentiality and integrity stated below apply with even greater force. The secure link studied here applies in principle to any such sensor whose current is digitised by a delta-sigma modulator and transmitted wirelessly.

A low-noise transimpedance amplifier (TIA) with four gain settings (3.30 kΩ to 3.06 MΩ) provides 140.55 dB of dynamic range and 9.48 pA<sub>rms</sub> of input-referred noise over 100 kHz, and a second-order 1-bit continuous-time delta-sigma modulator clocked at 10 MHz digitises the current.

Because these readings drive the control loop, their **confidentiality and integrity** are essential [1]:

* an eavesdropper on the link learns the state of the process, which the manufacturer treats as confidential;
* a man-in-the-middle intercepts the packets, alters them and forwards them to the server, so that the control loop acts on false data, with consequences ranging from reduced yield to the loss of a batch or, in pharmaceutical production, a health hazard.

Fig. 1 shows where these threats act: the readings, which close the control loop, cross an open radio link between the capsules and the receiver, on which **the attacker can listen and inject** forged, replayed or altered frames; the attacker can also choose what the sensor measures or obtain a sensor chip and attack the chip itself.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 1.</b> Application context and threats. Left: stirred-tank bioreactor with floating sensor capsules. Right: uplink of the encrypted ΔΣ bitstream to the receiver and the process-control server; orange: the attacker, who listens to the uplink and injects frames. Bottom: one capsule magnified (counter, reference and working electrodes CE, RE, WE; potentiostat and transimpedance amplifier (TIA); secure delta-sigma modulator (S-DSM); radio).</p>

The conventional solution, a standard cipher on the chip, conflicts with the resource constraints of the capsule, which render conventional cryptography impractical [1]. The chip of [1] dissipates about 1.35 mW in its front end, TIA, buffer and modulator; an on-chip Trivium stream cipher [5] adds 220 µW, and a conventional design must in addition decimate the modulator output into words before encrypting them. Secure links therefore appear costly precisely where energy is most constrained.

### B. Physical-layer encryption in the delta-sigma modulator [1]

Yasar *et al.* [1] encrypt at the output of the data converter itself. The sensor current is digitised by a second-order 1-bit delta-sigma modulator (Section II), whose output is a high-rate bit stream that toggles frequently even for a constant input, because the loop shapes the quantisation noise towards high frequencies. In this secure delta-sigma modulator (S-DSM), each modulator output bit is XORed with one bit of the keystream of a 16-bit linear-feedback shift register (LFSR), whose key is shared with the receiver, and the result is transmitted. The receiver applies the same keystream, recovers the modulator bits and filters them into readings. According to [1], dither injected at the comparator of the modulator further reduces the predictability of the bitstream, and two channels of the chip that encrypt the same input with the same key disagree on about 50 % of their bits, so that an eavesdropper with a replica chip cannot predict the keystream. The security function then costs **24 µW, 1.8 % of the chip power without security** (the overhead measure of [1]), and because the bits are transmitted without decimation, the wireless energy for the same information remains up to **2.67× below** that of a decimate-then-encrypt design [1].

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chennakeshavadasa/secure-sensor-figures/f8600a404a4d61508ddf09cc77a4dd23b2eaedc9/img/primer_sdsm_vs_proposal.png" width="760" alt="primer" style="display:inline-block"></p>

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 2.</b> Signal chain and key path of the two designs. (a) S-DSM [1]: a 16-bit key stored in on-chip memory seeds a 16-bit LFSR; no message authentication code (MAC) tag. (b) Proposal: no key in non-volatile memory (NVM); a 128-bit key regenerated from 600 static random-access memory (SRAM) cells at every power-up keys Grain-128a, which adds a 32-bit MAC tag to every frame.</p>

Fig. 2 contrasts where the key lives: the S-DSM stores its 16-bit key on the chip and sends untagged frames, whereas the proposal of this work (Section IV) holds no key in non-volatile memory and authenticates every frame.

### C. Research questions

The S-DSM provides physical-layer security at low cost in power and area. Its evaluation in [1], however, covers an eavesdropper with a replica chip and two cryptanalyses (a zero input; the same key with the same message), and its circuit behaviour is that of one 65 nm chip measured at room temperature. Three features of the design are not tested there: the 16-bit key is **stored** on the chip, the LFSR keystream is **linear**, and the frames are **not authenticated**. This notebook asks four questions, and answers them with open-source tools and the SkyWater SKY130 process design kit (PDK):

1. **How secure is the S-DSM against a realistic attacker?** An attacker may also search the key space, learn a few keystream bits, obtain a chip, or transmit on the link. Answering this requires a bit-exact model of the link that reproduces the published chip measurements of [1] (Sections V and VI) and an evaluation of every attack on it (Section IX).
2. **Can the stored key be eliminated and every frame authenticated, without changing the analog front end, and at what cost?** We propose to regenerate the key at every power-up from the random start-up state of SRAM cells, a physically unclonable function (PUF), corrected by a Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) code and hashed into a 128-bit key; to replace the LFSR by the Grain-128a stream cipher [6]; and to authenticate every frame with Grain-128a's built-in message authentication code (MAC), a frame counter, and two nonces (a nonce, from "number used once", is a value never repeated under the same key): a session nonce chosen by the receiver and a chip nonce generated by the chip (Section IV). Its security is evaluated in Section IX, and its area, power and wireless energy in Section X.
3. **Do circuit non-idealities change these answers?** A transistor-level comparator has noise and offset, a transistor-level SRAM cell flips with noise and temperature, and both vary with process, supply voltage and temperature (PVT). Do these non-idealities degrade the sensor's accuracy, protect the original design, or make the PUF key unreliable? Answering this requires the circuits at block level (Section VII) and their effect at system level (Section VIII).
4. **Can the key generator be derived from a specification, and do the models hold together?** A key-generator compiler turns the reliability specification into generated RTL, verified in simulation against the model (Section XI), and one mixed-level simulation of the complete sensor checks the abstractions behind the system-level results (Section XII).

Subsection D lists the contributions of this work, and Section XV answers the four questions with the numbers of this run.

### D. Contributions

**Principal result.** Against 15 attacks, each verdict labelled simulated, analytic or assumed, **the original design of [1] fails 11 and the proposal withstands all 15** in the model (Section IX). Six of the 11 need an attacker who holds the chip or transmits on the link, beyond the eavesdropper evaluated in [1]; the others break the 16-bit key by brute force, recover the keystream from a few leaked bits, or exploit a replayed session nonce, and the cryptanalyses of [1] succeed once the attacker scans the whole capture (with a simplified representation of the dither of [1]). The proposal's verdicts are nine simulated, two analytic and four resting on stated assumptions, and it detects and rejects five of the attacks.

The main contributions of this work are the following, in the order in which the notebook establishes them:

1. **A new architecture: authenticated in-modulator encryption keyed by a physically unclonable function** (Section IV). No key is held in on-chip non-volatile memory (NVM), and the key exists only in volatile registers while the chip is powered: a 128-bit key is regenerated at every power-up from the start-up state of 600 static random-access memory (SRAM) cells, used as a physically unclonable function (PUF), through a fuzzy extractor with a Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) code and a hash, and used by Grain-128a with its message authentication code (MAC), a frame counter, a session nonce and a chip nonce. The analog front end, the modulator and the bit-level exclusive-OR (XOR) encryption of the secure delta-sigma modulator (S-DSM) of [1] are unchanged.
2. **A model consistent with the published measurements of [1]** (Section VI). Before it is used, the bit-exact model of the link is checked against the two measurements of [1]: the bit-flip probabilities (48.2 % and 50.0 % of bits differ, against 49.8 % and 50.05 % measured; the same-message value is the ceiling of independent channels, 48.4 % for the model's test sine, so this is a consistency check, not a validation) and the bit counts behind its energy table (bit ratios within 0.18 % of its energy ratios; no radio number used). The model reproduces the measured disagreement with its simplified dither and a small offset between the channels; this is a means of matching the measurement, not a claim about what decorrelates the channels of the chip, which [1] attributes to its dither.
3. **Circuit parameters from extracted SKY130 layouts** (Section VII, block level). A StrongARM comparator and a 6T SRAM cell, simulated in ngspice from their extracted layouts and across 45 process, voltage and temperature (PVT) conditions, replace the model's assumed parameters. The simulated SRAM cell has **about one third of the noise-to-mismatch ratio** that the model assumed before (0.0225 against 0.06). Sized from the simulated error rates over 1,000 Monte Carlo chips (a cell model fitted to the post-layout SPICE Monte Carlo), a 600-cell code enrolled at 25 °C needs t = 39 for a 10⁻⁶ key-failure probability from 0 to 85 °C (up to 46 over the 85 °C error rate's interval), whereas the bounded entropy budget (192 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy, for a 128-bit key with the hash margin) allows at most t = 35: **with a 25 °C enrolment, reliability and secrecy cannot both be met**. The system simulations use t = 45 (94–137 secret bits) as a working setting; an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C meets both: t = 17 holds 10⁻⁶ for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips at every corner and leaves 284–352 secret bits (935 cells, 600 kept; Section VIII-F); the key-generator compiler of Section XI generates hardware, verified in simulation bit for bit against the model, for an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C (repetition-3 and BCH t = 4 code, 1,395 cells, 194 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound, the same 192-bit budget). At the fast-nMOS corners up to 26 % of the cells reverse their preferred state at 85 °C.
4. **A circuit-to-system analysis across 45 PVT conditions** (Section VIII, system level). Each effect is predicted by a first-order theory and then simulated. **In the model, with its simplified dither, the analog circuits do not secure the original design**: against an attacker who scans every window of the capture, comparator noise protects it only from 160 mV, 197× its worst PVT value, at a cost of 7.5 dB of signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio (SNDR), and comparator offset does not at any value tested (up to σ<sub>os</sub> = 3,000 mV, beyond the supply). **The proposal's key reliability is set by the SRAM cell's process corner**: the code must be sized for the worst corner, and an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C lets every corner meet 10⁻⁶ with t = 17 (935 cells, 284–352 secret bits).
5. **A security evaluation beyond the cryptanalyses of [1]** (Section IX). Both designs face 15 attacks, each verdict labelled simulated, analytic or assumed. In the model and under this work's wider threat model, the original design **fails 11**: its 16-bit key is found by brute force, read from memory or recovered by Berlekamp-Massey; the cryptanalyses of [1] succeed once the attacker scans the whole capture with the public polynomial of its linear-feedback shift register (LFSR), trims the replica and votes over frames; a replayed session nonce repeats its keystream; and it accepts cloned, spoofed, replayed and bit-flipped data. In the model, the proposal **withstands all 15** (nine verdicts simulated, two analytic, four assumed), and detects and rejects 5 of them.
6. **A quantified, open implementation** (Section X). Register-transfer-level (RTL) descriptions verified against published test vectors, synthesised, placed and routed in SKY130 in a low-power form applied equally to every compared design (radix-16 parallel state update and clock gating): 9,869 gate equivalents (GE), zero design-rule-check (DRC) violations, clean layout-versus-schematic (LVS) check, timing met at three corners, 64.3 µW at 10 MHz from gate-level simulation (73.4 µW with OpenRCX-extracted wires; 16 antenna violations remain in the routed block). In the same SKY130 flow and at the same conditions, the simulated power of this block is 3.6× that of the S-DSM in the same low-power form. A figure of merit, FOM = E<sub>bit</sub>/(L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> S K) (energy per bit, measured or simulated, over the minimum gate length and nominal supply squared of the design's own process, per bit of security level, per security property provided), compares designs across processes without scaling any number: 29.1 aJ/(nm·V²) for the proposal (SKY130 gate-level simulation) against 1,603 for [1]'s measured S-DSM. For the same information at an oversampling ratio (OSR) of 50 it sends **1.44–1.60× fewer bits than the decimate-then-Trivium design of [1]**, but 3.1× more than an information-equivalent design that decimates to 16-bit words before encrypting; no radio is designed, so no radio energy is claimed.
7. **A key-generator compiler: from specification to a verified, laid-out decoder** (Section XI). From a reliability and secrecy specification it searches concatenated repetition and BCH codes with the corner models, writes the Verilog, verifies it bit for bit against the model, synthesises the most promising candidates and places and routes the selected one. It shows that, under the cell models, no concatenated repetition and BCH code with r ≤ 7 and n ≤ 1023 makes a 25 °C enrolment meet the target at all five corners, that the two-temperature enrolment does, and that both requirements, including the 192-bit secrecy budget, are then met with 1,395 cells and a repetition-3 and BCH t = 4 code, and that in this serial template the selected decoder (8,984 GE) is close to the low-power keystream block (9,869 GE); with a synthesised SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm) core the complete key generator and keystream block total 38,638 GE.
8. **One simulation of the complete sensor across abstraction levels** (Section XII). The SRAM array and the StrongARM comparator, inside the modulator loop, are simulated at transistor level together with the RTL of the key decoder and of Grain-128a and the behavioural rest of the link. This regenerates the key from transistor-level cells and tests the behavioural comparator model decision by decision.

Every number is recomputed by running this notebook in one Colab session (Section VII-A), except those of the seven recorded runs listed in the Appendix, which are shown from records of the same code and can be re-run with their switches.

### E. Methodology and organisation of the notebook

The proposed design is evaluated along three lines (Fig. 3): security (the 15 attacks on both designs), the circuit-to-system evaluation across PVT (transistor-level circuits carried to the accuracy, power and security of the sensor), and implementation cost (verified RTL, synthesis, place-and-route, power and wireless energy). Each line is a sequence of open-source steps executed in the present session or loaded from a recorded run of the same code. The sections take these steps in the order below; the table after it lists the code that computes them.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chennakeshavadasa/secure-sensor-figures/f8600a404a4d61508ddf09cc77a4dd23b2eaedc9/img/method_flow.png" width="900" alt="Methodology: the three lines of evaluation and their open-source steps" style="display:inline-block"></p>

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 3.</b> Evaluation method. Rows: the three lines of evaluation (security, circuit to system, implementation cost); boxes: the four open-source steps of each line in order (arrows), with the quantities and tools of each step.</p>

The sections follow one rule: nothing is used before it has been established. The model is checked for consistency with the published measurements of [1] before any result relies on it, the circuits are simulated at block level before their effect on the system is evaluated, and the design is fixed by the security evaluation before it is implemented.

1. **Foundations.** Section I states the application, the design of [1] and the research questions; Section II reviews the four concepts the work builds on (delta-sigma modulation, stream ciphers, message authentication, PUFs and fuzzy extractors); Section III reviews prior art; Section IV fixes the threat model, which defines the 15 attacks, and describes the proposed architecture.
2. **A model, checked before use.** Section V builds a bit-exact model of both designs: front end, modulator, keystreams, PUF and fuzzy extractor, framing, receiver and attacks. Section VI checks it for consistency with two measurements of [1] before any later section relies on it.
3. **Block level: the analog circuits.** Section VII simulates the two circuits whose non-idealities the model needs, the modulator's StrongARM comparator and the 6T SRAM cell, in SKY130 from extracted layouts and across 45 PVT conditions, and replaces the model's assumed parameters with the simulated ones.
4. **System level.** Section VIII carries these block-level values to the accuracy, power and security of the sensor, in six studies, each a first-order theory tested by simulation.
5. **Security.** Section IX runs the 15 attacks on both designs with the SKY130-derived circuit parameters, and evaluates the reliability of the PUF key.
6. **Implementation: the digital blocks.** Section X implements the digital blocks of both designs and of a Trivium reference at block level (verified RTL, synthesis, place-and-route, gate-level power, with Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout and Icarus Verilog) and counts the bits each design sends for the same information; Section XI compiles the key generator from a reliability specification into verified, routed hardware. The digital blocks come after the system and security sections because they do not change those results: they are verified bit for bit against the model, and they implement the design that the security evaluation has fixed.
7. **Integration.** Section XII runs one mixed-level simulation of the complete sensor, with transistor-level circuits, RTL digital blocks and the behavioural rest of the link, as a final check of the abstractions on which Sections VIII and IX rely.
8. **Closing.** Section XIII opens the interactive explorer, Section XIV compares this work with prior art (Table XXIV), and Section XV concludes with the limitations and next steps, followed by the references.

### Summary of Section I

1. The readings of a floating bioreactor sensor drive a control loop, so they need **confidentiality** (against an eavesdropper) and **integrity** (against a man-in-the-middle) [1].
2. A conventional cipher is costly on such a sensor: an on-chip Trivium adds 220 µW to a front end of about 1.35 mW, and the modulator output must first be decimated [1].
3. The S-DSM of [1] instead XORs every modulator bit with a 16-bit LFSR keystream, for 24 µW (1.8 % of the chip power without security) and, according to [1], up to 2.67× lower wireless energy than decimate-then-encrypt in its OSR-30 comparison.
4. Its security rests on a stored 16-bit key, a linear keystream and the unpredictability of the modulator bits, and was tested in [1] against two cryptanalyses; the four research questions above examine what lies beyond them.

Section II next reviews the four concepts these questions rely on. The remaining sections then answer the questions in the order given in Section I-E: the model is checked against the published measurements of [1] before it is used, and the circuits are simulated at block level before their effect on the system is evaluated.

# **II. Background**
---
**The question.** This work joins four fields: data conversion, stream ciphers, message authentication and hardware security. Which ideas from each does the rest of the notebook rely on, and why does each matter for a low-power sensor link?

**Why it matters.** The abstract's claims are made in these terms. The original S-DSM fails 11 of 15 attacks because its keystream is *linear*, its key is *short and stored*, and its frames are not *authenticated*. The proposal closes them with a *PUF* key, a *fuzzy extractor*, a *nonlinear* cipher with a fresh initialisation vector (IV) per frame and a *MAC* with a counter and nonces. A reader who meets these words for the first time should be able to follow every later section after reading this one.

**What it takes from earlier sections.** Section I described the sensor (a current front end and a second-order 1-bit delta-sigma modulator clocked at 10 MHz) and the S-DSM of [1], which XORs every modulator bit with a 16-bit LFSR keystream. This section explains the principles behind those words. It does not evaluate either design; that starts in Section IV.

**Roadmap.** Each subsection treats one concept in the same steps: Goal (why the concept is needed here), Theory (what it is and how it works, as numbered steps, with every symbol defined), the illustrating figures, Result (what the figures show, with their numbers) and Interpretation (what it means for this work).

* **A. Delta-sigma modulation**: how a fast 1-bit converter digitises a slow signal, and why its bitstream is busy and hard to predict.
* **B. Stream ciphers**: encryption by XOR with a keystream; the LFSR; the two attacks that recover a short linear keystream (exhaustive key search and Berlekamp-Massey); nonlinear ciphers.
* **C. Message authentication and freshness**: why encryption alone does not stop forged, altered or replayed frames, and how a MAC, a counter and a nonce do.
* **D. PUFs and fuzzy extractors**: how a chip can regenerate a key from its own transistor mismatch instead of storing it.

**How the figures were made.** The figures and animations in this section are recorded, not executed in this session. They are drawn by `python dev/assets/make_assets.py` from this notebook's behavioural model (`secsensor.py`, Section V), with a recorded fit of the SRAM-PUF cell model that is close to, but not identical to, the parameters this run derives in Section VII. Their numbers are therefore illustrative; where one differs from the run, the text gives both.

### A. Delta-sigma modulation: an oversampling 1-bit converter

**Goal.** The S-DSM encrypts the raw output bits of the sensor's delta-sigma (ΔΣ) modulator. To see why this costs little power, and why an attacker may find these bits hard to predict, one must first know how the modulator produces them.

**Theory.**

1. *What it is.* A ΔΣ modulator digitises a slowly varying signal with a **1-bit quantiser that runs much faster than the signal**. In [1] the clock is f<sub>s</sub> = 10 MHz and the signal bandwidth f<sub>B</sub> = 100 kHz. The Nyquist rate of the signal is 2 f<sub>B</sub> = 200 kHz, so the modulator oversamples by OSR = f<sub>s</sub> / (2 f<sub>B</sub>) = 50: one output reading per 50 bits.
2. *How it works: feedback makes the bits average to the input.* An integrator accumulates the difference between the input u and the fed-back output bit, taken as v = ±1 (the transmitted bit is y ∈ {0, 1}, v = 2y − 1). When the integrator is high, the comparator (the 1-bit quantiser) outputs +1, which pulls the integrator back down; when it is low, it outputs −1. In the model of this notebook (Section V) the second-order loop is, at clock k,
   x<sub>1</sub>[k] = x<sub>1</sub>[k−1] + ½ (u[k] − v[k−1]),  x<sub>2</sub>[k] = x<sub>2</sub>[k−1] + ½ (x<sub>1</sub>[k] − v[k−1]),  v[k] = +1 if x<sub>2</sub>[k] ≥ 0, else −1.
   (The model of Section V adds leakage, noise, offset and dither to these two lines.)
   Because the integrators stay bounded, the long-run average of v must equal the average of u: the **density of ones follows the input**.
3. *Noise shaping.* The quantiser makes a large error e at every clock (it rounds x<sub>2</sub> to ±1). Treating e as additive noise, with the quantiser written as v = κ x<sub>2</sub> + e for a gain κ, the loop above has exactly the noise and signal transfer functions (NTF and STF)
   NTF(z) = (1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)² / D(z),  STF(z) = (κ/4) / D(z),  D(z) = 1 + (3κ/4 − 2) z<sup>−1</sup> + (1 − κ/2) z<sup>−2</sup>.
   At low frequency D ≈ D(1) = κ/4, so the input passes with unit gain and the error is filtered by NTF ≈ (4/κ)(1 − z<sup>−1</sup>)², whose magnitude, (4/κ)(2 sin(π f / f<sub>s</sub>))², grows as f² (40 dB per decade) for any κ. The quantisation noise is therefore pushed out of the signal band, to high frequencies, where the receiver's decimation filter removes it, leaving a high-resolution reading at f<sub>s</sub> / OSR = 200 kHz.
4. *Assumptions.* The additive-noise picture of a 1-bit quantiser is an approximation (the quantiser's gain is not defined), so it predicts the *slope* of the shaped noise, not its exact level, which scales with 1/κ. The circuit adds comparator noise and offset, integrator noise and, in [1], dither; Section V adds them to the model.

**Prediction.** The output spectrum should show the signal tone on a low noise floor inside 0–100 kHz, and noise that rises at 40 dB per decade (f², in power) above the band. The bits should toggle often even for a slowly varying input, and their 50-bit mean should track the input.

Recorded animation (<code>python dev/assets/make_assets.py dsm</code>).</p>

Shading: 0–100 kHz signal band; dashed orange: 40 dB/decade slope. Recorded animation (<code>python dev/assets/make_assets.py noise_shaping</code>).</p>

**Result.** Both predictions hold. In Fig. 4 the output bits toggle every few clocks, yet their 50-bit mean follows the input. In Fig. 5 the noise rises along the +40 dB/decade line above the band and is low inside it, where the 20 kHz tone stands out; the longer the FFT, the lower the in-band floor reads, because the noise power is spread over more frequency bins.

**Interpretation.** Two properties matter for this work.
* *Cost.* The modulator bits are the sensor's raw output. Encrypting them one by one needs one XOR gate per bit and no decimation filter on the sensor; this is the low cost of the S-DSM (Section I).
* *Security.* Each bit depends on the whole history of the input, on circuit noise and on every earlier comparator decision. [1] relies on this: an attacker who builds a replica chip and drives it with the same input still does not reproduce the bits. Whether that holds is tested in Sections VIII and IX. The bit density, however, still carries the input: encrypting the bits is what hides it, which is the subject of the next subsection.

### B. Stream ciphers: XOR with a keystream

**Goal.** Both designs encrypt each modulator bit with a stream cipher. This subsection explains what makes a keystream secure, how the S-DSM's 16-bit LFSR generates one, and the two attacks that recover it.

**Theory.**

1. *Encryption by XOR.* The transmitter sends C = D ⊕ K, where D is the data bit and K a keystream bit generated from a secret key k. The receiver generates the same keystream and computes C ⊕ K = D, because K ⊕ K = 0. If K is unpredictable to an eavesdropper, every C is equally likely to be 0 or 1 whatever D is: C reveals nothing about D. All the security rests on the keystream.
2. *Two requirements on the keystream.* (a) It must be unpredictable without the key, even to an attacker who has seen some of it. (b) It must never be reused: if two frames are encrypted with the same keystream, C<sub>1</sub> ⊕ C<sub>2</sub> = D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ D<sub>2</sub>, and the key no longer matters. A stream cipher therefore takes a public initialisation vector (IV), different for each frame, as well as the key.
3. *The linear feedback shift register (LFSR).* An LFSR of length L is a shift register whose new input bit is the XOR of a few of its own bits (the *taps*). With well-chosen taps it cycles through all 2<sup>L</sup> − 1 non-zero states (the all-zero state would stay at zero, so it is not a valid key) and outputs a long, balanced, random-looking sequence for a handful of gates. The S-DSM uses a 16-bit LFSR (taps 0, 2, 3 and 5) whose initial state is the key: 2<sup>16</sup> − 1 = 65,535 possible keys.
4. *Attack 1: exhaustive key search (brute force).* An attacker who knows a few plaintext bits (for example a fixed field of the frame) tests every key until the generated keystream matches. The work grows as 2<sup>key length</sup>: at a rate of R keys per second, a 16-bit key falls in at most 65,535 / R seconds, a 128-bit key in 2<sup>128</sup> / R seconds.
5. *Attack 2: linear complexity and Berlekamp-Massey.* The linear complexity L(n) of a bit sequence is the length of the shortest LFSR that generates its first n bits. The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm [3] computes that LFSR, taps and state, from the bits alone. For an LFSR of length L, L(n) stops growing at L, and **2L observed bits** are enough to recover the whole register: 32 bits for the S-DSM, after which every future keystream bit is known, without searching for the key at all. For a truly random sequence, L(n) instead grows as about n/2 for ever, and no short LFSR fits.
6. *Nonlinear stream ciphers.* Modern lightweight ciphers avoid both attacks. Trivium [5] (80-bit key) uses three shift registers with nonlinear (AND) feedback. Grain-128a [6], used in the proposal, combines a 128-bit LFSR with a 128-bit *nonlinear* feedback shift register, a 128-bit key and a 96-bit IV, and passes their bits through a nonlinear output function. Its keystream's linear complexity grows with its length, so Berlekamp-Massey does not converge, and its key space is 2<sup>128</sup>.

**Prediction.** On the S-DSM's keystream, L(n) should rise to 16 and stay there, and a register rebuilt from 32 bits should predict every later bit. On Grain-128a, L(n) should follow n/2, and a register rebuilt from any prefix should predict later bits no better than a coin toss (50 %). A 16-bit key should fall to exhaustive search in a fraction of a millisecond on one processor core; a search over a 128-bit key is infeasible.

**Result.** The predictions hold. With a guessed key, the attacker's decryption is wrong on 50.1 % of the 107,400 bits of a frame, the error rate of a coin toss, while the receiver makes no errors (Fig. 6). In Fig. 7 the LFSR's linear complexity stops at 16; Berlekamp-Massey rebuilds the register from 32 bits and predicts the next 1,000 bits 100 % right. Grain-128a's L(n) tracks n/2, and the prediction is right 52 % of the time, the level of chance. An exhaustive search (Fig. 8) at 6.6 × 10⁸ keys/s, the rate measured on one laptop core when the background figures were recorded, finds the model's 16-bit key after 50,085 of its 65,535 values, in 76 µs; the whole 16-bit key space takes about 0.1 ms, whereas trying all 2¹²⁸ keys of the proposal would take 5.1 × 10²⁹ s, about 1.2 × 10¹² times the age of the universe.

**Interpretation.** The XOR itself is sound; **the weakness of the S-DSM lies in its keystream generator**. Its key is short enough to be searched in well under a millisecond, and its keystream is linear, so 32 known bits give away all future bits. Both attacks need only a few known plaintext bits, which a frame with fixed fields provides. They are two of the 15 attacks of Section IX. A 128-bit nonlinear cipher such as Grain-128a resists both. Encryption alone, however, still lets an attacker alter or invent frames, which the next subsection addresses.

### C. Message authentication and freshness: encryption does not provide integrity

**Goal.** In the bioreactor, a forged reading is as harmful as a stolen one (Section I). This subsection explains why encryption does not prevent forgery, and what does.

**Theory.**

1. *Encryption is malleable.* Inverting a bit of C inverts the same bit of D after decryption: (C ⊕ Δ) ⊕ K = D ⊕ Δ for any change Δ. An attacker can thus alter a reading without knowing the key. An attacker who has recovered the key or the keystream (subsection B) can do more: encrypt a fabricated reading and send it.
2. *Message authentication code (MAC).* A MAC is a short tag τ computed from the message and the secret key. The receiver recomputes τ from what it received and rejects the frame if the two differ. Without the key, an attacker can only guess a b-bit tag, and succeeds with probability 2<sup>−b</sup> per attempt; for the 32-bit tag used here, 2<sup>−32</sup>. Grain-128a has a built-in MAC [6]: in its authenticated mode, selected by the first IV bit, it generates two bits per data bit, one to encrypt and one to update the tag.
3. *Freshness: the frame counter.* A MAC alone does not stop replay, the re-sending of an old, valid frame. Each frame therefore carries a 32-bit frame counter c that is incremented with every frame, and the receiver accepts only a counter larger than the last one it accepted.
4. *The nonce and the initialisation vector.* A **nonce** (from "number used once") is a value that a protocol uses only once under a given key; it need not be secret, only never repeated. It is needed because of requirement (b) of subsection B: a stream cipher started from the same key in the same way produces the same keystream, and two frames encrypted with the same keystream K give C<sub>1</sub> ⊕ C<sub>2</sub> = (D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ K) ⊕ (D<sub>2</sub> ⊕ K) = D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ D<sub>2</sub>, which reveals the data without the key. The cipher is therefore started from the key and an IV that is different for every frame, and the IV is built from three fields:
   * **N, the session nonce**: a fresh random 32-bit value that the receiver sends to the chip in clear at the start of each session, so that every session has different keystreams;
   * **c, the frame counter** of item 3: it makes the IV of every frame within a session different;
   * **N<sub>c</sub>, the chip nonce**: 31 bits that the chip derives from its own noisy SRAM power-up state, which differs at every power-up. Because N travels in clear, an attacker can send an old N to the chip again; the counter restarts with each session, so without N<sub>c</sub> the old IV, and with it the old keystream, would be repeated (attack A15 of Section IX). N<sub>c</sub> changes at every power-up even when N is replayed (Section IV-B).

   The IV of each frame is 1 ‖ N ‖ c ‖ N<sub>c</sub> (‖: concatenation; the leading 1 selects the authenticated mode; the 96-bit IV is completed with zeros). It differs for every frame of a session and, except for a chance collision of the 31-bit chip nonce, between sessions, so no keystream is reused. The S-DSM of [1] has no IV: its LFSR is started from the stored key alone.

**Prediction.** A frame whose payload, counter or encrypted chip ID has been changed should fail the MAC check, except with probability 2<sup>−32</sup>; a frame recorded in an earlier session or with an old counter should be rejected.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chennakeshavadasa/secure-sensor-figures/f8600a404a4d61508ddf09cc77a4dd23b2eaedc9/img/frame_format.png" width="760" alt="frame" style="display:inline-block"></p>

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 9.</b> Frame format of the proposal. (a) Uplink frame in transmission order, field widths in bits; blue: encrypted fields (not to scale); lower bracket: fields the 32-bit tag authenticates. (b) Per-frame IV, 1 ‖ N ‖ ctr ‖ N<sub>c</sub>, and the Grain-128a output streams. (c) Downlink at session start: receiver nonce N and helper data h.</p>

**Result.** Fig. 9 shows where each mechanism sits in the frame. The counter, the nonce, the MAC tag and the helper data cost the link little: the proposal adds **96 bits to each frame** (32-bit counter, 32-bit field for the 31-bit chip nonce N<sub>c</sub> of Section IV, and 32-bit MAC tag, against a 107,400-bit payload) and 482 bits once per session on the downlink (the 32-bit nonce and the 450-bit helper data of the t = 45 code). This subsection states the mechanisms only; the attacks that test them (spoofing, replay and bit-flipping) are run in Section IX.

**Interpretation.** The S-DSM has no MAC, counter or nonce, so **its receiver cannot tell a genuine frame from a forged or replayed one**. In the proposal these cost one extra Grain-128a output bit per data bit and 96 bits per frame (counter, chip nonce and tag). All of them depend on the key, so the remaining question is where the key comes from, which the next subsection answers.

### D. Physically unclonable functions and fuzzy extractors

**Goal.** The S-DSM stores its key in on-chip memory, where an attacker who obtains the chip can read it, and every chip made from the same design could be programmed with a copy. The proposal instead derives its key from the chip's own transistors. This subsection explains how such a key is produced and why it is reproduced exactly at every power-up.

**Theory.**

1. *The SRAM cell at power-up.* A 6T SRAM cell is two cross-coupled inverters, with storage nodes Q and Q̄, plus two access transistors. When the supply V<sub>DD</sub> ramps up with the access transistors off, both nodes start near 0 V and the two inverters contend. Random transistor mismatch (mainly threshold-voltage differences) gives one inverter the advantage, and the cell settles to 0 or 1 [13].
2. *Physically unclonable function (PUF).* Mismatch is random from chip to chip, fixed for a given chip, and not stored anywhere. The power-up pattern of n cells is therefore a fingerprint w: different chips should differ in about half of their cells, and the same chip should reproduce nearly the same pattern. Because it cannot be copied into another chip, it is a physically unclonable function.
3. *Noise makes some cells unstable.* Write the cell's preference as a mismatch term with spread σ<sub>m</sub> and the thermal noise at the moment of decision as a random term with spread σ<sub>n</sub>. Cells whose mismatch is small compared with the noise resolve differently from one power-up to the next. The fraction of such cells grows with the ratio s = σ<sub>n</sub> / σ<sub>m</sub>, and s grows with temperature. Section VII extracts s from SKY130 transistor-level simulation.
4. *Fuzzy extractor: from a noisy fingerprint to an exact key* [4]. A key must be reproduced bit for bit, so the noise is removed with an error-correcting code, here a Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) code over the Galois field GF(2¹⁰) that corrects up to t bit errors.
   * *Enrolment* (once, at test): the chip's fingerprint w is read; its syndrome h, a set of parity checks of w, is stored at the receiver as public helper data; the key is k = Hash(w), the first 128 bits of SHA-256 in the model.
   * *Reconstruction* (at every power-up): the chip reads a noisy w′ = w ⊕ e and receives h. Because the code is linear, the syndrome of w′ combined with h is the syndrome of the error pattern e alone; the BCH decoder finds e if it has at most t ones, restores w = w′ ⊕ e and recomputes k = Hash(w).
5. *Key failure.* Reconstruction fails when more than t cells flip. If each of the n cells flips independently with probability p, the number of flips is binomial and P(key fails) = Σ<sub>j>t</sub> C(n, j) p<sup>j</sup> (1 − p)<sup>n−j</sup>. The code is sized so that this stays below 10⁻⁶ over the operating temperature range.
6. *Leakage of the helper data.* A BCH syndrome over GF(2¹⁰) holds 10 bits per correctable error, so h reveals 10t bits about w. The fingerprint must therefore hold at least 128 bits of secrecy *beyond* them: n · H<sub>∞</sub> − 10t ≥ 128, where H<sub>∞</sub> is the min-entropy (worst-case unpredictability) of one cell in bits.

**Prediction.** Two chips should differ in about 50 % of their cells. A genuine chip at a later power-up should have a few to a few tens of flipped cells, fewer than t, and recover the same key; a counterfeit chip given the same helper data should have about n/2 errors, far beyond t, and fail. The number of flips, and hence P(key fails), should rise steeply with temperature.
