<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 17.</b> Reference frame of the proposal without attack (behavioural model, 37 °C). (a) Bits over 48 clocks, each row 0 (lower) or 1: <i>D</i>, <i>K</i> (red), <i>C</i> = <i>D</i> ⊕ <i>K</i>, decrypted <i>D</i><sub>rx</sub>, and <i>D</i> ⊕ <i>D</i><sub>rx</sub> (blue). (b) Modulator input <i>u</i> (grey; delayed and scaled to the receiver filters) and server reading (black); below: their difference.</p>

**Result.** The card reports, in order: chip ID check passed; MAC verified; all decrypted bits equal to the modulator bits; recovered SNDR 60.3 dB; 27 PUF cells flipped at this power-up, all corrected (t = 40); an expected number of flips Σp<sub>i</sub> = 26.6; and a key-failure probability of 1.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> at 37 °C. Fig. 17 shows the two tests of transparency: D ⊕ D<sub>rx</sub> is 0 on every one of the 107,400 bits (panel (a), whose last row states the count over the whole frame), and the server's reading follows the modulator input, with a residual error that the lower plot of panel (b) gives in % of full scale, together with its rms over the frame and the delay and gain of the receiver filters fitted by least squares. Every prediction holds.

**Interpretation.** The model operates end to end, and the blocks that the proposal adds (PUF, fuzzy extractor, Grain-128a, MAC) do not change the accuracy: the SNDR is set by the modulator alone. The 27 flips agree with the expected 26.6, but they use two thirds of the correction capability, and the resulting key-failure probability of 1.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> per power-up is far above the 10<sup>−6</sup> target of Section II-D. **The code must therefore be sized from the actual cell statistics**, across temperature and process: Section VII obtains them from SKY130 simulation and sizes t, and Section VIII evaluates the result across process, voltage and temperature.

#### Summary of Section V

1. **One model, two designs.** The link of [1] and the proposal are implemented bit for bit in one behavioural, cycle-accurate model. Its settings are held in one dictionary, each with its source, and every random stream is seeded, so every run is repeatable (Subsection A).
2. **The cipher matches its specification on every published test vector:** the model's Grain-128a reproduces 22 of 22 values (Subsection B).
3. **The modulator includes the modelled effects that can decorrelate two chips:** comparator noise and offset, first-integrator thermal noise (from the 9.48 pA of [1]), input-referred mismatch, integrator leak and capacitor-ratio errors, clipping, and dither at the comparator or in the feedback; the receiver uses a CIC filter and a 31-tap compensation FIR (Subsection C).
4. **The key path is implemented exactly on a fitted PUF cell model:** BCH syndrome fuzzy extractor over GF(2¹⁰), hash, and an exact (not sampled) key-failure probability of that cell model (Subsection D).
5. **The attacks are defined once:** exhaustive key search, Berlekamp-Massey, the windowed replica attack (80 windows of 64 bits, success when one window predicts 512 bits with more than 99 % accuracy) the full scan of the LFSR-16 confirmed by the chip ID, and the helper-data oracle, and 15 attacks with explicit verdict rules (Subsections E and G).
6. **The reference frame passes:** ID, MAC, 60.3 dB SNDR, and 27 flipped PUF cells, all corrected; with the assumed cell noise the key-failure probability is 1.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> at 37 °C, so the code must be sized from simulated cell statistics (Subsection H).

The model is only as reliable as its agreement with the published measurements of [1]. Section VI therefore tests it against the two measurements of [1] that it can reproduce directly, before any attack is evaluated.

# **VI. Consistency check against the measurements of [1]**
---
**The question.** Does the model of Section V reproduce what the chip of [1] was measured to do?

**Why it matters.** Every later verdict is computed on this model. Two of them depend on it directly: the security of the original design against the cryptanalyses of [1], which [1] argues from the measured disagreement between two channels of its chip, and the energy comparison of the designs, which later sections extend to the proposal. If the model did not reproduce these two measurements, neither the attacks of Section IX nor the energy figures of Section X could be trusted. The comparison also addresses a question that [1] leaves open: which physical effect makes the two channels disagree.

**What it takes from earlier sections.** The modulator and receiver filters of Section V-C with the `DEFAULTS` of V-A, before any SKY130 circuit parameter is used; the replica and same-key attacks of the threat model (Section IV), whose outcome rests on the effect measured here; and, for the energy, the block powers reported in [1].

**Roadmap.**

* **A. Two channels, same key, same input (Fig. 4(c) of [1])**: the experiment, the theory of why two channels disagree, and the decomposition into dither, thermal noise and analog mismatch.
* **B. Transmitted bits behind the energy table (Fig. 4(b) of [1])**: the bits each design sends, checked against the energy ratios of [1].
* **C. Runs, results and interpretation**: both experiments are run in two code cells, and their numbers are compared with [1] and interpreted.

The section closes with a summary of what the model reproduces and what this implies for the attacks.

### A. Two channels, same key, same input (Fig. 4(c) of [1])

**Goal.** Reproduce the measurement of [1] in which two channels of one chip encrypt the same input with the same key, and identify which modelled effect makes their outputs differ.

**Theory: the measurement of [1].** The chip of [1] has two nominally identical channels; the only deliberate difference between them is their dither sequence. With the same key, their ciphertext bits differ in 50.05 % of positions for a zero input and in 49.8 % for the same message. [1] relies on the dither and on the activity of the bitstream to conceal the keystream.

**Theory.**

1. *What the measurement observes.* With the same keystream K, C<sub>1</sub> ⊕ C<sub>2</sub> = (D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ K) ⊕ (D<sub>2</sub> ⊕ K) = D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ D<sub>2</sub>: the fraction of differing ciphertext bits equals the fraction of differing modulator bits. Identical modulators give 0 %; independent bit streams give 50 %. An eavesdropper who XORs the two ciphertexts learns D<sub>1</sub> ⊕ D<sub>2</sub>, which conceals the data only if the fraction is close to 50 %.
2. *Perturbations at the quantiser are suppressed.* Dither (d ∈ {0, ±0.022}, Section V-C) and comparator noise (σ<sub>c</sub> = 10<sup>−3</sup>) act at the comparator. They change a decision only when x<sub>2</sub> lies within the perturbation of the threshold, and the loop then corrects the changed decision as it corrects quantisation error (noise shaping), which returns the two channels to the same decisions.
3. *Perturbations ahead of the integrators are not suppressed.* An input-referred difference between the channels (analog mismatch, modelled as an offset δ added to the input u of channel 2) and the first integrator's thermal noise (σ<sub>i</sub>) are integrated twice before the quantiser and are not shaped. A constant δ acts at every clock: the two state trajectories diverge until their decision sequences are shifted relative to each other, after which the bits are uncorrelated.
4. *A zero input does not discriminate.* With u = 0 the loop idles in a short repetitive pattern whose phase is set by the first decisions and by the smallest perturbation; two channels out of phase disagree on about half of their bits, independently of the cause.
5. *The ceiling of the same-message test.* Once the two channels are fully decorrelated, their bits are independent, each a one with probability (1 + u)/2 at input u. Two such channels differ with probability (1 − u²)/2 at each clock, (1 − A²/2)/2 on average for a sine of amplitude A: about 48.4 % for the test signal of this model (A ≈ 0.25 FS), and 50 % for a zero input. No effect can push the disagreement above this value; any mismatch large enough to decorrelate the channels reaches it.

**Prediction.** (i) Zero input: about 50 % for every combination of effects. (ii) Same message: at most a few per cent from dither and comparator noise alone; at the independence value of item 5 once mismatch is present, for any mismatch above a small threshold; an intermediate value from integrator noise, whose level this first-order argument does not predict.

**Setup.**

| Item | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| level | behavioural, the modulator of Section V-C (`dsm2`) | Section V |
| settings | `DEFAULTS`, dither at the comparator | Section V-A, [1] |
| inputs | zero input (u = 0), and the same message: the 0.93 µA, 20 kHz sine test signal through the TIA and buffer | Section V-A |
| channel 2 differs from channel 1 by | its own dither seeds (0x3A17, 0x6E29 instead of 0x1D2B, 0x7A31); its own comparator and integrator noise stream (`seed` + 12 instead of `seed` + 11); an input offset δ = 0.10 % FS (0.6 mV at the modulator input) | δ assumed, as a typical input-referred mismatch between two channels |
| effects switched | dither on/off; integrator thermal noise σ<sub>i</sub> = 0.9 × 10<sup>−5</sup> at the first integrator's output (1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> referred to the input) on/off; mismatch on/off: 8 combinations, plus dither in the feedback with all effects on | comparator noise σ<sub>c</sub> = 10<sup>−3</sup> is on in every row |
| length, seeds | 30,000 clocks per run; the same seeds in every combination (master seed 2026), so that the rows differ only in the effects switched | Section V-A |
| mismatch sweep | same message, all effects on: δ = 0, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1 and 0.3 % FS, each with four independent seed sets (dither seeds and noise streams of both channels) | tests whether the result depends on the assumed δ |
| metrics | fraction of bits that differ (D<sub>1</sub> ≠ D<sub>2</sub>) over the run, and its running value after each clock; the SNDR of channel 1 for each dither placement, on one full frame of 107,400 clocks with integrator noise on (Section V-C) | |

### B. Transmitted bits behind the energy table (Fig. 4(b) of [1])

**Goal.** Check what the energy table of [1] rests on, which compares the S-DSM with a conventional design (a decimating ADC followed by the Trivium cipher [5]) for sending the same information, without using any radio number: no radio is designed in this work, so no radio energy is computed or claimed anywhere in this notebook.

**Theory.** Both designs send 20 Nyquist samples. The number of bits each sends per reading (Nyquist sample) is set by the architecture alone:
* *S-DSM:* one encrypted bit per modulator clock, OSR bits per reading.
* *ADC + Trivium:* 16-bit words at SR/NR times the Nyquist rate (SR: the decimated output rate; NR: the Nyquist rate), 16 × SR/NR bits per reading.

If the energies of [1] are set by the bits transmitted, as [1] states, the ratio of its two energies equals the ratio of the bits, 16 × (SR/NR) / OSR, whatever the radio.

**Prediction.** The bit ratio should equal the energy ratio of [1] in all four configurations, to the rounding of the table of [1].

**Setup.** The four configurations of Fig. 4(b) of [1]: OSR 50 and 30, each with SR/NR = 4.5 and 5. The metric is the largest relative difference between the bit ratio and the energy ratio reported in [1], over the four configurations. No radio or security power enters.

### C. Runs, results and interpretation

Both experiments are run in the two code cells below: the first defines them, the second runs them, reports the numbers against [1] and draws Fig. 18. The results of Subsection A are discussed first, then those of Subsection B, then their interpretation.

> **Next cell.** 1. Defines `channel_pair_flips`: one input through two modulators that differ in dither seeds, noise streams and an optional input offset, and the fraction (and running fraction) of bits that differ. 2. Defines `channel_experiments()`, which runs it for the zero input and the same message, for the 8 combinations of dither, integrator noise and mismatch and for dither in the feedback, and measures the SNDR for each dither placement. 3. Enters the table of Fig. 4(b) of [1]. The cell only defines functions; no simulation is run.


```python
#@title Fig. 4(b) and 4(c) of [1]: experiment definitions
# ---------- Fig. 4(c) of the paper: two channels of one chip, same key, same input, different dither
PAPER_FIG4C = dict(zero=0.5005, same=0.498)

def channel_pair_flips(P, u, mismatch_fs, seeds2=(0x3A17, 0x6E29)):
    D1 = dsm2(u, P, noise_seed=P["seed"] + 11)["D"]
    D2 = dsm2(u + mismatch_fs, P, seeds=seeds2, noise_seed=P["seed"] + 12)["D"]
    d = (D1 != D2)
    return float(d.mean()), np.cumsum(d) / np.arange(1, len(d) + 1)

def channel_experiments(P=None, mismatch_pct=0.1, n=LAB_N):
    """Bit-flip probability between two channels, split by what makes them differ."""
    P = {**DEFAULTS, **(P or {})}
    noise = P["int_noise"] if P["int_noise"] > 0 else 0.9e-5
    u_zero = np.full(n, s2d(tia(0.0, P["rtia"]), P["buffer"]))
    u_same = s2d(tia(sensor_current({**P, "sig": "sine"}, n), P["rtia"]), P["buffer"])
    rows = []
    for dith in (True, False):
        for nz in (noise, 0.0):
            for mm in (mismatch_pct / 100, 0.0):
                Q = {**P, "dither": dith, "int_noise": nz, "dither_at": "comparator"}
                z, _ = channel_pair_flips(Q, u_zero, mm); s, tr = channel_pair_flips(Q, u_same, mm)
                rows.append(dict(dither=dith, noise=nz, mismatch=mm * 100, at="comparator", zero=z, same=s, trace=tr))
    Q = {**P, "dither": True, "int_noise": noise, "dither_at": "feedback"}
    z, _ = channel_pair_flips(Q, u_zero, mismatch_pct / 100); s, tr = channel_pair_flips(Q, u_same, mismatch_pct / 100)
    rows.append(dict(dither=True, noise=noise, mismatch=mismatch_pct, at="feedback", zero=z, same=s, trace=tr))
    def sndr_at(at):
        Q = {**P, "int_noise": noise, "dither_at": at, "sig": "sine"}
        u = s2d(tia(sensor_current(Q, N_DSM), Q["rtia"]), Q["buffer"])
        return sndr(decode(dsm2(u, Q, noise_seed=Q["seed"])["D"]), Q["bin"])
    # independence value: two channels whose bits are independent, each with P(1) = (1 + u)/2, differ with
    # probability mean((1 - u^2)/2), i.e. (1 - A^2/2)/2 for a sine of amplitude A
    indep = dict(zero=float(np.mean((1 - u_zero ** 2) / 2)), same=float(np.mean((1 - u_same ** 2) / 2)),
                 amp=float(np.abs(u_same).max()))
    # mismatch sweep of the same-message test, all effects on, four independent seed sets per value
    Q = {**P, "dither": True, "int_noise": noise, "dither_at": "comparator"}
    dsweep = []
    for d in (0.0, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3):
        v = [float(np.mean(dsm2(u_same, Q, noise_seed=Q["seed"] + 11 + 100 * k)["D"]
                           != dsm2(u_same + d / 100, Q, seeds=(0x3A17 + 97 * k, 0x6E29 + 89 * k),
                                   noise_seed=Q["seed"] + 12 + 100 * k)["D"])) for k in range(4)]
        dsweep.append((d, v))
    return dict(rows=rows, noise=noise, mismatch=mismatch_pct, indep=indep, dsweep=dsweep,
                sndr=dict(comparator=sndr_at("comparator"), feedback=sndr_at("feedback")))

# ---------- Fig. 4(b): energy for the same information (radio 3.1 mW at 200 kb/s, 20 Nyquist samples)
PAPER_FIG4A_UW = dict(fe=321, tia=271, s2d=250, dsm=510, sdsm=24, trivium=220)
PAPER_FIG4B = [(50, 11.1, 4.5, 22.35, 15.5), (50, 10, 5, 24.82, 15.5), (30, 6.67, 4.5, 22.36, 9.3), (30, 6, 5, 24.84, 9.3)]
RADIO_J_PER_BIT, T_INFO, NYQ = 3.1e-3 / 200e3, 100e-6, 20

def energy_sdsm(osr, p_sec_uw, extra_bits=0.0):        # the S-DSM sends OSR bits per Nyquist sample
    return (osr * NYQ + extra_bits) * RADIO_J_PER_BIT + p_sec_uw * 1e-6 * T_INFO

def energy_words(srnr, p_sec_uw, bits=16):             # a decimating ADC + cipher sends 16-bit words
    return bits * srnr * NYQ * RADIO_J_PER_BIT + p_sec_uw * 1e-6 * T_INFO
```

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs `channel_experiments()` (30,000 clocks per run) and compares the all-effects row with Fig. 4(c) of [1]. 2. Tabulates every combination (Table III) and reports, in a second card, each effect on its own for the same message. 3. Computes the bits per reading of both designs in the four configurations of Fig. 4(b) of [1], compares their ratio with the energy ratio of [1] (fourth card) and tabulates them (Table IV). 4. Draws Fig. 18. Run time: about 2 s after compilation.


```python
#@title Fig.: the measurements of [1] and the model
cal = channel_experiments()
pct = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.1f} %"
r0 = cal["rows"][0]
card("Fig. 4(c) of [1] reproduced: two channels, same key, same input, all effects on",
     [("zero input", f"model <b>{pct(r0['zero'])}</b> of bits differ &nbsp;·&nbsp; measured in [1] 50.05 %"),
      ("same message", f"model <b>{pct(r0['same'])}</b> of bits differ &nbsp;·&nbsp; measured in [1] 49.8 %"),
      ("SNDR", f"{cal['sndr']['comparator']:.1f} dB with dither at the comparator, {cal['sndr']['feedback']:.1f} dB in the feedback")])
name = lambda r: (("feedback dither" if r["at"] == "feedback" else "dither" if r["dither"] else "no dither") + ", "
                  + ("thermal noise" if r["noise"] else "no noise") + ", " + (f"{r['mismatch']:.2f} % mismatch" if r["mismatch"] else "no mismatch"))
table(["The two channels differ by", "Zero input", "Same message"], [(name(r), pct(r["zero"]), pct(r["same"])) for r in cal["rows"]],
      caption="Table III: bits that differ between two channels with the same key and input, over 30,000 clocks, for each "
              "combination of dither, first-integrator thermal noise and 0.10 % FS input mismatch (comparator noise is on in every "
              "row; measured in [1]: 50.05 % and 49.8 %)")
one = lambda d, nz, mm: next(r for r in cal["rows"] if r["at"] == "comparator" and r["dither"] == d and bool(r["noise"]) == nz and bool(r["mismatch"]) == mm)
card("Same message: which effect decorrelates the two channels, each on its own",
     [("analog mismatch (0.10 % FS, ahead of the quantiser)", f"<b>{pct(one(False, False, True)['same'])}</b>"),
      ("first-integrator thermal noise", pct(one(False, True, False)["same"])),
      ("dither at the comparator", pct(one(True, False, False)["same"])),
      ("none of the three (comparator noise only)", pct(one(False, False, False)["same"]))])
ind = cal["indep"]; dsw = cal["dsweep"]
ms = lambda v: f"{100 * np.mean(v):.1f} % (range {100 * min(v):.1f}–{100 * max(v):.1f} %)"
card("Same message: what the test can resolve (all effects on, four independent seed sets per mismatch)",
     [("independent channels, analytic: mean of (1 − u²)/2", f"<b>{pct(ind['same'])}</b> for the test sine (amplitude {ind['amp']:.3f} FS); {pct(ind['zero'])} for the zero input")]
     + [(f"input mismatch {d:g} % FS", ms(v)) for d, v in dsw]
     + [("amplitude for which independence gives the measured 49.8 %", f"{np.sqrt(2 * (1 - 2 * 0.498)):.3f} FS")])

# Fig. 4(b) of [1] through the transmitted bits per reading, which the architecture sets (no radio number used): the decimating
# ADC with Trivium sends 16-bit words at SR/NR times the Nyquist rate, the S-DSM OSR bits; their ratio against the energy ratio
# that [1] itself reports, which holds if [1]'s energies are set by the transmitted bits.
rows = [(osr, dr, sr, tri, sd, 16 * sr, osr, 16 * sr / osr, tri / sd) for osr, dr, sr, tri, sd in PAPER_FIG4B]
worst = max(abs(r[7] / r[8] - 1) for r in rows)
card("Fig. 4(b) of [1]: transmitted bits for the same information",
     [("largest difference between the bit ratio and [1]'s energy ratio", f"<b>{100 * worst:.2f} %</b> over all {len(rows)} rows"),
      ("bits per reading at OSR 50", f"S-DSM 50; decimating ADC with Trivium {16 * 4.5:.0f}–{16 * 5:.0f} (16-bit words at 4.5–5× Nyquist)")],
     note="No radio number is used: [1]'s published energies are compared only through their ratio.", tone="ok" if worst < 0.01 else "bad")

table(["OSR", "SR/NR", "Bits per reading, ADC + Trivium", "Bits per reading, S-DSM", "Bit ratio", "Energy ratio reported in [1]"],
      [(r[0], r[2], f"{r[5]:.0f}", f"{r[6]}", f"{r[7]:.3f}", f"{r[8]:.3f}") for r in rows],
      caption="Table IV: bits sent per reading (Nyquist sample) for the same information by a decimating ADC with Trivium "
              "(16-bit words at SR/NR times the Nyquist rate) and by the S-DSM (OSR bits), and the ratio of the two against the "
              "ratio of the energies reported in Fig. 4(b) of [1]")

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(W2, 3.3), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.05]))
pick = [((True, True, True), "dither + noise + mismatch", COL["ok"], "-"), ((True, False, True), "dither + mismatch", COL["bad"], "--"),
        ((True, True, False), "dither + thermal noise", COL["aqua"], "-."), ((True, False, False), "dither only", COL["yellow"], ":")]
for (d, nz, mm), lab, c, ls in pick:                 # each run's final value at the right edge (the two mismatch runs apart)
    r = next(r for r in cal["rows"] if r["dither"] == d and bool(r["noise"]) == nz and bool(r["mismatch"]) == mm and r["at"] == "comparator")
    tr = 100 * np.asarray(r["trace"])
    a1.plot(np.arange(1, len(tr) + 1), tr, color=c, ls=ls, lw=1.5, label=lab)
    a1.annotate(f"{tr[-1]:.1f} %", xy=(len(tr), tr[-1]), xytext=(4, (5 if ls == "--" else -5) if mm else 0),
                textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=c, va="center", ha="left", annotation_clip=False)
a1.axhline(49.8, color=COL["ink"], ls=(0, (1, 1)), lw=0.9)
a1.text(2.6e4, 55, "measured in [1]: 49.8 %", fontsize=9, va="bottom", ha="right")        # clear of the curves' peak
a1.set_xscale("log"); a1.set_ylim(-5, 90); a1.set_xlim(10, LAB_N)
a1.set_xticks([10, 100, 1000, 10000]); a1.set_yticks([0, 25, 50, 75])
a1.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
a1.set_xlabel("Clock cycles since start"); a1.set_ylabel("Bits that differ (%)")
a1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8, handlelength=2.0); panel(a1, "a", "Same-message test")
x = np.arange(len(rows)); w = 0.34                   # (b) Fig. 4(b) of [1]: bit ratio (model) against [1]'s energy ratio
a2.bar(x - w / 2, [r[8] for r in rows], w, color="white", ec=COL["ink"], hatch="////", lw=0.8, label="energy ratio reported in [1]")
a2.bar(x + w / 2, [r[7] for r in rows], w, color=COL["ok"], ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.5, label="bit ratio, ADC + Trivium / S-DSM")
for xi, r in zip(x, rows):
    a2.text(xi + w / 2, r[7] + 0.05, f"{r[7]:.2f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8)
a2.set_xticks(x, [f"OSR {r[0]}\nSR/NR {r[2]}" for r in rows]); a2.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8.5, top=False)
a2.set_ylabel("ADC + Trivium relative to S-DSM"); a2.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
a2.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=1, loc="upper left"); a2.set_ylim(0, max(r[8] for r in rows) * 1.4)
panel(a2, "b", "Fig. 4(b) of [1] reproduced")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=2.5); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 18.</b> Model against the measurements of [1]. (a) Same-message test: running fraction of differing bits between two channels with the same input and key, with dither at the comparator and the effects in the legend; dotted: measured in [1]. (b) The ADC with Trivium relative to the S-DSM in the four configurations of Fig. 4(b) of [1]: energy ratio reported in [1] (hatched) and ratio of transmitted bits (solid, labelled); no radio number used.</p>

**Result: the two channels (first card, Table III, second card, Fig. 18).**

1. *Agreement with [1].* With all effects on, the model gives **50.0 %** of bits differing for the zero input (measured 50.05 %) and **48.2 %** for the same message (measured 49.8 %): within 0.1 percentage point of the measurement for the zero input, and 1.6 percentage points below it for the same message.
2. *Zero input.* All nine rows of Table III give 47.9–54.6 %, within 5 percentage points of 50 %, including the row with no dither, no integrator noise and no mismatch (49.9 %). Prediction (i) holds: the zero-input test cannot distinguish the effects.
3. *Same message, decomposed (second card).* Mismatch alone, without dither and integrator noise, gives **48.2 %**; adding noise or dither changes this by at most 0.3 percentage points (48.2–48.5 %). Integrator thermal noise without mismatch gives 26.2 % (26.6 % with dither). Dither alone gives **4.8 %**, and with none of the three effects, comparator noise alone gives 0.3 %. Prediction (ii) holds for the effects at the quantiser and for mismatch; integrator noise decorrelates about one quarter of the bits.
4. *Time course (Fig. 18(a)).* The two runs with mismatch rise to about 47–48 % within the first thousand clocks and end at 48.2 % and 48.5 %. The run with integrator noise and no mismatch rises more slowly, to about 21 % at the thousandth clock, stays between 21 % and 30 % thereafter and ends at 26.6 %. The run with dither alone stays below about 16 % after the first 100 clocks and settles near 5 %.
5. *Mismatch sweep and ceiling (third card).* The independence value for the test sine (amplitude 0.249 FS) is **48.4 %**. Without mismatch the four seed sets give 24.7 % on average (23.9–26.6 %); 0.003 % FS gives 45.7 %; from 0.01 % FS upwards every value lies between 47.4 % and 48.9 %, with means of 48.3–48.5 %, at the independence value whatever δ is. Prediction (ii) holds: above about 0.01 % FS the result no longer depends on the assumed mismatch, and the 48.2 % of the first card is the ceiling, not a fitted value. The measured 49.8 % would be the independence value for a sine of amplitude 0.089 FS.
6. *Dither placement (first card, last row of Table III).* Dither in the feedback, with all effects on, gives 47.9 % (zero input) and 47.2 % (same message), no more than mismatch already gives, but the modulator's SNDR decreases from **60.3 dB** (dither at the comparator) to **39.5 dB**.

**Result: the transmitted bits (fourth card, Table IV, Fig. 18(b)).** At OSR 50 the S-DSM sends 50 bits per reading and the ADC with Trivium 72 or 80; at OSR 30, 30 against 72 or 80. The bit ratios, 1.44, 1.60, 2.40 and 2.67, agree with the energy ratios of [1], 1.44, 1.60, 2.40 and 2.67, within **0.18 %**, inside the rounding of the table of [1], as predicted. Fig. 18(b) draws both ratios side by side for the four configurations.

**Interpretation.**

* *A consistency check, not a validation.* The model agrees with the channel disagreement of [1] within 1.6 percentage points and with the bit ratios behind its energy table within 0.18 %, with no parameter fitted to either (the channel offset δ = 0.10 % FS is assumed, and every value above about 0.01 % FS gives the same result), but neither comparison can discriminate between models. The zero input gives about 50 % for any combination of effects; the same-message value saturates at the independence value (1 − A²/2)/2 as soon as any mismatch above about 0.01 % FS is present, so it confirms that the channels are decorrelated, not how strongly; and **the remaining 1.6-point gap could be explained by a smaller test amplitude in [1]** (0.089 FS would give 49.8 %), which [1] does not state; the comparison cannot exclude a deficiency of the model. The bit check confirms the bit counts behind the energy table of [1], not a measurement, and uses no radio number. Within these limits, the attacks and the comparisons of later sections act on a model that is consistent with the silicon where the silicon has been measured; the circuit parameters themselves come from the SKY130 simulations of Section VII.
* *With the dither as modelled, the model needs a further effect to reach the measured disagreement.* [1] attributes the disagreement of its two channels to the dither, and its chip measurements are the stronger evidence. The model represents that dither in a simplified form: a discrete-time loop without excess loop delay, with the ladder ratio of 0.978 to 1.022 read as ±0.022 of full scale at the comparator input. In this form the loop corrects most dither-induced decisions, and the dither alone changes 4.8 % of the bits of the same message; integrator thermal noise alone changes 26.2 %; a small input-referred difference between the channels (from 0.01 % FS upwards) brings the value to the measured one. **This is a statement about the model, not about the chip of [1]:** the measurement cannot separate the effects, and the model's low dither contribution most likely reflects the simplified representation of the dither and of the continuous-time loop. The notebook therefore does not claim that the security of [1] rests on mismatch rather than on dither; it uses the channel offset only as the model's means of reproducing the measured decorrelation. Section IX-C sweeps the dither amplitude and shows that, in the model, a stronger dither does decorrelate the victim and the replica. Moving the dither into the feedback gives 47.2 % but reduces the SNDR by 21 dB (60.3 to 39.5 dB), which is consistent with the choice of [1] to dither at the comparator.
* *Consequence for the security evaluation.* In the model, the original design's resistance to the same-key test, and to the replica attack that rests on the same disagreement, depends on how strongly the victim's and the replica's bits decorrelate, through the dither and through analog differences together. Section VIII sweeps these quantities, and Section IX evaluates the attacks that do not depend on them at all (key search, Berlekamp-Massey, frame forgery).
* *Consequence for the comparisons of Section X.* The comparison of [1] rests on the bits each architecture sends; Section X therefore compares the proposal by its transmitted bits, which the architecture sets, and claims no radio energy.

#### Summary of Section VI

1. **Fig. 4(c) of [1] is matched within 1.6 percentage points:** two channels with the same key and input differ in 50.0 % (zero input) and 48.2 % (same message) of their bits, against 50.05 % and 49.8 % measured.
2. **The same-message value is a ceiling:** independent channels give (1 − A²/2)/2 = 48.4 % for the test sine; every mismatch from 0.01 to 0.3 % FS gives 47.4–48.9 % over four seed sets, so the test confirms decorrelation but not the mismatch, and the gap to 49.8 % would correspond to a smaller input amplitude in [1] (0.089 FS), which [1] does not state. This section is therefore a consistency check, not a validation.
3. **With the dither as modelled, the model reaches the measured disagreement only with a small channel offset:** 0.10 % FS of input-referred offset alone gives 48.2 %; integrator thermal noise alone 26.2 %; the modelled dither alone 4.8 %; none of them 0.3 %. [1] attributes the disagreement to its dither; the low dither contribution here is taken as a limit of the model's simplified dither, not as a finding about the chip. The zero-input test gives 48–55 % for every combination and cannot separate the effects.
4. **Dither placement:** at the comparator, as in [1], the dither preserves the 60.3 dB SNDR (in the model it contributes little to the disagreement); in the feedback it adds nothing beyond mismatch (47.2 %) and reduces the SNDR by 21 dB (39.5 dB).
5. **The bit counts behind Fig. 4(b) of [1] are confirmed:** the ratio of transmitted bits equals the energy ratio of [1] within 0.18 % in all four configurations; no radio number is used.

The analog parameters of the model are so far those of [1] or assumptions (comparator noise, channel mismatch, PUF noise). Section VII replaces the assumed comparator and SRAM-cell parameters by SKY130 transistor-level simulation, so that the system studies and the attacks run on simulated circuit values.

# **VII. Circuit-level simulation in SKY130**
---
**Question.** The bit-exact model of Section V contains a few settings that describe circuits rather than algorithms: the input-referred noise and the offset of the modulator's comparator (`comp_noise` and a per-chip offset), and the noise-to-mismatch ratio, temperature coefficient and bias of an SRAM cell's power-up value (`puf_sigma`, `puf_tc`, `puf_bias`). Section V set them to illustrative values (`comp_noise` = 10⁻³, `puf_sigma` = 0.06, `puf_tc` = 0.008, `puf_bias` = 0.5) and the BCH code strength to a placeholder, t = 40. This section determines what these settings are for transistor-level models of SKY130 devices: in the SkyWater SKY130 process, after layout extraction, and across process, voltage and temperature (PVT).

**Why it matters.** The security of both designs rests on these numbers. In the model of Section VI, analog differences between two channels ahead of the quantiser strongly affect whether their bits agree; the size of such analog differences, between the channels of one chip or between a victim's chip and an attacker's copy, is a circuit property. For the proposal, the noise-to-mismatch ratio of the physically unclonable function (PUF) sets how many fingerprint bits flip at each power-up, and therefore the BCH code strength, the key-failure probability and the number of secret bits that remain. The circuit numbers of the abstract (comparator noise and offset, the PUF's noise-to-mismatch ratio and error rates, the working code strength t = 45 and its 94-137 secret bits, lower bound to point estimate) are all obtained here.

**Approach and roadmap.** Each circuit is simulated at transistor level in ngspice with the PDK's own device, noise and mismatch models, first as a schematic and then as an extracted layout; the results are then mapped onto the model's settings. The subsections follow that order, block by block:

* **A. Simulation setup:** the open-source tools and their versions, installed in the session.
* **B. The StrongARM comparator** (schematic): transient operation, noise, energy and offset, and their conversion to model units.
* **C. The SRAM-PUF cell** (schematic): the power-up race between mismatch and noise, its Monte Carlo over temperature, and the fit of the cell model.
* **D. Post-layout extraction:** both cells drawn, checked (DRC, LVS) and extracted, then simulated again with the same seeds, so that every difference is caused by the layout.
* **E. The model with SKY130 parameters:** the post-layout values replace the illustrative settings, and the BCH code is sized from the simulated error rates of the extracted SRAM cell.
* **F. Process, voltage and temperature corners:** the extracted comparator at the five process corners, three supplies and three temperatures, and the extracted SRAM cell at the five corners and three temperatures (recorded grids); the comparator's energy separated into its dynamic and leakage terms; and the SRAM-PUF error law, which separates noise from reproducible flips.
* **Summary**, with the SKY130-derived settings handed to Section VIII.

> **Role of the circuits.** The StrongARM latch and the 6T SRAM cell are standard topologies, and drawing them in SKY130 is not a contribution of this work. They serve one purpose: to replace assumed model parameters with values obtained from a real PDK, including layout parasitics and process spread. This section therefore remains at block level (one comparator, one SRAM cell); the consequences of the values for the accuracy, power and security of the complete sensor are evaluated in Section VIII.

### A. Simulation setup

**Goal.** Install one fixed, open-source tool set in the session, so that every circuit number in this and the later sections can be traced to the same tools and versions.

**Setup.** All circuits are simulated with ngspice 41 on the SkyWater SKY130 open PDK (open_pdks build 1689ac3f): the 1.8 V devices `sky130_fd_pr__nfet_01v8` and `pfet_01v8`, the typical (tt) corner unless stated otherwise, and the PDK's own mismatch models. The layouts of Section VII-D are drawn with KLayout 0.30 (its Python API) and checked and extracted with Magic 8.3 and netgen 1.5. The digital blocks of Sections X, XI and XII are synthesised with Yosys 0.69 on the `sky130_fd_sc_hd` standard cells, placed and routed with OpenROAD, and simulated at gate level with Icarus Verilog; these tools are installed here as well, so that one cell prepares the whole notebook. Every version is pinned in the cell. The conda packages are installed with a static micromamba binary into separate prefixes, so that the installations run in parallel, and the PDK is enabled with the `ciel` PDK manager. If the conda builds of ngspice, Magic or netgen are unavailable in Colab, the cell installs the distribution's packages instead and reports the substitution. ngspice reads a start-up file that enables the HSPICE-compatible parameter handling the SKY130 libraries require (`ngbehavior=hsa`). Every simulation module of this section runs each ngspice process pinned to one processor core, because unpinned single-threaded processes ran up to 3.5 times slower on a two-core machine. The installation takes about 1–2 minutes in Colab; the cell prints the version of every tool it finds.

> **Next cell.** 1. Downloads a static micromamba binary, so that neither a conda installation nor a kernel restart is required. 2. Installs, in parallel: ngspice 41 (conda-forge); Magic 8.3 and netgen 1.5 (litex-hub conda builds); OpenROAD and Icarus Verilog (litex-hub conda builds); and from PyPI the `ciel` PDK manager, Yosys 0.69 (the WebAssembly build) and KLayout 0.30. 3. Enables one pinned build of the SkyWater SKY130 PDK with `ciel`: the transistor models, the high-density standard cells and the tools' setup files. 4. Writes the ngspice start-up file and prints the version of every tool. A re-run skips every tool already installed. Run time: about 1–2 minutes in Colab.


```python
#@title **Setup:** install ngspice, the SkyWater SKY130 PDK, Yosys, KLayout, Magic, netgen, OpenROAD and Icarus Verilog (about 1–2 minutes in Colab) { display-mode: "form" }
# Everything this notebook needs is installed from official open-source distributions:
#   ngspice 41      conda-forge build, via a static micromamba binary (no conda install, no kernel restart)
#   SKY130 PDK      open_pdks build 1689ac3f (2026-08-27) via the ciel PDK manager: the transistor models
#                   (sky130_fd_pr), the high-density standard cells (sky130_fd_sc_hd) and the tool setup files
#   Yosys 0.69      yowasp-yosys, Yosys compiled to WebAssembly and installed with pip
#   KLayout 0.30    the klayout Python package (layout drawing, GDS), from pip
#   Magic 8.3, netgen 1.5   litex-hub conda builds (DRC, parasitic extraction, LVS), via the same micromamba
#   OpenROAD 2.0, Icarus Verilog 13   litex-hub conda builds (place-and-route, timing and power; gate-level simulation)
# The installs run in parallel; re-running the cell skips whatever is already installed.
import os, sys, subprocess, shutil, pathlib, platform, time

IN_COLAB = "google.colab" in sys.modules
WORK = pathlib.Path("/content/cac" if IN_COLAB else os.environ.get("CAC_WORK", os.path.abspath("cac_work")))
TOOLS, PDK_ROOT = WORK / "tools", WORK / "pdk"
SKY130_VERSION = "1689ac3f2dc763876eaf967227c7dfe831b031ae"
PINS = dict(ngspice="41", ciel="3.0.0", yowasp_yosys="0.69.0.0.post1233", klayout="0.30.12", magic="8.3.465", netgen="1.5.272",
            openroad="2.0_12381_g01bba3695", iverilog="0_8_6897_g58dcf39db")
WORK.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def sh(cmd, cwd=None, timeout=1800):
    """Run a shell command; raise with its output if it fails."""
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, cwd=cwd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout)
    if r.returncode:
        raise RuntimeError(f"command failed: {cmd}\n{r.stdout[-3000:]}\n{r.stderr[-3000:]}")
    return r.stdout

def micromamba(env):
    """The static micromamba binary, from its own site or from its GitHub release. Each environment gets its own root
    prefix (package cache), so that the three installs below can run at the same time."""
    TOOLS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if not (TOOLS / "bin" / "micromamba").exists():
        try:
```

### B. The StrongARM comparator

**Goal.** Measure the three properties of the modulator's comparator that the model requires: its input-referred noise σ<sub>n</sub>, the spread σ<sub>os</sub> of its offset caused by device mismatch, and its energy per decision; then express the noise and the offset in the model's units.

**Theory: operation and regeneration.** The modulator of [1] quantises the output of its second integrator with a StrongARM latch clocked at f<sub>clk</sub> = 10 MHz [1, 7] (Fig. 19). While the clock φ is low, the reset devices M8–M11 precharge the internal nodes d<sub>p</sub>, d<sub>n</sub> and the outputs out<sub>p</sub>, out<sub>n</sub> to V<sub>DD</sub>. When φ rises, the tail M7 turns on and the input pair M1/M2 discharges d<sub>p</sub> and d<sub>n</sub> with currents I<sub>D</sub> ± g<sub>m</sub>ΔV<sub>in</sub>/2, where ΔV<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>in+</sub> − V<sub>in−</sub> is the differential input, I<sub>D</sub> the drain current of each input device and g<sub>m</sub> its transconductance. This integration phase lasts a time T<sub>int</sub>, until the nodes have fallen by about one threshold voltage V<sub>TH</sub> and the cross-coupled latch M3–M6 turns on. The latch then regenerates: the small differential voltage v<sub>0</sub> left by the integration grows as v(t) = v<sub>0</sub>·e<sup>t/τ</sup>, where τ ≈ C<sub>out</sub>/g<sub>m,latch</sub> is the regeneration time constant set by the output capacitance and the latch transconductance, until the outputs reach the rails. Because the decision time grows only with ln(V<sub>DD</sub>/v<sub>0</sub>), a smaller input requires little additional time: for these device sizes τ = 36 ps (the slope of the simulated decision delay against ln ΔV<sub>in</sub>, `dev/spice_comparator/RESULTS.md`), so even a 10 µV input reaches the latch's half-swing about 0.62 ns after the clock edge, far inside the 50 ns half-period of the 10 MHz clock. **Metastability therefore does not limit this comparator, and its accuracy is set by noise and offset alone.** Two inverters buffer out<sub>p</sub> and out<sub>n</sub>, so that both outputs see identical loads irrespective of the state of the following NOR SR latch, which holds the decision q through the reset phase.

**Theory: input-referred noise and kT/C.** During integration, each input device adds channel noise of one-sided power spectral density (PSD) S<sub>i</sub> = 4kTγg<sub>m</sub> to its drain node of capacitance C<sub>P</sub> (k is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and γ the channel-noise factor, 2/3 for a long-channel device). The signal deposits a charge g<sub>m</sub>ΔV<sub>in</sub>T<sub>int</sub> on the same node, and the noise a charge whose variance grows in proportion to T<sub>int</sub>. Referring the noise to the input and using T<sub>int</sub> ≈ C<sub>P</sub>V<sub>TH</sub>/I<sub>D</sub> gives the first-order result [7]

σ<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup> ≈ 4kTγ / (g<sub>m</sub>T<sub>int</sub>) = (kT/C<sub>P</sub>) · 4γ(I<sub>D</sub>/g<sub>m</sub>)/V<sub>TH</sub>.

The comparator integrates its input for a time T<sub>int</sub>, and a longer integration averages more noise; the result is the kT/C noise of the integrating node, scaled by a bias-dependent factor. A larger node capacitance or a longer integration lowers σ<sub>n</sub>; a higher temperature raises it as √T. With C<sub>P</sub> of a few femtofarads (√(kT/C<sub>P</sub>) = 0.91 mV at 5 fF and 300 K), I<sub>D</sub>/g<sub>m</sub> ≈ 0.1 V and V<sub>TH</sub> ≈ 0.5 V, the factor 4γ(I<sub>D</sub>/g<sub>m</sub>)/V<sub>TH</sub> is about 0.5. **Prediction: σ<sub>n</sub> between a few tenths of a millivolt and about 1 mV.** The noise is Gaussian, so the probability of deciding 1 against a constant input follows a probit curve, P(q = 1) = Φ((ΔV<sub>in</sub> − μ)/σ<sub>n</sub>), with Φ the standard normal cumulative distribution and μ the comparator's systematic offset; fitting this curve to many simulated decisions measures σ<sub>n</sub> and μ. The analysis, like the measurement below, includes white channel noise only. The input pair's 1/f noise is not negligible in itself: from the PDK's `.noise` analysis it has a corner near 22 MHz and amounts to about 95 µV rms over 10 Hz–100 kHz, the signal band at OSR 50 (`dev/spice_comparator/RESULTS.md`). It changes little within a clock period and acts as a slowly varying offset, about a sixth of σ<sub>n</sub> and 2 % of the offset σ<sub>os</sub> measured below, which the loop treats as it treats the offset; it is not part of σ<sub>n</sub>.

**Theory: offset from mismatch (Pelgrom's law).** Two nominally identical transistors differ in threshold voltage by a random amount whose standard deviation decreases with gate area: each device varies with σ(V<sub>T</sub>) = A/√(WL), and the difference of a pair with σ(ΔV<sub>T</sub>) = √2·A/√(WL) (Pelgrom's law; A is a process constant, W and L the device width and length). The input pair's mismatch appears directly at the input; the latch's mismatch is divided by the gain of the integration phase before it is referred to the input. The input devices are therefore drawn long (W/L = 4/0.5 µm, WL = 2 µm²). With the per-device coefficient of the SKY130 nMOS threshold in the PDK's model, A = 3.356 mV·µm, one input device has σ(V<sub>T</sub>) = 2.4 mV, and the pair difference √2 × 2.4 = 3.4 mV from this term alone. The PDK also varies the subthreshold offset and the oxide thickness of each device, and the latch adds its own share, so **the prediction is an offset σ<sub>os</sub> somewhat above 3.4 mV, of the order of 4–5 mV**: an order of magnitude above the noise. The offset is a constant of each chip, Gaussian over chips, and to first order independent of temperature.

**Theory: energy and model units.** The comparator draws charge only when it switches, so its energy per decision is E = C<sub>sw</sub>V<sub>DD</sub><sup>2</sup>, with C<sub>sw</sub> the total capacitance charged per cycle (internal nodes, outputs, buffers and the clock gates); its power is E·f<sub>clk</sub>. In the model the comparator compares the normalised integrator state x<sub>2</sub> with zero, x<sub>2</sub> = ±1 being the feedback reference, and decides y = 1 when x<sub>2</sub> + offset + `comp_noise`·N(0, 1) ≥ 0. The mapping from volts takes x<sub>2</sub> = 1 to V<sub>unit</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>/4 = 0.45 V differential at the SKY130 supply of 1.8 V. This is the value that keeps the second integrator within the output swing of a 1.8 V operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) when the model clips x<sub>2</sub> at ±2.5 (±0.56 V on each output around the 0.9 V common mode). Hence `comp_noise` = σ<sub>n</sub>/V<sub>unit</sub>, and the per-chip offset has standard deviation σ<sub>os</sub>/V<sub>unit</sub>.

**Setup.** Transistor level, schematic netlist, SKY130 tt corner, 27 °C, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, input common mode 0.9 V, ideal 10 MHz clock with 100 ps edges and 50 % duty cycle. Device sizes (W/L in µm, all from the design choices above): input pair M1/M2 4/0.5, tail M7 2/0.15, latch nMOS M3/M4 1/0.15 and pMOS M5/M6 2/0.15 (twice the nMOS width for the mobility ratio), reset devices M8–M11 1/0.15, followed by inverter buffers and a NOR SR latch on a separate supply, so that their current can be measured apart from the core. Every transistor carries the source and drain junction areas and perimeters of a single-finger layout with 0.29 µm of diffusion, without which the models contain no junction capacitance. The schematic assumes 1 fF of wiring capacitance on d<sub>p</sub>, d<sub>n</sub>, out<sub>p</sub> and out<sub>n</sub> (Section VII-D replaces this assumption with the extracted values) and a 5 fF load on each output of the SR latch. Only the two device models used are loaded from the PDK's corner file, which gives the same device currents as the complete library in a fraction of its loading time. Around every rising clock edge the simulator's time step is held at 20 ps by breakpoints, because a larger step during regeneration can place the latch on the wrong side.

* **Transient.** Six consecutive decisions with inputs of ±1, ±0.2 and ±20 mV, without mismatch or noise, to show the operation and to check the decisions.
* **Noise.** ngspice's transient analysis contains no device noise, so the noise is injected in three steps. (i) A noiseless transient at ΔV<sub>in</sub> = +0.5 mV records the terminal voltages of the 11 core transistors on a 20 ps grid around the third rising clock edge (the first cycle starts from the DC operating point and differs from the periodic steady state). (ii) For each device and each grid point, a copy of the device biased at those voltages gives the PDK's channel thermal-noise PSD from one `.noise` analysis at 1 GHz, where the 1/f noise is a few per cent of the thermal noise (corner near 22 MHz); the two devices of each symmetric pair receive their average. (iii) In the noisy runs, each core transistor receives an independent drain–source noise current with samples of variance S/(2·20 ps), linearly interpolated, in a window from 0.2 ns before to 0.5 ns after each rising clock edge; outside this window the decision is either latched or being reset. The injection method was checked on a test RC circuit driven by the resistor's 4kT/R noise through the same windowed, interpolated sources: at the 20 ps grid used here, the rms node voltage is 0.874 ± 0.044 of √(kT/C) for RC = 35 ps and 0.950 ± 0.044 for RC = 150 ps (0.939 and 0.977 at a 10 ps grid; `dev/spice_comparator/RESULTS.md`). The linear interpolation loses noise on nodes whose time constant is comparable to the grid; if the nodes that set the decision behaved like these test nodes, **σ<sub>n</sub> would be underestimated by about 5–13 %**. Refining the grid to 10 and 5 ps in a development run raised σ<sub>n</sub> by 1 and 2 %, within its standard error. These grid and window checks were made at tt and 27 °C only; at the PVT conditions of Section VII-F the same grid and window are assumed. A pilot run (9 inputs within ±2 mV, 20 decisions each) gives a first estimate of σ<sub>n</sub>; the main run then applies eleven inputs spread over ±2.5 times that estimate, 100 decisions each (1,100 decisions, independent noise per decision, one comparator per netlist, the input order shuffled), and the probit curve is fitted by maximum likelihood; the standard errors follow from the curvature of the likelihood.
* **Offset.** 96 Monte Carlo comparators with the PDK's mismatch on threshold voltage, oxide thickness and subthreshold offset of every device (4 comparators per netlist, one mismatch seed per netlist, noise off). Each instance finds its own switching threshold with a successive-approximation search built from ideal behavioural elements inside the same transient: in each clock cycle the input moves by one step towards the threshold, in the direction opposite to the decision. There are 16 steps, the first 16 mV, each 1.8 times smaller than the last, so that the final step is 2.4 µV; the ratio below 2 makes the search redundant, so that a wrong early decision is corrected, and limits it to ±36 mV.
* **Energy.** The supply current integrated over one clock period, with an input of ±1 mV alternating so that the output toggles in every cycle (the worst case), for the core, for the buffers and SR latch, and for the clock, counted as V<sub>DD</sub> times the charge the clock source delivers (the charge a CMOS clock driver would draw); the first cycle is discarded.
* **Seeds, statistics and run mode.** All seeds are fixed, so every run reproduces the same numbers. The cells below run all measurements live in this session with the quick statistics, which give σ<sub>n</sub> to about ±5 % (one standard error) and σ<sub>os</sub> to −12 %/+17 % (95 % interval of a standard deviation from 96 samples); `quick=False` in the noise cell gives about four times as many decisions and Monte Carlo instances.
