<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 40.</b> Study A: accuracy against the comparator. (a) Modulator SNDR against the comparator noise σ<sub>n</sub>: simulation at tt, 27 °C, 1.8 V (solid), theory (dashed), 45 PVT conditions (markers). (b) DC error of the reading against offset |o| (circles); diamond: 3× the largest PVT σ<sub>os</sub>; dotted: 0.1 % of full scale; orange: beyond the theory's integrator range. Grey: PVT ranges.</p>

**Result.**

* *Noise at PVT.* The SNDR is 60.3–60.4 dB at all 45 PVT conditions (Fig. 40(a)).
* *Noise margin.* In simulation the SNDR falls by 3 dB at σ<sub>n</sub> ≈ 72 mV, 88× the largest PVT value (0.812 mV), that is about 90-fold.
* *Theory against simulation.* The describing function predicts the −3 dB point at about 99 mV, 1.4× the simulated 72 mV. Without noise it gives 58.8 dB against the simulated 60.4 dB, so it underestimates the low-noise SNDR by 1.6 dB. Up to σ<sub>n</sub> = 300 mV the two differ by at most 1.6 dB. At σ<sub>n</sub> = 1 V the theory overestimates the SNDR by about 12 dB. There the quantiser's input is dominated by noise, and the linearised relay no longer describes it, as the theory's assumptions anticipated.
* *Offset identity.* The bare loop with an offset and the offset-free loop started from the shifted state give identical bits for all three offsets tested (`True`).
* *DC error.* With an offset of 3× the largest PVT σ<sub>os</sub>, the decoded reading changes by 0.47 ppm of full scale. Over the sweep the error stays far below 0.1 % of full scale up to 1 V and exceeds it from 1.2 V on (Fig. 40(b)). The theory's integrator range is 700 mV, so it is conservative by 1.7×. The sweep has no point between 1.0 and 1.2 V, so the true limit lies in that interval.

**Interpretation.** Both predictions hold in form. The comparator noise is shaped like quantisation error and has no measurable effect on the SNDR until it is about 90× its worst PVT value. The offset is absorbed as a shift of the loop's state up to an integrator range more than 100× the largest PVT σ<sub>os</sub> (5.85 mV). The theory gives the right mechanism and the right order of magnitude, not the exact numbers: its noise limit is 1.4× too high and its offset limit 1.7× too low. **Design consequence:** for accuracy, this comparator can be sized for energy, not for noise or offset. The next study asks the opposite question for the same two quantities: could the comparator's noise or offset at least make two chips different enough to protect the original design?

### B. Security of the original design: comparator noise and offset

**Goal.** The original design's only defence against an attacker who owns a second chip (the threat model of Section IV) is the analog difference between the two chips. This study asks whether the comparator provides that difference at any PVT condition and, if not, how large its noise or offset would have to be, and at what cost in accuracy.

**Theory.** With the replica attack of the simulation setup, the attacker's keystream estimate is $\hat{K} = K \oplus (D \oplus \hat{D})$. Wherever the victim and the replica make the same decisions over the last 48 bits of a 64-bit window (Berlekamp-Massey tolerates wrong bits only within the first $L + 1 = 17$ bits, $L = 16$ being the LFSR's length), Berlekamp-Massey recovers the LFSR from that window, and the whole keystream follows. A clean window, with no differing bit, always qualifies.

* *The full-scan attacker* examines every window of the frames it records, so it succeeds as soon as one frame contains one such stretch. Its success probability falls to zero only where the two chips no longer agree on 48 consecutive bits anywhere in the capture.
* *The 80-window attacker of [1]* examines $W = 80$ random windows of one frame. If a fraction $f_{64}$ of all 64-bit windows is clean, and the windows are drawn independently,
$$P_{\text{succ}} \;\ge\; 1 - \left(1 - f_{64}\right)^{W},$$
where $P_{\text{succ}}$ is the probability that this attack succeeds on a chip pair. This is a lower bound, because a window whose only errors lie in its first 17 bits also yields the key.

Two facts decide $f_{64}$:

* *Disagreements come in bursts.* Two second-order loops driven by the same input follow nearly the same trajectory. Their decisions differ only where $x_2$ passes close to the threshold, and the state difference that a differing decision leaves is bounded by the loop, so the two loops resynchronise. If disagreements were independent with rate $p$, then $f_{64} = (1-p)^{64}$, negligible at $p$ of a few tens of per cent. Because they cluster, long clean stretches remain, and the attack needs only one.
* *An offset does not change the dynamics* (study A). A chip with offset $o$ is the same dynamical system as one without it, started from a shifted state. An offset therefore cannot decorrelate two chips, however large, until it pushes the loop into clipping beyond the integrator range of study A (700 mV). Noise, in contrast, randomises every decision with $|x_2 + o| \lesssim \sigma_n$, so as σ<sub>n</sub> grows it eliminates the clean windows, and $f_{64}$ and $P_{\text{succ}}$ decrease steeply.

*Predictions.* (i) Two chips that differ only in their comparator offsets agree on most bits, and the attack always succeeds. (ii) At the PVT noise, the 80-window attack succeeds whenever $f_{64}$ is a few per cent: $f_{64} = 5\,\%$ already gives $P_{\text{succ}} \ge 98\,\%$; it falls below 10 % of pairs only for $f_{64}$ below about 0.13 %. The full-scan attacker needs only one qualifying stretch in about 119,000 windows (four frames), so it should resist far more noise: protection against it needs $f_{64}$ well below 10<sup>−5</sup>, that is, comparator noise well above the level that defeats the 80-window attack. (iii) An offset protects only through clipping. Because σ<sub>os</sub> is the standard deviation of a random offset, some chips exceed the integrator range before σ<sub>os</sub> does: the fraction of chips with $|o| > 700$ mV is $2\,[1 - \Phi(700\,\text{mV}/\sigma_{os})]$, with Φ the standard normal distribution function. This fraction is 2 % at σ<sub>os</sub> = 300 mV and 24 % at 600 mV. The success rate should therefore begin to decrease slightly below the integrator range, and, since clipped loops emit long runs of equal bits that both chips share, it should not reach zero.

#### Part 1: the comparator offset alone

**Setup.** Behavioural model; this tests prediction (i). The victim and the replica are identical except for their comparators: each chip draws its offset independently from the SKY130 offset distribution of the schematic comparator (Section VII-B), and each has its own comparator-noise sequence. There is no analog input mismatch, and the integrator's thermal noise is set to zero. Both chips receive the same constant input (0.5 µA) for 30,000 clocks. The run is repeated without dither and with dither (the replica with its own dither seeds), for 24 chip pairs each, from a fixed seed. Metrics: the fraction of bits that differ between the two chips, and the number of pairs that the replica attack compromises.

> **Next cell.** 1. Draws 24 pairs of comparator offsets from the SKY130 distribution. 2. Runs the victim's and the replica's modulators on the same input, without and with dither. 3. Counts the bits that differ, and runs Berlekamp-Massey (`window_attack`, 80 windows) on the XOR of the victim's ciphertext and the replica's bits. 4. Prints the card (the result is marked in the figure of part 2). Part 1 uses the 80-window attacker of [1] only: where it already breaks every pair, the full-scan attacker of part 2, which examines every window, does so as well.


```python
#@title Fig.: study B, part 1: the comparator offset alone
r = rng_for(4242); u = np.full(LAB_N, s2d(tia(0.5e-6, DEFAULTS["rtia"]), DEFAULTS["buffer"]))
P0 = {**DEFAULTS, "comp_noise": COMP["comp_noise"], "int_noise": 0.0}
K = lfsr16_bits(DEFAULTS["key16"], ID_BITS + LAB_N)[ID_BITS:]
res = {}
for dith in (False, True):
    flips, broken = [], []
    for k in range(24):
        o1, o2 = r.normal(0, COMP["comp_offset_sigma"], 2)
        P = {**P0, "dither": dith}
        D1 = dsm2(u, P, noise_seed=1, offset=o1)["D"]; D2 = dsm2(u, P, seeds=(0x2C4D, 0x51E7), noise_seed=2, offset=o2)["D"]
        flips.append(np.mean(D1 != D2))
        broken.append(window_attack(D1 ^ K ^ D2, K, 100 + k)["broken"] > 0)      # Berlekamp-Massey on C xor replica
    res[dith] = (np.array(flips), np.array(broken))
card("Victim and replica differ only in their SKY130 comparator offsets",
     [(f"{'with' if d else 'without'} dither", f"median {np.median(res[d][0]) * 100:.1f} % of bits differ; Berlekamp-Massey breaks the original design "
       f"in <b>{res[d][1].sum()} of {len(res[d][1])}</b> chip pairs") for d in (False, True)],
     note="The loop absorbs the offset as a shift of its state (study A), so it gives no protection.", tone="bad")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(W1 + 1.0, 2.8))
ax.hist([res[False][0] * 100, res[True][0] * 100], bins=np.linspace(0, 12, 25), color=["white", COL["ok"]], ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.6,
        hatch="", label=["no dither", "dither"])
ax.set_xlabel("Bits that differ, victim vs replica (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("Chip pairs"); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_xlim(0, 12); ax.legend(loc="upper right"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
OFFREP = res                                     # part 1, also marked in panel (b) of the figure of part 2
```


<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #eb6834;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Victim and replica differ only in their SKY130 comparator offsets</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">without dither</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">median 2.3 % of bits differ; Berlekamp-Massey breaks the original design in <b>24 of 24</b> chip pairs</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">with dither</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">median 6.1 % of bits differ; Berlekamp-Massey breaks the original design in <b>24 of 24</b> chip pairs</td></tr></table><div style="margin-top:4px;opacity:.85">The loop absorbs the offset as a shift of its state (study A), so it gives no protection.</div></div>

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 41.</b> Study B, part 1: the comparator offset alone. Histogram, over 24 simulated chip pairs (behavioural model) that differ only in their SKY130 comparator offsets and noise, of the modulator bits that differ between victim and replica; white: no dither; blue: dither.</p>

**Result.** Without dither, a median of 2.3 % of the bits differ between victim and replica; with dither, 6.1 %. The replica attack compromises the original design in 24 of 24 chip pairs in both cases (card above; Fig. 41), as prediction (i) states.

**Interpretation.** In the model, the comparator offset provides **no protection**. It acts at the quantiser, inside the loop, where study A shows that it only shifts the loop's state. A replica that differs from the victim only in this respect still agrees with it on about 94–98 % of the bits (medians), which leaves Berlekamp-Massey enough clean windows to recover the 16-bit LFSR in every pair. In the model, the disagreement of the two channels of [1] on 50 % of their bits must therefore be produced before the quantiser: Section VI reproduces it with a small input-referred offset between the channels, whereas the model's simplified dither alone does not; this is how the model matches the measurement, not a claim about the chip, which [1] attributes to its dither. Part 2 asks whether the comparator's noise, or an offset far larger than SKY130 gives, changes this.

#### Part 2: comparator noise and offset, at PVT and swept

**Setup.** Behavioural model with the full testbench settings, including the integrator's thermal noise of [1]; this tests predictions (ii) and (iii).

* *PVT:* 8 chip pairs at each of the 45 conditions (360 pairs), each with that condition's σ<sub>n</sub>, σ<sub>os</sub> and supply.
* *Noise sweep:* σ<sub>n</sub> from 0.3 mV to 300 mV (12 points, denser between 30 and 200 mV, where the attack begins to fail) with the post-layout σ<sub>os</sub> = 4.37 mV.
* *Offset sweep:* σ<sub>os</sub> from 1 mV to 3 V (10 points) with the post-layout σ<sub>n</sub> = 0.575 mV.
* *Pairs:* 24 independent pairs per swept point, raised to 100 at the points in the transition and at the first point beyond it where no pair is broken (simulation setup). Each pair has its own offsets, noise, dither and seeds, and each of its frames its own noise realisation.
* *Attackers:* the full-scan attacker over up to four frames (the security criterion), and the 80-window attacker of [1] on the first frame, on the same pairs.
* *Metrics:* for every point, the fraction of pairs each attacker breaks with its 95 % Clopper-Pearson interval, the disagreement rate p and the clean-window fraction f<sub>64</sub> (first frame, clocks 200 to 30,000), and the theory's bound for the 80-window attacker. The protection point is the first swept value from which on no pair is broken (simulation setup); its SNDR cost is interpolated from the noise sweep of study A. For the illustration of panel (c), one pair is shown at the post-layout noise and at the protection point: 600 clocks around the longest clean stretch of the post-layout capture, with each pair's disagreement rate and clean-window fraction over the whole capture.

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs the replica attack, with both attackers, over the noise sweep, the offset sweep and the 45 PVT conditions, raising the points near the protection point to 100 pairs. 2. Finds the noise and the offset from which the full-scan attacker breaks no pair, with the confidence bounds per pair and per frame, and the SNDR that noise costs (from study A). 3. Compares the theory's bound with the 80-window attacker. 4. Prints the card and draws Fig. 42, including where one victim/replica pair disagrees around its longest clean stretch.


```python
#@title Fig.: study B, part 2: security of the original design
# Study B: security of the original design. The replica attack against the comparator's noise and offset, at the 45 PVT
# conditions and swept far beyond them: the full-scan, multi-frame attacker (security criterion) with Clopper-Pearson
# intervals, the 80-window attacker of [1] and the theory's bound for it
t0 = time.time()
SN_SEC = np.array([0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 50, 70, 100, 130, 160, 200, 300]) * 1e-3             # comparator noise for the attack (V)
rep_sn = replica_sweep(lambda x, n, k0: replica_pairs(Qn(x), os0, 1.8, n, 3, k0=k0), SN_SEC)
rep_os = replica_sweep(lambda x, n, k0: replica_pairs(Qn(sn0), x, 1.8, n, 4, k0=k0), OS_SWEEP)
rep_pvt = [rp_summary(replica_pairs(Qn(r["sigma_n"], r["vdd"]), r["sigma_os"], r["vdd"], 8, 11 + i)) for i, r in enumerate(PVT["cmp"])]
g = lambda rs, k: np.array([x[k] for x in rs])
k_pvt, n_pvt, k80_pvt = int(g(rep_pvt, "k").sum()), int(g(rep_pvt, "n").sum()), int(g(rep_pvt, "k80").sum())
sn_p, sn_b, sn_S = protection(SN_SEC, rep_sn); os_p, os_b, os_S = protection(OS_SWEEP, rep_os)
SYS.update(rep_pvt=k_pvt / n_pvt, rep_pvt_ci=cp95(k_pvt, n_pvt), rep80_pvt=k80_pvt / n_pvt, n_pvt=n_pvt, sn_prot=sn_p, sn_brk=sn_b,
           sn_prot_n=sn_S["n"] if sn_S else None, os_prot=os_p, os_min=g(rep_os, "success").min(),
           f64_pvt=g(rep_pvt, "f64").mean(), p_pvt=g(rep_pvt, "p").mean(), sn_10_80=crossing(SN_SEC, g(rep_sn, "success80"), 0.1))
SYS["sndr_at_snp"] = float(np.interp(np.log(sn_p), np.log(SN_SWEEP), sndr_sweep)) if sn_p else None
pct = lambda S: f"{S['k']}/{S['n']} [{100 * S['ci'][0]:.0f}–{100 * S['ci'][1]:.0f} %]"
card("Study B, security of the original design: the replica attack against the comparator",
     [("full-scan attacker at the 45 PVT conditions (8 pairs each)", f"<b>breaks {k_pvt} of {n_pvt} pairs</b> (95 % interval "
       f"{100 * SYS['rep_pvt_ci'][0]:.0f}–{100 * SYS['rep_pvt_ci'][1]:.0f} %); the 80-window attacker of [1]: {k80_pvt} of {n_pvt}"),
      ("why: clean 64-bit windows at PVT (theory's f<sub>64</sub>)", f"{100 * SYS['f64_pvt']:.1f} % of windows, although the chips disagree on "
       f"{100 * SYS['p_pvt']:.0f} % of bits; independent errors would leave (1 − p)<sup>64</sup> = {(1 - SYS['p_pvt']) ** 64:.0e}"),
      ("comparator noise that protects (no pair broken by the full-scan attacker, ≥ 100 pairs)",
       (f"σ<sub>n</sub> = <b>{1e3 * sn_p:.0f} mV</b> ({sn_S['k']} of {sn_S['n']} pairs, {N_FRAMES} frames each: success ≤ "
        f"{100 * sn_S['ci'][1]:.1f} % per pair and ≤ {100 * sn_S['frame_hi']:.2f} % per frame at 95 % confidence; last break at "
        f"{1e3 * sn_b:.0f} mV); <b>{sn_p / sn_max:.0f}×</b> the PVT maximum, at a cost of <b>{sndr_sweep[0] - SYS['sndr_at_snp']:.1f} dB</b> "
        "of SNDR (study A)") if sn_p else "none in the sweep"),
      ("the 80-window attacker of [1] (secondary): below 10 % of pairs from", (f"σ<sub>n</sub> ≈ {1e3 * SYS['sn_10_80']:.0f} mV"
       if SYS["sn_10_80"] else "not in the sweep")),
      ("full-scan attack against σ<sub>n</sub>: pairs broken [95 % interval]",
       ", ".join(f"{1e3 * x:g} mV: {pct(S)}" for x, S in zip(SN_SEC, rep_sn))),
      ("comparator offset that protects", (f"σ<sub>os</sub> = {1e3 * os_p:.0f} mV" if os_p else
       f"<b>none</b>: up to σ<sub>os</sub> = {1e3 * OS_SWEEP[-1]:.0f} mV, beyond the supply, the full-scan attack breaks "
       f"{100 * SYS['os_min']:.0f} % or more of pairs")),
      ("full-scan attack against σ<sub>os</sub> (integrator range of study A: {:.0f} mV)".format(1e3 * o_abs),
       ", ".join(f"{1e3 * x:g} mV: {pct(S)}" for x, S in zip(OS_SWEEP, rep_os))),
      ("theory bound 1 − (1 − f<sub>64</sub>)<sup>80</sup> vs the 80-window attacker", "mean |difference| "
       f"{np.mean(np.abs(g(rep_sn, 'bound') - g(rep_sn, 'success80'))):.2f} over the noise sweep; the bound is conservative "
       "(Berlekamp-Massey also succeeds on windows whose only errors lie in their first 17 bits)"),
      ("pairs simulated", f"{int(g(rep_sn, 'n').sum()) + int(g(rep_os, 'n').sum()) + n_pvt:,}, each with its own seeds"),
      ("run time", f"{time.time() - t0:.0f} s")], tone="bad")

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W2, 5.2))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1.25, 1])
axs = [fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1, :])]
def err_curve(ax, xs, rs, key="success", ci="ci", **kw):     # a success curve with its Clopper-Pearson 95 % intervals
    y = 100 * g(rs, key); lo, hi = (100 * np.array([x[ci][j] for x in rs]) for j in (0, 1))
    ax.errorbar(xs, y, yerr=[y - lo, hi - y], capsize=2, elinewidth=0.8, **kw)
def sec_panel(ax, xs, rs, xp, rng, xlabel, lab, title):
    ax.axvspan(*rng, color=COL["faint"], alpha=0.3, lw=0, label="PVT range")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    err_curve(ax, 1e3 * xs, rs, fmt="o-", color=COL["ink"], ms=3, lw=1.5, label=f"full scan, {N_FRAMES} frames (95 % interval)")
    ax.plot(1e3 * xs, 100 * g(rs, "success80"), "s:", color=COL["faint"], ms=2.5, lw=1.0, label="80 windows, one frame [1]")
    ax.plot(1e3 * xs, 100 * g(rs, "bound"), "--", color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, label=r"bound $1 - (1 - f_{64})^{80}$")
    for r, y in zip(PVT["cmp"], g(rep_pvt, "success")):
        ax.plot(1e3 * r[xp], 100 * y, vmark[r["vdd"]], color=tcol[r["temp"]], ms=4, mec=COL["ink"], mew=0.3)
    ax.set_ylim(-5, 108); ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel("Pairs broken (%)"); panel(ax, lab, title)
sec_panel(axs[0], SN_SEC, rep_sn, "sigma_n", [1e3 * min(r["sigma_n"] for r in PVT["cmp"]), 1e3 * sn_max],
          r"Comparator noise $\sigma_\mathrm{n}$ (mV)", "a", "security vs noise")
if sn_p:
    axs[0].axvline(1e3 * sn_p, color=COL["key"], lw=0.9, ls=":")
    axs[0].annotate(f"protects from {1e3 * sn_p:.0f} mV:\n0 of {sn_S['n']} pairs broken;\nSNDR −{sndr_sweep[0] - SYS['sndr_at_snp']:.1f} dB",
                    (1e3 * sn_p, 62), xytext=(0.33, 62), textcoords="data", fontsize=7.5, ha="left", va="center", color=COL["key"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.6, color=COL["key"], shrinkA=2))   # three short lines: clear of the curves
axs[0].legend(fontsize=6.5, loc="lower left")
sec_panel(axs[1], OS_SWEEP, rep_os, "sigma_os", [1e3 * min(r["sigma_os"] for r in PVT["cmp"]), 1e3 * os_max],
          r"Comparator offset $\sigma_\mathrm{os}$ (mV)", "b", "security vs offset")
axs[1].axvline(1e3 * o_abs, color=COL["bad"], lw=0.9, ls=":")             # the same integrator range as study A
if "OFFREP" in globals():                                                # part 1: the offset alone, 24 pairs each
    axs[1].annotate(f"part 1, offset alone: {OFFREP[True][1].sum()} of {len(OFFREP[True][1])} pairs", (1e3 * os_max, 100),
                    xytext=(1.2, 45), fontsize=7.5, ha="left", va="center", color=COL["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.6, color=COL["ink"]))
axs[1].annotate("integrator range (study A)", (1e3 * o_abs, 20), xytext=(-4, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=7.5, ha="right", color=COL["bad"])
# (c) why: where the victim's and the replica's bits differ, at the post-layout noise and at the noise that protects. The
# clean-window fraction is measured over the whole capture (clocks 200 to 30,000, as in the theory); the panel shows 600
# clocks around the longest clean stretch of the post-layout pair, so that single disagreements can be seen
ax = axs[2]; n_show, rows_c = 600, []
for sn_v in (sn0, sn_p or SN_SEC[-1]):
    o1, o2 = np.random.default_rng(3).normal(0, os0 / VU(1.8), 2)
    D1 = dsm2(u_dc, Qn(sn_v), noise_seed=1, offset=o1)["D"]; D2 = dsm2(u_dc, Qn(sn_v), seeds=REPLICA_DITHER, noise_seed=2, offset=o2)["D"]
    x = (D1 ^ D2).astype(int); c = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(x)]); clean = (c[64:] - c[:-64]) == 0   # clean[s]: s..s+63
    rows_c.append((sn_v, x, clean, float(clean[200:30000 - 63].mean()), float(x[200:30000].mean())))
st = np.flatnonzero(rows_c[0][2][1000:29000]) + 1000                       # clean windows of the post-layout pair
runs = np.split(st, np.flatnonzero(np.diff(st) != 1) + 1) if len(st) else [np.array([1000])]
r0 = max(runs, key=len); k0 = int(max(200, (r0[0] + r0[-1] + 64) // 2 - n_show // 2))
for row, (sn_v, x, clean, f64_c, p_c) in enumerate(rows_c):
    cov = np.zeros(n_show, bool)
    for s0 in np.flatnonzero(clean[k0 - 63:k0 + n_show]) + k0 - 63:
        cov[max(0, s0 - k0):max(0, s0 - k0 + 64)] = True
    y0 = 1 - row
    ax.fill_between(np.arange(k0, k0 + n_show), y0 - 0.38, y0 + 0.38, where=cov, color=COL["ok"], alpha=0.35, lw=0, step="mid")
    ax.vlines(k0 + np.flatnonzero(x[k0:k0 + n_show]), y0 - 0.3, y0 + 0.3, color=COL["ink"], lw=0.6)
    ax.text(k0 + n_show * 1.02, y0, f"$\\sigma_\\mathrm{{n}}$ = {1e3 * sn_v:.{2 if sn_v < 1e-2 else 0}f} mV" + (" (post-layout)" if row == 0 else " (protects)")
            + f"\n{100 * p_c:.0f} % of bits differ; clean\nwindows {100 * f64_c:.{1 if f64_c > 1e-3 else 2}f} % of the capture",
            fontsize=7.5, va="center")
ax.set_xlim(k0, k0 + n_show * 1.36); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.6); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(int(np.ceil(k0 / 100) * 100), k0 + n_show + 1, 100))
ax.set_xlabel("Clock (of the attack's 30,000)")
panel(ax, "c", "one chip pair: disagreements (ticks) and clocks inside a clean 64-bit window (shaded)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 42.</b> Study B, part 2: security of the original design. Pairs broken by the replica attack against (a) the comparator noise σ<sub>n</sub> and (b) its offset σ<sub>os</sub>; markers: PVT conditions, as in Fig. 40; dotted vertical: protection point (a), integrator range (b). (c) One pair's disagreements (ticks) and clean 64-bit windows (shading), at the post-layout and the protecting noise (top, bottom).</p>

**Result.**

* *PVT.* The full-scan attacker breaks 360 of the 360 simulated chip pairs at the 45 PVT conditions (95 % interval 99–100 %; Fig. 42(a), (b), markers); the 80-window attacker of [1] breaks 356 of them.
* *Why.* The two chips disagree on 25 % of their bits (a quarter), yet 4.9 % of all 64-bit windows remain clean (mean over the PVT pairs): the disagreements come in bursts, separated by clean stretches such as the one in Fig. 42(c). Independent errors at that rate would leave (1 − p)<sup>64</sup> = 1 × 10<sup>−8</sup>. With f<sub>64</sub> = 4.9 %, the bound gives a success rate close to 100 % even for 80 windows (prediction ii). The chips disagree far more here than in part 1 (2.3–6.1 %). The main difference between the two setups is the integrator's thermal noise, present here and absent there; study D examines it.
* *Noise that protects.* The full-scan attacker breaks all 24 pairs up to σ<sub>n</sub> = 50 mV, 87 of 100 at 70 mV, 14 of 100 at 100 mV and 3 of 100 at 130 mV (95 % interval 1–9 %), and **none of 100 from σ<sub>n</sub> = 160 mV** (and none of 24 at 200 and 300 mV). At 160 mV its success probability is below 3.6 % per pair and below 0.92 % per frame at 95 % confidence. This noise is 197× the largest PVT value, and costs **7.5 dB of SNDR** (study A, interpolated): more than the 3 dB at which study A counts the accuracy as lost (72 mV).
* *The weaker attacker.* The 80-window attacker of [1] falls below 10 % of the pairs from σ<sub>n</sub> ≈ 60 mV and breaks none of 100 at 70 mV, where the full scan still breaks 87. Protection defined by that attacker, as in earlier versions of this study, understates the required noise by more than 2×.
* *Offset.* No offset tested (up to 3 V) protects the original design. Up to σ<sub>os</sub> = 300 mV the full-scan attacker breaks every pair. It breaks 75 of 100 at 600 mV, where a quarter of the chips already exceed the integrator range (prediction iii), 41 of 100 at 1 V and still 24 of 100 (95 % interval 16–34 %) at 3 V, beyond the supply (the card lists every point). With the SKY130 offsets alone (part 1) the 80-window attacker already compromises 24 of 24 pairs (label in Fig. 42(b)). Beyond the integrator range the loops clip, their bits become nearly constant, and the clean windows do not disappear.
* *Theory against simulation.* Over the noise sweep, the bound 1 − (1 − f<sub>64</sub>)<sup>80</sup> differs from the 80-window attacker's success by 0.05 on average (as a fraction of pairs), and lies below it, as a lower bound should.

**Interpretation.** **In the model, with its simplified dither, the comparator cannot give the original design its security at any of the 45 PVT conditions.** Its offset only shifts the loop's state. Its noise would have to be about 200× its worst value before an attacker who scans every window of four frames fails on 100 pairs out of 100, and then the sensor has lost 7.5 dB of SNDR: in the original design, analog "protection" and accuracy are in direct conflict. Even that point is a statistical statement, a 95 % upper bound of 3.6 % per pair, not a negligible probability; an attacker who records more frames gains further chances. This is why the proposal derives its security from a key instead of from analog differences. Before turning to the other analog blocks (studies D and E), study C completes the comparator with its power.

### C. Power: the comparator in the sensor's power budget

**Goal.** Find the comparator's share of the sensor's power at the 45 PVT conditions, and whether it affects the comparison of designs in Section X.

**Theory.** The comparator decides once per modulator clock, so its power is $P = E\,f_{clk}$, with $E$ the energy per decision of Section VII-F and $f_{clk}$ = 10 MHz. The relevant reference at system level is the power of the modulator it belongs to, 510 µW in [1] (Fig. 4(a) therein). *Prediction:* with $E$ below 1 pJ at every condition, $P$ stays below 10 µW, under 2 % of the modulator; and because every design compared in Section X uses the same modulator and comparator, the comparator's power cancels in that comparison.

**Setup.** No new simulation: the energies per decision of the extracted comparator at the 45 PVT conditions (recorded grid, Section VII-F, Fig. 35) and at the nominal condition (post-layout, Section VII-D). Metrics: $P$ at 10 MHz and $P/510$ µW.

> **Next cell.** 1. Converts the energy per decision at each of the 45 conditions and at the nominal condition into power at 10 MHz. 2. Expresses it as a share of the 510 µW modulator of [1]. 3. Prints the card.

**Result.** The extracted SKY130 comparator dissipates 1.4–8.2 µW in simulation at 10 MHz over the 45 PVT conditions, the largest value at the hot, fast-nMOS condition of Fig. 35. This is at most 1.6 % of the 510 µW measured for the 65 nm modulator of [1]; at the nominal condition the share is about 0.4 %.

**Interpretation.** At system level **the comparator's power is negligible at every condition**, and since it is common to every design compared in Section X, it does not affect the comparison. Studies A to C have covered the comparator; studies D and E turn to the modulator's other analog blocks, the integrators.

### D. The modulator's own non-idealities: integrator noise and OTA gain

**Goal.** Find what the integrators of [1] require for accuracy (thermal noise, OTA DC gain), and whether their noise, which differs from chip to chip, could protect the original design where the comparator could not (study B). The integrators are not simulated at transistor level in this work. Their non-idealities enter the behavioural model (Section V-C) as parameters, and are swept here.

**Theory.**

* *Integrator noise is not shaped.* Noise of rms $\sigma_i$ (in units of full scale, per clock) added at the first integrator's output appears at the modulator input as $\sigma_i/g_1$, white and before any noise shaping. Only the fraction $1/\mathrm{OSR}$ of its power falls in the signal band, where it competes with the in-band quantisation noise $P_q = P_{sig}\,10^{-\mathrm{SNDR}_0/10}$. Here $P_{sig}$ is the power of the input sine (amplitude 0.249, so $P_{sig} = 0.249^2/2$) and $\mathrm{SNDR}_0$ the SNDR without integrator noise (the simulated low-noise SNDR of study A). Then
  $$\mathrm{SNDR}(\sigma_i) \approx -10\log_{10}\!\left(10^{-\mathrm{SNDR}_0/10} + \frac{\sigma_i^2}{g_1^2\,\mathrm{OSR}\,P_{sig}}\right), \qquad \sigma_{i,\,-3\,\mathrm{dB}} = g_1\sqrt{\mathrm{OSR}\,P_q}.$$
  *Prediction:* the −3 dB point lies at about 66× the integrator noise derived from [1] (the next cell evaluates it).
* *Finite OTA gain makes the integrators leak.* With an OTA DC gain $A$, each integrator becomes $x[k] = p\,x[k-1] + \dots$ with the pole $p = A/(1+A)$, and the zeros of the NTF move from $z = 1$ to $z = p$. In the signal band $|1 - p\,e^{-j\omega}|^2 \approx \varepsilon^2 + \omega^2$ with $\varepsilon = 1/(1+A)$. Integrating $|\mathrm{NTF}|^2 \propto (\varepsilon^2 + \omega^2)^2$ over $0 \le \omega \le B = \pi/\mathrm{OSR}$ gives the rise of the in-band quantisation noise:
  $$R(A) = 1 + \frac{10}{3}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{B}\right)^{2} + 5\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{B}\right)^{4}, \qquad \mathrm{SNDR}(A) = \mathrm{SNDR}_0 - 10\log_{10}R(A).$$
  *Prediction:* the loss stays below 1 dB for $\varepsilon/B \lesssim 0.27$, that is $A \gtrsim 1.2\,\mathrm{OSR}$ (about 36 dB at OSR = 50): the classic rule that the OTA gain must exceed the oversampling ratio. The approximation assumes small leakage ($\varepsilon \ll 1$) and the ideal loop otherwise.
* *Integrator noise decorrelates two chips faster than comparator noise, but not before the accuracy is lost.* Comparator noise changes a decision only where $x_2$ is near the threshold. Integrator noise enters the state at every clock, accumulates in the loop and pushes two chips' trajectories apart, so it removes the clean windows of the replica attack more effectively. *Prediction:* the 80-window attacker's success falls with the integrator noise, but stretches on which the two chips agree, and with them the full-scan attack, persist as long as the SNDR is intact.

**Setup.** Behavioural, at the nominal corner only (the integrators have no PVT data in this work).

* *Accuracy:* the integrator noise from 0.1 to 300× the value derived from [1] (8 points), and the OTA gain from 20 to 100 dB (9 points), three noise seeds each. The two theory curves use the simulated $\mathrm{SNDR}_0$ and no other simulated or fitted value.
* *Security:* the replica attack of study B, with both attackers and the post-layout comparator offsets, at 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300 and 1,000× the integrator noise of [1]; 24 independent pairs per point, raised to 100 near the protection point (simulation setup). The full-scan attacker replaces the inference of earlier versions, which estimated from f<sub>64</sub> how many clean windows a full scan would find.

> **Next cell.** 1. Sweeps the integrator noise and the OTA gain, and simulates the SNDR. 2. Evaluates the two theory curves and their −3 dB and −1 dB points. 3. Runs the replica attack (full-scan and 80-window attackers) against the integrator noise, with Clopper-Pearson intervals, and measures f<sub>64</sub>. 4. Prints the card and draws Fig. 43.


```python
#@title Fig.: study D, modulator non-idealities
# Study D: accuracy against the modulator's own non-idealities (behavioural in this work): the first integrator's thermal
# noise and the OTA's DC gain, with the two theory curves (unshaped input noise; the leaky integrators' NTF), and the
# replica attack against the integrator noise (full-scan attacker with Clopper-Pearson intervals, and the 80-window attacker)
t0 = time.time()
NI0 = P_sys["int_noise"]
NI_SWEEP = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300])                     # multiples of the value derived from [1]
A_SWEEP = np.array([20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100])                   # OTA DC gain (dB)
sndr_ni = np.array([np.mean([sndr_at({**P_sys, "int_noise": NI0 * m}, k) for k in range(3)]) for m in NI_SWEEP])
sndr_A = np.array([np.mean([sndr_at({**P_sys, "ota_gain": 10 ** (a / 20)}, k) for k in range(3)]) for a in A_SWEEP])
s_ref = sndr_sweep[0]                                                      # the low-noise SNDR of study A
P_sig, g1 = amp_in ** 2 / 2, 0.5
ni_th = np.logspace(-1, np.log10(300), 100)
sndr_ni_th = -10 * np.log10(10 ** (-s_ref / 10) + (ni_th * NI0) ** 2 / (g1 ** 2 * OSR * P_sig))
ni_3db_th = g1 * np.sqrt(OSR * P_sig * 10 ** (-s_ref / 10)) / NI0
A_th = np.linspace(18, 100, 200); x_ = (1 / (1 + 10 ** (A_th / 20))) / (np.pi / OSR)
sndr_A_th = s_ref - 10 * np.log10(1 + 10 / 3 * x_ ** 2 + 5 * x_ ** 4)
A_1db_th = float(A_th[np.argmax(sndr_A_th >= s_ref - 1)])
NI_SEC = np.array([1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000])                          # integrator noise for the attack (x value of [1])
rep_ni = replica_sweep(lambda m, n, k0: replica_pairs({**P_sys, "int_noise": NI0 * m}, os0, 1.8, n, 5, k0=k0), NI_SEC)
ni_p, ni_b, ni_S = protection(NI_SEC, rep_ni)
SYS.update(ni_prot=ni_p, ni_3db=crossing(NI_SWEEP, sndr_ni, s_ref - 3), ni_3db_th=ni_3db_th, A_1db_th=A_1db_th,
           A_1db=next((a for a, s in zip(A_SWEEP, sndr_A) if all(x >= s_ref - 1 for x in sndr_A[list(A_SWEEP).index(a):])), None))
card("Study D, the modulator's own non-idealities: accuracy and security",
     [("integrator noise for −3 dB: simulation | theory g<sub>1</sub>√(OSR·P<sub>q</sub>)",
       f"<b>{SYS['ni_3db']:.0f}×</b> | {ni_3db_th:.0f}× the value derived from [1]: the SNDR is limited by quantisation, not by thermal noise"),
      ("OTA DC gain for less than 1 dB loss: simulation | theory R(A)", f"<b>≥ {SYS['A_1db']:.0f} dB</b> (sweep grid) | {A_1db_th:.0f} dB; "
       f"at 30 dB the SNDR decreases by {s_ref - np.interp(30, A_SWEEP, sndr_A):.1f} dB (theory {s_ref - np.interp(30, A_th, sndr_A_th):.1f} dB)"),
      (f"full-scan attacker ({N_FRAMES} frames) against the integrator noise: pairs broken [95 % interval]", ", ".join(
       f"{m}×: {x['k']}/{x['n']} [{100 * x['ci'][0]:.0f}–{100 * x['ci'][1]:.0f} %]" for m, x in zip(NI_SEC, rep_ni))
       + ("; <b>no protection in the sweep</b>" if ni_p is None else f"; protects from {ni_p:g}×")),
      ("the 80-window attacker of [1] (secondary)", ", ".join(f"{m}×: {x['k80']}/{x['n']}" for m, x in zip(NI_SEC, rep_ni))
       + "; f<sub>64</sub>: " + ", ".join(f"{100 * x['f64']:.2g} %" for x in rep_ni)),
      ("run time", f"{time.time() - t0:.0f} s")], tone="ok")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(W2, 3.2))
ax = axs[0]
ax.semilogx(NI_SWEEP, sndr_ni, "o-", color=COL["ink"], ms=3.5, lw=1.5, label="simulation")
ax.semilogx(ni_th, sndr_ni_th, "--", color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, label="theory (unshaped input noise)")
ax.axvline(1, color=COL["ok"], lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.text(1.15, 0.5, "from [1]", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), fontsize=7.5, color=COL["ok"])
ax.set_ylim(min(np.min(sndr_ni), np.min(sndr_ni_th)) - 2, np.max(sndr_ni) + 1.5)              # every point inside the frame
ax.set_xlabel("Integrator noise (× value of [1])"); ax.set_ylabel("Modulator SNDR (dB)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left")
panel(ax, "a", "SNDR vs integrator noise")
ax = axs[1]
ax.plot(A_SWEEP, sndr_A, "o-", color=COL["ink"], ms=3.5, lw=1.5, label="simulation")
ax.plot(A_th, sndr_A_th, "--", color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, label="theory $R(A)$")
ax.axvline(20 * np.log10(OSR), color=COL["faint"], lw=0.9, ls=":")
ax.text(20 * np.log10(OSR) + 1.5, 0.55, "$A$ = OSR", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), fontsize=7.5, color=COL["faint"])
ax.set_ylim(sndr_A.min() - 2, s_ref + 3)
ax.set_xlabel("OTA DC gain $A$ (dB)"); ax.set_ylabel("Modulator SNDR (dB)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right")
panel(ax, "b", "SNDR vs OTA gain")
ax = axs[2]
if SYS["ni_3db"]:
    ax.axvspan(SYS["ni_3db"], NI_SEC[-1] * 1.25, color=COL["bad"], alpha=0.10, lw=0)
    ax.text(SYS["ni_3db"] * 1.15, 72, "SNDR\nbelow\n−3 dB", fontsize=7, ha="left", va="center", color=COL["bad"])
ax.set_xscale("log")
err_curve(ax, NI_SEC, rep_ni, fmt="o-", color=COL["ink"], ms=3.5, lw=1.5, label=f"full scan, {N_FRAMES} frames")
ax.plot(NI_SEC, [100 * x["success80"] for x in rep_ni], "s:", color=COL["faint"], ms=2.5, lw=1.0, label="80 windows [1]")
ax.plot(NI_SEC, [100 * x["bound"] for x in rep_ni], "--", color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, label="bound (80 windows)")
ax.set_ylim(-5, 165); ax.set_yticks(range(0, 101, 20)); ax.set_xlim(0.7, NI_SEC[-1] * 1.25)   # headroom: the legend above the data
ax.set_xlabel("Integrator noise (× value of [1])"); ax.set_ylabel("Pairs broken (%)")
ax2 = ax.twinx()                                                            # f64 on a log scale
ax2.semilogy(NI_SEC, [max(100 * x["f64"], 1e-3) for x in rep_ni], "s:", color=COL["ok"], ms=3.5, lw=1.0, label="clean windows $f_{64}$ (right)")
ax2.set_ylim(5e-4, 3e3); ax2.set_yticks([1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]); ax2.set_ylabel("Clean 64-bit windows $f_{64}$ (%)", color=COL["ok"]); ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors=COL["ok"])
ax2.grid(False)
hs = [a.get_legend_handles_labels() for a in (ax, ax2)]
ax.legend(hs[0][0] + hs[1][0], hs[0][1] + hs[1][1], fontsize=6.5, loc="upper left")
panel(ax, "c", "security vs integrator noise")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 43.</b> Study D: modulator non-idealities (nominal corner). SNDR against (a) the first integrator's thermal noise relative to the value derived from [1] (dotted) and (b) the OTA DC gain (dotted: A = OSR): simulation (solid) and theory (dashed). (c) Replica attack against the integrator noise: pairs broken (left) and clean-window fraction f<sub>64</sub> (blue, right); orange: over 3 dB of SNDR lost.</p>

**Result.**

* *Integrator noise.* The SNDR falls by 3 dB at 68× the integrator noise derived from [1]; the theory predicts 66× (Fig. 43(a)). The SNDR is limited by quantisation, not by thermal noise.
* *OTA gain.* In simulation a DC gain of 40 dB or more keeps the loss below 1 dB. The sweep has points at 35 and 40 dB, so the true limit lies between them; the theory gives 36 dB. At 30 dB the SNDR falls by 3.9 dB, against 3.2 dB from $R(A)$ (Fig. 43(b)). The theory follows the simulation with no fitted parameter, but at 30 dB it underestimates the loss by 0.7 dB. The dotted line marks A = OSR (34 dB at OSR = 50), the classic rule of thumb: the loss begins just above it, which is why the theory asks for about 1.2 × OSR rather than OSR itself.
* *Security.* The full-scan attacker breaks all 24 pairs at every integrator noise from the value of [1] to 300×, and 97 of 100 (95 % interval 91–99 %) at 1,000× (Fig. 43(c)). The 80-window attacker of [1] breaks 24 of 24 pairs up to 3×, 20 at 10×, 12 at 30×, 6 at 100×, 2 at 300× and 2 of 100 at 1,000×; it follows the fall of f<sub>64</sub> from 5.1 % at the value of [1] to 0.0047 % at 1,000× (Fig. 43(c), right axis); f<sub>64</sub> stays above zero over the whole sweep.

**Interpretation.** For accuracy, the integrators need an OTA DC gain of at least about 1.2 × OSR: 36 dB from the theory, between 35 and 40 dB in the simulation. Their thermal noise has a margin of about 68×. The integrator noise decorrelates the two chips' trajectories enough to defeat an attacker who tries 80 windows, but **not an attacker who scans every window**: even at 1,000×, fifteen times beyond the 68× at which the SNDR has lost 3 dB (shaded in Fig. 43(c)), the full scan breaks 97 of 100 pairs. **In the behavioural model, the integrators' noise gives the original design no security without destroying its accuracy, and almost none against the full scan (97 of 100 pairs broken even at 1,000×).** The other chip-to-chip difference of the integrators, the mismatch of their capacitors, is the subject of study E.

### E. Security of the original design: integrator capacitor mismatch

**Goal.** The integrators' coefficients $g_1$ and $g_2$ are capacitor ratios. Their chip-to-chip mismatch is an analog difference that a replica cannot copy, and therefore a candidate for the protection that the comparator fails to give (study B). This study asks whether it protects the original design, and at what mismatch.

**Theory.** Let each chip's coefficients be $g_1(1+\epsilon_1)$ and $g_2(1+\epsilon_2)$, with $\epsilon_1$, $\epsilon_2$ the relative errors of the two capacitor ratios.

* *The second coefficient cannot matter.* The 1-bit quantiser sees only the sign of $x_2$. Given the decisions, $x_2$ is linear in $g_2$: multiplying $g_2$ by $(1 + \epsilon_2)$ multiplies $x_2$ by $(1 + \epsilon_2)$ at every clock. This leaves every sign, and so every decision, unchanged. *Prediction:* without offset, dither and clipping, the bitstream is **exactly independent of $g_2$**; with them, only weakly dependent.
* *Which spread is relevant.* In a switched-capacitor loop, $g_1$ and $g_2$ are capacitor ratios, which match chip to chip to about 0.1–1 %. The modulator of [1] is a continuous-time loop (Section V): its coefficients are RC or g<sub>m</sub>/C products, set by absolute resistor, transconductance and capacitor values, which spread by ±10–30 % from chip to chip unless they are trimmed. For the continuous-time loop the relevant range is therefore 10–30 %, not the 1 % of a capacitor ratio; the sweep covers both. A spread common to both integrators of a chip moves $g_1$ and $g_2$ together, and since only $g_1$ matters, it acts like the independent errors simulated here.
* *The first coefficient does matter*, because it scales $x_1$ but not the feedback $v$ that enters $x_2$, which changes the trajectory. Even so, two chips with different $g_1$ make the same decisions over long stretches, by the argument of study B. *Prediction:* an error in $g_1$ changes a fraction of the decisions; the full-scan attacker fails only once the mismatch removes every stretch of about 48 bits on which the two chips agree, in every frame.

**Setup.** Behavioural, at the nominal corner only.

* *Scale-invariance check:* the bare loop on the first 20,000 clocks of the sine, with a relative error of 0.01 % to 10 % (5 points) in $g_1$ alone or in $g_2$ alone. The metric is the fraction of decisions unchanged from the error-free loop.
* *Replica attack:* each chip draws independent errors of both coefficients from $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, for σ = 0.01 % to 50 % (9 points), with both attackers of study B; 24 independent pairs per point, raised to 100 near the protection point. The comparator offsets are the post-layout ones, and all other settings are those of the testbench.

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs the bare loop with an error in $g_1$ only and in $g_2$ only, and counts the unchanged decisions. 2. Runs the replica attack (full-scan and 80-window attackers) over the mismatch sweep, with Clopper-Pearson intervals. 3. Finds the mismatch from which the full-scan attacker breaks no pair, if any. 4. Prints the card and draws Fig. 44.


```python
#@title Fig.: study E, capacitor mismatch
# Study E: security of the original design against the integrators' capacitor-ratio mismatch: the scale-invariance check
# on the bare loop (g2 cannot change a decision, g1 can), then the replica attack with mismatched chips
t0 = time.time()
E_SWEEP = np.array([1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2, 0.1])                         # relative error of one coefficient
ref_bits = bare_loop(u_id)
agree_g1 = np.array([np.mean(bare_loop(u_id, g1=0.5 * (1 + e)) == ref_bits) for e in E_SWEEP])
agree_g2 = np.array([np.mean(bare_loop(u_id, g2=0.5 * (1 + e)) == ref_bits) for e in E_SWEEP])
CM_SWEEP = np.array([0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 50]) * 1e-2       # sigma of each capacitor ratio, chip to chip
rep_cm = replica_sweep(lambda x, n, k0: replica_pairs(P_sys, os0, 1.8, n, 6, coef_sigma=x, k0=k0), CM_SWEEP)
s_cm = g(rep_cm, "success"); cm_p, cm_b, cm_S = protection(CM_SWEEP, rep_cm); cm_1 = rep_cm[list(CM_SWEEP).index(1e-2)]
SYS.update(cm_prot=cm_p, cm_1pc=cm_1["success"], cm_1pc_ci=cm_1["ci"], cm_10_80=crossing(CM_SWEEP, g(rep_cm, "success80"), 0.1),
           g2_exact=bool((agree_g2 == 1).all()))
card("Study E, security of the original design: integrator capacitor mismatch",
     [("theory check: g<sub>2</sub> error alone (bare loop)", f"decisions unchanged at every error up to 10 %: <b>{SYS['g2_exact']}</b>"),
      ("theory check: g<sub>1</sub> error alone", ", ".join(f"{100 * e:g} %: {100 * a:.1f} %" for e, a in zip(E_SWEEP, agree_g1))
       + " of decisions unchanged"),
      (f"full-scan attacker ({N_FRAMES} frames), capacitor-ratio mismatch between chips: pairs broken [95 % interval]",
       ", ".join(f"{100 * x:g} %: {S['k']}/{S['n']} [{100 * S['ci'][0]:.0f}–{100 * S['ci'][1]:.0f} %]" for x, S in zip(CM_SWEEP, rep_cm))),
      ("protection by capacitor mismatch", f"at σ = 1 %: <b>{cm_1['k']} of {cm_1['n']}</b> pairs broken; " + (
       f"no pair broken from σ = {100 * cm_p:g} % ({cm_S['k']} of {cm_S['n']})" if cm_p else
       f"<b>none in the sweep</b>: still {cm_S['k'] if cm_S else rep_cm[-1]['k']} of {rep_cm[-1]['n']} pairs at σ = {100 * CM_SWEEP[-1]:.0f} %")),
      ("the 80-window attacker of [1] (secondary)", ", ".join(f"{100 * x:g} %: {S['k80']}/{S['n']}" for x, S in zip(CM_SWEEP, rep_cm))),
      ("run time", f"{time.time() - t0:.0f} s")], tone="bad")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(W2, 2.9))
ax = axs[0]
ax.semilogx(100 * E_SWEEP, 100 * agree_g2, "s-", color=COL["ok"], ms=4, lw=1.5, label="error in $g_2$ only (theory: 100 %)")
ax.semilogx(100 * E_SWEEP, 100 * agree_g1, "o-", color=COL["bad"], ms=4, lw=1.5, label="error in $g_1$ only")
ax.set_ylim(0, 105); ax.set_xlabel("Relative coefficient error (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("Decisions unchanged (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left"); panel(ax, "a", "scale invariance of the 1-bit loop")
ax = axs[1]
ax.set_xscale("log")
err_curve(ax, 100 * CM_SWEEP, rep_cm, fmt="o-", color=COL["ink"], ms=3.5, lw=1.5, label=f"full scan, {N_FRAMES} frames (95 % interval)")
ax.plot(100 * CM_SWEEP, 100 * g(rep_cm, "success80"), "s:", color=COL["faint"], ms=2.5, lw=1.0, label="80 windows, one frame [1]")
ax.plot(100 * CM_SWEEP, 100 * g(rep_cm, "bound"), "--", color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, label=r"bound $1 - (1 - f_{64})^{80}$")
ax.axvline(1, color=COL["bad"], lw=0.9, ls=":")                            # a realistic chip-to-chip mismatch of matched capacitors
ax.plot(1, 100 * SYS["cm_1pc"], "o", ms=7, mfc="none", mec=COL["bad"], mew=1.2)
ax.annotate(f"realistic 1 %:\n{cm_1['k']} of {cm_1['n']} pairs\nbroken", (1, 100 * SYS["cm_1pc"]), xytext=(0.7, 72),
            textcoords="data", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=COL["bad"],
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", lw=0.6, color=COL["bad"]))
ax.set_ylim(-5, 108); ax.set_xlabel(r"Capacitor-ratio mismatch $\sigma$ (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("Pairs broken (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left"); panel(ax, "b", "security vs capacitor mismatch")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 44.</b> Study E: capacitor mismatch (nominal corner). (a) Fraction of decisions unchanged against the relative error of g<sub>2</sub> alone (blue squares) or g<sub>1</sub> alone (orange circles), bare loop without dither, noise or clipping. (b) Pairs broken by the replica attack against the chip-to-chip mismatch σ of both coefficients; dotted vertical and circle: 1 %, a matched capacitor ratio.</p>

**Result.** The bare loop confirms both predictions (Fig. 44(a)). An error in $g_2$ alone leaves every decision unchanged at every error up to 10 % (`True`). An error in $g_1$ alone changes decisions: 99.7 % stay unchanged at 0.01 %, 96.8 % at 0.1 %, and 76–82 % from 1 % to 10 %. In the replica attack (Fig. 44(b)), the full-scan attacker breaks all 24 pairs at every mismatch up to 3 %, including the 1 % of a matched capacitor ratio (circle); 78 of 100 pairs at 10 % (95 % interval 69–86 %), 31 of 100 at 30 % (22–41 %) and still 16 of 100 at 50 % (9–25 %). No mismatch in the sweep protects the design. The 80-window attacker of [1] breaks fewer: 44 of 100 at 10 %, 13 at 30 % and 6 at 50 %.

**Interpretation.** No mismatch of the integrators' coefficients protects the original design, neither the 1 % of a matched capacitor ratio nor the ±10–30 % absolute spread of the RC or g<sub>m</sub>/C products of a continuous-time loop such as that of [1]: at 30 % the full-scan attacker still breaks about a third of the pairs. **The integrators give the original design no security either.** Studies A to E together show that, in the model with its simplified dither, neither the comparator nor the integrators of the original design protect it. The proposal instead rests its security on one circuit, the SRAM-PUF cell, which study F carries to the key.

### F. Security of the proposal: from SRAM-PUF cell to key

**Goal.** The proposal does not rely on any analog difference between chips. Its security rests on one transistor-level quantity: the power-up behaviour of the SRAM cells from which the key is regenerated. This study derives what the cell's noise and temperature behaviour do to the key (reliability) and to the secret it holds (secrecy), at all five process corners and over a population of chips. It asks whether the BCH code of Section VII-E (t = 45) makes the key reliable at every corner, which enrolment removes the reproducible flips, and which code then meets both requirements.

**Theory.**

The cell's error law is that of Section VII-F: noise of noise-to-mismatch ratio $s(T)$, estimated from repeated simulated power-ups, and at high temperature, at the fast-nMOS corners, a rotation θ(T) of the mismatch that makes a fixed set of cells change sign. Section VII-E turned this law into a two-component cell model; three steps lead from it to the key.

1. *Key failure over a population.* With per-cell error probabilities $p_i$, the number of errors $E$ in the 600-bit fingerprint follows a Poisson-binomial distribution, and the key fails when $E$ exceeds the BCH code's correction capability $t$: $P_{\text{fail}} = P(E > t)$, computed exactly for each chip. Because the flipped cells are the same at every hot power-up, chips with many flips fail almost surely and the others almost never; the study therefore reports, per corner, the fraction of simulated chips that meet 10<sup>−6</sup> and the 99th percentile of the t they require.
2. *Secrecy.* The BCH code over GF(2¹⁰) publishes 10 helper bits per correctable error. With $H_\infty = -\log_2\max(P_1, 1 - P_1)$ the min-entropy of a cell that powers up to 1 with probability $P_1$, $n H_\infty - 10t$ bits remain secret, and the requirement of Section VII-E is 192 bits (128 + 2·log<sub>2</sub>(1/ε), ε = 2⁻³²) at the 95 % lower confidence bound on $H_\infty$. A two-temperature enrolment publishes a keep-mask; the attacker knows which cells are kept, so the entropy is that of the kept cells, estimated from them alone. *Prediction:* with 512 cells per corner the lower bound lies near 0.8 bit, so 600 cells allow at most t ≈ 27.
3. *Why enrolling at two temperatures removes the flips, and which two.* If the mismatch rotates monotonically with temperature, the sign of a cell's mismatch, as a function of θ, is a sinusoid, which changes sign at most once over any range of θ shorter than π. A cell with the same sign at the two enrolment temperatures therefore keeps it at every temperature between them, but not outside. An enrolment at 25 and 85 °C thus says nothing about 0 °C, the bottom of the specified range, where θ has the opposite sign; an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C, the ends of the simulated range, covers 0–85 °C. The cost is the fraction of cells whose sign changes, about θ(85 °C)/π, plus the unstable ones. *Prediction:* with the −40 and 85 °C enrolment the held-out error rate of the kept cells is low at all three temperatures, whereas the 25 and 85 °C enrolment leaves errors at −40 °C wherever θ(−40 °C) is large; and the key-failure probability no longer depends on the flips at any corner.

**Setup.** Behavioural level: the two-component cell model of Section VII-E, anchored at each corner to the recorded transistor-level Monte Carlo of Section VII-F (Table X: 512 cells × 5 power-ups at −40, 25 and 85 °C per corner). The noise s(T) comes from the disagreement between the power-ups at each temperature, the rotation θ(T) from the error rate against the first 25 °C power-up; both are interpolated linearly in T.

* *Population:* 1,000 simulated chips per corner and enrolment, each with its own cells and its own enrolment reads, seeded from `chip_seed`. For the two-temperature enrolment each chip has a 1,000-cell array, is read three times at each enrolment temperature, keeps the cells that are stable and equal at both, and uses the first 600 kept cells (a chip with fewer fails).
* *Enrolments:* one read at 25 °C; and three reads at −40 and at 85 °C. The 25 and 85 °C enrolment of Table XI is compared on the recorded bits.
* *Cross-validation on the recorded bits:* for each two-temperature enrolment, the mask is chosen from power-ups 1–3 and the error rate of the kept cells against the enrolled value is evaluated on the held-out recorded power-ups 4–5 at −40, 25 and 85 °C, with a 95 % Clopper–Pearson interval (reads of the same cell are treated as independent, so the intervals are somewhat narrow). Three screening reads leave two held-out reads; more screening reads would leave too few to validate. The fraction of cells the −40 and 85 °C enrolment keeps is also predicted by the model, which is not fitted to it.
* *Code and ranges:* t from 0 to 120 (t = 45, the working setting of the system simulations (Section VII-E), marked); worst case over 0, 25 and 85 °C, where the piecewise-linear s(T) and θ(T) put the maximum over 0–85 °C. Panel (a) follows this chip (`chip_seed`) from −40 to 85 °C in 5 °C steps; the figure draws probabilities below 10<sup>−16</sup> at 10<sup>−16</sup>.
* *Secrecy:* the 95 % lower bound and the point estimate of $H_\infty$ per corner, from the 512 cells (25 °C enrolment) or from the kept cells (−40 and 85 °C); the limit is set by the corner with the lowest bound.
* *Metrics:* the fraction of chips meeting 10<sup>−6</sup> at t = 45; the 99th percentile of the required t; the held-out error rates; the secret bits as an interval; the array size for which 99.9 % of the simulated chips keep 600 cells.

> **Next cell.** 1. Anchors the two-component model at each corner and simulates 1,000 Monte Carlo chips for each enrolment. 2. Cross-validates both two-temperature enrolments on the recorded bits, with confidence intervals. 3. Bounds the min-entropy of all cells and of the kept cells per corner and derives the secrecy limits. 4. Evaluates this chip against temperature. 5. Prints the card and draws Fig. 45.


```python
#@title Fig.: study F, SRAM-PUF to key
# Study F: from SRAM-PUF cell to key, at the five corners. Each corner gets the two-component cell model of Section
# VII-E (chip_population: noise s(T) from repeated power-ups, rotation theta(T) from the error rate), anchored to its
# recorded PVT Monte Carlo (512 cells x 5 power-ups at -40, 25 and 85 °C). Key reliability over 1,000 simulated chips for a
# 25 °C enrolment and for the enrolment at -40 and 85 °C; both two-temperature enrolments (25 + 85 and -40 + 85 °C) are
# also cross-validated on the recorded bits (mask from power-ups 1-3, error rates on the held-out power-ups 4-5, with 95 %
# Clopper-Pearson intervals); the secret budget uses the lower confidence bound on the min-entropy of the kept cells.
t_used = CAL["bch_t"]
E_RD, H_RD, N_ARR = [0, 1, 2], [3, 4], 1000              # screening reads, held-out reads, simulated array (two-temperature)
ENROL = {"25": (25,), "−40+85": (-40, 85)}
cp95 = lambda k, n: (float(_beta.ppf(0.025, k, n - k + 1)) if k else 0.0, float(_beta.ppf(0.975, k + 1, n - k)) if k < n else 1.0)
PUF_SYS = {}
for j, c in enumerate(PVT["puf"]["corners"]):
    k, b, mu = c["corner"], BITS[j].astype(np.int8), c["fit"]["mu"]; w0 = b[i25, 0]; R = b.shape[1]
    ber = {T: float(((b[i, 1:] if T == 25 else b[i]) != w0).mean()) for i, T in enumerate(TEMPS)}
    q = {T: float(np.mean([(b[i, x] != b[i, y]).mean() for x in range(R) for y in range(x + 1, R)])) for i, T in enumerate(TEMPS)}
    sT, th = two_component(mu, ber, q)
    st3 = lambda i: b[i][E_RD].min(axis=0) == b[i][E_RD].max(axis=0)
    xv = {}
    for name, (Ta, Tb) in (("25+85", (25, 85)), ("−40+85", (-40, 85))):          # recorded-bit cross-validation
        ia, ib = TEMPS.index(Ta), TEMPS.index(Tb)
        keep = st3(ia) & st3(ib) & (b[ia, E_RD[0]] == b[ib, E_RD[0]]); w = b[ia, E_RD[0]]
        err = {T: (int((b[i][H_RD][:, keep] != w[keep]).sum()), int(keep.sum()) * len(H_RD)) for i, T in enumerate(TEMPS)}
        xv[name] = dict(keep=float(keep.mean()), err=err, h=h_bounds(int(w[keep].sum()), int(keep.sum())))
    pop = {name: chip_population(mu, sT, th, enrol=e, n_arr=PUF_BITS if len(e) == 1 else N_ARR, tmax=120 if len(e) == 1 else 60,
                                 seed=DEFAULTS["chip_seed"] * 100 + j) for name, e in ENROL.items()}
    PUF_SYS[k] = dict(PUF_CELL[k], sT=sT, th=th, xv=xv, pop=pop, h_all=h_bounds(int(w0.sum()), len(w0)),
                      t99={n: int(np.percentile(p["treq"], 99, method="higher")) for n, p in pop.items()},
                      frac={n: float(np.mean(p["treq"] <= t_used)) for n, p in pop.items()},
                      keep_model=float(np.mean(pop["−40+85"]["kept"]) / N_ARR))
# this chip (chip_seed) at every temperature, 25 °C enrolment, t = t_used (one chip of the population model per corner)
TT, t_grid = np.arange(-40, 86, 5), np.arange(0, 121)
key_T = {k: np.array([chip_population(q["mu"], q["sT"], q["th"], n_chips=1, temps=(int(T),), seed=DEFAULTS["chip_seed"])["worst"][0, t_used]
                      for T in TT]) for k, q in PUF_SYS.items()}
p99 = lambda wst: np.percentile(wst, 99, axis=0)                                # the 99th-percentile chip, for each t
# the key generator these models support: -40 + 85 °C enrolment, 600 kept cells, the largest 99th-percentile t of the corners
t_fin = max(q["t99"]["−40+85"] for q in PUF_SYS.values())
h_keep = {k: q["xv"]["−40+85"]["h"] for k, q in PUF_SYS.items()}
k_h = min(h_keep, key=lambda x: h_keep[x][0])                                  # corner with the lowest entropy bound
lim = lambda h: int(np.floor((PUF_BITS * h - SECRET_REQ) / 10))                 # largest t leaving SECRET_REQ secret bits
t_lim25 = lim(min(q["h_all"][0] for q in PUF_SYS.values())); t_lim2 = lim(h_keep[k_h][0])
kf = {k: np.quantile(q["pop"]["−40+85"]["kept"] / N_ARR, 0.001) for k, q in PUF_SYS.items()}
k_kf = min(kf, key=kf.get); n_cells_fin = int(np.ceil(PUF_BITS / kf[k_kf]))      # 99.9 % of chips keep 600 cells
xmax = lambda name, k: max(PUF_SYS[k]["xv"][name]["err"].items(), key=lambda e: e[1][0] / e[1][1])
ci = lambda e: "{:.2f} % ({:.2f}–{:.2f})".format(100 * e[0] / e[1], *(100 * x for x in cp95(*e)))
pc_ = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.1f} %"
card(f"Study F, security of the proposal: from SRAM-PUF cell to key (two-component cell model, 1,000 chips per corner)",
     [(f"this chip, t = {t_used}, 25 °C enrolment: first temperature from −40 °C up with P(key fails) above 10<sup>−6</sup>",
       ", ".join(f"{k} " + next((f"{T} °C".replace("-", "−") for T, v in zip(TT, key_T[k]) if v > 1e-6), "none") for k in PUF_SYS)),
      (f"chips meeting 10<sup>−6</sup> over 0–85 °C at t = {t_used}, 25 °C enrolment", ", ".join(f"{k} {pc_(q['frac']['25'])}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items())),
      ("t required for 10<sup>−6</sup>, 99th percentile of the chips, 25 °C enrolment",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {q['t99']['25'] if q['t99']['25'] <= 120 else '&gt; 120'}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items())),
      ("recorded bits, enrolment at 25 and 85 °C: held-out error rate of the kept cells at −40 °C (95 % interval)",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {ci(q['xv']['25+85']['err'][-40])}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items())),
      ("recorded bits, enrolment at −40 and 85 °C: highest held-out error rate of the kept cells over −40, 25, 85 °C",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {ci(xmax('−40+85', k)[1])} at {xmax('−40+85', k)[0]} °C".replace("-4", "−4") for k in PUF_SYS)),
      ("cells kept by the −40 + 85 °C enrolment: recorded | model (not fitted to it)",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {pc_(q['xv']['−40+85']['keep'])} | {pc_(q['keep_model'])}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items())),
      ("t required for 10<sup>−6</sup>, 99th percentile, enrolment at −40 and 85 °C",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {q['t99']['−40+85']}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items()) + f"; chips meeting 10<sup>−6</sup> at t = {t_fin}: at least "
       f"{pc_(min(np.mean(q['pop']['−40+85']['treq'] <= t_fin) for q in PUF_SYS.values()))} at every corner"),
      ("min-entropy per cell, 95 % lower bound – point estimate: all cells | cells kept at −40 and 85 °C",
       ", ".join(f"{k} {q['h_all'][0]:.3f}–{q['h_all'][1]:.3f} | {h_keep[k][0]:.3f}–{h_keep[k][1]:.3f}" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items())),
      (f"secrecy limit (≥ {SECRET_REQ} secret bits at the lower bound of the worst corner)",
       f"t ≤ {t_lim25} with {PUF_BITS} cells; t ≤ {t_lim2} with {PUF_BITS} cells kept at −40 and 85 °C"),
      (f"key generator: enrolment at −40 and 85 °C, {PUF_BITS} kept cells, t = {t_fin}",
       f"<b>{int(np.floor(PUF_BITS * h_keep[k_h][0] - 10 * t_fin))}–{int(np.floor(PUF_BITS * h_keep[k_h][1] - 10 * t_fin))} secret bits</b> "
       f"at {k_h}; <b>{n_cells_fin} cells</b> so that 99.9 % of the chips keep {PUF_BITS} at {k_kf}")],
     tone="ok" if t_fin <= t_lim2 else "bad")
pcol = {"tt": COL["ink"], "ss": COL["ok"], "ff": COL["bad"], "sf": COL["aqua"], "fs": COL["yellow"]}
lsty = lambda k: dict(ls="--", lw=1.8, zorder=5) if k == "tt" else dict(ls="-", lw=1.4, zorder=3)   # tt on top, dashed
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(W2, 3.1), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.12))
ax = axs[0]
ax.axvspan(0, 85, color=COL["faint"], alpha=0.2, lw=0)
for k in PUF_SYS:
    ax.semilogy(TT, np.maximum(key_T[k], 1e-16), color=pcol[k], label=k, **lsty(k))
ax.axhline(1e-6, color=COL["key"], lw=0.9, ls=":"); ax.set_ylim(1e-17, 30); ax.set_xticks([-40, 0, 25, 85])
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)"); ax.set_ylabel("P(key fails)")
ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=7, loc="upper left", handlelength=1.8, columnspacing=0.8)
panel(ax, "a", f"This chip, t = {t_used}")
for ax, name, lab, title, tl in ((axs[1], "25", "b", "25 °C enrolment", t_lim25),
                                 (axs[2], "−40+85", "c", "−40 and 85 °C enrolment", t_lim2)):
    ax.axvspan(tl + 0.5, t_grid[-1], color=COL["faint"], alpha=0.3, lw=0, hatch="//", label=f"< {SECRET_REQ} secret bits")
    for k, q in PUF_SYS.items():
        y = np.pad(p99(q["pop"][name]["worst"]), (0, len(t_grid)), mode="edge")[:len(t_grid)]   # beyond tmax: below 1e-16
        ax.semilogy(t_grid, np.maximum(y, 1e-16), color=pcol[k], **lsty(k))
        if q["t99"][name] < q["pop"][name]["worst"].shape[1]:                                         # the t this corner requires for 1e-6
            ax.plot(q["t99"][name], 1e-6, "o", ms=4, color=pcol[k], mec="white", mew=0.5, zorder=6)
    ax.axhline(1e-6, color=COL["key"], lw=0.9, ls=":"); ax.axvline(t_used, color=COL["ink"], lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.set_ylim(1e-17, 30); ax.set_xlim(0, t_grid[-1]); ax.set_xlabel("BCH correction t")
    ax.tick_params(labelleft=False)
    panel(ax, lab, title)
axs[1].legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower left")
axs[1].text(t_used + 2, 1e-9, f"t = {t_used}", fontsize=7.5, color=COL["ink"], ha="left")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.085, right=0.99, bottom=0.17, top=0.9)
plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 45.</b> Study F: SRAM-PUF to key (cell model per corner). (a) Key-failure probability of the model's reference chip against temperature; t = 45, 25 °C enrolment; grey: 0–85 °C. (b), (c) Worst case over 0–85 °C of the 99th-percentile chip against t; enrolment at 25 °C (b), −40 and 85 °C (c); dotted: 10<sup>−6</sup> target; dots: t required; hatched: under 192 secret bits.</p>

**Result.**

* *25 °C enrolment, t = 45.* For one simulated chip (Fig. 45(a)) the key-failure probability stays below 10<sup>−6</sup> from −40 to 85 °C at tt and ss; it exceeds the target from 55 °C at ff and from 40 °C at fs, where θ grows, and already at −40 °C at sf, whose cell is the noisiest. Over the population of Monte Carlo chips (the per-corner cell model), all meet the target at tt and ss, 72.9 % at sf and none at ff and fs.
* *The t each corner requires* (25 °C enrolment, 99th percentile of the chips; dots in Fig. 45(b)): 33 at tt, 29 at ss, 55 at sf, 89 at ff and more than 120 at fs. The secrecy limit with 600 cells is t ≤ 27 (lower bound 0.772 bit at ff): **with a 25 °C enrolment no corner, not even tt, meets both requirements.**
* *Which two temperatures (recorded bits).* With the enrolment at 25 and 85 °C, the kept cells' held-out error rate at −40 °C is 1.72 % (95 % interval 1.01–2.75 %) at ss and 3.09 % (2.08–4.40 %) at sf, as predicted by item 3, and 0.31–0.98 % at the other corners. With the enrolment at −40 and 85 °C, the highest held-out error rate over the three temperatures is at most 1.01 % (0.46–1.91 %, ff at 25 °C) at every corner; at sf it is 0.11 %.
* *Kept cells.* The −40 and 85 °C enrolment keeps 95.3, 94.5, 86.9, 88.5 and 68.9 % of the recorded cells at tt, ss, ff, sf and fs; the model, which is not fitted to these fractions, predicts 94.7, 94.9, 85.6, 88.4 and 68.7 %.
* *Enrolment at −40 and 85 °C, population.* The 99th percentile of the required t is 9 at tt, 10 at ss, 13 at ff, 16 at sf and 17 at fs (Fig. 45(c)); at t = 17, at least 99.7 % of the chips meet 10<sup>−6</sup> at every corner.
* *Secrecy.* The min-entropy of the kept cells lies between 0.758 bit (95 % lower bound, fs) and 0.941 bit (point estimate, sf); the mask removes little entropy (at fs, 0.758 against 0.777 bit for all cells). With 600 kept cells the limit is t ≤ 26. The key generator with this enrolment, 600 kept cells and t = 17 leaves **284–352 secret bits** at fs, the corner with the lowest bound, and needs 935 cells so that 99.9 % of the simulated chips keep 600 at fs.

**Interpretation.** The two mechanisms of Section VII-F act on the key in different ways. Noise is what the BCH code is sized for; the reproducible flips at ff and fs, and the higher noise at sf, would need codes far beyond the secrecy limit, and once the entropy is bounded and the hash margin included, even tt with a 25 °C enrolment needs more correction (t = 33) than the secret allows (t ≤ 27). **The two-temperature enrolment excludes the flipping cells from the key, provided its two temperatures bracket the operating range**: the recorded bits show that an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C leaves the cells that flip at −40 °C, whereas one at −40 and 85 °C does not, and the model's prediction of the kept fraction agrees with the recorded bits to within 1.3 percentage points at every corner. With that enrolment a code of t = 17 on 600 kept cells (935 cells in all) meets 10<sup>−6</sup> for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips at every corner and leaves 284–352 secret bits, above the 192 required. These results rest on the two-component model, anchored to 512 simulated cells per corner, and on independent cells; the held-out error rates are measured on two reads per cell. Section XII regenerates the key from transistor-level cells as an independent check, at one condition per run (tt and 37 °C in the published run; any corner and temperature in its settings form), and Section XI sizes the decoder and the array of the complete key generator.

### G. The circuit-to-system map

**Goal.** Collect the results of studies A to F in one table. For every transistor-level quantity, the table answers the question a designer asks of each circuit: does this block need attention, and for what?

**Setup.** No new simulation: the table reads the values that studies A to F computed in this session. Its columns are the circuit quantity, its value (nominal and PVT range), the system quantity it determines, that system quantity over the PVT grid, and the margin to failure. The PVT coverage of each row is that of the paths table at the start of this section.

> **Next cell.** 1. Collects the results of studies A to F. 2. Prints them as Table XII, one row per circuit quantity and system metric.

```python
e_lo, e_hi = (1e15 * x for x in f1("energy"))
t99_ = lambda n, k: (str(PUF_SYS[k]["t99"][n]) if PUF_SYS[k]["t99"][n] <= 120 else "&gt; 120")
keep_min = min(q["keep"] for q in PUF_SYS.values())

     f"{1e6 * SYS['dc_err']:.2f} ppm FS at 3σ", "absorbed by the loop"),
    ("Comparator offset σ<sub>os</sub>", "", "security: full-scan replica attack on the original design",

    ("Integrator thermal noise (swept)", "", "security: full-scan replica attack on the original design",

     f"{rep_ni[-1]['k']} of {rep_ni[-1]['n']} at {NI_SEC[-1]}×, far beyond the −3 dB SNDR point ({SYS['ni_3db']:.0f}×)"),
    ("OTA DC gain (behavioural, swept)", "–", "accuracy: modulator SNDR", "–", f"≥ {SYS['A_1db']:.0f} dB for less than 1 dB loss"),
    ("Capacitor-ratio mismatch, chip to chip (swept)", "–", "security: full-scan replica attack on the original design",
     f"breaks {cm_1['k']} of {cm_1['n']} pairs at σ = 1 %", (f"no pair broken only from σ = {100 * SYS['cm_prot']:g} %"
     if SYS["cm_prot"] else f"still {rep_cm[-1]['k']} of {rep_cm[-1]['n']} at σ = {100 * CM_SWEEP[-1]:.0f} %")),
    ("Comparator energy per decision", f"{1e15 * f1('energy')[0]:.0f}–{1e15 * f1('energy')[1]:.0f} fJ", "power at 10 MHz",
     f"{e_lo * 1e-2:.1f}–{e_hi * 1e-2:.1f} µW", f"≤ {100 * e_hi * 1e-2 / DSM_UW_1:.1f} % of the modulator of [1]; common to all designs"),
    ("SRAM-PUF error rate, 25 °C enrolment", "BER at 85 °C: " + ", ".join(f"{c['corner']} {100 * c['rows'][TEMPS.index(85)]['ber']:.1f} %"
     for c in PVT["puf"]["corners"]), f"security: key reliability, t = {t_used}, 0–85 °C (1,000 chips per corner)",
     "chips meeting 10<sup>−6</sup>: " + ", ".join(f"{k} {100 * q['frac']['25']:.0f} %" for k, q in PUF_SYS.items()),
     "t required (99th percentile): " + ", ".join(f"{k} {t99_('25', k)}" for k in PUF_SYS) + f"; secrecy limit t ≤ {t_lim25}"),
    ("SRAM-PUF, enrolment at −40 and 85 °C (cross-validated)", f"{100 * min(q['xv']['−40+85']['keep'] for q in PUF_SYS.values()):.0f}–"
     f"{100 * max(q['xv']['−40+85']['keep'] for q in PUF_SYS.values()):.0f} % of cells kept", f"security: key reliability, t = {t_fin}, 0–85 °C",
     "chips meeting 10<sup>−6</sup>: ≥ " + f"{100 * min(np.mean(q['pop']['−40+85']['treq'] <= t_fin) for q in PUF_SYS.values()):.1f} % at every corner",
     "t required (99th percentile): " + ", ".join(f"{k} {t99_('−40+85', k)}" for k in PUF_SYS) + f"; secrecy limit t ≤ {t_lim2}; "
     f"{n_cells_fin} cells for {PUF_BITS} kept"),
    ("SRAM-PUF bias P(1) and min-entropy (kept cells, −40 and 85 °C enrolment)", f"P(1) = {CAL['puf_bias']:.3f} (tt, 25 °C); "
     f"min-entropy ≥ {h_keep[k_h][0]:.3f} bit per cell (95 % lower bound, {k_h})", f"security: secret fingerprint bits, t = {t_fin}",
     f"{int(np.floor(PUF_BITS * h_keep[k_h][0] - 10 * t_fin))}–{int(np.floor(PUF_BITS * h_keep[k_h][1] - 10 * t_fin))} at {k_h}",
     f"≥ {SECRET_REQ} up to t = {t_lim2}")]
```
