**Result.** Read row by row, Table XII sorts the circuit quantities into four groups.

* *No requirement.* The comparator's noise (0.58 mV nominal, 0.37–0.81 mV over PVT) keeps the SNDR at 60.3–60.4 dB, with a margin of 88× to the −3 dB point. Its offset (4.37 mV nominal, 4.01–5.85 mV) leaves a DC error of 0.47 ppm of full scale at 3σ. Its simulated SKY130 energy (144–822 fJ per decision) is 1.4–8.2 µW at the 10 MHz clock, at most 1.6 % of the power measured for the modulator of [1] in 65 nm. The integrator's thermal noise has a margin of 68×.
* *A modest requirement.* The OTA needs a DC gain of 40 dB or more for less than 1 dB of loss.
* *No protection for the original design (in the model, with its simplified dither).* The full-scan replica attacker breaks 360 of 360 pairs at the PVT conditions. Comparator noise resists it (no pair of 100 broken) only from 160 mV (197×), at a cost of 7.5 dB of SNDR. The comparator offset never resists it (24 % or more of the pairs broken up to 3 V). The integrator noise does not resist it either: 97 of 100 pairs are still broken at 1,000×, far beyond the −3 dB point. No capacitor mismatch in the sweep resists it: 16 of 100 pairs are still broken at σ = 50 %.
* *The one circuit that sets the security of the proposal.* The SRAM-PUF cell, with a 25 °C enrolment and t = 45, meets 10<sup>−6</sup> for all simulated chips at tt and ss only, and the 99th-percentile chip needs t = 55, 89 and more than 120 at sf, ff and fs, beyond the secrecy limit of t = 27 (192 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy over the five corners, study F; t = 35 at tt alone). With the enrolment at −40 and 85 °C, t = 17 meets it for at least 99.7 % of the chips at every corner, with 935 cells for 600 kept cells and 284–352 secret bits at fs.

**Interpretation.** In the original design, the analog quantities that could make two chips differ enough to stop the attack either do so only at a cost in accuracy (7.5 dB of SNDR for the comparator noise) or do not do so at all within the sweeps (integrator noise up to 1,000×, comparator offset up to 3 V, coefficient mismatch up to 50 %). In the proposal, among the circuits studied here, **the only one that matters for security is the SRAM-PUF cell**, and what it requires (a code and an enrolment sized for the worst corner) is a system-level design choice, not a circuit fix.

#### Summary of Section VIII

1. **Accuracy is insensitive to the comparator across PVT** (study A). The SNDR is 60.3–60.4 dB at all 45 PVT conditions. The comparator noise would have to grow 88× (to 72 mV) before 3 dB are lost, and an offset of 3× the largest PVT σ<sub>os</sub> changes the reading by 0.47 ppm. The loop shapes the noise like quantisation error and absorbs the offset as a change of initial state, up to an integrator range that the theory puts at 700 mV (conservative by 1.7×). The describing-function theory gives the mechanism and the order of magnitude, but places the noise limit 1.4× too high and overestimates the SNDR once the quantiser is noise-dominated.
2. **No analog block protects the original design against the full-scan replica attacker without a direct cost in accuracy** (studies B, D and E). Security is judged against an attacker who scans every 64-bit window of up to four frames, with independent seeds for every chip pair and 95 % Clopper–Pearson intervals; a point counts as protected when none of at least 100 pairs is broken (at most 3.6 % per pair at 95 %), which is the strongest statement a simulation of this size can make. The replica attack breaks 360 of 360 pairs over the 45 PVT conditions, because two chips that disagree on 25 % of their bits still leave 4.9 % of 64-bit windows clean. The offset alone never protects (24 of 100 pairs broken even at 3 V, interval 16–34 %). Comparator noise protects only from σ<sub>n</sub> = 160 mV, 197× the largest PVT value, at a cost of 7.5 dB of SNDR; integrator noise does not protect even at 1,000× its value (97 of 100 pairs broken), and the capacitor mismatch not even at σ = 50 % (16 of 100). The second integrator's coefficient cannot change a single decision.
3. **The comparator's power is negligible at every corner** (study C): 1.4–8.2 µW at 10 MHz in post-layout SKY130 simulation, at most 1.6 % of the measured 65 nm modulator of [1].
4. **The modulator's own requirement is an OTA gain of 40 dB or more** (study D), as the leaky-integrator theory predicts (36 dB). Its thermal noise has a margin of 68×.
5. **The security of the proposal depends on the circuit only through the key, and the theory says how** (study F). Noise sets the error rate at room temperature (the closed form is within 28 % at every corner). A temperature-dependent rotation of the mismatch, up to 50° at fs and 85 °C, adds reproducible flips at the fast-nMOS corners. With a 25 °C enrolment, the 99th percentile of the chips needs t = 33 at tt, 29 at ss, 55 at sf, 89 at ff and more than 120 at fs, whereas the bounded secret of 600 cells allows at most t = 27: no corner meets both requirements. Enrolled at −40 and 85 °C, t = 17 meets 10<sup>−6</sup> for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips at every corner and leaves 284–352 secret bits with 600 kept cells (935 cells in all).

**Design implications.**

* **Size the key generator for the worst corner, not the typical one.** With a 25 °C enrolment, no code meets the target at every corner within the secrecy limit.
* **Enrol at both ends of the temperature range.** Dark-bit masking [15] based on stability at 25 °C removes the noisy cells that dominate at sf, but not the reproducible flips that dominate at ff and fs. Retaining only the cells that are stable and equal at the two enrolment temperatures removes them, provided the two temperatures bracket the operating range: an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C leaves the cells that flip at −40 °C (held-out error rate up to 3.09 % at sf), one at −40 and 85 °C keeps 68.9–95.3 % of the cells and holds the held-out error rate at or below 1.01 % at every corner and temperature. 935 cells then provide 600 usable bits for 99.9 % of the simulated chips at fs.
* **Screen at the maximum operating temperature.** The corners at risk cannot be identified at room temperature (fs has the lowest BER of all corners at 25 °C), so key reconstruction must be tested hot.
* **No measure is required for the comparator; the integrators need an OTA gain of 40 dB or more.** Neither affects the security of the proposal, which does not rely on analog quantities.

**Limits.** The SRAM-PUF results cover process × temperature at the nominal supply. The secrecy limit uses the nominal bias. Studies D and E are behavioural sweeps at the nominal corner. The key-failure probabilities rest on the cell model anchored to the recorded Monte Carlo, with the flips represented as noise.

**What comes next.** Section IX takes the model with SKY130 parameters to the full security evaluation: all 15 attacks on both designs, of which the replica attack studied here is one. Section XI sizes the complete key generator for the two-temperature enrolment at every corner, and Section XII replaces the behavioural comparator and SRAM cell with their transistor-level netlists to test the abstraction used throughout this section.

# **IX. Security evaluation**
---
This section answers the first research question: **what security does each design provide?** It supports the central claim of the abstract: against an attacker who uses every capability of the threat model, the original S-DSM [1] fails 11 of the 15 attacks, including the replica, same-message and saturation attacks that [1] considered, whereas the proposal withstands all 15. The threat model here is wider than the evaluation of [1], which considers an eavesdropper with a replica chip: six of the 11 (A7, A8, A9, A13, A14 and A15) need an attacker who holds the chip or transmits on the link. Those verdicts show which protections the proposal adds; they are not failures of [1] against the attacker it evaluates. Against that attacker, the original design fails only when its key is searched or the attacks of [1] are carried further than in [1] (A2 to A6). The verdicts of A4 to A6 rest on analog decorrelation and use the model's simplified dither of [1] (Section VI); Subsection C shows that a stronger dither protects the original design against the attacker of [1], so these three verdicts hold for the dither as modelled. The verdict table states for each verdict whether it rests on a simulated attack, on an analytic argument or on an assumption.

The section builds on the earlier sections. Section IV-A defined the attacker, the attacker's five capabilities C1 to C5 and the 15 attacks A1 to A15 (Table I). Section V implemented both designs bit for bit, together with the attack tools and the decision rule of every attack. Section VI showed that the model is consistent with the two measurements of [1], and Section VII replaced its circuit parameters by SKY130 post-layout values (Table VIII). Section VIII showed with the replica attack that neither the comparator nor the integrators make two chips different enough to protect the original design, and that the PUF key must be sized for its worst process corner. The attacks below therefore act on the link with SKY130-derived parameters.

The section has three subsections and a summary:

* **A. Attack evaluation.** All 15 attacks are run once on each design. The results are a verdict table, figures of three attacks, an interactive version and a closer analysis of the helper-data manipulation attack.
* **B. PUF reliability.** The one new failure mode of the proposal is quantified: a power-up at which the PUF does not regenerate the key.
* **C. Parameter sweeps.** The parameters that set the security boundaries are swept, to measure the margin that the current settings leave.
* **Summary.** The numbered findings, and the transition to the cost of the proposal (Section X).

### A. Attack evaluation: 15 attacks on both designs

**Goal.** To run every attack of the threat model on both designs at the current settings, and to judge each run by a decision rule fixed in advance. The result is one verdict per attack and design.

**Theory.** *Notation.* The modulator produces one bit *D* per clock. The keystream generator produces one bit *K* per clock: a 16-bit LFSR in the original design, Grain-128a in the proposal. The chip transmits *C* = *D* ⊕ *K*. The attacker's estimate of the keystream is *K̂*, and the corresponding estimate of the data is *D̂* = *C* ⊕ *K̂*. The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm (BM) [3] returns the shortest linear feedback shift register that generates a bit sequence; its length *L* is the linear complexity of the sequence. BM determines an *L*-bit register from 2*L* consecutive correct bits, that is, from 32 bits for the 16-bit LFSR. In the proposal, *w* is the 600-bit SRAM fingerprint enrolled at 25 °C, and *h* is the public helper data: the BCH syndrome of *w*, 10*t* bits long for a code that corrects *t* = 45 flipped cells. The key is the hash of the corrected fingerprint. Each frame carries a 32-bit counter and a 32-bit MAC tag, and the initialisation vector (IV) of the cipher contains the session nonce of the receiver and the counter, so that every frame has its own keystream.

*Capabilities.* Section IV-A defines five capabilities of the attacker: C1, recording the radio link; C2, choosing the sensor input; C3, learning a short run of keystream bits; C4, possessing a chip; C5, transmitting on the link (the uplink and the helper-data downlink). Each attack below states the capabilities it requires.

*Decision tests.* Every attack ends in one of three tests, which `run_attack` (Section V-G) applies after the frame has been simulated:

* *Keystream test* (A1 to A4, A6, A7, A15). The attacker's estimate *K̂* is compared with the true keystream *K* over the bits of the frame that the attacker did not already know. If they agree on more than 99 % of these bits, the attacker reads the data and the attack succeeds: DATA BREACHED. Otherwise the verdict is DATA SAFE; an estimate unrelated to the key agrees on about 50 % of the bits.
* *Receiver test* (A8 to A10, A13, A14). If the receiver accepts the frame that the attacker forged, cloned, replayed or altered, the attack succeeds: FAKE DATA ACCEPTED. If the receiver rejects it, the verdict is ATTACK DETECTED.
* *Leakage tests* (A5, A11, A12). A5 succeeds, INFORMATION LEAKS, if the fraction of ones in *C*₁ ⊕ *C*₂ differs from ½ by more than 0.03, or if it lets the attacker estimate the amplitude of the reading within 25 % (the estimator is given with A5 below). A11 succeeds, KEY WEAKENED, if fewer than 128 fingerprint bits remain secret. A12 succeeds, INFORMATION LEAKS, if any answer of the attacked chip differs from the answer of a chip with another fingerprint. Otherwise the verdict is DATA SAFE.

NOT APPLICABLE marks an attack on a mechanism that the design does not have: the helper data (A10 to A12) in the original design.

*The 15 attacks*, numbered as in Table I and in the verdict table below (*[1]*: also considered in [1]):

* **A1. Passive eavesdropping** *[1]* (C1). The attacker records *C* and decrypts it with a key that is not the chip's key (in the model, the original key with 0x5A5A added bit-wise, or a random 128-bit key). *Test:* keystream. *Prediction:* safe for both designs, because a wrong key yields a *K̂* that is correct on only about half of the bits.
* **A2. Brute-force key search** (C1). The chip ID identifies the sensor and is not secret, so the encrypted ID reveals the first 16 keystream bits. The attacker tests all 65,535 non-zero seeds of the 16-bit LFSR against these bits and generates the keystream of the seed that matches. *Test:* keystream, over the whole frame. *Prediction:* the original design fails, because exactly one seed matches 16 output bits. In this frame model the search is even unnecessary: the first 16 outputs of the LFSR are its seed, so the decrypted ID field *is* the key. [1] does not state whether its frame carries an encrypted known field at the start; without one, the same search runs against any 16 consecutive known keystream bits (A3) and still ends in well under a millisecond (Section II-B), so the verdict does not depend on this detail of the frame. The 2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸ keys of the proposal cannot be searched; the model represents any feasible search by one random 128-bit guess, so this verdict is assumed from the key length, not tested.
* **A3. Berlekamp-Massey keystream recovery** (C3). The attacker knows the first *m* = 64 keystream bits of the frame. BM returns the register that generates them, and the register predicts the remaining keystream bits. *Test:* keystream, over the bits after the 64 known ones. *Prediction:* the original design fails, because *L* = 16 and 64 bits exceed 2*L*. For Grain-128a, BM returns a register of about *m*/2 = 32 bits whose predictions agree with *K* no better than chance.
* **A4. Zero/DC input with a replica chip** *[1]* (C2). The attacker forces a DC input of 0.5 µA and applies the same input to a replica chip of the same design, whose bits *D*<sub>r</sub> the attacker can read. The replica differs from the victim by an input-referred offset of 0.1 % of full scale (FS), its own dither sequence and its own noise. The keystream estimate is *K̂* = *C* ⊕ *D*<sub>r</sub> = *K* ⊕ (*D* ⊕ *D*<sub>r</sub>), which is correct wherever the two chips make the same decision. The attack proceeds in two stages. First, as in [1] and in Section VIII, BM is run on 80 windows of 64 bits of *K̂* at random positions within the first 30,000 clocks (`window_attack`, Section V-E); a window succeeds when its register predicts the next 512 keystream bits with more than 99 % accuracy, and the earliest successful window is extended forwards and backwards. Second, if this fails, the attacker of the original design uses what the threat model allows: the LFSR polynomial is public, so any 16 correct keystream bits are its state. Every position of *K̂* is tried (`lfsr16_scan`): a candidate state must predict the following 1,024 bits of *K̂* better than chance (at least 62 %), and its seed, run back to the start of the frame, must decrypt the encrypted chip ID to the public ID, a test that a wrong seed passes with probability 2⁻¹⁶. Because the replica's input is under the attacker's control (C2), the scan is repeated with the replica's input trimmed by 0, ±0.03, ±0.1 and ±0.2 % FS until a seed is confirmed. *Test:* keystream. For the proposal, BM cannot extend a Grain-128a keystream; if *K̂* agrees with *K* on more than 97 % of the bits, the attacker reads only the frame whose input it forced, which carries nothing it does not know, and a fresh IV per frame gives every other frame a different keystream, so the verdict is DATA SAFE. *Prediction:* the full scan finds a clean stretch of at least 16 + a few bits in a capture of 107,400 clocks, because the bits of the two chips agree on about half of the clocks and in runs (Section VIII-B), so **the original design fails**; the proposal is safe.
* **A5. Same key, same message** *[1]* (C1). The attacker records two transmissions of the same reading. If both use the same keystream, *C*₁ ⊕ *C*₂ = *D*₁ ⊕ *D*₂ reveals where the two bit streams differ. The model produces the second transmission on a second modulator channel with a 0.1 % FS input offset and its own dither and noise; in the proposal, the second frame carries the next counter value and therefore its own IV. Where two independent bit streams carry the same input *u*, they differ with probability (1 − *u*²)/2, so the fraction of ones in *C*₁ ⊕ *C*₂ is not ½ but (1 − ⟨*u*²⟩)/2: it reveals the mean square of the reading. For a sine of amplitude *A* the attacker's estimate is *Â* = √(2(1 − 2·⟨*C*₁ ⊕ *C*₂⟩)). *Test:* leakage, as defined above. *Prediction:* **the original design leaks the amplitude of the reading**, because its keystream is the same in both transmissions, however well noise, dither and the offset decorrelate *D*₁ and *D*₂ (Section VI); in the proposal the two frames use different keystreams, so *C*₁ ⊕ *C*₂ is uniformly random.
* **A6. Forced-input saturation** (C2). The attacker forces a large current into the electrode in order to drive the modulator towards overload, where its bits become nearly constant. In one frame at 10 µA, the attacker takes the more frequent bit value as the estimate *D̂* of every bit and applies the window procedure of A4 to *K̂* = *C* ⊕ *D̂*. The S2D buffer gain of 0.5 limits the modulator input to half of full scale, so the bits keep toggling (three of four are ones). The attacker therefore records 21 frames at a forced current of about 1.7 µA (input about 0.45 FS), stepped by 5 nA per frame so that the frames' bits differ, and takes the majority of *C* over the frames at each position: the model assumes that in the original design the LFSR restarts from the stored key in every frame, which [1] does not state, so *K* is the same in all of them and the majority recovers it at almost every position; the full scan of A4 then confirms the seed. If the register instead ran on across frames, every frame would have a different keystream and the multi-frame attack would fail as the single-frame one does; the verdict of A6 rests on this assumption. *Test:* keystream. *Prediction:* the single-frame attack fails against both designs, but **the multi-frame attack breaks the original design**, whose keystream repeats from frame to frame; the proposal's per-frame IV gives every frame a different keystream, so the majority carries no information. Subsection C sweeps the buffer gain for the single-frame attack.
* **A7. Key extraction from memory** (C4). The attacker reads the stored key from an unpowered chip. *Test:* keystream. *Prediction:* the original design fails, because its 16-bit key is stored on the chip. The proposal holds no key in non-volatile memory; the key exists only in volatile registers while the chip is powered, so the attacker is reduced to a guess. This verdict is assumed: it presumes that the enrolment read-out of the fingerprint is disabled after test (Section IV-A) and it excludes physical attacks on a powered chip, such as probing, laser fault injection and the cloning of an SRAM fingerprint by photonic emission analysis.
* **A8. Spoofing (forged frames)** *[1]* (C5, after A2). The attacker encrypts a fake reading of 0.3 µA with the key recovered by brute force (original) or with a guessed key (proposal), gives the frame the next counter value and a tag computed with that key (proposal), and substitutes it for the chip's frame. *Test:* receiver. *Prediction:* the original receiver accepts the frame. The proposal rejects it, because a frame made with a wrong key passes the 32-bit tag check with probability 2⁻³².
* **A9. Cloned or counterfeit sensor** (C4 + C5). The attacker deploys a chip of the same design that carries the genuine chip ID and reports a reading of the attacker's choice (0.3 µA). *Test:* receiver. *Prediction:* the counterfeit of the original design, loaded with the extracted key, is accepted. The clone of the proposal has a different SRAM fingerprint; with the genuine helper data it reconstructs a different key, so the receiver's ID and MAC checks fail. The model's clone is a chip with another fingerprint, so this verdict assumes that the fingerprint cannot be copied; a physical clone of the SRAM fingerprint is outside the threat model.
* **A10. Helper-data tampering** (C5). The attacker inverts one bit of *h* on the downlink. *Test:* the key that the chip reconstructs is compared with the enrolled key. A changed key causes the receiver's ID and MAC checks to fail (ATTACK DETECTED); an unchanged key means that the tampering had no effect (DATA SAFE). *Prediction:* the decoder either fails or corrects towards a different fingerprint, the hash yields a different key, and the attack is detected.
* **A11. Helper-data leakage** (C1). The helper data is public, and its 10*t* bits reveal part of the fingerprint. For cells that power up to 1 with probability *p*, each cell carries a min-entropy of *H*<sub>∞</sub> = −log₂ max(*p*, 1 − *p*) bits, so at least 600·*H*<sub>∞</sub> − 10*t* bits of the fingerprint remain secret (rounded down; `puf_residual`). *Test:* leakage (at least 128 secret bits). *Prediction:* with *p* = 0.4928 (Table VIII), *H*<sub>∞</sub> ≈ 0.979 and *t* = 45, 137 bits remain secret at the point estimate of the bias, more than the 128 bits of the key; over the bias interval the count falls to 94 bits, and the bounded budget of Section VII-E (192 bits at the 95 % lower bound) is not met, so this verdict holds only at the point estimate. This verdict is analytic and rests on the bias estimate; Section VII-E gives its confidence interval.
* **A12. Helper-data manipulation oracle** (C5). The attacker adds the syndrome of an error pattern of its choice to *h*, 200 times, and observes whether the chip still produces frames that the receiver accepts. *Test:* leakage; a twin chip with a different fingerprint and the same noise answers the same queries. *Prediction:* the answers depend on the chosen pattern and on the noise, but not on the fingerprint, so they reveal nothing. The closer analysis at the end of this subsection derives this prediction. The verdict is analytic: because the syndrome is linear, the twin chip's decoder receives the same input by construction, so the comparison illustrates the identity rather than testing it.
* **A13. Replay of a recorded frame** (C1 + C5). The attacker retransmits a genuine frame recorded earlier, after the true reading has decreased to 0.4 times its former value. *Test:* receiver. *Prediction:* the original receiver, which has no counter, accepts the old frame. The proposal rejects it, because its counter is not larger than the last counter accepted.
* **A14. Bit-flipping in transit** (C5). The attacker inverts each payload bit of *C* with probability 0.1, which inverts the same bits of *D*, and leaves the header and the encrypted ID unchanged. *Test:* receiver. *Prediction:* the original receiver checks only the ID and accepts the altered data. The MAC of the proposal covers every payload bit and detects the change.
* **A15. Keystream reuse through a replayed session nonce** (C1 + C2 + C5). The receiver's session nonce *N* travels in clear on the downlink, which the attacker can alter (C5). The attacker records a frame, then, in 11 later sessions, replays its nonce *N* to the chip while forcing a large current (about 1.7 µA, stepped by 5 nA per session), and takes the majority of *C* over these sessions as the estimate *K̂*; the earlier reading follows as *C* ⊕ *K̂*. If the keystream of the new sessions equals that of the recorded one, the majority recovers it. *Test:* keystream, judged on the recovered reading (correlation with the true reading above 0.9: DATA BREACHED; above 0.5: INFORMATION LEAKS). *Prediction:* the original design fails, because its keystream restarts from the stored key in every frame (assumed, as in A6). A proposal whose IV held only *N* and the counter would fail too, since the counter restarts at each session; the chip nonce *N*<sub>c</sub> in the IV (Section IV-B), taken from the raw power-up fingerprint, gives every session its own keystream, so **the proposal is safe**. The cell below also runs the proposal without *N*<sub>c</sub> (`chip_nonce=False`) to show the flaw it closes.

*Overall prediction.* **Eleven of the 15 attacks succeed against the original design and none against the proposal.** Against the original design, six attacks recover the keystream (A2, A3, A4, A6, A7 and A15), because its key is short, its keystream linear and repeated in every frame, and its key stored; A5 leaks the amplitude of the reading; four attacks place fake data on the server (A8, A9, A13 and A14), because the original design has neither an integrity check nor a freshness check.

**Setup.**

* *Level.* The evaluation uses the behavioural, bit-exact model of Section V with the post-layout SKY130 circuit values of Table VIII; it contains no transistor-level part. The analog parameters are those of the nominal corner; Section VIII covers process, voltage and temperature.
* *Frame.* Each attack is run on one frame of 107,400 modulator clocks per design. The sensor input is the 0.93 µA sine of Section V-A, except where the attack sets the input: the DC input of A4, the forced current of A6, the reading of the counterfeit in A9 and the reduced reading of A13.
* *Design settings* (`DEFAULTS`). Dither on, with the ±2.2 % amplitude of [1]; S2D buffer gain 0.5; for the proposal, *t* = 45, counter and MAC on, and the PUF read at the operating temperature of 37 °C after enrolment at 25 °C.
* *Attacker settings* (`ATK_DEF`, Section V-A): a replica offset of 0.1 % FS and trims of 0, ±0.03, ±0.1 and ±0.2 % FS (A4); a second-channel offset of 0.1 % FS (A5); *m* = 64 known keystream bits (A3); 21 frames at 1.7 µA, stepped by 5 nA (A6); a fake reading of 0.3 µA (A8, A9); one inverted helper bit (A10); 200 manipulation queries (A12); a payload inversion probability of 0.1 (A14); 11 sessions with a replayed nonce (A15). The single-frame forced current of 10 µA (A6) is the setting `force_uA` of `DEFAULTS`.
* *Seeds and repetitions.* Every random stream is derived from `seed` = 2026 with a fixed offset per attack, so each verdict results from one deterministic run without repetition; the verdicts of A4, A5, A6 and A15 are therefore single samples of random processes, and Subsection C and Section VIII give their dependence on the settings.
* *Metric.* The verdict of each attack on each design, and the number of successful attacks per design.

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs each of the 15 attacks once on each design with the current settings (`verdict_table()`). 2. Prints the verdicts as Table XIII, with the security property each attack targets, the mechanism that defeats it, what each verdict rests on (simulated, analytic or assumed) and the number of successful attacks per design, and a card with the details of A4, A5, A6 and A15, including the proposal without its chip nonce. 3. Defines `attack_figure`, which draws both designs side by side under one or more attacks, with only the rows that show what the attack does, for the figures below.


```python
#@title Attack evaluation: verdict table
import ipywidgets as W
if IN_COLAB:
    from google.colab import output as _colab_output
    _colab_output.enable_custom_widget_manager()

GOOD = {"safe", "detected"}
STOPS = dict(eaves="encryption (both)", brute="128-bit PUF key", bm="Grain-128a's nonlinearity", knownin="Grain-128a; per-frame IV",
             samekey="per-frame IV", saturate="per-frame IV", extract="no stored key (PUF); read-out disabled",
             spoof="unrecoverable key + MAC", clone="unclonable PUF", htamper="key = hash(w) + ID check", hleak="n·H∞ − 10t ≥ 128",
             hmanip="syndrome construction + hash", replay="frame counter + MAC", bitflip="MAC over the payload",
             reuse="chip nonce N<sub>c</sub> in the IV")

ICON = {k: f'<img src="{ASSETS}/icons/{f}.svg" width="18" height="18" style="vertical-align:-4px;margin-right:6px" alt="{k}">'
        for k, f in (("good", "happy"), ("bad", "sad"), ("na", "neutral"))}

def verdict_html(T):
    """The verdict table: booktabs rules, a face per verdict (happy: safe or detected, sad: the attack succeeds)."""
    def cell(v):
        kind = "good" if v in GOOD else "na" if v == "na" else "bad"
        return f'<td style="padding:4px 14px;white-space:nowrap">{ICON[kind]}{"<b>" if kind == "bad" else ""}{VERDICT[v]}{"</b>" if kind == "bad" else ""}</td>'
    ev = lambda a: f'<td style="padding:4px 10px;opacity:.8;white-space:nowrap">{EVIDENCE[a][0]} / {EVIDENCE[a][1]}</td>'
    rows = "".join(f'<tr><td style="padding:4px 14px">A{k + 1}. {name}{" <i>[1]</i>" if paper else ""}</td>'
                   f'<td style="padding:4px 10px;opacity:.8">{PROPERTY[a]}</td>{cell(T[a][0])}{cell(T[a][1])}{ev(a)}'
                   f'<td style="padding:4px 14px;opacity:.8">{STOPS[a]}</td></tr>' for k, (a, name, paper) in enumerate(ATTACKS))
    bad = lambda k: sum(T[a][k] not in GOOD | {"na"} for a in T)
    th = lambda s: f'<th style="text-align:left;padding:5px 14px;border-bottom:1px solid currentColor">{s}</th>'
    return (f'<div style="font-family:\'STIX Two Text\',\'Times New Roman\',Times,serif;font-size:15px;max-width:980px;margin:8px 0">'
            f'<div style="text-align:center;font-variant:small-caps;letter-spacing:.04em;margin-bottom:4px">Table XIII: verdict of every attack on both designs '
            f'(<i>[1]</i>: considered in [1])</div>'
            f'<table style="border-collapse:collapse;border-top:1.6px solid currentColor;border-bottom:1.6px solid currentColor">'
            f'<thead><tr>{th("Attack")}{th("Property")}{th("Original S-DSM [1]")}{th("Proposed")}{th("Evidence (original / proposed)")}{th("What stops it")}</tr></thead><tbody>{rows}</tbody></table>'
            f'<div style="margin-top:6px">Attacks that succeed: <b>original {bad(0)} of {len(T)}</b>, <b>proposed {bad(1)} of {len(T)}</b>. '
            f'Evidence: <i>simulated</i>, the attack is run on the model; <i>analytic</i>, a formula or an identity; '
            f'<i>assumed</i>, a property taken as given (the length of the key, the unclonability of the PUF, or a physical '
            f'attack outside the threat model). By property, the original fails ' +
            ", ".join(f"{p} {sum(T[a][0] not in GOOD | {'na'} for a in T if PROPERTY[a] == p)} of {sum(1 for a in T if PROPERTY[a] == p and T[a][0] != 'na')}"
                      for p in dict.fromkeys(PROPERTY[a] for a, _, _ in ATTACKS) if any(PROPERTY[a] == p and T[a][0] != 'na' for a in T)) +
            '.</div></div>')

T = verdict_table()
display(HTML(verdict_html(T)))
# the attacks that the competent attacker changes, and the proposal without its chip nonce
_a4, _a5 = simulate(scheme="baseline", attack="knownin")["atk"], simulate(scheme="baseline", attack="samekey")["atk"]
_a6, _a15 = simulate(scheme="baseline", attack="saturate")["atk"], simulate(scheme="baseline", attack="reuse")["atk"]
_p15, _p15n = simulate(attack="reuse")["atk"], simulate(attack="reuse", chip_nonce=False)["atk"]
card("Attacks A4, A5, A6 and A15 in detail",
     [("A4, original: 80 random windows / full scan", f"{_a4['win']['broken']} of 80 windows; full scan: seed confirmed "
       f"at a replica trim of {_a4.get('scan_trim', 0):+.2f} % FS ({_a4.get('scan_cand', 0)} candidate states)" if "scan_seed" in _a4 else
       f"{_a4['win']['broken']} of 80 windows; full scan: no seed confirmed"),
      ("A5, original: fraction of ones in C₁ ⊕ C₂, amplitude estimate", f"{_a5['xfrac']:.4f}; Â = {_a5['a_hat']:.3f} against A = {_a5['a_true']:.3f} FS"),
      ("A6, original: majority over frames", f"{_a6.get('frames', 0)} frames, keystream estimate {100 * _a6.get('mf_kacc', 0):.1f} % correct; "
       + ("seed confirmed" if "scan_seed" in _a6 else "no seed confirmed")),
      ("A15, original: reading recovered from replayed sessions", f"correlation {_a15['corr']:.2f} with the true reading ({_a15['sessions']} sessions)"),
      ("A15, proposal with the chip nonce", f"correlation {_p15['corr']:+.2f}; {_p15['cn_distinct']} distinct chip nonces in {_p15['sessions']} sessions"),
      ("A15, proposal without the chip nonce", f"correlation {_p15n['corr']:.2f}: <b>{VERDICT[_p15n['v']]}</b>")],
     tone="bad" if _p15["v"] != "safe" else "ok")

from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch

def attack_figure(attack, mac=True, dither=True, buffer=0.5):
    """Both designs under one attack, side by side, or under several attacks, one row of panels each: the bits that show
    what the attack does over 200 clocks, grouped by where they are observed, each group headed by what happens there;
    then the readings. Returns the simulated frames, (original, proposed) per attack."""
    attacks = (attack,) if isinstance(attack, str) else tuple(attack)
    over = dict(mac=mac, dither=dither, buffer=buffer)
    rows = []
    for a in attacks:
        sims = [simulate(scheme=sc, attack=a, **over) for sc in ("baseline", "proposed")]
        ratios = [chain_ratios(S) for S in sims]
        n = max(len(r) for r in ratios)
        ratios = [r[:-1] + [0.0] * (n - len(r)) + r[-1:] for r in ratios]      # same rows in both panels
        hr = [max(a_, b_) for a_, b_ in zip(*ratios)]
        rows.append((a, sims, n, hr, 0.27 * sum(hr) + 1.05))                    # inches: rows + titles and the x axis
    leg_h = 0.42
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W2, sum(r[-1] for r in rows) + leg_h))
    subs = fig.subfigures(len(rows) + 1, 1, height_ratios=[r[-1] for r in rows] + [leg_h], hspace=0.0)
    names = dict((x, nm) for x, nm, _ in ATTACKS)
    for k, ((a, sims, n, hr, h), sub_row) in enumerate(zip(rows, subs)):
        for c, (sub, S, name) in enumerate(zip(sub_row.subfigures(1, 2, wspace=0.0), sims, ("original S-DSM", "proposed"))):
            items = len(chain_items(S))
            axs = sub.subplots(n, 1, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=hr, hspace=0.25))
            for ax in axs[items:-1]:
                ax.remove()
            sub.subplots_adjust(left=0.34, right=0.95, top=1 - 0.66 / h, bottom=0.42 / h)
            plot_chain(S, axs=list(axs[:items]) + [axs[-1]], legend=False)
            v = S["atk"]["v"]
            good, na = v in ("safe", "detected"), v == "na"
            col = COL["faint"] if na else COL["ok"] if good else COL["bad"]
            # the outcome at a glance: the whole panel tinted (blue: the design holds, orange: the attacker gains), a
            # filled verdict banner under the title, and the reading on white
            sub.add_artist(FancyBboxPatch((0.012, 0.006), 0.976, 0.988, transform=sub.transSubfigure, zorder=-10,
                                          boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.015", lw=0.9, ec=col,
                                          fc="#f4f5f7" if na else "#edf3fc" if good else "#fdf0e8"))
            for ax_ in axs[:items]:
                ax_.patch.set_alpha(0.0)
            axs[-1].set_facecolor("white")
            title = (f"({'abcdefgh'[2 * k + c]}) " + (f"{names[a].split(':')[0].split(' of ')[0]}: {name}" if len(rows) > 1 else name[0].upper() + name[1:]))
            sub.text(0.04, 1 - 0.10 / h, title, fontsize=10, va="top")
            sub.text(0.04, 1 - 0.36 / h, " " + VERDICT[v] + " ", fontsize=10, va="top", fontweight="bold", color="white",
                     bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=col, ec="none"))
    hl = {}                                    # one legend for all panels, under the figure
    for ax in fig.axes:
        for hd, l in zip(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels()):
            hl.setdefault(l, hd)
    if "attacker's forged reading" in hl and "old reading replayed" in hl:     # same line style: one entry
        hl["attacker's reading: forged (a, b) or replayed (c, d)"] = hl.pop("attacker's forged reading"); del hl["old reading replayed"]
    subs[-1].legend(hl.values(), hl.keys(), loc="center", ncol=min(4, len(hl)), frameon=False, fontsize=9,
                    columnspacing=1.2, handlelength=1.8)
    plt.show()
    return [r[1] for r in rows] if len(rows) > 1 else rows[0][1]
```

<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #2a78d6;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Attacks A4, A5, A6 and A15 in detail</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A4, original: 80 random windows / full scan</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">0 of 80 windows; full scan: seed confirmed at a replica trim of +0.03 % FS (441 candidate states)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A5, original: fraction of ones in C₁ ⊕ C₂, amplitude estimate</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">0.4849; Â = 0.246 against A = 0.249 FS</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A6, original: majority over frames</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">21 frames, keystream estimate 98.4 % correct; seed confirmed</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A15, original: reading recovered from replayed sessions</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">correlation 0.95 with the true reading (11 sessions)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A15, proposal with the chip nonce</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">correlation -0.01; 11 distinct chip nonces in 11 sessions</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">A15, proposal without the chip nonce</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">correlation 0.95: <b>DATA BREACHED</b></td></tr></table></div>


**Result.** Table XIII agrees with the prediction for every attack. **Against the original design, 11 of 15 attacks succeed.** Six breach the data: brute-force key search (A2), Berlekamp-Massey recovery (A3), the replica attack (A4, through the full scan; the card gives the trim at which the seed was confirmed), the multi-frame saturation attack (A6), key extraction (A7) and keystream reuse (A15). Same key and same message (A5) leaks the amplitude of the reading. Four place fake data on the server: spoofing (A8), the cloned sensor (A9), replay (A13) and bit-flipping (A14). Only passive eavesdropping (A1) does not succeed, and the three helper-data attacks (A10 to A12) are not applicable. **Against the proposal, 0 of 15 attacks succeed.** The receiver detects and rejects five of them: spoofing, the clone, helper-data tampering, replay and bit-flipping. For the other ten the verdict is DATA SAFE. Without the chip nonce, the proposal falls to A15 (card below the table), as predicted.

**Interpretation.** **The failures of the original design have three architectural causes.** Its key is short, its keystream linear and its key stored, so three independent attacks recover the keystream. Its keystream restarts in every frame, so any repetition, of the message (A5), of the forced input (A6) or of the session (A15), exposes it. And its frames carry neither authentication nor freshness, so any attacker who can transmit places data on the server, with or without the key. The analog attacks that [1] considered do not hold either once the attacker uses the capabilities of the threat model: the bits of two chips agree in runs long enough for a scan of every window, the replica's input can be trimmed, and frames can be repeated. Section VIII reached the same conclusion for the comparator and the integrators.

**The proposal's verdicts rest on three kinds of evidence**, given in the column "Evidence". Nine are simulated: the attack runs on the model and the decision test is applied. Two are analytic: the secret-bit budget (A11), whose confidence interval is given in Section VII-E, and the manipulation oracle (A12), an identity of the syndrome construction. Four are assumed: eavesdropping and brute force rest on the 128-bit key, extraction on the absence of a key in non-volatile memory and of a usable read-out path, and the clone on the unclonability of the fingerprint. These verdicts hold for the attacks as implemented; they are not a proof of security, and the physical attacks listed in Section IV-A are outside the threat model.

#### Three attacks, block by block

The verdict table states who wins; the next two figures show where in the link each attack succeeds or is stopped. They answer one question for three attacks: brute-force key search (Fig. 46), which tests the key, and spoofing and replay (Fig. 47), which test the receiver. Both designs are drawn side by side over the same 200 modulator clocks. Only the rows that show what the attack does are drawn: the bits *C* on the air, the attacker's keystream estimate or forged frame, the frame the receiver gets, its checks, the bits *D*<sub>rx</sub> it decrypts and the reading the server shows. The chip's internal signals (the sensor current, the integrator state, *D* and *K*) are the same under every attack and are left out; the interactive version below draws them where the attacker sets the input. The ciphertext rows of the two designs look alike, as they must: an encrypted bitstream is indistinguishable from random bits whatever the key, so the difference cannot be seen in the bits themselves. Each group of rows therefore opens with a line that states what happens there in this frame, and the rows mark what changes: the bits the attacker altered are marked in orange, the row of the keystream estimate ends with the share of wrong bits (*K̂* = *K* when the attacker has the keystream), each receiver check is marked ✓ (passes) or × (fails), *D*<sub>rx</sub> is orange when it carries the attacker's bits to the server and grey when the frame is discarded, and the reading panel shows what the server displays and, in red, what the attacker decrypts, forges or replays. Each panel is tinted by its outcome, orange when the attacker gains something and blue when the attack is stopped or learns nothing, under a verdict banner of the same colour, so that the two designs can be told apart at a glance.

Runs attack A2, the brute-force key search, on both designs: the attacker tests all 65,535 seeds of the 16-bit LFSR against the 16 keystream bits that encrypt the known chip ID, and makes one random 128-bit guess against the proposal. 2. Draws the transmitted bits, the attacker's keystream estimate, the receiver's checks and the reading shown by the server.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 46.</b> Brute-force key search (A2) on (a) the original S-DSM and (b) the proposed design. Rows: bits <i>C</i> on the air; the attacker's keystream estimate <i>K̂</i> (orange: wrong bits; right: share of wrong bits); the receiver's checks. Reading: server output (black) and the attacker's decryption (red, dashed). Panel tint and banner: the outcome (orange: the attacker gains; blue: the design holds). **Result.** The search recovers the key of the original design: in Fig. 46(a), *K̂* contains no wrong bit (100 % of the bits equal *K*, marked *K̂* = *K*), and the data decrypted by the attacker coincide with the true reading (DATA BREACHED). In (b), a random 128-bit guess yields a *K̂* that is wrong on 50 % of the bits (marked in orange), and the decrypted data are noise unrelated to the reading (DATA SAFE). In both panels the receiver's checks pass, because the attack is passive: **the 16-bit key falls to a search of the whole key space**, and nothing at the receiver can detect it.

Runs attack A13, replay: the attacker retransmits a frame recorded earlier, after the true reading has decreased to 0.4 times its value. 3. Draws both attacks on both designs, one row of panels per attack: the bits on the air, the attacker's or the received frame, the receiver's checks, the bits it decrypts and the reading shown by the server.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 47.</b> Spoofing (A8) and replay (A13) on the original S-DSM, (a) and (c), and the proposed design, (b) and (d). Rows and colours as in Fig. 46, with the attacker's forged <i>C</i> or the <i>C</i> at the receiver (orange: bits changed) and the decrypted bits <i>D</i><sub>rx</sub> (orange: passed to the server; grey: discarded). Reading: server output carrying the attacker's data (orange) and the forged or replayed reading (red, dashed); box: frame rejected.</p>

**Result.** *Spoofing.* In Fig. 47(a) the receiver accepts the forged frame, and the server shows the constant 0.3 µA reading of the attacker in place of the true sine (FAKE DATA ACCEPTED). The original design has no MAC and no counter, so its only check, the chip ID, passes because the attacker encrypted the correct ID with the recovered key. In (b) the forged frame was encrypted and tagged with a guessed key; the chip-ID check and the MAC check both fail, the receiver rejects the frame and the server shows nothing (ATTACK DETECTED).

*Replay.* In (c) the receiver accepts the old frame, and the server shows the earlier, larger reading although the true reading has decreased to 0.4 times its value (FAKE DATA ACCEPTED). In (d) the chip ID and the MAC of the replayed frame are valid, since the chip itself produced them, but its counter is not larger than the last counter accepted; the counter check fails and the frame is rejected (ATTACK DETECTED). The two attacks are stopped by different checks: **a wrong key by the MAC, a stale frame by the counter**. Two animations follow. The first (Fig. 48) is the spoofing attack on the original design in the interactive explorer: the attacker recovers the 16-bit key by brute force from a known part of the frame, encrypts a fake reading with it and replaces the chip's frame on the channel; the receiver finds a valid frame and ID and accepts the forged frame, and the server shows the attacker's constant reading. The second (Fig. 49) runs spoofing, replay and the third frame attack, bit-flipping, on both designs: the original receiver accepts all three frames, and the proposal's MAC tag and frame counter reject them. Both are recorded, not results of this run.

#### Interactive attack evaluation

The figures above show 3 of the 15 attacks at the current settings, with the rows that matter for them. The next cell shows any of the 15 attacks and allows the defences on which the verdicts depend to be switched off; it opens on the replica attack (A4). Switching off the counter and MAC of the proposal also removes its per-frame IV, so that the same-message attack, replay and bit-flipping succeed against the proposal as well. The dither and the buffer gain of the original design can be changed too; with the full-scan attacker of Table XIII they change no verdict of the original design, which falls to A4 to A6 with the model's simplified dither on or off. After each change the figure and a new verdict table are computed. The cell requires a live kernel: a static copy of the notebook, such as the one on GitHub, shows only its default view as a still image. All 15 attacks are therefore also drawn as one still figure after it (Fig. 51).

> **Next cell.** 1. Shows a menu of the 15 attacks and switches for the counter and MAC of the proposal, the dither and the S2D buffer gain. 2. On every change, draws the selected attack on both designs with `attack_figure`. 3. Runs all 15 attacks again with these settings and prints a new verdict table below the figure. Requires a live kernel.


```python
#@title Attack evaluation: interactive
w_atk = W.Dropdown(options=[(("[paper] " if p else "") + n, a) for a, n, p in ATTACKS], value="knownin", description="Attack", layout=W.Layout(width="420px"))
w_mac = W.Checkbox(value=True, description="proposal: counter + MAC"); w_dith = W.Checkbox(value=True, description="dither")
w_buf = W.ToggleButtons(options=[("S2D ×0.5", 0.5), ("no buffer (×1)", 1.0)], value=0.5, description="buffer")
w_out = W.Output()
def _show(*_):
    with w_out:
        w_out.clear_output(wait=True)
        show.plain = True                  # figures in a widget: plain PNG (see show())
        try:
            attack_figure(w_atk.value, w_mac.value, w_dith.value, w_buf.value)
        finally:
            show.plain = False
        T2 = verdict_table(mac=w_mac.value, dither=w_dith.value, buffer=w_buf.value)
        display(HTML(verdict_html(T2)))
for w in (w_atk, w_mac, w_dith, w_buf):
    w.observe(_show, "value")
show.capture = []                          # a static copy of the default view, for viewers without a kernel
try:
    attack_figure(w_atk.value, w_mac.value, w_dith.value, w_buf.value)
finally:
    _static, show.capture = show.capture, None
display_widget(W.VBox([W.HBox([w_atk, w_buf]), W.HBox([w_mac, w_dith]), w_out]), _static[0] if _static else None); _show()
```

#### All 15 attacks at a glance

**Goal.** Show the outcome of every attack of Table XIII on both designs in one still figure, so that each verdict can be seen without a running kernel.

**Setup.** Behavioural level, with the settings of Table XIII (the proposal's counter and MAC on, dither on, S2D buffer gain 0.5). Each of the 15 attacks is run once on each design with `simulate()`, which gives the same frames as the verdict table. Each panel is the reading panel of Fig. 46 for one attack and one design, over output samples 60 to 179: the true reading, the server's output and what the attacker decrypts, forges or replays. The metric is the verdict of each attack and the evidence it rests on (simulated, analytic or assumed, as in Table XIII).

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs each of the 15 attacks on both designs. 2. Draws one row per attack: for each design the reading panel, tinted by the outcome, with the verdict and the evidence it rests on. 3. Prints a card that counts the attacks in which the attacker gains something on each design and checks the 30 verdicts against Table XIII.


```python
#@title Fig.: all 15 attacks at a glance
# All 15 attacks on both designs, one row each, for a reader without a running kernel (the interactive figure above shows
# one attack at a time). Each panel is the reading panel of the attack figures: the true reading (grey), the server's
# output (black; orange when it is the attacker's data) and what the attacker decrypts, forges or replays (red, dashed),
# tinted by the outcome, with the verdict and the evidence it rests on (simulated, analytic or assumed)
import time as _t
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
_t0 = _t.time()
SHORT = dict(breached="BREACHED", spoofed="FAKE ACCEPTED", leak="LEAKS", weak="KEY WEAKENED", safe="SAFE",
             detected="DETECTED", na="N/A")
ATLAS = {a: [simulate(scheme=sc, attack=a) for sc in ("baseline", "proposed")] for a, _, _ in ATTACKS}

def attack_atlas(atlas):
    n = len(ATTACKS)
    h_row, h_top, h_bot = 0.47, 0.42, 0.62
    H = n * h_row + h_top + h_bot
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W2, H))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(n, 2, left=0.335, right=0.99, top=1 - h_top / H, bottom=h_bot / H, hspace=0.16, wspace=0.05)
    for c, head in enumerate(("Original S-DSM [1]", "Proposed")):
        x = gs[0, c].get_position(fig)
        fig.text((x.x0 + x.x1) / 2, 1 - 0.16 / H, head, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10)
    for r, (a, name, paper) in enumerate(ATTACKS):
        for c, S in enumerate(atlas[a]):
            ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[r, c])
            plot_reading(ax, S, small=True)
            v = S["atk"]["v"]
            good, na = v in ("safe", "detected"), v == "na"
            col = COL["faint"] if na else COL["ok"] if good else COL["bad"]
            ax.set_facecolor("#f4f5f7" if na else "#edf3fc" if good else "#fdf0e8")
            ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
            for sp in ax.spines.values():
                sp.set_color(col); sp.set_linewidth(0.9)
            ax.text(0.985, 0.90, SHORT[v], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=7, color="white",
                    fontweight="bold", zorder=7, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=col, ec="none"))
            ax.text(0.012, 0.08, EVIDENCE[a][c], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=6.5,
                    color=COL["ink"], zorder=7, style="italic",
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.9))
        y = gs[r, 0].get_position(fig)
        fig.text(0.012, (y.y0 + y.y1) / 2, f"A{r + 1}  {name}" + ("  [1]" if paper else ""), ha="left", va="center",
                 fontsize=8.5)
    handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["faint"], lw=1.0, label="true reading"),
               plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["ink"], lw=1.2, label="server output"),
               plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["bad"], lw=2.0, label="server output, attacker's data"),
               plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["key"], lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 1.6)), label="attacker's decryption, forgery or replay"),
               Patch(fc="#fdf0e8", ec=COL["bad"], label="attacker gains"), Patch(fc="#edf3fc", ec=COL["ok"], label="design holds"),
               Patch(fc="#f4f5f7", ec=COL["faint"], label="not applicable")]
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", ncol=4, fontsize=8, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0),
               columnspacing=1.2, handlelength=1.8)
    plt.show()

attack_atlas(ATLAS)
_gain = lambda v: v not in ("safe", "detected", "na")
_won = [sum(_gain(ATLAS[a][k]["atk"]["v"]) for a, _, _ in ATTACKS) for k in (0, 1)]
_same = all(tuple(S["atk"]["v"] for S in ATLAS[a]) == T[a] for a, _, _ in ATTACKS)
card("All 15 attacks on both designs, as drawn in the atlas",
     [("attacks in which the attacker gains something", f"original {_won[0]} of {len(ATTACKS)}, proposal {_won[1]} of {len(ATTACKS)}"),
      ("verdicts against the verdict table above", "all 30 agree" if _same else "<b>differ</b>"),
      ("frames simulated", f"{2 * len(ATTACKS)}, in {_t.time() - _t0:.0f} s")], tone="info" if _same else "bad")
```

**Result.** In Fig. 51, 11 of the original design's 15 panels are orange. After the key-recovery attacks A2 to A4, A6 and A7 the attacker's decryption lies on the true reading, and A15 recovers the reading from replayed sessions (BREACHED); A5 reveals the reading from two frames under the same key (LEAKS); and the forged, cloned, replayed and altered frames of A8, A9, A13 and A14 reach the server in place of the true reading (FAKE ACCEPTED). Eavesdropping alone (A1) fails against it, and the helper-data attacks A10 to A12 do not apply, since the original design has no helper data. In the proposal's column every panel is blue: the attacker decrypts only noise or learns nothing (SAFE: A1 to A7, A11, A12 and A15), and every frame that the simulated chip did not produce in the current session is rejected (DETECTED: A8 to A10, A13 and A14). The card checks that the 30 verdicts agree with Table XIII: **the original design falls to 11 of the 15 attacks and the proposal to none**.

#### A closer analysis: the helper-data manipulation attack

**Goal.** To determine whether an attacker who can modify the helper data, and who observes whether the receiver accepts the result, can learn the fingerprint *w* bit by bit. Such attacks have broken fuzzy extractors whose helper data was not constructed as a syndrome. This is attack A12, the one verdict that the figures above do not show.

**Theory.** With the syndrome construction [4], *h* = *H**w*, where *H* is the parity-check matrix of the BCH code. At power-up the chip reads *w*′ = *w* ⊕ *ε*, where *ε* marks the cells that flipped. The decoder receives the syndrome *H**w*′ ⊕ *h* = *H**ε* and corrects *ε*. If the attacker sends *h* ⊕ *H**e* instead, with an error pattern *e* of the attacker's choice, the decoder receives *H*(*ε* ⊕ *e*). Whether decoding succeeds therefore depends only on *ε* and *e*, never on *w*. When it succeeds, it returns *w* ⊕ *e*, whose hash is a wrong key, so the frame is rejected. *Predictions:* (1) no tampered power-up is accepted; (2) the decoder fails when *e* and the noise together flip more than *t* cells; (3) a chip with a different fingerprint and the same noise gives the same answer to every query, so the answers carry no information about *w*.

**Setup.** Behavioural model of Section V-D (`manip_oracle`), with the simulated PUF parameters, read at 37 °C and *t* = 45. The attacker makes *Q* = 200 queries (`manip_q`). Query *q* adds the syndrome of a random error pattern of weight 1 + (*q* mod 55) to *h*, so that the weight cycles from 1 to *t* + 10 = 55. Each query is a new power-up with its own noise. A twin chip with a random fingerprint *w*₂ and its own helper data receives the same noise pattern and the same added syndrome. For each query the model records whether the attacked chip reconstructs the enrolled key (the receiver accepts) and whether its decoder reports a failure, and compares both answers with those of the twin. All random streams are derived from `seed` + 57. The metrics are the numbers of accepted power-ups and of decoder failures, and the number of queries on which the two chips give the same answers; the verdict is DATA SAFE only if all 200 answers agree.

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs attack A12 on the proposal (`simulate(attack="hmanip")`): 200 power-ups, each with the syndrome of a chosen error pattern added to the helper data. 2. Records for each query whether the receiver accepts and whether the decoder fails, and the answers of a twin chip with a different fingerprint and the same noise. 3. Reports the counts and the verdict.


```python
#@title Helper-data manipulation
# helper-data manipulation: does tampering with h and watching accept/reject reveal the fingerprint?
Sm = simulate(attack="hmanip")
M = Sm["manip"]
card("Helper-data manipulation attack",
     [("tampered power-ups", f"{M['Q']} (chosen error patterns added to <i>h</i>)"),
      ("receiver accepted / decoder failed", f"{M['acc']} / {M['fails']}"),
      ("same answer from a chip with a different fingerprint", f"{M['same']} of {M['Q']}"),
      ("verdict", "<b>no information about the fingerprint leaks</b>" if M["same"] == M["Q"] else "<b>some information leaks</b>")],
     tone="ok" if M["same"] == M["Q"] else "bad")
```


<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #2a78d6;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Helper-data manipulation attack</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">tampered power-ups</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">200 (chosen error patterns added to <i>h</i>)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">receiver accepted / decoder failed</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">0 / 57</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">same answer from a chip with a different fingerprint</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">200 of 200</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">verdict</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>no information about the fingerprint leaks</b></td></tr></table></div>


**Result.** The card reports, row by row: 200 tampered power-ups; 0 accepted by the receiver, as predicted (1), and 57 decoder failures (28.5 %); the same answers from the twin chip in **200 of 200** queries, as predicted (3); and the verdict that no information about the fingerprint leaks. The 57 failures are consistent with prediction (2): the pattern weights extend to 55, and the heavier patterns, together with the cells flipped by noise, exceed the 45 cells that the code corrects.

**Interpretation.** The accept/reject oracle exists, but it measures only the noise and the attacker's own pattern. **By the linearity of the syndrome, the syndrome construction and the hashed key defeat this attack in the model without any additional circuit.** This completes the attack evaluation. The remaining cost of the PUF key is reliability: the key must be regenerated correctly at every power-up, which Subsection B quantifies.

### B. PUF reliability: probability of key failure per power-up

**Goal.** The proposal introduces one failure mode that the original design does not have: at power-up, the PUF may fail to regenerate the key, and the chip then cannot communicate until the next power-up. A product specification requires this probability per power-up. This subsection computes it exactly over temperature, for one modelled chip and for 16 others, checks the computation by Monte Carlo simulation, and computes how many fingerprint bits the code leaves secret.

**Theory.** The cell model is that of Section V-D. Cell *i* has a fixed mismatch *m*<sub>i</sub>, drawn once from a Gaussian distribution of unit variance whose mean sets the bias. At each power-up the cell reads 1 when *m*<sub>i</sub> + *s*(*T*)·*ν* > 0, where *ν* is new standard Gaussian noise and *s*(*T*) = *s*<sub>25</sub>(1 + *a*·|*T* − 25 °C|) is the noise-to-mismatch ratio at temperature *T*, with temperature coefficient *a*. Enrolment reads the fingerprint *w* once at 25 °C. At temperature *T*, cell *i* therefore differs from its enrolled bit with probability

$$p_i(T) = \Phi\!\left(-\frac{m_i}{s(T)}\right) \text{ if } w_i = 1, \qquad p_i(T) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{m_i}{s(T)}\right) \text{ if } w_i = 0,$$

where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. Let *N*<sub>i</sub> = 1 if cell *i* flips and 0 otherwise. The number of flipped cells, *N* = Σ<sub>i</sub> *N*<sub>i</sub>, is a sum of 600 independent Bernoulli variables with different *p*<sub>i</sub>, and its distribution is the Poisson-binomial distribution. The BCH decoder corrects up to *t* flipped cells, so the key fails when more than *t* cells flip:

$$P_{\text{fail}}(T) = P(N > t) = \sum_{k > t} P(N = k).$$

`fail_tail` (the tail) and `err_dist` (the full distribution) evaluate this exactly by a recursion that adds one cell at a time, and remain accurate down to about 10⁻³⁰⁰, far below the reach of sampling.

*Mechanism.* Only cells with |*m*<sub>i</sub>| comparable to *s*(*T*) can flip. Away from 25 °C, *s*(*T*) increases, more cells become unstable, and the tail beyond *t* grows by many orders of magnitude. A stronger code moves the threshold *t* further into the tail.

*The opposing constraint.* The helper data is the syndrome of *w*, 10*t* bits long. With the min-entropy per cell *H*<sub>∞</sub> = −log₂ max(*p*, 1 − *p*), for cells that power up to 1 with probability *p*, at least 600·*H*<sub>∞</sub> − 10*t* fingerprint bits remain secret. A stronger code is more reliable but leaves fewer secret bits, so reliability and secrecy set opposite limits on *t*. Section VII-E bounds *H*<sub>∞</sub> from below (95 % confidence) and requires 192 secret bits, 128 for the key plus the margin of the leftover-hash lemma.

*Assumptions.* The cells are independent. The noise is Gaussian and thermal only, so the SPICE value of *s*<sub>25</sub> is a lower bound (Table VIII). The chip has not aged (`puf_years` = 0). Temperature acts only through *s*(*T*); the reproducible flips caused by the rotation of the mismatch are not in this subsection's model: Section VII-E and Section VIII-F size the code with a two-component model over 1,000 Monte Carlo chips. Probabilities far below 10⁻¹⁰ are statements about the model's Gaussian tail, not about silicon, and are given to one significant figure.

*Predictions.* (1) *P*<sub>fail</sub> is lowest at the enrolment temperature of 25 °C and increases on both sides. (2) With *t* = 45, the working setting of the system simulations (Section VII-E), the linear law keeps *P*<sub>fail</sub> far below 10⁻⁶ over 0–85 °C. This prediction is optimistic, because the law underestimates the simulated error rate at 85 °C (1.75 % against 3.14 %, Table VIII). (3) The Monte Carlo histogram of *N* follows the exact distribution. (4) With *p* = 0.4928 the point estimate leaves 600·*H*<sub>∞</sub> − 450 ≈ 137 secret bits and the lower bound about 94, both short of the 192 required.

**Setup.**

* *Level and model.* Behavioural: the `SRAMPUF` model with the parameters fitted to the post-layout SKY130 Monte Carlo simulation of the extracted 6T cell (Table VIII): *s*<sub>25</sub> = 0.02253, *a* = 0.02051 per °C and *p* = 0.4928, all at the nominal corner, with the linear temperature law *s*(*T*) of the cell model. Section VIII-F covers the five process corners.
* *Chips.* "This chip" is the modelled chip with seed 7 (`chip_seed`), on which the earlier, noise-only sizing of t = 45 was made. Sixteen other chips, with seeds 107 to 1,607, are enrolled in the same way at 25 °C.
* *Codes.* The code strength is *t* = 45; this chip is also evaluated with *t* − 10 = 35 and *t* + 10 = 55. The other chips use *t* = 45.
* *Temperature.* −40 to 85 °C in steps of 5 °C, the range over which the SRAM-PUF cell is simulated; the specified range is 0–85 °C.
* *Monte Carlo check.* 4,000 power-ups of this chip at the operating temperature of 37 °C (`temp`, the bioreactor), each compared bit by bit with the enrolled fingerprint, seeded from `seed` + 909; the exact distribution of *N* at 37 °C is computed for comparison. With no failure among *M* power-ups, *P*<sub>fail</sub> < 1 − 0.05<sup>1/*M*</sup> at 95 % confidence, about 3/*M* = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴: the sample tests the body of the distribution, not its tail.
* *Metrics.* *P*<sub>fail</sub> per power-up against the target of 10⁻⁶; the mean and maximum number of flipped cells; the number of secret bits against 128.

> **Next cell.** 1. Defines `puf_reliability()`, which computes the exact key-failure probability over −40 to 85 °C for this chip with *t* − 10, *t* and *t* + 10, and for 16 other chips with *t*. 2. Adds a Monte Carlo simulation of 4,000 power-ups of this chip at the operating temperature and the exact distribution of flipped cells there. The cell only defines functions; no simulation is run.


```python
#@title PUF reliability: definitions
def puf_reliability(P=None, temps=np.arange(-40, 86, 5), n_chips=16, n_mc=4000):
    """Exact key-failure probability per power-up against temperature (this chip and others), plus a Monte
    Carlo check of the error-count distribution at the current temperature."""
    P = {**DEFAULTS, **(P or {})}; age = puf_age(P)
    def chip(seed):
        puf = SRAMPUF(seed, PUF_BITS, P["puf_sigma"], P["puf_bias"], P["puf_tc"])
        return puf, enroll(puf, P["bch_t"], rng_for(seed * 7919 + 1))["w"]
    puf, w = chip(P["chip_seed"])
    ts = [t for t in (P["bch_t"] - 10, P["bch_t"], P["bch_t"] + 10) if t >= 1]
    curves = {t: np.array([fail_tail(puf.p_err(w, T, age), t) for T in temps]) for t in ts}
    others = np.array([[fail_tail(o.p_err(wo, T, age), P["bch_t"]) for T in temps]
                       for o, wo in (chip(P["chip_seed"] + 100 * c) for c in range(1, n_chips + 1))])
    r = rng_for(P["seed"] + 909); errs = np.array([int((puf.read(P["temp"], r, age) != w).sum()) for _ in range(n_mc)])
    p_now = fail_tail(puf.p_err(w, P["temp"], age), P["bch_t"])
    return dict(temps=temps, curves=curves, band=(others.min(0), others.max(0)), errs=errs,
                dist=err_dist(puf.p_err(w, P["temp"], age)), p_now=p_now, t=P["bch_t"], temp=P["temp"])
```

> **Next cell.** 1. Runs `puf_reliability()` with the current settings. 2. Reports the failure probability at the operating temperature (exact and Monte Carlo), the temperatures that meet 10⁻⁶, the flipped-cell statistics, the worst of the other chips and the secret bits. Fig. 52 plots these quantities.


```python
#@title PUF reliability: key failure probability and flipped cells
pr = puf_reliability()
res = puf_residual(DEFAULTS)
ok_T = [T for T, p in zip(pr["temps"], pr["curves"][pr["t"]]) if p < 1e-6]
spec = (pr["temps"] >= 0) & (pr["temps"] <= 85)                       # the specified 0-85 °C
mean_exact = float((np.arange(len(pr["dist"])) * pr["dist"]).sum())
mc_ub = 1 - 0.05 ** (1 / len(pr["errs"]))                # 95 % upper bound on P(fail) when no power-up of the sample failed
def sci1(v, d=0):                                         # 1 + d significant figures: 9.79e-40 -> 1 × 10^-39
    m, e = f"{v:.{d}e}".split("e")
    return f"{m} × 10<sup>{int(e)}</sup>".replace("-", "−")
card(f"Key reliability of this chip, BCH t = {pr['t']} (linear temperature law of the cell model)",
     [(f"P(key fails at one power-up), {pr['temp']} °C", f"<b>{sci1(pr['p_now'])}</b> (exact within the cell model; a figure this small "
       "states only that the model's Gaussian tail lies far below the target, not a property of silicon)"),
      ("Monte Carlo power-ups", f"{(pr['errs'] > pr['t']).sum()} of {len(pr['errs']):,} failed: P(key fails) &lt; {sci1(mc_ub, 1)} at 95 % confidence; "
       "the sample tests the body of the distribution, not its tail"),
      ("temperatures below 10<sup>−6</sup>", f"{ok_T[0]} to {ok_T[-1]} °C" if ok_T else "none"),
      (f"flipped cells per power-up, {pr['temp']} °C", f"mean {pr['errs'].mean():.2f} (Monte Carlo), {mean_exact:.2f} (exact); "
       f"largest seen {pr['errs'].max()}"),
      ("16 other chips, worst over 0–85 °C", f"{sci1(pr['band'][1][spec].max())}"),
      ("secret bits left after publishing <i>h</i>: 95 % lower bound – point estimate", f"<b>{budget(H_TT[0], pr['t'])}–{res}</b> "
       f"(need ≥ {SECRET_REQ}, Section VII-E)")],
     tone="ok" if ok_T and budget(H_TT[0], pr["t"]) >= SECRET_REQ else "bad")
```


<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #eb6834;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Key reliability of this chip, BCH t = 45 (linear temperature law of the cell model)</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">P(key fails at one power-up), 37 °C</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>1 × 10<sup>−39</sup></b> (exact within the cell model; a figure this small states only that the model's Gaussian tail lies far below the target, not a property of silicon)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">Monte Carlo power-ups</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">0 of 4,000 failed: P(key fails) &lt; 7.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> at 95 % confidence; the sample tests the body of the distribution, not its tail</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">temperatures below 10<sup>−6</sup></td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">-40 to 85 °C</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">flipped cells per power-up, 37 °C</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">mean 11.23 (Monte Carlo), 11.24 (exact); largest seen 19</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">16 other chips, worst over 0–85 °C</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">3 × 10<sup>−23</sup></td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">secret bits left after publishing <i>h</i>: 95 % lower bound – point estimate</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>94–137</b> (need ≥ 192, Section VII-E)</td></tr></table></div>

```python

for (t, p), c, ls in zip(pr["curves"].items(), (COL["ok"], COL["bad"], COL["aqua"]), ("-", "--", "-.")):
    a1.plot(pr["temps"], lg(p), color=c, ls=ls, lw=2.0 if t == pr["t"] else 1.4,
            label=f"this chip, $t$ = {t}" + (" (below the plotted range)" if np.all(lg(p) < -24) else ""))
a1.axhline(-6, color=COL["ink"], ls=(0, (1, 1)), lw=0.9); a1.text(25, -5.4, "$10^{-6}$ target", fontsize=9, ha="center")
a1.set_ylim(-24, 0.5); a1.set_xlim(pr["temps"][0], pr["temps"][-1])
a1.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)"); a1.set_ylabel("$\\log_{10}$ P(key fails)"); 
panel(a1, "a", "Key failure vs temperature")
k = np.arange(len(pr["dist"])); lo, hi = max(0, pr["errs"].min() - 3), max(pr["errs"].max(), pr["t"]) + 3
a2.hist(pr["errs"], bins=np.arange(lo, hi + 1) - 0.5, density=True, color=COL["ok"], alpha=0.35, ec=COL["ok"], lw=0.5, label="Monte Carlo power-ups")
a2.plot(k[lo:hi + 1], pr["dist"][lo:hi + 1], color=COL["bad"], lw=1.6, marker="o", ms=2.5, label="exact distribution")
a2.axvline(pr["t"] + 0.5, color=COL["ink"], lw=1.0, ls="--")
a2.text(pr["t"] - 0.6, a2.get_ylim()[1] * 0.97, f"$t$ = {pr['t']}:\ndecoder fails\nbeyond", fontsize=9, ha="right", va="top")
a2.set_xlabel("Flipped cells per power-up"); a2.set_ylabel("Probability"); a2.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="center right")
panel(a2, "b", f"Flipped cells at {pr['temp']} °C")
fig.legend(*a1.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=4, fontsize=8.5, frameon=False, handlelength=2.0)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.5, rect=(0, 0.1, 1, 1)); plt.show()
```
