<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 52.</b> Key-failure probability and flipped cells with the linear temperature law. (a) log₁₀ P(key fails) against temperature: this chip with <i>t</i> = 35 (solid) and 45 (dashed); 16 other chips with <i>t</i> = 45 (band); 10⁻⁶ target (dotted). (b) Flipped cells per power-up at 37 °C: 4,000 Monte Carlo power-ups (bars), exact distribution (dots) and correction limit <i>t</i> (dashed).</p>

**Result.** In the order of the card rows and of the panels of Fig. 52:

* **Operating temperature.** At 37 °C, the exact key-failure probability of this chip is **1 × 10⁻³⁹** per power-up within the cell model. None of the 4,000 Monte Carlo power-ups failed, which bounds *P*<sub>fail</sub> only below 7.5 × 10⁻⁴ (95 % confidence); the exact value rests on the model's tail, which the sample cannot test.
* **Temperature range at *t* = 45.** With the linear law, *P*<sub>fail</sub> remains below 10⁻⁶ over the whole grid, −40 to 85 °C, as predicted (2). This result inherits the law's underestimate of the 85 °C error rate. With the two-component model and the simulated error rates, Section VII-E finds that all of 1,000 simulated chips meet 10⁻⁶ at *t* = 45 from 0 to 85 °C, and 98.9 % at the upper end of the 85 °C error-rate interval (99th percentile of the required *t*: 39, between 33 and 46 over the interval); Section VIII-F finds 100 % at tt and ss with the separate 512-cell corner run, and far fewer at sf, ff and fs.
* **Flipped cells at 37 °C.** The card gives a mean of 11.23 flipped cells per power-up in the Monte Carlo simulation against 11.24 from the exact distribution, and at most 19 flipped cells in any of the 4,000 power-ups, less than half of the 45 that the code corrects.
* **Other chips.** The worst key-failure probability of the 16 other chips over 0–85 °C, with the same law, is 3 × 10⁻²³.
* **Secrecy.** The card gives **94–137** secret bits, from the lower bound to the point estimate, as predicted (4): fewer than the 192 required.
* **Shape over temperature** (Fig. 52(a)). *P*<sub>fail</sub> is lowest at 25 °C and increases steeply on both sides, as predicted (1). With the linear law, even the weaker code, *t* = 35, stays below the target from −40 to 85 °C. The stronger code, *t* = 55, lies below the plotted range at every temperature, but would leave at most 600·*H*<sub>∞</sub> − 550, that is 37, secret bits at the point estimate, far fewer than 192. At every temperature, this chip lies above the band of the 16 other chips, which enters the plotted range only at its two ends, so a code sized on this chip is conservative for the other chips sampled.
* **Distribution of flipped cells** (Fig. 52(b)). The Monte Carlo histogram follows the exact distribution, as predicted (3), and lies far below the correction limit *t* = 45.

**Interpretation.** **At the operating temperature the modelled key-failure probability of this chip lies far below the 10⁻⁶ target**, as far as the cell model's tail can be trusted; the Monte Carlo sample confirms the body of the distribution, not the tail. The margin is smallest at the ends of the temperature range, and there it depends on how the error rate is modelled: the linear law of the cell model, used in this subsection, underestimates the 85 °C error rate, which is why Section VII-E sizes the code with a two-component model over a chip population. The binding limit is secrecy: with the entropy bounded and the hash margin included, *t* = 45 on 600 cells leaves 94–137 secret bits, short of 192, and the conservative *s*<sub>25</sub> = 0.06 would need *t* = 60, which leaves none (Table VIII). Section VIII-F added the process corners and shows that an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C meets the reliability target at every corner with *t* = 17 for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips and leaves 284–352 secret bits on 600 kept cells, and Section XI sizes a complete key generator for the worst corner, with an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C. Within this chip, reliability sets a lower limit on *t* and secrecy an upper limit. Subsection C maps both limits together over temperature and *t*.

### C. Parameter sweeps: security boundaries of both designs

**Goal.** Subsection A judged each design at a single operating point. This subsection measures how far that point lies from the boundary at which a verdict changes. Each of the three experiments below is repeated over a grid of the two parameters that govern it.

**Theory.**

1. **Replica attack: dither amplitude *a*<sub>d</sub> against replica offset *δ*.** As in A4, the attacker's keystream estimate is *K̂* = *K* ⊕ (*D* ⊕ *D*<sub>r</sub>). BM determines the 16-bit LFSR from 2*L* = 32 consecutive correct bits, so a 64-bit window succeeds when the victim bits *D* and the replica bits *D*<sub>r</sub> agree throughout it, or disagree only within its first L + 1 = 17 bits, which BM absorbs into the register's initial state (an error at any later position makes it return a wrong register).
   * The offset *δ*, in % of full scale (FS), is a DC difference between the modulator inputs of the two chips. It acts ahead of the quantiser, changes the trajectories of the loops and therefore decorrelates the two bit streams once it is large enough (Section VI).
   * The dither multiplies the comparator input by 1 + *d* and adds *d*, where *d* ∈ {−*a*<sub>d</sub>, 0, +*a*<sub>d</sub>} is set by a pair of LFSRs with the chip's own seeds (Section V-C). A large *a*<sub>d</sub> decorrelates the chips even at *δ* = 0.

   *Prediction:* the attack succeeds against the original design only at small *δ* combined with small *a*<sub>d</sub>. It succeeds nowhere against the proposal: BM cannot extend a Grain-128a keystream, and even an exact estimate of *D* would expose only the keystream of the one frame whose input the attacker chose, because the per-frame IV changes the keystream of every other frame.
2. **Saturation attack: buffer gain *g* against forced current *I*.**
   * The TIA output is *v* = clip(*V*<sub>CM</sub> + *I*·*R*<sub>TIA</sub>, 0, *V*<sub>DD</sub>), and the modulator input, normalised to full scale, is *u* = *g*(*v* − *V*<sub>CM</sub>)/(*V*<sub>DD</sub>/2). The model uses *V*<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V, *V*<sub>CM</sub> = 0.6 V and *R*<sub>TIA</sub> = 321.88 kΩ (Section V-A).
   * For *I* ≥ *V*<sub>CM</sub>/*R*<sub>TIA</sub> ≈ 1.86 µA the TIA output is at the supply rail, and *u* = *g*.
   * A 1-bit loop with feedback ±1 can track only inputs with |*u*| < 1. For *u* ≥ 1 its bits become constant, the attacker's constant estimate of *D* is correct, and BM recovers the LFSR.

   *Prediction:* the attack succeeds against the original design for *I* ≳ 1.86 µA and *g* ≳ 1. At the design value *g* = 0.5, *u* does not exceed 0.5. The attack succeeds nowhere against the proposal, for the reasons given under experiment 1.
3. **PUF key: temperature *T* against code strength *t*.** *P*<sub>fail</sub>(*T*, *t*) follows from the theory of Subsection B. Rows with 600·*H*<sub>∞</sub> − 10*t* < 192, the secrecy requirement of Section VII-E with *H*<sub>∞</sub> at its 95 % lower bound (0.908 bit), that is *t* ≥ 36, leave too few secret bits. The *design window* is the set of grid points with *P*<sub>fail</sub> < 10⁻⁶ and at least 192 secret bits. *Prediction:* a V-shaped window centred near the enrolment temperature of 25 °C, widening as *t* increases, and bounded at the top by the secrecy limit, which lies below the current *t* = 45. The window is computed with the linear temperature law of the cell model, which underestimates the 85 °C error rate (Subsection B), so it is wider at high temperature than the sizing from the simulated error rates of Section VII-E allows.

**Setup.**

* *Level and settings.* Behavioural model with the post-layout settings of Table VIII at the nominal corner. Every parameter that is not swept keeps its value of Subsection A.
* *Replica and saturation grids.* Each grid point simulates 30,000 modulator clocks (`LAB_N`) of DC input: 0.5 µA for the replica attack, *I* for the saturation attack.
  * Replica grid: *a*<sub>d</sub> ∈ {off, 0.01, 0.022, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4}, where 0.022 is the dither of [1]; *δ* ∈ {0, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1} % FS, where 0.1 % FS is the replica of Subsection A. The victim and the replica have their own dither seeds and noise.
  * Saturation grid: *g* ∈ {0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2}; *I* ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20} µA. The attacker's estimate of *D* is the more frequent bit value.
* *Decision rules.* The attack succeeds against the original design when at least one of the 80 windows of A4 succeeds, that is, when its register predicts the next 512 keystream bits with more than 99 % accuracy; this is the criterion of Section VIII. It succeeds against the proposal only if the estimate agrees with the Grain-128a keystream on more than 97 % of the bits while the counter and MAC are switched off; here they are on.
* *Seeds and repetitions.* Each grid point is a single run with fixed seeds: the victim from `seed` = 2026, the replica with its own dither and noise seeds. There are no repetitions, so a grid point near a boundary may change with the seed.
* *PUF grid.* This chip, *T* from −40 to 80 °C in steps of 10 °C and at 85 °C, and *t* from 10 to 58 in steps of 4, evaluated with the exact distribution of Subsection B.
* *Metrics.* The replica attack is characterised by the fraction *f*<sub>64</sub> of 64-bit windows in which the replica bits equal the victim bits (clocks 200 to 30,000, as in Section VIII-B), the quantity on which BM succeeds or fails; the saturation attack by the longest run of equal modulator bits; and the PUF key by log₁₀ *P*<sub>fail</sub>. Every grid point of the first two grids also receives the verdict of each design. The ring in each map marks the grid point nearest to the current settings. The card above each figure gives the number of grid points at which the attack succeeds, and the verdicts at the ring; for the PUF grid, it gives the largest *t* that leaves 128 secret bits and the extent of the design window in the row of the ring.

> **Next cell.** 1. Defines `replica_experiment`, the replica attack of A4 on 30,000 clocks of DC input, judged for both designs, with the fraction of 64-bit windows in which victim and replica agree. 2. Defines `sweep(kind)`, which runs the replica attack over dither amplitude and replica offset, the saturation attack over buffer gain and forced current, or the PUF key-failure computation over temperature and *t*. The cell only defines functions; no simulation is run.


```python
#@title Sweeps: definitions
def replica_experiment(P, mm_pct, ki_input, Kb, Kp, mac):
    """The attack lab's zero/DC-input replica attack on LAB_N clocks, for both designs' keystreams."""
    u = np.full(LAB_N, s2d(tia(0.0 if ki_input == "zero" else 0.5e-6, P["rtia"]), P["buffer"]))
    Dv = dsm2(u, P, noise_seed=P["seed"])["D"]
    Dr = dsm2(u + mm_pct / 100, P, seeds=(0x2C4D, 0x51E7), noise_seed=P["seed"] + 2)["D"]
    x = (Dv ^ Dr)[200:].astype(np.int64); c = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(x)])
    out = dict(flip=float(np.mean(Dv != Dr)), f64=float(np.mean(c[64:] - c[:-64] == 0)))   # f64: clean 64-bit windows (replica_pairs)
    for name, K in (("base", Kb), ("prop", Kp)):
        kg = Dv ^ K ^ Dr
        w = window_attack(kg, K, P["seed"] + 3); raw = float(np.mean(kg == K))
        out[name] = "breached" if (w["broken"] > 0 if name == "base" else (raw > 0.97 and not mac)) else "safe"
    return out

def sweep(kind, P=None):
    """kind: 'replica' (dither x replica mismatch), 'saturate' (buffer gain x forced current), 'puf' (T x BCH t)."""
    P = {**DEFAULTS, **(P or {})}
    if kind == "puf":
        temps, ts = np.append(np.arange(-40, 81, 10), 85), np.arange(10, 61, 4)
        puf = SRAMPUF(P["chip_seed"], PUF_BITS, P["puf_sigma"], P["puf_bias"], P["puf_tc"])
        w = enroll(puf, P["bch_t"], rng_for(P["chip_seed"] * 7919 + 1))["w"]
        Z = np.zeros((len(ts), len(temps)))
        for i, T in enumerate(temps):
            d = err_dist(puf.p_err(w, T, puf_age(P)))
            for j, t in enumerate(ts):
                Z[j, i] = d[t + 1:].sum()
        weak = np.array([PUF_BITS * min_ent_bit(P["puf_bias"]) - 10 * t < 128 for t in ts])
        return dict(kind=kind, x=temps, y=ts, z=Z, weak=weak, cur=(P["temp"], P["bch_t"]))
    Kb = lfsr16_bits(P["key16"], ID_BITS + LAB_N)[ID_BITS:]
    Kp = simulate(**{**P, "scheme": "proposed", "attack": "none"})["K"][:LAB_N]
    if kind == "replica":
        amps, mms = [0, 0.01, 0.022, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4], [0, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0]
        Z = np.zeros((len(mms), len(amps))); F = np.zeros(Z.shape); VB = np.empty(Z.shape, object); VP = np.empty(Z.shape, object)
        for j, m in enumerate(mms):
            for i, a in enumerate(amps):
                X = replica_experiment({**P, "dither": a > 0, "dither_amp": a or P["dither_amp"]}, m, "dc", Kb, Kp, P["mac"])
                Z[j, i], F[j, i], VB[j, i], VP[j, i] = X["flip"], X["f64"], X["base"], X["prop"]
        return dict(kind=kind, x=amps, y=mms, z=Z, f64=F, vb=VB, vp=VP, cur=(P["dither_amp"] if P["dither"] else 0, ATK_DEF["mismatch"]))
    if kind == "saturate":
        gains, cur = [0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2], [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16, 20]
        Z = np.zeros((len(cur), len(gains))); VB = np.empty(Z.shape, object); VP = np.empty(Z.shape, object)
        for j, c in enumerate(cur):
            for i, g in enumerate(gains):
                Q = {**P, "buffer": g}
                D = dsm2(np.full(LAB_N, s2d(tia(c * 1e-6, Q["rtia"]), g)), Q, noise_seed=Q["seed"])["D"]
                guess = 1 if D.mean() >= 0.5 else 0
                Z[j, i] = longest_run(D)
                kb = D ^ Kb ^ guess; VB[j, i] = "breached" if window_attack(kb, Kb, Q["seed"] + 23)["broken"] > 0 else "safe"
                kp = D ^ Kp ^ guess; VP[j, i] = "breached" if (np.mean(kp == Kp) > 0.97 and not P["mac"]) else "safe"
        return dict(kind=kind, x=gains, y=cur, z=Z, vb=VB, vp=VP, cur=(P["buffer"], P["force_uA"]))
    raise ValueError(kind)
```

> **Next cell.** 1. Defines `show_sweep`, which prints a card with the number of grid points at which the attack succeeds (or the PUF design window) and draws one sweep as a map, with a ring at the grid point nearest to the current settings. No simulation is run.


```python
#@title Sweeps: plotting helper
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

def show_sweep(o, report=True, draw=True):
    """The card of one sweep (report) and its map (draw). Replica attack: (a) the clean-window fraction f64, (b) the
    original design's verdict. Saturation attack: one map, the run length with the original design's breached points
    hatched and the predicted boundary dashed. PUF key: the key-failure probability with the secrecy rows and the window."""
    kind = o["kind"]
    if kind == "puf":                                  # secrecy rows from the bounded budget of Section VII-E
        o["weak"] = np.array([budget(H_TT[0], int(t)) < SECRET_REQ for t in o["y"]])
    nx, ny = len(o["x"]), len(o["y"])
    ci = int(np.argmin(np.abs(np.array(o["x"], float) - o["cur"][0]))); cj = int(np.argmin(np.abs(np.array(o["y"], float) - o["cur"][1])))
    if report and kind != "puf":                       # count the breached grid points of each design
        nb_, np_ = int((o["vb"] == "breached").sum()), int((o["vp"] == "breached").sum())
        rows = [("original S-DSM", f"<b>{nb_} of {o['vb'].size}</b>"), ("proposed", f"<b>{np_} of {o['vp'].size}</b>"),
                ("at the ring (nearest grid point to the current settings)", f"original {o['vb'][cj, ci]}, proposed {o['vp'][cj, ci]}")]
        if kind == "replica":
            F, br = o["f64"], o["vb"] == "breached"
            rows += [("clean 64-bit windows f<sub>64</sub> at the ring", f"{100 * F[cj, ci]:.3f} %"),
                     ("grid points with f<sub>64</sub> = 0 (no clean window in 30,000 clocks)", f"{int((F == 0).sum())} of {F.size}"),
                     ("f<sub>64</sub> at the breached points", f"{100 * F[br].min():.3f} to {100 * F[br].max():.2f} %; {int((F[br] == 0).sum())} of "
                      f"{int(br.sum())} breached points have f<sub>64</sub> = 0" if br.any() else "none"),
                     ("f<sub>64</sub> with an identical replica (δ = 0), a<sub>d</sub> = " + ", ".join("off" if v == 0 else f"{v:g}" for v in o["x"]),
                      ", ".join(f"{100 * v:.2f}" for v in F[0]) + " %"),
                     ("largest f<sub>64</sub> at δ > 0", f"{100 * F[1:].max():.2f} %")]
        card(f"{'Replica' if kind == 'replica' else 'Saturation'} attack: grid points at which the attack succeeds", rows,
             tone="bad" if nb_ else "ok")
    elif report:                                       # the design window at the ring's row, and the secrecy limit on the grid
        win_T = np.array(o["x"])[(~o["weak"][cj]) & (o["z"][cj] < 1e-6)]
        card("PUF key: design window (linear temperature law)",
             [(f"largest t on the grid that leaves ≥ {SECRET_REQ} secret bits (95 % lower bound of the min-entropy)",
               f"{int(np.array(o['y'])[~o['weak']].max())}"),
              (f"grid temperatures in the window at t = {o['y'][cj]} (the ring's row)",
               f"{win_T.min()} to {win_T.max()} °C" if len(win_T) else "none")])
    if not draw:
        return
    ring = lambda ax: (ax.plot(ci, cj, "o", ms=12, mfc="none", mec="white", mew=3.2),
                       ax.plot(ci, cj, "o", ms=12, mfc="none", mec=COL["ink"], mew=1.4))
    def hatch(ax, V, ec):
        for j in range(ny):
            for i in range(nx):
                if V[j, i]:
                    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i - 0.5, j - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, hatch="///", ec=ec, lw=0))
    def axes_style(ax, xlabel, ylabel, yticks=True):
        ax.grid(False); ax.tick_params(top=False, right=False, direction="out")
        ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, nx, 1), minor=True); ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, ny, 1), minor=True)
        ax.grid(which="minor", color="white", linewidth=0.7, linestyle="-"); ax.tick_params(which="minor", length=0)   # thin cell borders
        sx = max(1, int(np.ceil(nx / 6))); sy = max(1, int(np.ceil(ny / 9)))     # thin the ticks so labels stay >= 9 pt
        ax.set_xticks(range(0, nx, sx), [("off" if (kind == "replica" and v == 0) else f"{v:g}".replace("-", "−")) for v in o["x"]][::sx], fontsize=9)
        ax.set_yticks(range(0, ny, sy), [f"{v:g}" for v in o["y"]][::sy] if yticks else [], fontsize=9)
        ax.set_xlabel(xlabel, fontsize=9.5)
        if ylabel:
            ax.set_ylabel(ylabel, fontsize=9.5)
    breached = lambda k: np.vectorize(lambda v: v == "breached")(o[k]).astype(float)
    ring_h = plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="none", ms=9, mfc="none", mec=COL["ink"], mew=1.4, label="current settings")
    def verdict(ax, key, lab, title, xlabel, ylabel):               # one design's verdict at every grid point
        V = breached(key)
        ax.imshow(V, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap=ListedColormap(["#dbe8fb", COL["bad"]]), vmin=0, vmax=1)
        hatch(ax, V, "white")
        ring(ax); axes_style(ax, xlabel, ylabel, yticks=ylabel is not None)
        panel(ax, lab, title + f": {int(V.sum())} of {V.size}")
    verdict_legend = [Patch(fc="#dbe8fb", ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.5, label="safe"),
                      Patch(fc=COL["bad"], ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.5, hatch="///", label="breached: the attack succeeds")]
    if kind == "replica":
        XL, YL = "Dither amplitude $a_{\\rm d}$", "Replica offset $\\delta$ (% FS)"
        fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(W2, 6.4))
        a0, a1, a2, a3 = axs.ravel()
        im = a0.imshow(o["z"], origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="Blues", vmin=0)        # (a) replica bits that differ
        cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=a0, fraction=0.06, pad=0.03); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9, direction="out")
        cb.set_label("Replica bits wrong", fontsize=9); cb.outline.set_linewidth(0.6)
        ring(a0); axes_style(a0, XL, YL)
        panel(a0, "a", "Replica bits that differ from the victim")
        FL = np.log10(np.maximum(o["f64"], 1e-5))                          # (b) f64 = 0 is drawn at 10^-5
        im = a1.imshow(FL, origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="Blues", vmin=-5, vmax=-1)
        cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=a1, fraction=0.06, pad=0.03); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9, direction="out")
        cb.set_ticks([-5, -4, -3, -2, -1], labels=["0", "0.01", "0.1", "1", "10"]); cb.ax.set_title("$f_{64}$ (%)", fontsize=9)
        cb.outline.set_linewidth(0.6)
        cb.ax.axhline(np.log10(0.0013), color=COL["bad"], lw=2.0, ls="--", zorder=10)     # the theory's protection level (replica_pairs)
        hatch(a1, breached("vb"), COL["bad"])
        ring(a1); axes_style(a1, XL, YL)
        panel(a1, "b", "Clean 64-bit windows $f_{64}$")
        verdict(a2, "vb", "c", "Original S-DSM, breached", XL, YL)
        verdict(a3, "vp", "d", "Proposed, breached", XL, YL)
        fig.legend(handles=verdict_legend + [plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["bad"], ls="--", lw=1.6, label="$f_{64}$ = 0.13 %: 80-window protection level (colour bar)"), ring_h],
                   loc="lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False, fontsize=9, columnspacing=1.2)
        fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, h_pad=1.0, rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))
    elif kind == "saturate":
        XL, YL = "S2D buffer gain $g$", "Forced current $I$ (µA)"
        fig, (ax, a2, a3) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(W2, 3.4), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.35, 1, 1]))
        im = ax.imshow(np.log10(1 + o["z"]), origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="Blues", vmin=0)
        cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.06, pad=0.03); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9, direction="out")
        cb.set_label("$\\log_{10}$(1 + longest run of equal bits)", fontsize=9); cb.outline.set_linewidth(0.6)
        hatch(ax, breached("vb"), COL["bad"])
        gx = float(np.interp(1.0, o["x"], np.arange(nx))) - 0.5            # predicted boundary: g = 1 (between grid columns)
        iy = float(np.interp(VCM / DEFAULTS["rtia"] * 1e6, o["y"], np.arange(ny)))   # and I = V_CM / R_TIA
        ax.plot([gx, gx, nx - 0.5], [ny - 0.5, iy, iy], color=COL["bad"], ls="--", lw=1.6)
        ring(ax); axes_style(ax, XL, YL)
        panel(ax, "a", "Longest run, original")
        verdict(a2, "vb", "b", "Original", XL, None)
        verdict(a3, "vp", "c", "Proposed", XL, None)
        fig.legend(handles=verdict_legend + [plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["bad"], ls="--", lw=1.6, label="predicted boundary"), ring_h],
                   loc="lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False, fontsize=9, columnspacing=1.2)
        fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, rect=(0, 0.09, 1, 1))
    else:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.6))
        im = ax.imshow(np.log10(np.maximum(o["z"], 1e-20)), origin="lower", aspect="auto", cmap="Blues_r", vmin=-20)
        cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.06, pad=0.03); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=9, direction="out")
        cb.set_label("$\\log_{10}$ P(key fails)", fontsize=9); cb.outline.set_linewidth(0.6)
        for j in np.flatnonzero(o["weak"]):
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((-0.5, j - 0.5), nx, 1, fill=False, hatch="///", ec=COL["ink"], lw=0))
        win = (~o["weak"][:, None]) & (o["z"] < 1e-6)
        ax.contour(np.arange(nx), np.arange(ny), win.astype(float), levels=[0.5], colors=COL["ink"], linewidths=2)
        ring(ax); axes_style(ax, "Temperature (°C)", "BCH correction $t$")
        ax.set_title("Key-failure probability per power-up", loc="left", fontsize=10)
        fig.legend(handles=[Patch(fc="white", ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.5, hatch="///", label=f"< {SECRET_REQ} secret bits left"),
                            plt.Line2D([], [], color=COL["ink"], lw=2, label="design window"),
                            plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="none", ms=9, mfc="none", mec=COL["ink"], mew=1.4, label="current")],
                   loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
        fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1))
    plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 53.</b> Replica attack sweep (30,000 clocks per grid point). Horizontal: dither amplitude <i>a</i><sub>d</sub>; vertical: replica offset <i>δ</i>. (a) Fraction of replica bits that differ from the victim's. (b) Clean-window fraction <i>f</i><sub>64</sub>, logarithmic with 0 at the bottom; orange mark: 80-window protection level (Section VIII-B). (c), (d) Verdict on the original and the proposed design. Hatched: attack succeeds; ring: current settings.</p>

**Result.**

* **Original design** (Fig. 53(c)). The attack succeeds at **10 of the 56** grid points: at four points with an identical replica (*δ* = 0), without dither and with *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.01, 0.022 and 0.1; at *δ* = 0.01 % FS without dither and with *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.05; at *δ* = 0.03 % FS without dither and with *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.01 and 0.022; and at *δ* = 0.1 % FS with *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.1. No point with *a*<sub>d</sub> ≥ 0.2, and no point in the *δ* = 0.001 and 0.003 % FS rows, is breached. At the working settings (*a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.022, *δ* = 0.1 % FS) the attacker of [1] does not break the original design (one seed).
* **Proposal** (Fig. 53(d)). The attack succeeds at 0 of the 56 points: the whole map is light, because a replica's bits, however close to the victim's, do not reveal a keystream that Berlekamp-Massey could rebuild. The two verdict maps side by side show where the original design's protection depends on the analog settings and that the proposal's does not.
* **Decorrelation** (Fig. 53(a)). For *δ* ≥ 0.01 % FS the replica bits differ from the victim bits on close to half of the clocks. Only in the bottom rows does the replica agree with the victim on substantially more than half of the clocks, unless the dither is strong. The fraction of differing bits alone does not decide the attack, however: it is the clean windows of panel (b) that the attack uses.
* **Clean windows** (Fig. 53(b)). With an identical replica (*δ* = 0), *f*<sub>64</sub> is 6.80, 5.99, 3.55, 2.06 and 0.20 % for *a*<sub>d</sub> = off, 0.01, 0.022, 0.05 and 0.1, and 0.00 % for stronger dither; the attack succeeds at four of these five points. At every *δ* > 0 the replica bits differ from the victim bits on close to half of the clocks and *f*<sub>64</sub> is at most 0.11 %, below the 0.13 % at which the theory of Section VIII-B expects the 80-window attacker of [1] to fail (Section VIII-B defines protection by a stricter, full-scan attacker); 42 of the 56 points have no clean window at all. Yet 6 of the 10 breached points lie at *δ* > 0, one of them with *f*<sub>64</sub> = 0 (card): the theory's bound is a lower bound, because BM also succeeds on windows whose only errors lie within their first 17 bits, and a single pair per grid point can be lucky where the theory, an average over pairs, predicts protection.
* **Comparison with the prediction.** Prediction (1) holds only in part: every successful point has *a*<sub>d</sub> ≤ 0.1, but the successes extend to *δ* = 0.1 % FS, the offset assumed for the replica, and include points at *δ* = 0.01 to 0.1 % FS where the replica bits differ from the victim bits on close to half of the clocks and *f*<sub>64</sub> is at most 0.11 %. With one seed per grid point (Setup), these isolated successes mark offsets at which the protection is not reliable rather than a sharp boundary. The *δ* = 0 row also agrees with Section VIII-B: without an input offset, two chips that differ only in their noise and dither sequences disagree on about a quarter of the bits but leave enough clean windows, and the attack succeeds against the original design with the dither of [1].
* **Margin.** With the dither of [1], the attack succeeds at *δ* = 0 and again at *δ* = 0.03 % FS, one grid step below the assumed 0.1 % FS, although the offsets 0.001 to 0.01 % FS are safe; at *δ* = 0.1 % FS it succeeds with the stronger dither *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.1. The assumed offset therefore leaves a margin of one grid step, not a wide one.

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 55.</b> PUF key sweep (this chip, linear temperature law). Colour: log₁₀ of the key-failure probability per power-up (clipped at −20) against temperature and BCH strength <i>t</i>; hatched: fewer than 192 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound; thick outline: design window; ring: grid point nearest to the current <i>t</i> and 37 °C.</p>

**Result.** The map of Fig. 55 uses the linear temperature law and is therefore optimistic at 85 °C.

* **Secrecy rows.** The largest *t* on the grid that leaves at least 192 secret bits at the lower bound is 34; the hatched rows are *t* ≥ 38, as predicted (3).
* **Shape of the window.** The window is V-shaped. It is narrowest at small *t*, at the 20 and 30 °C columns, widens as *t* increases, and is bounded at the top by the secrecy limit.
* **Working point.** The working setting *t* = 45 lies between the grid rows *t* = 42 and *t* = 46, both beyond the secrecy limit. The ring, at the grid point *t* = 46 and 40 °C nearest to the current *t* = 45 and 37 °C, falls in a hatched row, so the card reports no grid temperature in the window in that row. In the top row of the window, *t* = 34, and with the linear law, the window spans the whole grid from −40 to 85 °C.

**Interpretation.** The sweeps convert the verdicts of Subsection A into margins.

* **Original design: analog margins.** Against the analog attacks as [1] performs them (windowed Berlekamp-Massey on one frame), the original design is protected only by two analog quantities. The replica offset is a property of the attacker's own replica, and the buffer gain is a design choice made for the signal path, not for security. Within this model the gain margin is wide, a factor of two, but the offset margin is not: with the dither of [1] the replica attack already succeeds at 0.03 % FS, one grid step below the assumed 0.1 % FS, and at 0.1 % FS itself with *a*<sub>d</sub> = 0.1. They are, however, the only barrier, and an attacker able to trim the input offset of the replica can search for a matching value. The attack lab of Section IX-A includes such a search (trims of 0, ±0.03, ±0.1 and ±0.2 % FS with a scan of every position) and finds the key; the maps here use the attacker of [1] alone, so they show the margin against that attacker, not against a competent one.
* **Proposal: no analog margin required.** The attacks succeed against the proposal at none of the 137 replica and saturation grid points. None of its verdicts depends on these parameters.
* **Proposal: the PUF window.** The one design constraint that the proposal adds is the PUF window. At the operating temperature it is met with a wide margin, and the margin decreases towards the ends of the temperature range. With the two-component cell model over a chip population instead of the linear law, the reliability limit over 0–85 °C (99th percentile *t* = 39, up to 46 over the 85 °C error-rate interval; Section VII-E) lies above the secrecy limit (*t* = 35 at the lower bound): for 600 cells enrolled at 25 °C the window closes, and the enrolment at −40 and 85 °C of Section VIII-F reopens it (*t* = 17 against a limit of 26 on 600 kept cells).

### Summary of Section IX

1. **Verdicts.** Of the 15 attacks, **11 succeed against the original design and 0 against the proposal** (Table XIII), as predicted. Seven recover or leak the data of the original design, because its key is short and stored, its keystream linear and its keystream repeated whenever the session nonce repeats: brute-force search (A2), Berlekamp-Massey recovery (A3), the three attacks of [1] carried out by a competent attacker (A4 replica with a full scan, A5 same key and message, A6 saturation with multi-frame voting), key extraction (A7) and keystream reuse (A15). Four place fake data on the server, because the original design has neither an integrity nor a freshness check: spoofing (A8), the clone (A9), replay (A13) and bit-flipping (A14). The receiver of the proposal detects and rejects five attacks.
2. **Analog attacks on the original design.** Against the attacker of [1], the original design is protected only by analog margins, which a competent attacker removes (Section IX-A):
   * the replica attack succeeds at 10 of 56 grid points, all with a dither amplitude of at most 0.1 and a replica offset of at most 0.1 % FS, including 0.03 % FS with the dither of [1] (Fig. 53);
   * the saturation attack succeeds at 21 of 81 points, all with a buffer gain of at least 1.0 and a forced current of at least 2 µA (Fig. 54);
   * neither attack succeeds against the proposal at any of these points.
3. **Helper data.** None of the three helper-data attacks recovers the key or passes undetected. Tampering is detected. Publishing the helper data of the working setting *t* = 45 leaves 94–137 secret bits (95 % lower bound to point estimate), short of the 192 that a 128-bit key with the hash margin requires (Section VII-E). The manipulation oracle accepted 0 of 200 tampered power-ups and answered all 200 queries exactly as a chip with a different fingerprint did, so it reveals nothing.
4. **Key reliability.** The new failure mode is rare at the operating temperature. At 37 °C and *t* = 45, the cell model gives a key-failure probability of 1 × 10⁻³⁹ per power-up, and none of 4,000 Monte Carlo power-ups failed (mean 11.23 flipped cells, at most 19), which bounds it only below 7.5 × 10⁻⁴. With the linear law the probability remains below 10⁻⁶ from −40 to 85 °C (Fig. 52), but the law underestimates the 85 °C error rate: with the two-component model, 98.9–100 % of 1,000 simulated chips meet 10⁻⁶ at *t* = 45 at tt (Table VIII), and no 600-cell code enrolled at 25 °C leaves 192 secret bits with that reliability (Fig. 55). Both requirements are met by the enrolment at −40 and 85 °C of Section VIII-F and by the compiled codes of Section XI.

The security of the proposal therefore rests on no analog margin of the signal path, but on the PUF key generator (SRAM cells and decoder), Grain-128a, the MAC and the counter. Section X determines what these blocks cost in area and power in SKY130.

# **X. Implementation cost on SKY130**
---
**Question.** What do the additional security functions of the proposal cost in SKY130 standard-cell area and gate-level power, and how many bits must they send, compared with the S-DSM of [1] and with the conventional alternative, an on-chip Trivium?

**Why it matters.** The case made in [1] for the S-DSM rests on efficiency: its security adds 24 µW, whereas an on-chip Trivium adds 220 µW (Fig. 4(a) of [1]). The proposal replaces the 16-bit keystream LFSR by Grain-128a with its message authentication code (MAC), a frame counter, a session nonce and a 128-bit key register. The cost claims of the abstract (the area and power of the block, and a wireless-energy advantage over a conventional cipher) must therefore rest on a design that is checked against published test vectors, laid out and simulated at gate level in SKY130, not on a gate-count estimate.

**What it takes from earlier sections.** The composition of the keystream block of the proposal (Section IV); the block powers measured in [1] (Fig. 4(a) of [1]) and its energy model (Fig. 4(b) of [1]), which Section VI reproduces; and the SkyWater SKY130 process design kit (PDK), the open-source tools, the Magic design-rule deck and the layout viewer installed and used in Section VII.

**Roadmap.** The section follows the digital flow from register-transfer level (RTL) to energy, one step per subsection:

* **A. The designs and their RTL:** the security blocks compared, written in Verilog, each in two forms: for one keystream bit per clock, and in a low-power form (radix 16, clock-gated) that applies the same techniques to every design.
* **B. Verification and synthesis:** each design checked bit for bit against published test vectors, at RTL and after synthesis, and its area on `sky130_fd_sc_hd` (Table XIV).
* **C. Place and route and sign-off:** the low-power block of the proposal carried to a layout, checked for design rules, antenna effects and timing, and re-simulated (Fig. 56).
* **D. Gate-level power:** the power of every design in both forms, from the same gate-level flow under identical conditions (Table XV), and where the power of the proposal goes (Table XVI).
* **E. A figure of merit across processes, and wireless energy:** what the difference between SKY130 and the 65 nm process of [1] changes and what it does not; a figure of merit, FOM = E<sub>bit</sub>/(L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> S K), that compares designs across processes without scaling any number or using any modelled one; and the bits each design sends for the same information at OSR 50, against the conventional design of [1] and an information-equivalent one (Table XVIII, Fig. 58).
* **F. Power breakdown of the chip:** the result drawn in the form of Fig. 4(a) of [1] (Fig. 59).
* **G. Complete system power:** the chip of [1] block by block with each security block, every number's source stated and none scaled, and the proposal compared with [1] both with actual numbers and under strictly equal treatment (Table XIX).

A summary with the numbered findings closes the section.

### A. The designs and their RTL

**Goal.** Describe every security block to be compared in synthesisable Verilog, so that the area and the power of all of them come from the same flow and the same standard-cell library.

**Setup.** Four designs, written as five Verilog top-level modules, are described at RTL. All are clocked at the modulator clock of [1], 10 MHz, and load their key and initialisation vector (IV) in parallel in one clock.

* **S-DSM** [1] (`sdsm_ks`): three 16-bit linear-feedback shift registers (LFSRs) with the polynomial $x^{16} + x^{14} + x^{13} + x^{11} + 1$, bit-exact with the model of Section V: one generates the keystream, which is XORed with the modulator bit, and two generate the dither. A zero seed is replaced by 1 to avoid the all-zero lock-up state.
* **Trivium**, radix 1 (`trivium_r1`): the 288-bit state of the specification, loaded with the 80-bit key and the 80-bit IV, followed by 4 × 288 = 1,152 initialisation clocks without output, then one keystream bit per clock. It is the conventional reference of [1].
* **Grain-128a** [6], built on one core (`grain_core`): a 128-bit nonlinear feedback shift register (NFSR) and a 128-bit LFSR, with the output function $h$ and the feedback functions $f$ and $g$ of the specification. A parameter W sets the number of pre-output bits per clock; for W = 2 the core evaluates two consecutive steps in the same clock, which is possible because every tap of the second step lies in the current state. Two forms are synthesised:
  * *encryption only* (`grain128a_enc1x`, W = 1): 256 initialisation clocks, then one keystream bit per clock, for reference;
  * *authentication mode* (`grain128a_auth2x`, "Grain-128a + MAC, 2×"): W = 2, so that each modulator clock yields one keystream bit (the even pre-output bit) and one MAC bit (the odd bit). The MAC (`grain_mac`) consists of a 32-bit accumulator and a 32-bit shift register, preloaded with the first 64 pre-output bits in 32 clocks after the 128 initialisation clocks; for each message bit equal to 1 the shift register is added to the accumulator, and the accumulator holds the 32-bit tag after the padding bit. A frame therefore starts 1 + 128 + 32 = 161 clocks after the load.
* **The complete keystream block of the proposal** (`secure_ks_top`): Grain-128a + MAC 2×; the 128-bit key register, shifted in serially from the fuzzy extractor once per power-up (128 clocks); the 32-bit session nonce, shifted in once per session (32 clocks), which also presets the 32-bit frame counter so that the first frame of a session uses counter 0; the 31-bit chip nonce N<sub>c</sub>, shifted in once per session (31 clocks) from the hash of the raw power-up read; the counter, incremented at the start of every frame; the IV, formed as 1 ‖ nonce ‖ counter ‖ N<sub>c</sub> as in the model; and the two dither LFSRs.

**Low-power forms.** Written for one keystream bit per clock, every design clocks all its flip-flops at 10 MHz, and the power of a standard-cell block is mostly that of its clocked flip-flops (Subsection D). Each design is therefore also written in a low-power form (`lowpower.v`), bit-exact with the form above and with the same ports, so that every design receives the same two techniques and none is compared in a form the others are denied:

* *Parallel state update (radix 16).* The cipher computes 16 keystream bits per state update and updates its state once every 16 clocks; an output multiplexer delivers one bit per 10 MHz clock. The S-DSM's three LFSRs advance 16 steps per update (`sdsm_lp`); Trivium computes 16 bits per update (`trivium_lp`, 72 initialisation clocks instead of 1,152); Grain-128a computes 32 pre-output bits, 16 keystream and 16 MAC bits, per update (`grain128a_lp`), so that a frame starts 11 clocks after the load instead of 161. The MAC buffers the 16 message bits of each update and adds them in one cycle, its logic held still in the other 15 (operand isolation).
* *Clock gating.* Each register receives a clock edge only in the cycles in which it is written, through an integrated clock-gating cell (`sky130_fd_sc_hd__dlclkp_1`): the state registers once every 16 clocks, and in the proposal (`secure_ks_lp`) the key, the two nonces and the counter only when they are loaded or incremented.

The clock-gating cells are instantiated for the implementation (`define ICG_CELLS`); for verification with the single-clock simulator of Subsection B, the same registers are written as enabled flip-flops, and the gated netlist itself is re-simulated after layout (Subsection C). A next-state value that is loaded is masked with the load signal on a kept net, so that a gate-level simulation starting from undefined flip-flops loads exactly as a fabricated circuit would.

Four parts of the proposal are not in these blocks. Three of them run once at power-up: the SRAM-PUF array, the BCH decoder and the hash. The decoder is generated and synthesised by the compiler of Section XI, which also synthesises the hash and collects the complete area (XI-E). The fourth is the per-frame MAC alignment: lock-step hardware would need a 32-bit delay line, estimated at about 170 gate equivalents (GE, defined in Subsection B), which is not included in the area.

Each design has a Python reference model, checked against the published test vectors: Table 3 and Appendix A of the Grain-128a specification [6], and the eSTREAM Trivium vectors.

> **Next cell.** Writes the RTL and verification flow to `rtl_flow.py`: 1. the Verilog of every design; 2. the Python reference models and the published test vectors; 3. the AIGER simulator; 4. the Yosys scripts.


```python
%%writefile rtl_flow.py
"""rtl_flow.py - RTL, verification and SKY130 synthesis helpers for the Code-a-Chip notebook.

Hardware cost of three ways to encrypt a 1-bit delta-sigma modulator stream:
  (a) S-DSM (ESSERC'25): modulator bit XOR a 16-bit LFSR keystream, plus two 16-bit dither LFSRs
  (b) Trivium, radix 1 (1 keystream bit per clock)
  (c) proposal: Grain-128a keyed from a PUF, authentication mode, 2 pre-output bits per modulator
      clock (even bits encrypt, odd bits feed the 32-bit MAC), with a 32-bit frame counter and a
      32-bit nonce forming the IV.

Standard library + numpy only. Every function that runs Yosys takes the binary name (`yosys` or
`yowasp-yosys`) and the liberty path as arguments; nothing here hard-codes a machine path.

Verification: the default engine ('aig') has Yosys write the design (RTL, or the synthesized sky130
netlist read with the liberty cell functions) as an AIGER file, which AigSim runs cycle by cycle in
numpy, every test job in its own bit lane and flip-flops starting from random values. It is needed
because yowasp-yosys (the WASM build used in Colab) has no `sim` command. Where `sim` exists,
run_all() also replays the same jobs as Verilog testbenches under Yosys `sim` ('yosys-sim').

Typical use (notebook):
    import rtl_flow as R
    res = R.run_all('yowasp-yosys', LIB, 'rtl_build')   # verify + synthesize everything
    print(R.area_table(res))

Bit conventions
  Grain-128a: as in the paper's test vectors (and model.js). Ports are declared [0:127] / [0:95], so
    a hex literal puts k_0 / IV_0 in the MSB (index 0) and port bit i is k_i / IV_i. The tag port is
    [0:31] with t_0 in the MSB, i.e. it prints as the paper's 8 hex digits.
  Trivium: the RTL follows the specification, port bit key[i] / iv[i] loads s_i / s_(93+i). The
    eSTREAM test vectors were produced by the reference code, which reverses the key/IV and maps bit
    sequences to bytes LSB first (see trivium.c's header comment); trivium_estream_bits() and
    trivium_bits_to_bytes() convert between the two.
  LFSR16: model.js class LFSR16, out = s & 1, s <- (s >> 1) | ((s ^ s>>2 ^ s>>3 ^ s>>5) & 1) << 15,
    seed 0 replaced by 1.
"""
import json
import os
import random
import re
import subprocess
import time

import numpy as np

# =====================================================================================
# 1. Verilog sources
# =====================================================================================
VERILOG = {}

VERILOG['lfsr16.v'] = r'''
// 16-bit LFSR, bit-exact with model.js class LFSR16 (x^16+x^14+x^13+x^11+1, right-shift form).
// out is the current bit (the model's bit() returns s & 1 and then shifts).
module lfsr16 (
  input         clk,
  input         load,              // synchronous seed load
  input  [15:0] seed,
  output        out
);
  reg [15:0] s;
  assign out = s[0];
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) s <= (seed == 16'd0) ? 16'd1 : seed;          // zero seed -> 1 (no lock-up)
    else      s <= {s[0] ^ s[2] ^ s[3] ^ s[5], s[15:1]};
endmodule
'''

VERILOG['sdsm_ks.v'] = r'''
// (a) ESSERC'25 S-DSM: c = d XOR LFSR16(key16); two more LFSR16s drive the dither
// (model.js dsm2: dither = amp * (l1.bit() - l2.bit())).
module sdsm_ks (
  input         clk,
  input         load,              // load the three seeds
  input  [15:0] key16, seed1, seed2,
  input         d,                 // modulator output bit
  output        c,                 // encrypted bit
  output        dith1, dith2       // dither bits
);
  wire k;
  lfsr16 u_key (.clk(clk), .load(load), .seed(key16), .out(k));
  lfsr16 u_d1  (.clk(clk), .load(load), .seed(seed1), .out(dith1));
  lfsr16 u_d2  (.clk(clk), .load(load), .seed(seed2), .out(dith2));
  assign c = d ^ k;
endmodule
'''

VERILOG['trivium_r1.v'] = r'''
// (b) Trivium (De Canniere & Preneel, eSTREAM), radix 1: one keystream bit per clock.
// s[1:288] uses the specification's numbering. load copies key/iv into the state (parallel load),
// then 4 x 288 = 1152 initialisation clocks run without output; ready marks z = z_1, z_2, ...
module trivium_r1 (
  input         clk,
  input         load,
  input  [1:80] key,               // key[i] -> s_i
  input  [1:80] iv,                // iv[i]  -> s_(93+i)
  output        z,
  output        ready
);
  reg [1:288] s;
  reg [10:0]  cnt;
  reg         busy;
  wire t1 = s[66]  ^ s[93];
  wire t2 = s[162] ^ s[177];
  wire t3 = s[243] ^ s[288];
  assign z     = t1 ^ t2 ^ t3;
  assign ready = ~busy;
  wire n1 = t1 ^ (s[91]  & s[92])  ^ s[171];
  wire n2 = t2 ^ (s[175] & s[176]) ^ s[264];
  wire n3 = t3 ^ (s[286] & s[287]) ^ s[69];
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin
      s    <= {key, 13'd0, iv, 4'd0, 108'd0, 3'b111};
      cnt  <= 11'd0;
      busy <= 1'b1;
    end else begin
      s <= {n3, s[1:92], n1, s[94:176], n2, s[178:287]};
      if (busy) begin
        cnt <= cnt + 11'd1;
        if (cnt == 11'd1151) busy <= 1'b0;
      end
    end
endmodule
'''

VERILOG['grain128a.v'] = r'''
// Grain-128a (Agren, Hell, Johansson, Meier 2011). Index i of b / s is b_(t+i) / s_(t+i);
// [0:N] ranges put index 0 in the MSB, so hex literals follow the paper (k_0 = MSB).

// Pre-output generator: NFSR b, LFSR s, W = 1 or 2 pre-output bits per clock (y[0] = y_t,
// y[1] = y_(t+1)). load copies key / IV in parallel (s_96..s_126 = 1, s_127 = 0); while init is
// high the pre-output is fed back into both registers.
module grain_core #(parameter W = 1) (
  input           clk,
  input           load,
  input           init,
  input  [0:127]  key,
  input  [0:95]   iv,
  output [0:W-1]  y
);
  reg [0:127] b, s;
  // One step at the current offset: {y, s_t+128 (LFSR f), b_t+128 (NFSR g + s_t)}.
  function [0:2] step(input [0:127] bb, input [0:127] ss);
    reg h;
    begin
      h = (bb[12] & ss[8]) ^ (ss[13] & ss[20]) ^ (bb[95] & ss[42]) ^ (ss[60] & ss[79])
        ^ (bb[12] & bb[95] & ss[94]);
      step[0] = h ^ ss[93] ^ bb[2] ^ bb[15] ^ bb[36] ^ bb[45] ^ bb[64] ^ bb[73] ^ bb[89];
      step[1] = ss[0] ^ ss[7] ^ ss[38] ^ ss[70] ^ ss[81] ^ ss[96];
      step[2] = ss[0] ^ bb[0] ^ bb[26] ^ bb[56] ^ bb[91] ^ bb[96]
              ^ (bb[3] & bb[67]) ^ (bb[11] & bb[13]) ^ (bb[17] & bb[18]) ^ (bb[27] & bb[59])
              ^ (bb[40] & bb[48]) ^ (bb[61] & bb[65]) ^ (bb[68] & bb[84])
              ^ (bb[88] & bb[92] & bb[93] & bb[95])
              ^ (bb[22] & bb[24] & bb[25]) ^ (bb[70] & bb[78] & bb[82]);
    end
  endfunction
  wire [0:2] r0 = step(b, s);              // step t
  wire [0:2] r1 = step(b << 1, s << 1);    // step t+1 (taps <= 97, all in the current state)
  wire fs0 = r0[1] ^ (init & r0[0]), fb0 = r0[2] ^ (init & r0[0]);
  wire fs1 = r1[1] ^ (init & r1[0]), fb1 = r1[2] ^ (init & r1[0]);
  generate
    if (W == 1) assign y = r0[0];
    else        assign y = {r0[0], r1[0]};
  endgenerate
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin
      b <= key;
      s <= {iv, {31{1'b1}}, 1'b0};
    end else if (W == 1) begin
      b <= {b[1:127], fb0};
      s <= {s[1:127], fs0};
    end else begin
      b <= {b[2:127], fb0, fb1};
      s <= {s[2:127], fs0, fs1};
    end
endmodule

// MAC (Section 2.4): accumulator A and shift register R. pre: A||R shifts in the pair
// (ya, yb) for 32 clocks, so A = y_0..y_31 and R = y_32..y_63. Afterwards R shifts in the
// macstream bit yb every clock and acc applies A ^= R (message bit m_i = 1, or the padding bit).
module grain_mac (
  input         clk,
  input         pre,
  input         ya, yb,
  input         acc,
  output [0:31] tag                 // A, t_0 in the MSB
);
  reg [0:31] A, R;
  assign tag = A;
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (pre) begin
      A <= {A[2:31], R[0:1]};
      R <= {R[2:31], ya, yb};
    end else begin
      if (acc) A <= A ^ R;
      R <= {R[1:31], yb};
    end
endmodule

// (c1) Grain-128a, encryption only, 1 bit per clock: z = y_i (IV_0 = 0). 256 init clocks.
module grain128a_enc1x (
  input          clk,
  input          load,
  input  [0:127] key,
  input  [0:95]  iv,
  output         z,
  output         ready
);
  reg [7:0] cnt;
  reg       busy;
  grain_core #(.W(1)) u_core (.clk(clk), .load(load), .init(busy), .key(key), .iv(iv), .y(z));
  assign ready = ~busy;
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin cnt <= 8'd0; busy <= 1'b1; end
    else if (busy) begin
      cnt <= cnt + 8'd1;
      if (cnt == 8'd255) busy <= 1'b0;
    end
endmodule

// (c2) Grain-128a, authentication mode, 2 pre-output bits per clock = one keystream bit
// z_i = y_(64+2i) and one macstream bit a = y_(65+2i) per modulator clock.
// After load: 128 init clocks (256 pre-output bits), 32 MAC preload clocks, then RUN:
// m is message bit m_i at keystream index i; pad (in RUN) adds the padding bit m_L = 1,
// after which tag_ok is high and tag holds the 32-bit tag.
module grain128a_auth2x (
  input          clk,
  input          load,
  input  [0:127] key,
  input  [0:95]  iv,              // IV_0 must be 1 (authentication mode)
  input          m,
  input          pad,
  output         z,
  output         a,
  output         run,
  output         tag_ok,
  output [0:31]  tag
);
  localparam INIT = 2'd0, PRE = 2'd1, RUN = 2'd2, DONE = 2'd3;
  reg  [1:0] ph;
  reg  [6:0] cnt;
  wire [0:1] y;
  grain_core #(.W(2)) u_core (.clk(clk), .load(load), .init(ph == INIT), .key(key), .iv(iv), .y(y));
  grain_mac u_mac (.clk(clk), .pre(ph == PRE), .ya(y[0]), .yb(y[1]),
                   .acc((ph == RUN) & (m | pad)), .tag(tag));
  assign z = y[0];
  assign a = y[1];
  assign run    = (ph == RUN);
  assign tag_ok = (ph == DONE);
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin ph <= INIT; cnt <= 7'd0; end
    else case (ph)
      INIT: begin cnt <= cnt + 7'd1; if (cnt == 7'd127) ph <= PRE; end   // cnt wraps to 0
      PRE:  begin cnt <= cnt + 7'd1; if (cnt == 7'd31)  ph <= RUN; end
      RUN:  if (pad) ph <= DONE;
      default: ;
    endcase
endmodule
'''

VERILOG['secure_ks_top.v'] = r'''
// (c3) Proposal keystream block: PUF key register + session nonce + chip nonce + frame counter feeding
// Grain-128a (auth mode, 2x), plus the two dither LFSR16s.
//   key_sh : shift the 128-bit key in from the fuzzy extractor, k_0 first (128 clocks)
//   nonce_sh: shift the receiver's 32-bit session nonce in, MSB first (32 clocks); this also
//            presets the counter to all-ones so the first frame of a session uses ctr = 0
//   cn_sh  : shift the 31-bit chip nonce N_c in, MSB first (31 clocks, once per session, from the hash of the raw
//            power-up read)
//   start  : new frame: ctr <= ctr + 1 and Grain loads key and IV = 1 | nonce | ctr | N_c
//            (the model's iv_bits); z / run / tag as in grain128a_auth2x
module secure_ks_top (
  input         clk,
  input         key_sh, key_in,
  input         nonce_sh, nonce_in,
  input         cn_sh, cn_in,
  input         start,
  input         m, pad,
  input         dith_load,
  input  [15:0] seed1, seed2,
  output        z,
  output        run, tag_ok,
  output [0:31] tag,
  output [31:0] ctr,               // counter value of the current frame (sent and MACed)
  output        dith1, dith2
);
  wire [0:127] key_r;
  wire [0:31]  nonce_r;
  wire [0:30]  cn_r;
  reg  [31:0]  ctr_r;
  wire [31:0]  ctr_n = ctr_r + 32'd1;
  assign ctr = ctr_r;
  shreg #(.N(128)) u_key   (.clk(clk), .sh(key_sh),   .din(key_in),   .q(key_r));
  shreg #(.N(32))  u_nonce (.clk(clk), .sh(nonce_sh), .din(nonce_in), .q(nonce_r));
  shreg #(.N(31))  u_cn    (.clk(clk), .sh(cn_sh),    .din(cn_in),    .q(cn_r));
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (nonce_sh)   ctr_r <= 32'hFFFF_FFFF;
    else if (start) ctr_r <= ctr_n;
  grain128a_auth2x u_grain (.clk(clk), .load(start), .key(key_r), .iv({1'b1, nonce_r, ctr_n, cn_r}),
                            .m(m), .pad(pad), .z(z), .a(), .run(run), .tag_ok(tag_ok), .tag(tag));
  lfsr16 u_d1 (.clk(clk), .load(dith_load), .seed(seed1), .out(dith1));
  lfsr16 u_d2 (.clk(clk), .load(dith_load), .seed(seed2), .out(dith2));
endmodule

// Serial-in shift register with shift enable; the first bit shifted in ends at index 0 (MSB).
module shreg #(parameter N = 8) (
  input            clk,
  input            sh,
  input            din,
  output reg [0:N-1] q
);
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (sh) q <= {q[1:N-1], din};
endmodule
'''

# Probes for the load-mux cost: the same logic with load tied low (the state can never be
# written, so the per-bit load multiplexers disappear). Synthesised only, never simulated.
VERILOG['probes.v'] = r'''
module sdsm_noload (input clk, input d, output c, output dith1, output dith2);
  sdsm_ks u (.clk(clk), .load(1'b0), .key16(16'd0), .seed1(16'd0), .seed2(16'd0), .d(d), .c(c),
             .dith1(dith1), .dith2(dith2));
endmodule
module trivium_noload (input clk, output z);
  trivium_r1 u (.clk(clk), .load(1'b0), .key(80'd0), .iv(80'd0), .z(z), .ready());
endmodule
module grain_core1_noload (input clk, input init, output y);
  grain_core #(.W(1)) u (.clk(clk), .load(1'b0), .init(init), .key(128'd0), .iv(96'd0), .y(y));
endmodule
module grain_core2_noload (input clk, input init, output [0:1] y);
  grain_core #(.W(2)) u (.clk(clk), .load(1'b0), .init(init), .key(128'd0), .iv(96'd0), .y(y));
endmodule
module grain_core1 (input clk, input load, input init, input [0:127] key, input [0:95] iv, output y);
  grain_core #(.W(1)) u (.clk(clk), .load(load), .init(init), .key(key), .iv(iv), .y(y));
endmodule
module grain_core2 (input clk, input load, input init, input [0:127] key, input [0:95] iv, output [0:1] y);
  grain_core #(.W(2)) u (.clk(clk), .load(load), .init(init), .key(key), .iv(iv), .y(y));
endmodule
'''

VERILOG['lowpower.v'] = r'''
// Low-power (radix-K, clock-gated) versions of the three designs, bit-exact with the 1-bit-per-clock RTL above.
// Every register that does not change in a cycle receives no clock edge in it: with `define ICG_CELLS (implementation)
// its clock passes through an integrated clock-gating cell (sky130_fd_sc_hd__dlclkp_1); without it (verification with the
// single-clock AIGER simulator) the same register is written as an enable flip-flop. The state of each cipher advances K
// keystream bits per update, once every K clocks, and an output multiplexer delivers one bit per 10 MHz clock.
module icg (input clk, input en, output gclk);
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  sky130_fd_sc_hd__dlclkp_1 u (.CLK(clk), .GATE(en), .GCLK(gclk));
`else
  assign gclk = clk;                                   // verification build: the enable is applied at the register
`endif
endmodule

// 16-bit LFSR of lfsr16.v, K steps per update: its next K outputs are s[0..K-1] (right-shifting register).
module lfsr16_lp #(parameter K = 16) (input clk, input load, input en, input [15:0] seed, input [3:0] c, output out);
  reg [15:0] s, t; integer i;
  always @* begin t = s; for (i = 0; i < K; i = i + 1) t = {t[0] ^ t[2] ^ t[3] ^ t[5], t[15:1]}; end
  reg o; integer j;                                    // out = s[c], written with constant indices
  always @* begin o = 1'b0; for (j = 0; j < 16; j = j + 1) if (c == j) o = s[j]; end
  assign out = o;
  // next state = (t AND NOT load) OR (seed AND load), the masked term kept as a net: during the load the old (possibly
  // still undefined) state reaches the register only through an AND with 0, so a gate-level simulation starting from
  // undefined flip-flops loads exactly as the silicon does
  (* keep *) wire [15:0] tm = t & {16{~load}};
  wire [15:0] nx = tm | ({16{load}} & ((seed == 16'd0) ? 16'd1 : seed));
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  wire g; icg u_g (.clk(clk), .en(load | en), .gclk(g));
  always @(posedge g) s <= nx;
`else
  always @(posedge clk) if (load | en) s <= nx;
`endif
endmodule

// (a') S-DSM of [1], low-power: the three LFSR16s advance 16 steps once every 16 clocks.
module sdsm_lp (input clk, input load, input [15:0] key16, seed1, seed2, input d, output c, output dith1, dith2);
  reg [3:0] cc; wire tick = (cc == 4'd15);
  always @(posedge clk) if (load) cc <= 4'd0; else cc <= cc + 4'd1;
  wire k;
  lfsr16_lp #(16) u_key (.clk(clk), .load(load), .en(tick), .seed(key16), .c(cc), .out(k));
  lfsr16_lp #(16) u_d1  (.clk(clk), .load(load), .en(tick), .seed(seed1), .c(cc), .out(dith1));
  lfsr16_lp #(16) u_d2  (.clk(clk), .load(load), .en(tick), .seed(seed2), .c(cc), .out(dith2));
  assign c = d ^ k;
endmodule

// (b') Trivium, low-power: 16 keystream bits per state update (Trivium allows up to 64), init at 16 steps per clock.
module trivium_lp (input clk, input load, input [1:80] key, input [1:80] iv, output z, output ready);
  reg [1:288] s, t; reg [0:15] zz; reg t1, t2, t3; integer i;
  always @* begin
    t = s;
    for (i = 0; i < 16; i = i + 1) begin
      t1 = t[66] ^ t[93]; t2 = t[162] ^ t[177]; t3 = t[243] ^ t[288];
      zz[i] = t1 ^ t2 ^ t3;
      t1 = t1 ^ (t[91] & t[92]) ^ t[171]; t2 = t2 ^ (t[175] & t[176]) ^ t[264]; t3 = t3 ^ (t[286] & t[287]) ^ t[69];
      t = {t3, t[1:92], t1, t[94:176], t2, t[178:287]};
    end
  end
  reg [6:0] cnt; reg busy; reg [3:0] cc; wire tick = (cc == 4'd15);
  reg zo; integer j;
  always @* begin zo = 1'b0; for (j = 0; j < 16; j = j + 1) if (cc == j) zo = zz[j]; end
  assign ready = ~busy; assign z = zo;
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin cnt <= 7'd0; busy <= 1'b1; cc <= 4'd0; end
    else if (busy) begin cnt <= cnt + 7'd1; if (cnt == 7'd71) busy <= 1'b0; end     // 72 x 16 = 1152 init steps
    else cc <= cc + 4'd1;
  (* keep *) wire [1:288] tm = t & {288{~load}};        // load masking as in lfsr16_lp
  wire [1:288] nx = tm | ({288{load}} & {key, 13'd0, iv, 4'd0, 108'd0, 3'b111});
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  wire g; icg u_g (.clk(clk), .en(load | busy | tick), .gclk(g));
  always @(posedge g) s <= nx;
`else
  always @(posedge clk) if (load | busy | tick) s <= nx;
`endif
endmodule

// Grain-128a core, W pre-output bits per update (W <= 32: every tap of the W steps lies in the current state).
module grain_core_lp #(parameter W = 32) (input clk, input load, input en, input init, input [0:127] key, input [0:95] iv,
                                          output [0:W-1] y);
  reg [0:127] b, s;
  function [0:2] step(input [0:127] bb, input [0:127] ss);
    reg h;
    begin
      h = (bb[12] & ss[8]) ^ (ss[13] & ss[20]) ^ (bb[95] & ss[42]) ^ (ss[60] & ss[79]) ^ (bb[12] & bb[95] & ss[94]);
      step[0] = h ^ ss[93] ^ bb[2] ^ bb[15] ^ bb[36] ^ bb[45] ^ bb[64] ^ bb[73] ^ bb[89];
      step[1] = ss[0] ^ ss[7] ^ ss[38] ^ ss[70] ^ ss[81] ^ ss[96];
      step[2] = ss[0] ^ bb[0] ^ bb[26] ^ bb[56] ^ bb[91] ^ bb[96]
              ^ (bb[3] & bb[67]) ^ (bb[11] & bb[13]) ^ (bb[17] & bb[18]) ^ (bb[27] & bb[59])
              ^ (bb[40] & bb[48]) ^ (bb[61] & bb[65]) ^ (bb[68] & bb[84])
              ^ (bb[88] & bb[92] & bb[93] & bb[95]) ^ (bb[22] & bb[24] & bb[25]) ^ (bb[70] & bb[78] & bb[82]);
    end
  endfunction
  wire [0:W-1] fs, fb; genvar k;
  generate for (k = 0; k < W; k = k + 1) begin : st
    wire [0:2] r = step(b << k, s << k);
    assign y[k] = r[0]; assign fs[k] = r[1] ^ (init & r[0]); assign fb[k] = r[2] ^ (init & r[0]);
  end endgenerate
  (* keep *) wire [0:127] bm = {b[W:127], fb} & {128{~load}}, sm = {s[W:127], fs} & {128{~load}};   // load masking
  wire [0:127] bn = bm | ({128{load}} & key), sn = sm | ({128{load}} & {iv, {31{1'b1}}, 1'b0});
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  wire g; icg u_g (.clk(clk), .en(load | en), .gclk(g));
  always @(posedge g) begin b <= bn; s <= sn; end
`else
  always @(posedge clk) if (load | en) begin b <= bn; s <= sn; end
`endif
endmodule

// (c2') Grain-128a + MAC, low-power: 32 pre-output bits = 16 keystream + 16 macstream bits per update, once every 16
// clocks; same ports and behaviour as grain128a_auth2x except the latencies (RUN 11 clocks after load instead of 161).
module grain128a_lp (input clk, input load, input [0:127] key, input [0:95] iv, input m, input pad,
                     output z, output a, output run, output tag_ok, output [0:31] tag);
  localparam INIT = 2'd0, PRE = 2'd1, RUN = 2'd2, DONE = 2'd3;
  reg [1:0] ph; reg [3:0] cnt, cc;
  wire tick = (cc == 4'd15);
  wire [0:31] y;
  grain_core_lp #(32) u_core (.clk(clk), .load(load), .en((ph == INIT) | (ph == PRE) | (((ph == RUN) | (ph == DONE)) & tick)),
                              .init(ph == INIT), .key(key), .iv(iv), .y(y));
  reg [0:31] A, R; reg [0:15] mb;
  assign tag = A; assign run = (ph == RUN); assign tag_ok = (ph == DONE);
  reg zo, ao; integer j;
  always @* begin zo = 1'b0; ao = 1'b0; for (j = 0; j < 16; j = j + 1) if (cc == j) begin zo = y[2 * j]; ao = y[2 * j + 1]; end end
  assign z = zo; assign a = ao;
  // MAC update for the 16 message bits of the block: bit i (i < cc from the buffer, i = cc the current m | pad); operand
  // isolation keeps the XOR network still except in the update cycle (tick, or pad for the last, partial block)
  integer i; reg [0:31] An, Rn; reg mi; wire upd = (ph == RUN) & (tick | pad);
  always @* begin
    An = A; Rn = R;
    for (i = 0; i < 16; i = i + 1) begin
      mi = upd & ((i < cc) ? mb[i] : (i == cc) ? (m | pad) : 1'b0);
      if (mi) An = An ^ Rn;
      Rn = {Rn[1:31], y[2 * i + 1]};
    end
  end
  wire mac_en = ~load & ((ph == PRE) | upd);
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  wire gm; icg u_gm (.clk(clk), .en(mac_en), .gclk(gm));
  always @(posedge gm) if (ph == PRE) {A, R} <= {A[0:31], R[0:31]} << 32 | {32'd0, y}; else begin A <= An; R <= Rn; end
`else
  always @(posedge clk) if (mac_en) begin if (ph == PRE) {A, R} <= {A[0:31], R[0:31]} << 32 | {32'd0, y}; else begin A <= An; R <= Rn; end end
`endif
  integer q;
  always @(posedge clk) for (q = 0; q < 15; q = q + 1) if ((ph == RUN) & (cc == q)) mb[q] <= m;   // mb[15] unused
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (load) begin ph <= INIT; cnt <= 4'd0; cc <= 4'd0; end
    else case (ph)
      INIT: begin cnt <= cnt + 4'd1; if (cnt == 4'd7) begin ph <= PRE; cnt <= 4'd0; end end    // 8 x 32 = 256 init steps
      PRE:  begin cnt <= cnt + 4'd1; if (cnt == 4'd1) ph <= RUN; end                            // 2 x 32 = 64 preload bits
      RUN:  begin cc <= cc + 4'd1; if (pad) ph <= DONE; end          // the keystream continues after the tag
      DONE: cc <= cc + 4'd1;
    endcase
endmodule

// (c3') Proposal keystream block, low-power: same ports and behaviour as secure_ks_top (latency aside); the key, nonce,
// chip-nonce and counter registers are clocked only when written.
module secure_ks_lp (
  input clk, input key_sh, key_in, nonce_sh, nonce_in, cn_sh, cn_in, start, m, pad, dith_load,
  input [15:0] seed1, seed2, output z, run, tag_ok, output [0:31] tag, output [31:0] ctr, output dith1, dith2);
  reg [0:127] key_r; reg [0:31] nonce_r; reg [0:30] cn_r; reg [31:0] ctr_r;
  wire [31:0] ctr_n = ctr_r + 32'd1;
  assign ctr = ctr_r;
`ifdef ICG_CELLS
  wire gk; icg u_gk (.clk(clk), .en(key_sh), .gclk(gk)); wire gn; icg u_gn (.clk(clk), .en(nonce_sh), .gclk(gn)); wire gc; icg u_gc (.clk(clk), .en(cn_sh), .gclk(gc)); wire gt; icg u_gt (.clk(clk), .en(nonce_sh | start), .gclk(gt));
  always @(posedge gk) key_r   <= {key_r[1:127], key_in};
  always @(posedge gn) nonce_r <= {nonce_r[1:31], nonce_in};
  always @(posedge gc) cn_r    <= {cn_r[1:30], cn_in};
  always @(posedge gt) ctr_r   <= nonce_sh ? 32'hFFFF_FFFF : ctr_n;
`else
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (key_sh)   key_r   <= {key_r[1:127], key_in};
    if (nonce_sh) nonce_r <= {nonce_r[1:31], nonce_in};
    if (cn_sh)    cn_r    <= {cn_r[1:30], cn_in};
    if (nonce_sh) ctr_r <= 32'hFFFF_FFFF; else if (start) ctr_r <= ctr_n;
  end
`endif
  grain128a_lp u_grain (.clk(clk), .load(start), .key(key_r), .iv({1'b1, nonce_r, ctr_n, cn_r}), .m(m), .pad(pad),
                        .z(z), .a(), .run(run), .tag_ok(tag_ok), .tag(tag));
  reg [3:0] dc; wire dt = (dc == 4'd15);
  always @(posedge clk) if (dith_load) dc <= 4'd0; else dc <= dc + 4'd1;
  lfsr16_lp #(16) u_d1 (.clk(clk), .load(dith_load), .en(dt), .seed(seed1), .c(dc), .out(dith1));
  lfsr16_lp #(16) u_d2 (.clk(clk), .load(dith_load), .en(dt), .seed(seed2), .c(dc), .out(dith2));
endmodule
'''

def write_verilog_files(outdir):
    """Write every Verilog source to outdir; returns the list of paths."""
    os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
    paths = []
    for name, text in VERILOG.items():
        p = os.path.join(outdir, name)
        with open(p, 'w') as f:
            f.write(text.lstrip('\n'))
        paths.append(p)
    return paths

# 2. Reference models (Python) and test vectors
# =====================================================================================
def hex_to_bits(h, n=None):
    """Hex -> bit list, bit 0 = MSB of the first digit (the Grain paper's convention)."""
    h = re.sub(r'\s+', '', h)
    bits = [(int(c, 16) >> (3 - j)) & 1 for c in h for j in range(4)]
    return bits if n is None else bits[:n]


def bits_to_hex(bits):
    bits = list(bits) + [0] * (-len(bits) % 4)
    return ''.join('%x' % (bits[i] << 3 | bits[i + 1] << 2 | bits[i + 2] << 1 | bits[i + 3])
                   for i in range(0, len(bits), 4))


def bits_to_int(bits):
    v = 0
    for b in bits:
        v = (v << 1) | (b & 1)
    return v


def int_to_bits(v, n):
    return [(v >> (n - 1 - i)) & 1 for i in range(n)]


class LFSR16:
    """Port of model.js class LFSR16."""
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.s = (seed & 0xFFFF) or 1

    def bit(self):
        s = self.s
        fb = (s ^ (s >> 2) ^ (s >> 3) ^ (s >> 5)) & 1
        self.s = (s >> 1) | (fb << 15)
        return s & 1

    def bits(self, n):
        return [self.bit() for _ in range(n)]


def grain_pre(key_bits, iv_bits, n):
    """Grain-128a pre-output y_0..y_(n-1) (port of model.js _grainRun / Grain128a)."""
    b = list(key_bits)
    s = list(iv_bits) + [1] * 31 + [0]
    out = []
    for t in range(256 + n):
        q = t
        b12, b95 = b[q + 12], b[q + 95]
        y = ((b12 & s[q + 8]) ^ (s[q + 13] & s[q + 20]) ^ (b95 & s[q + 42]) ^
             (s[q + 60] & s[q + 79]) ^ (b12 & b95 & s[q + 94]) ^ s[q + 93] ^
             b[q + 2] ^ b[q + 15] ^ b[q + 36] ^ b[q + 45] ^ b[q + 64] ^ b[q + 73] ^ b[q + 89])
        st = s[q]
        fs = st ^ s[q + 7] ^ s[q + 38] ^ s[q + 70] ^ s[q + 81] ^ s[q + 96]
        fb = (st ^ b[q] ^ b[q + 26] ^ b[q + 56] ^ b[q + 91] ^ b[q + 96] ^
              (b[q + 3] & b[q + 67]) ^ (b[q + 11] & b[q + 13]) ^ (b[q + 17] & b[q + 18]) ^
              (b[q + 27] & b[q + 59]) ^ (b[q + 40] & b[q + 48]) ^ (b[q + 61] & b[q + 65]) ^
              (b[q + 68] & b[q + 84]) ^ (b[q + 88] & b[q + 92] & b[q + 93] & b95) ^
              (b[q + 22] & b[q + 24] & b[q + 25]) ^ (b[q + 70] & b[q + 78] & b[q + 82]))
        if t < 256:
            fs ^= y
            fb ^= y
        else:
            out.append(y)
        s.append(fs)
        b.append(fb)
    return out


def grain_keystream(key_bits, iv_bits, n_enc):
    """model.js grainKeystream: auth mode (IV_0 = 1) -> dict(enc, auth, A0, R0); else dict(enc)."""
    if iv_bits[0] != 1:
        return {'enc': grain_pre(key_bits, iv_bits, n_enc)}
    n_auth = n_enc + 64
    y = grain_pre(key_bits, iv_bits, 64 + 2 * n_auth)
    return {'enc': y[64::2][:n_enc], 'auth': y[65::2][:n_auth],
            'A0': bits_to_int(y[0:32]), 'R0': bits_to_int(y[32:64])}


def grain_tag(msg_bits, ks):
    """model.js grainTag: 32-bit tag (t_0 in the MSB)."""
    A, R = ks['A0'], ks['R0']
    for i, m in enumerate(msg_bits):
        if m:
            A ^= R
        R = ((R << 1) | ks['auth'][i]) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return A ^ R


def iv_bits(nonce, ctr, cn=0):
    """The model's iv_bits: IV_0 = 1, nonce (32 bits, MSB first), counter (32 bits), chip nonce N_c (31 bits, MSB first)."""
    return [1] + int_to_bits(nonce, 32) + int_to_bits(ctr, 32) + int_to_bits(cn, 31)
```
