<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 61.</b> Compiled key-reconstruction unit of specification C in SKY130, drawn as Fig. 56(a): diffusion and poly of the standard-cell rows and vertical met4 power stripes, signal routing hidden; scale bar: 50 µm. Default mode: placed and globally routed in this session (title “Placement”); with <code>ROUTE_COMPILED = True</code>: routed in detail (title “Routed”).</p>

**Result.** The selected design (8,984 GE, 707 flip-flops) is placed and globally routed live on a 379 µm × 379 µm die with about 18,500 instances. With global-routing parasitics, its setup slack at 10 MHz is +90 ns and its hold slack +0.40 ns. The recorded detailed routing of the same design ends with 0 routing DRC violations and Magic finds 0 violations in the routed GDS; **2 antenna violations remain** after the insertion of 4 diodes. As for the keystream block, the clock period leaves a wide setup margin and the hold slack is small but positive.

Fig. 61 shows the placed unit, its standard cells spread over the core at the target utilisation of 25 %, dense where the decoder's logic and registers sit and sparse where only fill cells are; its title reads “Placement” because the default mode does not route it in detail. Its GDS is written in this session and can also be opened in the layout viewer of Section VII-D, as the card states.

**Interpretation.** The specification of step 1 ends in a placed layout in this session and in a routed layout in the recorded run of the same flow: **the key generator's decoder, like the keystream block, can be placed and routed DRC-clean in an open PDK, with 2 antenna violations left open**. They have the cause stated for the keystream block in Section X-C: the antenna repair of this OpenROAD version works on the global routes, and a few detailed routes end longer; three recorded settings (margins of 20 and 60 %, the latter also with buffered input ports) each left 2. A block for fabrication must close them with a diode or a jumper placed after detailed routing; this is not done here. Its die (379 µm on a side) is slightly smaller than that of the low-power keystream block (399 µm), consistent with a decoder slightly smaller than that block (8,984 against 9,869 GE).

### E. Step 6: the complete area

**Goal.** Give the area of everything the proposal adds to the chip of [1], not only the keystream block of Section X (9,869 GE in its low-power form): the key decoder, the hash, the SRAM-PUF array, the helper data and the parts that are not designed, each marked as synthesised, drawn, estimated or not costed; and place the decoder among published PUF key decoders.

**Theory.** The key generator runs once per power-up: it reads the array, corrects the fingerprint with the decoder, and hashes the corrected word into the 128-bit key and the chip nonce (SHA-256 in the model, Section V). The hash must therefore be on the chip. A SHA-256 core that computes one round per clock holds the eight chaining words, the eight working words and a 16-word message schedule, 1,024 bits of state, so it needs more than 1,000 flip-flops (about 5,500 GE in flip-flops alone at 5.33 GE each) before its adders and round constants. *Prediction:* the hash, not the decoder, is the largest part of the key generator. The helper data of specification C are the enrolment mask (one bit per physical cell, 1,395), the repetition helper bits ($r - 1$ per group, 648) and the BCH syndromes ($10t$, 40): 2,083 bits. They are public; the protocol sends them on the downlink at the start of a session (Section IV), so they need no storage on the chip if the decoder consumes them as they arrive, while the powered array keeps its power-up values.

**Setup.**

* *Hash:* a SHA-256 compression core in Verilog (one round per clock, 65 clocks per 512-bit block, message words entering serially), simulated with Icarus Verilog on five messages of one and two blocks, among them a 516-bit word of the size of specification C's fingerprint, and compared with Python's `hashlib`; synthesised with Yosys on `sky130_fd_sc_hd`. Padding and block sequencing are not included.
* *Decoder:* the selected design of specification C from step 3 (synthesised; placed in step 5).
* *Keystream block:* Table XIV (synthesised, placed and routed).
* *Array:* the physical cells of specification C times the area of the SRAM cell drawn in Section VII-D. This cell is drawn with the logic design rules, not as a foundry bit cell, so it overstates the array; the periphery (word-line drivers, read-out, power switching) is not designed.
* *Helper data:* zero on the chip if streamed; otherwise estimated as flip-flops. The delay line of Section X-A is its estimate there.
* *Not costed:* the array periphery, the downlink receiver, the hash's padding and control, and the power and energy of the decoder and the hash.
* *Metrics:* area in GE and µm² per part, with its source; the total of the designed parts and each part's share.

> **Next cell.** 1. Writes a SHA-256 compression core in Verilog. 2. Simulates it with Icarus Verilog on five messages and compares the digests with Python's hashlib. 3. Synthesises it on sky130_fd_sc_hd. 4. Collects the area of every part for specification C, with its source, and prints the table and the card.


```python
#@title Complete area of the proposal
# Step 6: the complete area of the proposal's digital security, specification C. The hash that turns the corrected fingerprint
# into the key (SHA-256 in the model) is written in RTL, checked against Python's hashlib and synthesised; the array area is
# its cells times the SRAM cell drawn in Section VII-D; the parts that are not designed are listed, not guessed
import hashlib, struct
SHA_V = r"""// SHA-256 compression, one round per clock: the 16 words of a block enter serially during rounds 0-15 (win, read at the
// round given by rnd); the message schedule is a 16-word shift register; init loads the initial hash value; after round 63
// the chaining value H is updated (feed-forward) and done pulses. Padding and block sequencing are left to the controller.
module sha256_core(input wire clk, input wire rst, input wire init, input wire start, input wire [31:0] win,
                   output reg done, output reg [6:0] rnd, output wire [255:0] digest);
  reg [31:0] H [0:7]; reg [31:0] a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h; reg [31:0] W [0:15]; reg busy; integer z;
  function [31:0] rotr(input [31:0] x, input [4:0] n); rotr = (x >> n) | (x << (32 - n)); endfunction
  function [31:0] K(input [5:0] i);
    case (i)
""" + "".join(f"      {i}: K = 32'h{k:08x};\n" for i, k in enumerate([
    0x428a2f98, 0x71374491, 0xb5c0fbcf, 0xe9b5dba5, 0x3956c25b, 0x59f111f1, 0x923f82a4, 0xab1c5ed5, 0xd807aa98, 0x12835b01,
    0x243185be, 0x550c7dc3, 0x72be5d74, 0x80deb1fe, 0x9bdc06a7, 0xc19bf174, 0xe49b69c1, 0xefbe4786, 0x0fc19dc6, 0x240ca1cc,
    0x2de92c6f, 0x4a7484aa, 0x5cb0a9dc, 0x76f988da, 0x983e5152, 0xa831c66d, 0xb00327c8, 0xbf597fc7, 0xc6e00bf3, 0xd5a79147,
    0x06ca6351, 0x14292967, 0x27b70a85, 0x2e1b2138, 0x4d2c6dfc, 0x53380d13, 0x650a7354, 0x766a0abb, 0x81c2c92e, 0x92722c85,
    0xa2bfe8a1, 0xa81a664b, 0xc24b8b70, 0xc76c51a3, 0xd192e819, 0xd6990624, 0xf40e3585, 0x106aa070, 0x19a4c116, 0x1e376c08,
    0x2748774c, 0x34b0bcb5, 0x391c0cb3, 0x4ed8aa4a, 0x5b9cca4f, 0x682e6ff3, 0x748f82ee, 0x78a5636f, 0x84c87814, 0x8cc70208,
    0x90befffa, 0xa4506ceb, 0xbef9a3f7, 0xc67178f2])) + r"""    endcase
  endfunction
  wire [31:0] s0 = rotr(W[1], 7) ^ rotr(W[1], 18) ^ (W[1] >> 3), s1 = rotr(W[14], 17) ^ rotr(W[14], 19) ^ (W[14] >> 10);
  wire [31:0] wt = (rnd < 16) ? win : W[0] + s0 + W[9] + s1;          // W[t] from W[t-16], W[t-15], W[t-7], W[t-2]
  wire [31:0] t1 = h + (rotr(e, 6) ^ rotr(e, 11) ^ rotr(e, 25)) + ((e & f) ^ (~e & g)) + K(rnd[5:0]) + wt;
  wire [31:0] t2 = (rotr(a, 2) ^ rotr(a, 13) ^ rotr(a, 22)) + ((a & b) ^ (a & c) ^ (b & c));
  assign digest = {H[0], H[1], H[2], H[3], H[4], H[5], H[6], H[7]};
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (rst) begin busy <= 0; done <= 0; rnd <= 0; end
    else begin
      done <= 0;
      if (init) begin
        H[0] <= 32'h6a09e667; H[1] <= 32'hbb67ae85; H[2] <= 32'h3c6ef372; H[3] <= 32'ha54ff53a;
        H[4] <= 32'h510e527f; H[5] <= 32'h9b05688c; H[6] <= 32'h1f83d9ab; H[7] <= 32'h5be0cd19;
      end else if (start && !busy) begin
        a <= H[0]; b <= H[1]; c <= H[2]; d <= H[3]; e <= H[4]; f <= H[5]; g <= H[6]; h <= H[7]; rnd <= 0; busy <= 1;
      end else if (busy) begin
        if (rnd == 64) begin
          H[0] <= H[0] + a; H[1] <= H[1] + b; H[2] <= H[2] + c; H[3] <= H[3] + d;
          H[4] <= H[4] + e; H[5] <= H[5] + f; H[6] <= H[6] + g; H[7] <= H[7] + h; busy <= 0; done <= 1;
        end else begin
          h <= g; g <= f; f <= e; e <= d + t1; d <= c; c <= b; b <= a; a <= t1 + t2;
          for (z = 0; z < 15; z = z + 1) W[z] <= W[z + 1];
          W[15] <= wt; rnd <= rnd + 1;
        end
      end
    end
  end
endmodule
"""
t0 = time.time(); wd_h = WORK / "hash"; wd_h.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); (wd_h / "sha256_core.v").write_text(SHA_V)
pad = lambda m: m + b"\x80" + b"\x00" * ((55 - len(m)) % 64) + struct.pack(">Q", 8 * len(m))
r_h = np.random.default_rng(256)
msgs = [b"abc", b"", r_h.bytes(55), r_h.bytes(100), np.packbits(r_h.integers(0, 2, 516).astype(np.uint8)).tobytes()]
blocks, tests = [], []
for m in msgs:
    p = pad(m); tests.append((len(blocks), len(p) // 64, hashlib.sha256(m).hexdigest())); blocks += [p[i:i + 64] for i in range(0, len(p), 64)]
(wd_h / "blk.mem").write_text("".join("%08x\n" % w for b in blocks for w in struct.unpack(">16I", b)))
tb = (f"module tb; reg clk = 0, rst = 1, init = 0, start = 0; wire done; wire [6:0] rnd; wire [255:0] dg; reg [31:0] mem [0:{16 * len(blocks) - 1}];\n"
      "  integer blk, fo; wire [31:0] win = mem[blk * 16 + rnd[3:0]];\n"
      "  sha256_core u(.clk(clk), .rst(rst), .init(init), .start(start), .win(win), .done(done), .rnd(rnd), .digest(dg));\n"
      "  always #50 clk = ~clk;\n  initial begin $readmemh(\"blk.mem\", mem); fo = $fopen(\"out.txt\"); blk = 0; @(posedge clk); rst <= 0;\n")
for b0, nb_, _ in tests:
    tb += "    @(posedge clk) init <= 1; @(posedge clk) init <= 0;\n"
    tb += "".join(f"    blk = {b0 + j}; @(posedge clk) start <= 1; @(posedge clk) start <= 0; @(posedge done); @(posedge clk);\n" for j in range(nb_))
    tb += '    $fwrite(fo, "%h\\n", dg);\n'
(wd_h / "tb.v").write_text(tb + "    $finish;\n  end\nendmodule\n")
subprocess.run([str(PNR_BIN / "iverilog"), "-g2012", "-o", "sha.vvp", "tb.v", "sha256_core.v"], cwd=wd_h, check=True, capture_output=True)
subprocess.run([str(PNR_BIN / "vvp"), "-n", "sha.vvp"], cwd=wd_h, check=True, capture_output=True)
sha_ok = [o == e for o, (_, _, e) in zip((wd_h / "out.txt").read_text().split(), tests)]
S_SHA = R.synthesize(YOSYS, "sha256_core", [str(wd_h / "sha256_core.v")], str(LIBERTY), str(wd_h))
t_sha = time.time() - t0

# the complete area, specification C (the design that meets the target at every corner)
cfg = DSE["C"]["best"]; dec = SYN[cfg["r"], cfg["n"], cfg["t"]]; nand2 = RTL["nand2_um2"]
lib = R.liberty_cells(str(LIBERTY)); ff_ge = lib["sky130_fd_sc_hd__dfxtp_1"]["area"] / nand2
help_bits = dict(mask=cfg["cells"], rep=cfg["n"] * (cfg["r"] - 1), bch=10 * cfg["t"]); n_help = sum(help_bits.values())
AREA = [("keystream block (Grain-128a + MAC, key, nonces, counter, IV, dither)", ge["proposal_lp"], "low-power form; synthesised, placed and routed (Section X)"),
        (f"key decoder (repetition vote, r = {cfg['r']}; BCH, n = {cfg['n']}, t = {cfg['t']})", dec["ge"], "synthesised, placed; routed in the recorded run"),
        ("hash (SHA-256 compression core)", S_SHA["ge"], "synthesised; padding and block control not included"),
        (f"SRAM-PUF array, {cfg['cells']} bit cells", cfg["cells"] * CELL_UM2 / nand2, f"drawn cell ({CELL_UM2:.2f} µm², Section VII-D) × cells; no periphery"),
        ("32-bit MAC delay line", 170, "estimate (Section X-A)")]
tot = sum(a for _, a, _ in AREA)
rows_a = [(n_, f"{a:,.0f}", f"{a * nand2 / 1e3:.1f}", src) for n_, a, src in AREA]
rows_a.append(("<b>total, designed parts</b>", f"<b>{tot:,.0f}</b>", f"<b>{tot * nand2 / 1e3:.1f}</b>", ""))
rows_a += [(f"helper data, {n_help:,} bits ({help_bits['mask']} mask, {help_bits['rep']} repetition, {help_bits['bch']} BCH)",
            "0 or " + f"{n_help * ff_ge:,.0f}", "0 or " + f"{n_help * ff_ge * nand2 / 1e3:.1f}",
            f"none if streamed from the receiver at power-up; if held on chip, as flip-flops ({ff_ge:.2f} GE each), an estimate"),
           ("array periphery (word lines, read-out, power switching)", "–", "–", "not designed"),
           ("downlink receiver (session nonce and helper data)", "–", "–", "not designed")]
table(["Part", "Area (GE)", "Area (10<sup>3</sup> µm²)", "Source"], rows_a,
      caption="Table XXII: complete area of the proposal's digital security for specification C, in GE of sky130_fd_sc_hd "
              "(NAND2 = %.2f µm²; the array's area converted at the same rate)" % nand2, align=["left", "right", "right", "left"])
card("Complete area of the proposal (specification C)",
     [("SHA-256 core in RTL", f"<b>{sum(sha_ok)}/{len(sha_ok)}</b> digests equal to Python's hashlib (1 and 2 blocks, incl. a 516-bit "
                             f"fingerprint); {S_SHA['ge']:,.0f} GE, {S_SHA['ffs']} flip-flops; 65 clocks per block ({t_sha:.0f} s)"),
      ("designed parts", f"<b>{tot:,.0f} GE</b> ({tot * nand2 / 1e3:.1f} × 10<sup>3</sup> µm²): keystream "
                         f"{100 * ge['proposal_lp'] / tot:.0f} %, decoder {100 * dec['ge'] / tot:.0f} %, hash {100 * S_SHA['ge'] / tot:.0f} %, "
                         f"array {100 * cfg['cells'] * CELL_UM2 / nand2 / tot:.0f} %"),
      ("helper data held on chip instead of streamed", f"+{n_help * ff_ge:,.0f} GE as flip-flops ({n_help:,} bits)"),
      ("not costed", "array periphery, downlink receiver, padding and control of the hash, and the power of the decoder and hash")],
     tone="ok" if all(sha_ok) else "bad")
```

if held on chip, as flip-flops (5.33 GE each), an estimate</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left;padding:3px 12px">array periphery (word lines, read-out, power switching)</td><td style="text-align:right;padding:3px 12px">–</td><td style="text-align:right;padding:3px 12px">–</td><td style="text-align:left;padding:3px 12px">not designed</td></tr><tr><td style="text-align:left;padding:3px 12px">downlink receiver (session nonce and helper data)</td><td style="text-align:right;padding:3px 12px">–</td><td style="text-align:right;padding:3px 12px">–</td><td style="text-align:left;padding:3px 12px">not designed</td></tr></tbody></table></div>



<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #2a78d6;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Complete area of the proposal (specification C)</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">SHA-256 core in RTL</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>5/5</b> digests equal to Python's hashlib (1 and 2 blocks, incl. a 516-bit fingerprint); 15,097 GE, 1065 flip-flops; 65 clocks per block (4 s)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">designed parts</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>38,638 GE</b> (145.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> µm²): keystream 26 %, decoder 23 %, hash 39 %, array 12 %</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">helper data held on chip instead of streamed</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">+11,109 GE as flip-flops (2,083 bits)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">not costed</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">array periphery, downlink receiver, padding and control of the hash, and the power of the decoder and hash</td></tr></table></div>


**Result.** The SHA-256 core reproduces Python's `hashlib` on 5/5 messages, and synthesises to 15,097 GE with 1,065 flip-flops. With it, the designed parts of the proposal's digital security for specification C total **38,638 GE (145.0 × 10³ µm²)** (Table XXII): the low-power keystream block 26 %, the key decoder 23 %, the hash 39 % and the SRAM-PUF array (1,395 drawn cells) 12 %, with the 32-bit delay line estimated at 170 GE. As predicted, **the hash, not the decoder, is the largest part**: its 1,065 flip-flops alone are about 5,700 GE. The 2,083 helper bits (1,395 mask, 648 repetition and 40 BCH bits) need no area if they are streamed from the receiver at power-up; held on the chip as flip-flops, they would add an estimated 11,109 GE. The array periphery, the downlink receiver and the hash's padding and control are not designed and not included.

*The decoder against published ones.* The decoders of this compiler are serial (one Berlekamp-Massey update and one Chien evaluation step per clock) and keep the received word, the syndromes and the two locator polynomials in flip-flops: 707 flip-flops and 8,984 GE for specification C, 9,980 GE for A. Published PUF key generators on FPGAs are smaller in this respect. In PUFKY [14], the BCH decoder is a small microcoded processor of 112 Spartan-6 slices, and the whole key generator, ring-oscillator PUF, decoder and a SPONGENT-128 hash, occupies 1,162 slices, 82 % of them for the PUF. FPGA slices and standard-cell GE cannot be converted exactly, but a bound shows the scale: a Spartan-6 slice holds eight flip-flops, so the 707 flip-flops of the decoder of C alone would fill at least 89 slices, most of PUFKY's whole decoder.

**Interpretation.** The complete area of the designed parts is about 39,000 GE plus the undesigned periphery and receiver, about 3.9× the low-power keystream block of Section X. Two choices of this work, not the scheme, make the key generator large: a round-per-clock SHA-256, where a serialised SHA-256 or a lightweight hash such as the SPONGENT-128 of PUFKY [14] would be several times smaller, and a decoder template that holds all its data in flip-flops, where a microcoded decoder with its word in a small memory, as in [14], would be smaller. **"The decoder dominates the cost" is therefore a property of this serial template, not of PUF key generation;** both blocks run only at power-up, so their area matters more than their power. The summary below collects what the compiler shows.

#### What the compiler shows

1. **At the typical corner, both requirements are met with a few more cells than the hand design** (specification A). With the tt cell model of Section VII-F (512 cells; 2.70 % at 85 °C), 611 cells with BCH $t$ = 36 meet the target with 194 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy, the bounded budget of the hand design. Section VII-E sizes the hand design from the larger post-layout run of the same cell (1,024 cells; 3.14 % at 85 °C), with which 600 cells would need $t$ ≥ 46 over the interval of the 85 °C error rate while secrecy allows $t$ ≤ 35; the system simulations use $t$ = 45 as a working setting (94–137 secret bits, below the 192 of the secrecy criterion of Section VII-E). The key-failure probability is very sensitive to the 85 °C error rate, so specification A, built on the smaller run, is the less conservative of the two. By total area, the compiler prefers a repetition code: $r$ = 3, $t$ = 7, 1,092 cells, 50.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> µm².
2. **No code makes a 25 °C enrolment work at every corner** (specification B). With any repetition factor up to 7 and any BCH length up to 1023, at least one corner exceeds the target; the error rates point to fs, where reproducible flips make 27.8 % of the bits wrong at 85 °C, more than a code can correct without publishing more helper data than the cells hold secret.
3. **The two-temperature enrolment makes every corner work, with a weaker code** (specification C). Removing the cells that change between 25 and 85 °C leaves a cleaner fingerprint, so $t$ decreases (4 instead of 7 at $r$ = 3). The selected design, $r$ = 3, 324 groups, $t$ = 4 and 1,395 cells, has a total area of 50.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> µm², the same as A's although it covers five corners instead of one, and leaves 194 secret bits at the lower bound; it needs more physical cells than A at the same $r$, because the enrolment discards cells.
4. **In this serial template, the decoder is larger than the cipher.** The selected decoders (8,984–9,980 GE) are 2.9–3.3× the Grain-128a + MAC core of Section X written for one bit per clock (3,068 GE). Without repetition, the BCH-only designs are estimated at 2.2× (A) and 1.5× (C) the selected totals (estimates, not synthesised). The compiler makes this trade between cells and decoder explicit and selects by synthesised total area. Published decoders are smaller (a 112-slice microcoded BCH decoder in PUFKY [14]), so this ranking belongs to the template, not to PUF key generation.
5. **The result is synthesised and laid-out RTL, verified in simulation, not an estimate.** The generated decoders reproduce the model's reconstruction bit for bit and in the success flag in 72/72 tests each (12 directed, 60 random), including every read beyond their capacity. In 4,000 random error patterns per code, every pattern within $t$ is corrected; beyond $t$, none of the three decoders miscorrects a read with the success flag set (C: 0 of 2,000, A: 0 of 1,712, hand design: 0 of 458; Table XXI). The selected design is placed at 10 MHz, live, with +89.9 ns of setup slack and +0.40 ns of hold slack (global-routing parasitics), and is routed in SKY130 with 0 routing DRC and 0 Magic DRC violations in the recorded run of the same flow, with 2 antenna violations left open (`ROUTE_COMPILED = True` repeats it).
6. **The complete area is about 39,000 GE, and the hash is its largest part.** For specification C, the low-power keystream block (9,869 GE), the decoder (8,984 GE), a round-per-clock SHA-256 core (15,097 GE, verified against hashlib) and the drawn array (1,395 cells) total 38,638 GE; holding the 2,083 helper bits on chip instead of streaming them would add about 11,109 GE (Table XXII).

*Limits.* The cell error probabilities are those of one simulated chip per corner, with independent cells and no supply-voltage axis; the selection is the smallest of the two synthesised candidates per specification, ranked by an estimate; the RTL is simulated on 72 reads per design, and the thousands of random patterns run on the model's decoder, which the RTL matches decision for decision; the detailed routing is shown from a recorded run by default; the array periphery, the downlink receiver that delivers the helper data, the hash's padding and control, and the power and energy of the decoder and the hash are not costed, and the array uses a cell drawn with logic rules rather than a foundry bit cell.

**Next.** Section XII uses the decoder generated here, at RTL, in the mixed-level simulation of the complete sensor, together with the keystream block of Section X.

# **XII. The complete sensor in one mixed-level simulation**
---
**The question.** Does the complete secure sensor still work, and do the security results of Section VIII still hold, when the circuits that set its analog behaviour are simulated at transistor level and the digital blocks are the RTL that would be built?

**Why it matters.** Every system-level result so far comes from the bit-exact behavioural model of Section V, with circuit parameters obtained from SPICE simulations in Section VII. That model makes two abstractions. It replaces the StrongARM comparator, the modulator's 1-bit quantiser, by a threshold with a constant offset and Gaussian noise. And it reconstructs the key in Python rather than in hardware. This section tests both abstractions where they could fail: inside the closed modulator loop, and in the hardware that regenerates the key from transistor-level simulations of the extracted SRAM cells. It supports the abstract's claim that the key is regenerated from transistor-level cells and that the comparator model holds decision by decision.

**What it takes from earlier sections.** The extracted 6T SRAM cell and StrongARM comparator, their PVT data and the BCH correction capability t (Section VII); the replica attack and its behavioural prediction (Section VIII-B) and the SRAM-PUF error law (Section VIII-F); the keystream block's RTL, placed and routed in Section X; and the BCH decoder generated by the compiler of Section XI.

**What is simulated.** One simulation of the complete sensor, in which every block runs at the level at which its behaviour matters and the blocks exchange the real signals:

| Block | Level | Simulator | What this level adds over the model |
|---|---|---|---|
| SRAM-PUF array: enrolment and field power-up of 640 extracted 6T cells (the first 600 form the fingerprint) | **transistor** (post-layout, mismatch + transient noise) | ngspice | the actual power-up race of each cell at the operating temperature |
| Key reconstruction: BCH decoder generated by the compiler of Section XI | **RTL** | Icarus Verilog | the hardware that will be built, cycle by cycle |
| Key derivation: hash of the corrected fingerprint | behavioural | Python | - |
| TIA, buffer, the two integrators, 1-bit DAC, dither | behavioural | ngspice (B-sources) | - |
| StrongARM comparator, the modulator's quantiser, **inside the loop** | **transistor** (post-layout, this chip's mismatch, transient noise) | ngspice | regeneration, memory and metastability of the post-layout circuit, in closed loop |
| Grain-128a keystream, MAC, XOR with the modulator bits | **RTL** (the block placed and routed in Section X) | Icarus Verilog | the hardware's bit order, counter and MAC timing |
| Radio frame, receiver, eavesdropper, replica attacker | behavioural | Python | - |

Two chips are simulated: the victim and an attacker's replica, each with its own transistor-level comparator (its own Monte Carlo mismatch and its own transient noise). The replica lets the replica attack of Section VIII-B be run with transistor-level bits, against both designs.

**Roadmap.**

* *Theory* and *Simulation setup* (the next two cells): why the loop may be simulated in segments, how accurately the behavioural integrators must be solved, the decision-by-decision test of the comparator model, and every parameter and seed of the run.
* **A. Settings**: process corner, temperature, input and run length.
* **B. Step 1** (transistor level): the SRAM-PUF array powers up at enrolment and in the field.
* **C. Step 2** (RTL): the generated BCH decoder reconstructs the key.
* **D. Step 3** (transistor level in the loop): the victim's and the replica's modulators, and the decision-by-decision test.
* **E. Step 4** (RTL): Grain-128a encrypts and authenticates the victim's bits.
* **F. Step 5** (behavioural): the server, a forger, an eavesdropper and a short, illustrative replica attack.
* **G. Step 6** (transistor level, recorded run): the replica attack over 30,000 clocks.
* **H. Summary**: Table XXIII, block by block, and the section's findings.

#### Theory

Four questions decide whether a mixed-level run of this length is both feasible and meaningful. Symbols: $x_1, x_2$ are the two integrator outputs and $u$ the modulator input, all in model units (full scale ±1); $v = \pm 1$ is the DAC output; $d$ is the dither; $\Delta V_k$ is the differential input of the comparator at clock $k$, $\Delta V_k = (V_{DD}/4)\,x_2'$ with the dithered state $x_2' = x_2(1+d)+d$; $V_{os}$ is the comparator's input-referred offset in volts (in the model units of Section VIII, its offset is $o = -V_{os}/(V_{DD}/4)$) and $\sigma_n$ its input-referred noise (rms).

**1. Why the loop can be simulated in segments without error.** The modulator's only state is the pair $(x_1, x_2)$. The StrongARM comparator is reset in every clock cycle and keeps no state beyond it. A long transient can therefore be cut into segments: each segment starts from the previous one's integrator state (an `.ic` statement) and spends one extra clock, a warm-up decision, to bring the comparator into its normal cycle. The cut is exact up to the comparator's reset, which the circuit performs anyway. Its benefit is that ngspice's cost per clock stays constant instead of growing with the length of the transient. *Assumption:* the comparator really resets fully each cycle; an incomplete reset would show up as memory in the decision test of point 3.

**2. The behavioural integrators must be solved exactly.** ngspice solves every node to a relative tolerance `reltol`, $10^{-3}$ by default. The integrators must add exactly one loop step per clock. During development (the numbers are recorded in the docstring of `mixedsim.py`) the default tolerance left effective integrator gains of 0.4993 and 0.4972 instead of 0.5, gain errors of 0.1 to 0.6 %, and per-clock errors of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$. These are far above the integrators' own thermal noise, $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ of full scale per clock referred to the input ($0.9 \times 10^{-5}$ at the first integrator's output), and they differ from chip to chip, so they would make two chips' loops drift apart over a long run for a reason that no real chip has. With `reltol` = $10^{-6}$ the gains are exact to $10^{-6}$ and the per-clock error, $8 \times 10^{-6}$, is below the thermal noise, at about twice the simulation time. *Prediction:* the transistor-level loop decodes to the same reading as the behavioural model of the same chip.

**3. What the behavioural comparator leaves out, and how to test it.** The model of Section VIII decides
$$v_k = \operatorname{sgn}(\Delta V_k - V_{os} + n_k), \qquad n_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2),$$
with a constant offset and Gaussian noise. A real comparator can deviate from this in three ways. (i) Its offset can depend on the input history, through memory from an incomplete reset or kickback. (ii) It can be metastable: the regeneration time grows as $\tau \ln(V_{DD}/|\Delta V|)$, with $\tau$ the regeneration time constant, so an input smaller than about $V_{DD}\,e^{-t_{avail}/\tau}$ ($t_{avail}$: the time available before the latch samples) may not resolve in time. (iii) Its noise need not be Gaussian. The decisive test is decision by decision. Given the input $\Delta V_k$ that the transistor-level comparator actually saw at clock $k$, the threshold model predicts the decision $[\Delta V_k > V_{os}]$. It can be wrong only through noise, with probability $\Phi(-|\Delta V_k - V_{os}|/\sigma_n)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution. The expected number of disagreements over a run is therefore
$$\mathbb{E}[N_{\neq}] = \sum_k \Phi\!\left(-\frac{|\Delta V_k - V_{os}|}{\sigma_n}\right).$$
*Prediction:* the observed count $N_{\neq}$ is consistent with $\mathbb{E}[N_{\neq}]$ (approximately a Poisson count of that mean), and every disagreement occurs at $|\Delta V_k - V_{os}|$ of a few $\sigma_n$ at most. More disagreements, or disagreements at large inputs, would expose an effect that the model lacks.

**4. Why the bitstreams are not compared bit for bit over time.** A single differing decision changes the integrator state. From then on the transistor-level loop and the behavioural loop produce different but statistically equivalent bitstreams, so a bit-for-bit comparison over time would measure only the time to the first noise-driven disagreement. The two loops are therefore compared decision by decision on the same input (point 3) and by what the receiver makes of their bits (the decoded reading). The same argument applies to two chips: the victim and the replica start from the same state and see the same input, but their offsets, dither and noise differ, and every decision on which they differ also changes their states, so they do not stay in step. The replica attack must account for this (steps 5 and 6).

#### Simulation setup

The run simulates one victim chip and one replica chip at a single process corner and temperature, chosen in the settings form (A). Every random quantity has a fixed seed, so the run is reproducible; it is one sample, not a statistic. The statistics over many Monte Carlo chips and all 45 PVT conditions come from the behavioural studies of Section VIII, which this run checks.

| Item | Value in this run | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| corner, temperature, supply | tt, 37 °C, 1.8 V by default; any of tt, ss, ff, sf, fs and −40 to 85 °C in the form | settings A; 37 °C is body or bioreactor temperature |
| SRAM-PUF cells | 640 cells of the extracted 6T layout are powered up: the Monte Carlo runs in chunks of 64 cells, with the mismatch seeding of the recorded runs of Section VII, so the 600 cells of the fingerprint need ten chunks; the first 600 cells form the fingerprint and the last 40 are discarded | Section VII-C (cell), Section V-D (600-cell fingerprint) |
| PUF seeds and power-ups | mismatch seed: chip 1 (one seed per 64-cell chunk, as the recorded runs); transient-noise seed 7; one power-up at 25 °C (enrolment) and one at the chosen temperature (field read); two at 25 °C if 25 °C is chosen | fixed in the cell |
| BCH code | correction capability t = 45, the working setting of the system simulations (the strongest code that leaves 128 secret bits at the point estimate of the min-entropy; Section VII-E finds that no code for a 25 °C enrolment meets both the 10⁻⁶ target and the 192-bit limit); helper data 10 t = 450 bits (BCH over GF(2<sup>10</sup>), n = 600) | Section VII-E |
| comparator | post-layout StrongARM, Monte Carlo mismatch seeds 1000 (victim) and 1004 (replica); transient noise from the devices' noise spectrum at the chosen corner and temperature; σ<sub>n</sub> interpolated from the PVT grid | Section VII-B and -F |
| comparator offset | determined for each simulated chip in a separate SPICE run, by the successive-approximation search of Section VII-B, before the loop runs | Section VII-B |
| rest of the modulator | behavioural B-sources in ngspice: integrator gains g<sub>1</sub> = g<sub>2</sub> = 0.5, clipping at ±2.5, DAC ±1, comparator input ΔV = (V<sub>DD</sub>/4) x<sub>2</sub>′; first-integrator thermal noise 0.9 × 10<sup>−5</sup> of full scale per clock added to x<sub>1</sub> (1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup> referred to the input; seeds 31 and 32); each chip's own dither sequence (the replica's dither seeds differ from the victim's) | Section V-C, `mixedsim.py` |
| segmenting and solver | segments of 250 clocks, each started from the previous integrator state (`.ic`) with one warm-up decision; `reltol` = 10<sup>−6</sup> | Theory, points 1 and 2 |
| clock and run length | 10 MHz; 1,000 clocks per chip by default (500 to 8,000 in the form); step 6 uses 30,000 clocks | settings A; 30,000 is the length of the attack runs of Section VIII-B |
| sensor input | constant 0.5 µA (a bioreactor reading, and the input the replica attack uses), or a sine | settings A |
| frame | session nonce 0x3A94C1E7, frame counter 1, the 16-bit chip ID | Section IV |
| eavesdropper and forger | a random 128-bit key (seed 99); one ciphertext bit flipped in the middle of the frame | fixed in the cell |
| replica attack | 80 windows of 64 bits; a window *breaks* the key when the register that Berlekamp-Massey finds in it predicts the next 512 keystream bits with more than 99 % accuracy; window starts drawn at random from clock 200 to clock N − 777 (N: run length, capped at 30,000) | Section VIII-B |

**What is compared with what.** Each step has a pass criterion that is stated before its code cell:

1. Step 1: the field read against the enrolment; its error rate against the recorded transistor-level Monte Carlo at the same corner (Section VII-F) and against the code's capability t.
2. Step 2: the RTL decoder's corrected word against the enrolled fingerprint and against the model's decoder; the resulting key against the key the server stored at enrolment.
3. Step 3: every transistor-level decision against the threshold model on the same input ΔV<sub>k</sub>, with the count of disagreements against $\mathbb{E}[N_{\neq}]$; the decoded reading against the behavioural model of the same chip (same offset and σ<sub>n</sub>) and against the input.
4. Step 4: the RTL ciphertext, encrypted chip ID and MAC tag against the model.
5. Step 5: the server's decrypted bits against the victim's bits; the forged frame and the eavesdropper against the expectations of Section IX; the replica attack on both designs (illustrative at this length).
6. Step 6: the two chips' clean-window fraction against the behavioural prediction of Section VIII-B, and the replica attack on both designs.

**Run time.** About 6 minutes at the defaults on two cores, as in a free Colab session; the two transistor-level steps (1 and 3) take almost all of it, and step 3 grows in proportion to the number of clocks. Each card gives its step's run time, and Table XXIII collects them. Step 6 is a recorded run (72 min on two cores) that the form option `LONG_RUN` re-runs.

> **Next cell.** 1. Writes the mixed-level engine to `mixedsim.py`: the modulator netlist (behavioural integrators, DAC and dither around the transistor-level comparator, run in 250-clock segments with the integrator state handed over and `reltol` = 10<sup>−6</sup>); 2. the SRAM power-up call (640 cells in 64-cell Monte Carlo chunks); 3. the test bench that drives the RTL keystream block with the modulator's bits. Nothing is simulated yet.


```python
%%writefile mixedsim.py
"""mixedsim.py - one simulation of the complete secure sensor across abstraction levels.

Each block is simulated at the level at which its behaviour matters, and the blocks exchange real signals:

  SRAM-PUF power-up (640 extracted 6T cells: ten 64-cell Monte
  Carlo chunks; the first 600 form the fingerprint), mismatch +
  transient noise                                                    transistor level   ngspice   puf_power_up()
  TIA, buffer, two integrators, 1-bit DAC, dither                    behavioural        ngspice   modulator()
  StrongARM comparator, the modulator's quantiser (extracted,
  with this chip's mismatch and its transient noise), in the loop    transistor level   ngspice   modulator()
  BCH fuzzy-extractor decoder (the compiler's Verilog)               RTL                Icarus    (keygen.simulate)
  Grain-128a keystream, MAC, XOR with the modulator bits             RTL                Icarus    keystream_rtl()
  radio frame, receiver, eavesdropper, replica attacker              behavioural        Python    (the notebook's model)

The modulator netlist follows the difference equations of the notebook's bit-exact model: x1 += g1 (u - v) + n1,
x2 += g2 (x1 - v), with g1 = g2 = 0.5, clipping at +-2.5 and, optionally, an OTA leak; the comparator sees
dVin = (VDD/4) x2' with the dither x2' = x2 (1 + d) + d, and its latched decision drives the DAC v = +-1.
The behavioural integrators update in the comparator's reset phase, from gate pulses of unit area, so the latch holds
the decision they use.
"""
import os, subprocess, time
import numpy as np


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- modulator: behavioural loop + SPICE quantiser
def _pwl(name, node, times, values, rise=1e-9):
    """A piecewise-constant source that steps to values[k] at times[k] (linear over `rise`)."""
    pts = ["0", f"{values[0]:.8g}"]
    for t, a, b in zip(times[1:], values[:-1], values[1:]):
        pts += [f"{t - rise:.10g}", f"{a:.8g}", f"{t:.10g}", f"{b:.8g}"]
    return f"V{name} {node} 0 PWL(" + " ".join(pts) + ")"


def modulator(cs, cfg, u, d, n1, seed, S, seg=250, ota_gain=None, waves=4, log=None, scaled=True, options=(".option reltol=1e-6",)):
    """Simulate len(u) modulator clocks with the transistor-level comparator in the loop.

    cs: the comparator module; cfg: its config with layout, corner, vdd, vcm and temp_c set; u, d, n1: per-clock input,
    dither and first-integrator noise (model units); seed: the Monte Carlo mismatch seed (the chip); S: the comparator's
    channel-noise PSD at this PVT (cs.channel_noise_psd), or None for a noiseless comparator.
    Runs in segments of `seg` clocks: each segment starts from the previous one's integrator state (.ic) with one
    warm-up decision, so that ngspice's cost per clock stays constant. scaled: unit-amplitude gate pulses into 12 nF
    integrating capacitors (the same unit-area update; the original 1/12 ns pulses into 1 F left the circuit matrix
    badly conditioned next to the comparator's currents); options: extra '.option' lines. The default reltol = 1e-6 makes
    the integrators exact: with ngspice's default 1e-3 their effective gains were 0.4993 and 0.4972 with per-clock errors
    of 1e-3 to 1e-2, which made two chips' loops drift apart over long runs; at 1e-6 the gains are 0.5000 to 1e-6 and the
    per-clock error, 8e-6, is below the integrator's own thermal noise (about twice the run time). Returns dict(D, x1,
    x2, waves, seconds)."""
    n, T, vu = len(u), 1.0 / cfg["f_clk"], cfg["vdd"] / 4
    leak = 0.0 if not ota_gain or not np.isfinite(ota_gain) else 1.0 / (1.0 + ota_gain)
    D, X1, X2, W = np.zeros(n, np.uint8), np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n), None
    x1, x2, t0 = 0.0, 0.0, time.time()
    for s0 in range(0, n, seg):
        m = min(seg, n - s0)
        te = cs.edge_times(cfg, m + 1)                     # edge 0 warms the comparator up; edges 1..m are clocks s0..s0+m-1
        # gate pulse 1 + 11 + 1 ns of amplitude amp into Cint: the update is amp * 12 ns / Cint = 1 times the bracket
        amp, cint = (1.0, 12e-9) if scaled else (1.0 / 12e-9, 1.0)
        gk = cint / 1e-9                                   # clamp conductance: a 1 ns time constant beyond +-2.5
        uu, dd, nn = [np.concatenate([[a[s0]], a[s0:s0 + m]]) for a in (u, d, n1)]
        lines = [
            _pwl("sys_u", "su", te, uu), _pwl("sys_d", "sd", te - 10e-9, dd), _pwl("sys_n", "sn", te + 30e-9, nn),
            f"Vsys_g1 sg1 0 PULSE(0 {amp:.8g} {te[1] + 55e-9:.10g} 1n 1n 11n {T:.6g})",
            f"Vsys_g2 sg2 0 PULSE(0 {amp:.8g} {te[1] + 70e-9:.10g} 1n 1n 11n {T:.6g})",
            "Bsys_v sv 0 V = tanh(20*(V(c0_q)-V(c0_qb)))",      # the 1-bit DAC, driven by the comparator's SR latch
            f"Cx1 x1 0 {cint:.6g}", "Rx1 x1 0 1e15", f"Bx1 0 x1 I = V(sg1)*(0.5*(V(su)-V(sv)) + V(sn) - {leak:.6g}*V(x1))",
            f"Cx2 x2 0 {cint:.6g}", "Rx2 x2 0 1e15", f"Bx2 0 x2 I = V(sg2)*(0.5*(V(x1)-V(sv)) - {leak:.6g}*V(x2))",
            f"Bk1 x1 0 I = {gk:.6g}*(max(V(x1)-2.5,0)+min(V(x1)+2.5,0))", f"Bk2 x2 0 I = {gk:.6g}*(max(V(x2)-2.5,0)+min(V(x2)+2.5,0))",
            *options,
            f".ic v(x1)={x1:.10g} v(x2)={x2:.10g}"]
        if S is not None:
            src, tstr = cs.noise_sources(cfg, "c0", S, te[1:], np.random.default_rng(seed * 1000 + s0 // seg))
            lines += src + ["Vbrk brk 0 PWL(0 0 " + " ".join(f"{x} 0" for x in tstr) + ")", "Rbrk brk 0 1e3"]
        x2in = "(V(x2)*(1+V(sd))+V(sd))"
        inputs = {"c0": [f"Bc0p c0_inp 0 V = {cfg['vcm']:.6g} + {vu / 2:.6g}*{x2in}",
                         f"Bc0n c0_inn 0 V = {cfg['vcm']:.6g} - {vu / 2:.6g}*{x2in}"]}
        saves = ["v(c0_q)", "v(x1)", "v(x2)"] + (["v(clk)", "v(c0_outp)", "v(c0_outn)", "v(c0_qb)"] if s0 == 0 and waves else [])
        name = f"seg{s0 // seg:03d}"
        net = cs.make_netlist(cfg, ["c0"], te[-1] + 0.9 * T, "secure sensor modulator, mixed level", mismatch=True, seed=seed,
                              saves=saves, wrfile=name + ".dat", tmax=5e-9, inputs=inputs, extra=lines, with_latch=True, fine_edges=te)
        cs.run_ngspice(cfg["ngspice_bin"], net, cfg["workdir"], name, 3600)
        w = cs.read_wrdata(os.path.join(cfg["workdir"], name + ".dat"))
        D[s0:s0 + m] = (cs.sample_at(w["time"], w["v(c0_q)"], te[1:] + 0.45 * T) > cfg["vdd"] / 2)
        X1[s0:s0 + m] = cs.sample_at(w["time"], w["v(x1)"], te[1:])
        X2[s0:s0 + m] = cs.sample_at(w["time"], w["v(x2)"], te[1:])
        x1 = float(cs.sample_at(w["time"], w["v(x1)"], [te[-1] + 0.88 * T])[0])
        x2 = float(cs.sample_at(w["time"], w["v(x2)"], [te[-1] + 0.88 * T])[0])
        if s0 == 0 and waves:
            k = (w["time"] >= te[1] - 0.2 * T) & (w["time"] <= te[1 + waves] - 0.2 * T)
            W = {key: np.asarray(w[key])[k] for key in w} | dict(te=te[1:1 + waves])
        if log:
            log(f"  modulator: {s0 + m}/{n} clocks, {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
    return dict(D=D, x1=X1, x2=X2, waves=W, seconds=time.time() - t0)


def loop_reference(u, d, n1, offset, noise=None, ota_gain=None):
    """The same loop, behavioural, in the netlist's order (decide on x2, then update with that decision): the reference
    for a bit-by-bit comparison. offset, noise: the comparator's, in x2 units (noise: per-clock samples or None)."""
    leak = 0.0 if not ota_gain or not np.isfinite(ota_gain) else 1.0 / (1.0 + ota_gain)
    x1 = x2 = 0.0; D = np.zeros(len(u), np.uint8)
    for k in range(len(u)):
        q = x2 * (1 + d[k]) + d[k] + offset + (0.0 if noise is None else noise[k])
        D[k] = q >= 0; v = 1.0 if D[k] else -1.0
        x1 = min(max(x1 + 0.5 * (u[k] - v) + n1[k] - leak * x1, -2.5), 2.5)
        x2 = min(max(x2 + 0.5 * (x1 - v) - leak * x2, -2.5), 2.5)
    return D


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- SRAM PUF: transistor-level power-ups
def puf_power_up(ps, pcfg, cell, n_cells, temps, repeats, chip, noise_seed, pu=None, name="sys_puf", log=None):
    """Power the first n_cells cells of chip `chip` (mismatch seeds chip, chip + 1, ... per 64-cell chunk, as the recorded
    runs) up `repeats` times at each temperature in `temps`. Returns bits[T, R, N] (uint8)."""
    env = ps.noise_envelope(pcfg, sorted(set(temps) | {25}), cell=cell, name=name + "_env")
    mc = ps.run_montecarlo(pcfg, n_cells, temps, repeats, env, chunk=64, mismatch_seed=chip, noise_seed=noise_seed,
                           cell=cell, pu=pu or ps.POWERUP, name=name, log=log or (lambda *a: None))
    return mc["bits"].astype(np.uint8)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Grain-128a keystream block: RTL in Icarus
TB_SYSTEM = r"""`timescale 1ns/1ps
// The proposal's keystream block (secure_ks_top) driven by the modulator bitstream, with IV = 1 | N | ctr | N_c:
// enc_id = ID ^ z_0..z_15,
// C[j] = D[j] ^ z_(16+j), tag = Grain-128a MAC over ctr(32) | enc_id(16) | C(N), as the model's build_frame.
module tb_system;
  reg clk = 1'b0;
  always #50 clk = ~clk;
  reg key_sh = 0, key_in = 0, nonce_sh = 0, nonce_in = 0, cn_sh = 0, cn_in = 0, start = 0, m = 0, pad = 0, dith_load = 0;
  reg [15:0] seed1 = 16'h1D2B, seed2 = 16'h7A31;
  wire z, run, tag_ok, dith1, dith2;
  wire [0:31] tag;
  wire [31:0] ctr;
  secure_ks_top dut (.clk(clk), .key_sh(key_sh), .key_in(key_in), .nonce_sh(nonce_sh), .nonce_in(nonce_in),
                     .cn_sh(cn_sh), .cn_in(cn_in), .start(start), .m(m), .pad(pad), .dith_load(dith_load), .seed1(seed1), .seed2(seed2),
                     .z(z), .run(run), .tag_ok(tag_ok), .tag(tag), .ctr(ctr), .dith1(dith1), .dith2(dith2));
  localparam integer NMAX = 1 << 18;
  reg dmem [0:NMAX-1];
  reg [127:0] KEY; reg [31:0] NONCE, CTR, CN; reg [15:0] CHIP_ID;
  integer N, k, i, fo; reg [31:0] dly; reg e; reg [1023:0] dfile, ofile;
  task tick; begin @(posedge clk); #1; end endtask
  initial begin
    if (!$value$plusargs("KEY=%h", KEY) || !$value$plusargs("NONCE=%h", NONCE) || !$value$plusargs("CTR=%d", CTR) ||
        !$value$plusargs("ID=%h", CHIP_ID) || !$value$plusargs("N=%d", N) || !$value$plusargs("D=%s", dfile) ||
        !$value$plusargs("OUT=%s", ofile) || !$value$plusargs("CN=%h", CN)) begin $display("missing plusarg"); $finish; end
    $readmemb(dfile, dmem, 0, N - 1);
    fo = $fopen(ofile, "w"); #1;
    dith_load = 1; tick; dith_load = 0;
    key_sh = 1; for (i = 0; i < 128; i = i + 1) begin key_in = KEY[127 - i]; tick; end key_sh = 0;       // key, k_0 first
    nonce_sh = 1; for (i = 0; i < 32; i = i + 1) begin nonce_in = NONCE[31 - i]; tick; end nonce_sh = 0;  // nonce, MSB first
    cn_sh = 1; for (i = 0; i < 31; i = i + 1) begin cn_in = CN[30 - i]; tick; end cn_sh = 0;               // chip nonce, MSB first
    start = 1; for (i = 0; i <= CTR; i = i + 1) tick; start = 0;                                        // counter = CTR
    while (run !== 1'b1) tick;                                                                          // 128 + 32 init clocks
    dly = 32'd0;
    for (k = 0; k < 48 + N; k = k + 1) begin
      if (k < 16) e = CHIP_ID[15 - k] ^ z; else if (k < 16 + N) e = dmem[k - 16] ^ z; else e = 1'b0;
      m = (k < 32) ? ctr[31 - k] : dly[31];                       // MAC message ctr | enc_id | C (32-clock delay line)
      if (k < 16 + N) $fdisplay(fo, "%s %b %b", (k < 16) ? "I" : "C", e, z);
      tick; dly = {dly[30:0], e};
    end
    m = 0; pad = 1; tick; pad = 0;
    $fdisplay(fo, "TAG_OK %b", tag_ok); $fdisplay(fo, "TAG %h", tag); $fclose(fo); $finish;
  end
endmodule
"""


def keystream_rtl(R, key_bits, nonce, ctr, chip_id, D, wd, iverilog, vvp, cn=0):
    """Run the RTL keystream block on the bitstream D (Icarus), with session nonce `nonce` and chip nonce `cn` (31 bits) in
    the IV. The counter is reached by ctr + 1 start pulses, as on the chip. Returns dict(enc_id, C, z (the keystream bits used), tag, tag_ok, seconds)."""
    os.makedirs(wd, exist_ok=True)
    src = os.path.join(wd, "src"); R.write_verilog_files(src)
    srcs = [os.path.join(src, f) for f in R.DESIGNS["proposal"][1]]
    with open(os.path.join(wd, "tb_system.v"), "w") as f:
        f.write(TB_SYSTEM)
    with open(os.path.join(wd, "D.mem"), "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(str(int(b)) for b in D) + "\n")
    t0 = time.time()
    subprocess.run([iverilog, "-g2012", "-o", "sys.vvp", "-s", "tb_system", *srcs, "tb_system.v"], cwd=wd, check=True,
                   capture_output=True, text=True)
    key_hex = "".join(f"{int(''.join(str(int(b)) for b in key_bits[i:i + 4]), 2):x}" for i in range(0, 128, 4))
    subprocess.run([vvp, "-n", "sys.vvp", f"+KEY={key_hex}", f"+NONCE={nonce:08x}", f"+CN={cn:08x}", f"+CTR={ctr}", f"+ID={chip_id:04x}",
                    f"+N={len(D)}", "+D=D.mem", "+OUT=out.txt"], cwd=wd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    out = dict(I=[], C=[], z=[])
    for line in open(os.path.join(wd, "out.txt")):
        f = line.split()
        if f[0] in ("I", "C"):
            out[f[0]].append(int(f[1])); out["z"].append(int(f[2]))
        elif f[0] == "TAG":
            out["tag"] = int(f[1], 16)
        elif f[0] == "TAG_OK":
            out["tag_ok"] = f[1] == "1"
    return dict(enc_id=np.array(out["I"], np.uint8), C=np.array(out["C"], np.uint8), z=np.array(out["z"], np.uint8),
                tag=out["tag"], tag_ok=out["tag_ok"], seconds=time.time() - t0)
```

    Overwriting mixedsim.py


### A. Settings

**Goal.** Fix the operating condition of the run and look up the comparator noise σ<sub>n</sub> that the decision test of step 3 needs at that condition.

**Setup.** The defaults simulate a constant sensor reading of 0.5 µA at 37 °C (body or bioreactor temperature) at the typical corner (tt) and 1.8 V, over 1,000 modulator clocks per chip. The form also offers a slow corner (ss), a fast corner (ff), the skewed corners (sf, fs), any temperature from −40 to 85 °C, a sine input and up to 8,000 clocks. One informative alternative is fs at 85 °C, where Section VIII-F predicts that the key fails with a 25 °C enrolment. σ<sub>n</sub> is interpolated in temperature from the comparator PVT grid of Section VII-F at the chosen corner and 1.8 V.

> **Next cell.** 1. Reads the form: corner, temperature, input, number of clocks; 2. fixes the chips' seeds, the nonce and the frame counter; 3. interpolates the comparator noise σ<sub>n</sub> at the chosen corner and temperature from the PVT grid of Section VII-F; 4. prints the settings.


```python
#@title Mixed-level simulation: settings
# Settings of the mixed-level simulation (Colab shows them as a form). At the defaults the run takes about 4 to 5 minutes: the
# transistor-level steps dominate (SRAM power-ups, then the two chips' modulators, simulated in parallel)
CORNER = "tt"                           #@param ["tt", "ss", "ff", "sf", "fs"]
TEMP_C = 37                             #@param {type:"slider", min:-40, max:85, step:1}
INPUT = "constant"                      #@param ["constant", "sine"]
N_CLOCKS = 1000                         #@param {type:"slider", min:500, max:8000, step:250}
import importlib, concurrent.futures as cf, mixedsim as MS
importlib.reload(MS)
VDD_M, CHIPS, PUF_CHIP, NONCE, CTR = 1.8, (1000, 1004), 1, 0x3A94C1E7, 1   # comparator MC seeds: victim, replica
MIX = WORK / "mixed"; MIX.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); TIM_M = {}
_rows = sorted((r for r in PVT["cmp"] if r["corner"] == CORNER and r["vdd"] == VDD_M), key=lambda r: r["temp"])
SIG_N_M = float(np.interp(TEMP_C, [r["temp"] for r in _rows], [r["sigma_n"] for r in _rows]))   # σn at this corner and T
card("Mixed-level simulation: settings",
     [("process corner, temperature, supply", f"{CORNER}, {TEMP_C} °C, {VDD_M} V"),
      ("sensor input", "constant 0.5 µA (a bioreactor reading; the input of the replica attack)" if INPUT == "constant"
       else "sine, two periods per run"),
      ("modulator clocks per chip", f"{N_CLOCKS:,}"),
      ("chips", f"victim and replica: comparator Monte Carlo seeds {CHIPS[0]} and {CHIPS[1]}; SRAM array of chip {PUF_CHIP}"),
      ("comparator noise at this corner and temperature (Section VII-F)", f"σ<sub>n</sub> = {1e3 * SIG_N_M:.3f} mV")], tone="info")
```

**Result.** The published run uses the defaults: tt, 37 °C, 1.8 V, 1,000 clocks, comparator seeds 1000 (victim) and 1004 (replica), the SRAM array of Monte Carlo chip 1, and σ<sub>n</sub> = 0.594 mV at this corner and temperature. All numbers quoted in the rest of this section are from this run.

### B. Step 1, transistor level: the SRAM-PUF array powers up

**Goal.** Produce the chip's fingerprint from transistor-level SRAM cells, once at enrolment and once in the field, and measure how many cells power up differently, which is the input the key reconstruction of step 2 must correct.

**Theory.** The key is not stored. It is the power-up pattern of 600 SRAM cells. Each cell races to 1 or 0 at power-up, decided by its fixed transistor mismatch and the transient noise of that power-up. At enrolment (in the factory, at 25 °C) the pattern $w$ is read once and the BCH helper data, its syndrome, are computed from it and published. In the field the array powers up again at the operating temperature with fresh noise, giving $w'$. A cell whose mismatch is small compared with the noise, or whose mismatch changes with temperature, can power up the other way. The fraction of cells that differ, the bit error rate $\mathrm{BER} = |w \oplus w'|/600$, follows the error law of Section VIII-F; at the typical corner and moderate temperatures it is set mainly by noise. The code corrects up to t differing cells (t = 45, Section VII-E).

*Prediction and pass criterion.* The number of differing cells is close to 600 × BER, with BER taken from the recorded transistor-level Monte Carlo of Section VII-F at this corner and temperature (the card quotes it), within the binomial spread $\sqrt{600\,\mathrm{BER}(1-\mathrm{BER})}$; the key can be recovered only if it is at most t.

**Setup.** Transient simulations in ngspice of the extracted 6T cell with this chip's Monte Carlo mismatch (chip 1) and transient noise (seed 7); 640 cells (ten 64-cell chunks), of which the first 600 form the fingerprint; one power-up at 25 °C and one at the chosen temperature.

> **Next cell.** 1. Powers the 640 cells up in ngspice at 25 °C (enrolment) and at the chosen temperature (field read) and keeps the first 600; 2. counts the cells that differ; 3. compares the error rate with the recorded Monte Carlo at this corner and with t; 4. draws the fingerprint and the differing cells. About three to three and a half minutes on two cores.


```python
#@title Fig.: mixed level, step 1: SRAM-PUF power-ups
# Step 1, transistor level: this chip's SRAM-PUF array powered up in ngspice: once at enrolment (25 °C, the factory) and
# once in the field at TEMP_C. 640 cells of the extracted layout (the first 600 form the fingerprint), mismatch and noise
t0 = time.time()
pcfg_m = ps.make_config(str(SKY130_LIB), ngspice=str(NGSPICE), workdir=str(MIX / "puf"), corner=CORNER, jobs=max(2, len(os.sched_getaffinity(0)) or 2))
POST_M = dict(ps.CELL, layout=LAY_PUF)
if TEMP_C == 25:
    _b = MS.puf_power_up(ps, pcfg_m, POST_M, 640, [25], 2, PUF_CHIP, 7, name="mixed_puf")
    W_EN, W_RD = _b[0, 0, :PUF_BITS], _b[0, 1, :PUF_BITS]
else:
    _b = MS.puf_power_up(ps, pcfg_m, POST_M, 640, [25, TEMP_C], 1, PUF_CHIP, 7, name="mixed_puf")
    W_EN, W_RD = _b[0, 0, :PUF_BITS], _b[1, 0, :PUF_BITS]
TIM_M["puf"] = time.time() - t0
_pc = next(c for c in PVT["puf"]["corners"] if c["corner"] == CORNER)       # the recorded Monte Carlo at this corner
ber_exp = float(np.interp(TEMP_C, TEMPS, [r["ber"] for r in _pc["rows"]]))
n_err = int((W_EN != W_RD).sum())
card("Step 1, transistor level: SRAM-PUF power-ups",
     [("fingerprint", f"{PUF_BITS} cells, P(1) = {W_EN.mean():.3f}"),
      (f"bits that differ from the enrolment at {TEMP_C} °C", f"<b>{n_err}</b> (BER {100 * n_err / PUF_BITS:.2f} %); the "
       f"recorded Monte Carlo at this corner gives {100 * ber_exp:.2f} %" + (f" (interpolated to {TEMP_C} °C)" if TEMP_C not in TEMPS else "")
       + f", that is {PUF_BITS * ber_exp:.1f} ± {np.sqrt(PUF_BITS * ber_exp * (1 - ber_exp)):.1f} expected (binomial)"),
      ("BCH correction t", f"{CAL['bch_t']}: the key is recovered if at most {CAL['bch_t']} bits differ"),
      ("run time (ngspice)", f"{TIM_M['puf']:.0f} s")], tone="ok" if n_err <= CAL["bch_t"] else "bad")
from matplotlib.patches import Patch, Rectangle
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(W1 + 0.9, 2.75))
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
ax.imshow(W_EN.reshape(20, 30), cmap=ListedColormap(["white", "#a3a3a3"]), vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")
for k in np.flatnonzero(W_EN != W_RD):                  # the cells that power up to the other value in the field read
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k % 30 - 0.5, k // 30 - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=COL["key"], ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.8))
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(fc="#a3a3a3", ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.4, label="1 at enrolment"), Patch(fc="white", ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.4, label="0 at enrolment"),
                   Patch(fc=COL["key"], ec=COL["ink"], lw=0.8, label=f"differs at {TEMP_C} °C ({n_err})")],
          fontsize=7.5, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), ncol=3, frameon=False, handlelength=1.1, columnspacing=1.0)
ax.set_title(f"{n_err} of {PUF_BITS} cells differ; the code corrects up to {CAL['bch_t']}", loc="left", fontsize=9.5, pad=4)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 62.</b> Mixed level, step 1: SRAM-PUF power-ups in ngspice. Fingerprint enrolled at 25 °C, drawn as a 20 × 30 grid of cells (grey: 1, white: 0); red: cells that power up to the other value in the field read at the chosen temperature.</p>

**Result.** The fingerprint has 600 cells with P(1) = 0.472. In the field read at 37 °C, **7 of 600 cells** power up differently from the enrolment (Fig. 62, red), a BER of 1.17 %; they are scattered over the array. The recorded Monte Carlo at tt, interpolated to 37 °C, gives 1.32 %, that is 7.9 ± 2.8 expected errors (binomial standard deviation); the observed 7 lies within one standard deviation. The code corrects up to 45.

**Interpretation.** The transistor-level cells are consistent with the PUF error model of Section VIII at this condition, and the code has a margin of 38 errors. This is one simulated chip (one Monte Carlo mismatch draw) and one power-up: the key-failure probability comes from the statistics of Sections VII-E and VIII-F, not from this single read. With a 25 °C enrolment, t = 45 meets the 10<sup>−6</sup> target for the simulated chip population at the point estimate but leaves only 94–137 secret bits (Section VII-E); the enrolment at −40 and 85 °C of Section VIII-F meets the target with t = 17. The field read and the published helper data now go to the hardware that must remove the 7 errors.

### C. Step 2, RTL: the key is reconstructed in hardware

**Goal.** Reconstruct the key from the transistor-level field read of step 1 in the hardware that would be built, and check that it equals the key the server stored at enrolment.

**Theory.** The helper data published at enrolment is the BCH syndrome of the enrolled fingerprint $w$, 10 t bits for a BCH code over GF(2<sup>10</sup>). Combined with the field read $w' = w \oplus e$, it gives the syndrome of the error pattern $e$ alone, from which the decoder locates and flips the differing cells. If $e$ has at most t ones, the corrected word is exactly $w$; the key is then the first 128 bits of SHA-256($w$), the same key the server derived at enrolment. The decoder is a deterministic algorithm, so its RTL and the model's decoder (`reconstruct()`) must produce the same word for the same inputs; a single differing bit would be a bug in one of them, not noise.

*Prediction and pass criterion.* With the errors of step 1 (7 in the published run) and t = 45, the decoder succeeds; the RTL's corrected word equals the enrolled fingerprint and the model's output bit for bit; the hashed key equals the server's key.

**Setup.** RTL level: the decoder that the compiler of Section XI generates for n = 600 and t of Section VII-E with no repetition stage, simulated cycle by cycle in Icarus Verilog on the field read and the helper data; the hash is behavioural (Python).

> **Next cell.** 1. Computes the helper data (BCH syndrome) of the enrolled fingerprint; 2. simulates the generated decoder in Icarus Verilog on the field read and the helper data; 3. runs the model's decoder on the same inputs; 4. hashes the corrected word into the key and compares it with the server's enrolled key. A few seconds.


```python
#@title Mixed level, step 2: key reconstruction in RTL
# Step 2, RTL: the key-reconstruction hardware generated by the compiler of Section XI (BCH over GF(2^10),
# n = 600, t of Section VII-E), simulated cycle by cycle in Icarus Verilog on the field read and the helper data
# published at enrolment, and checked against the model's fuzzy extractor
t0 = time.time(); t_m = CAL["bch_t"]
H_EN = bch_syndrome(W_EN, t_m)                                  # helper data stored at enrolment: 10 t bits
KG_M = KG.simulate(dict(r=1, n=PUF_BITS, t=t_m), str(MIX / "keygen"),
                   [dict(cells=W_RD, rhelp=np.zeros(PUF_BITS, np.uint8), bhelp=syn_to_bits(H_EN))],
                   str(PNR_BIN / "iverilog"), str(PNR_BIN / "vvp"))[0]
REC_M = reconstruct(W_RD, H_EN, t_m)
KEY_M, KEY_SRV = hash_key(KG_M["bits"]), hash_key(W_EN)         # the chip's key; the key the server stored at enrolment
TIM_M["bch"] = time.time() - t0
card("Step 2, RTL: key reconstruction in the generated hardware",
     [("errors in the field read", f"{n_err} of {PUF_BITS} (t = {t_m})"),
      ("RTL decoder", f"success flag {KG_M['ok']}; corrected word equals the enrolled fingerprint: <b>{np.array_equal(KG_M['bits'], W_EN)}</b>"),
      ("RTL against the model's reconstruct()", f"identical bit for bit: <b>{np.array_equal(KG_M['bits'], REC_M['w'])}</b>"),
      ("key (SHA-256 of the corrected fingerprint, 128 bits)", f"equals the server's enrolled key: <b>{np.array_equal(KEY_M, KEY_SRV)}</b>"),
      ("latency", f"{KG_M['cycles']:,} clock cycles = {KG_M['cycles'] / 10:.0f} µs at 10 MHz, once per power-up"),
      ("run time (Icarus Verilog)", f"{TIM_M['bch']:.0f} s")], tone="ok" if np.array_equal(KEY_M, KEY_SRV) else "bad")
```


<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #2a78d6;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Step 2, RTL: key reconstruction in the generated hardware</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">errors in the field read</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">7 of 600 (t = 45)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">RTL decoder</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">success flag True; corrected word equals the enrolled fingerprint: <b>True</b></td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">RTL against the model's reconstruct()</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">identical bit for bit: <b>True</b></td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">key (SHA-256 of the corrected fingerprint, 128 bits)</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">equals the server's enrolled key: <b>True</b></td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">latency</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">91,127 clock cycles = 9113 µs at 10 MHz, once per power-up</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">run time (Icarus Verilog)</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">2 s</td></tr></table></div>


**Result.** The RTL decoder reports success. Its corrected word equals the enrolled fingerprint and is identical bit for bit to the model's `reconstruct()`, and the 128-bit key equals the server's enrolled key. Decoding takes 91,127 clock cycles, 9.1 ms at 10 MHz, once per power-up.

**Interpretation.** **The key generator works on transistor-level cells**: the RTL decoder regenerates the enrolled key from a simulated field read with the power-up errors of the transistor-level cells, and the generated RTL agrees with the model that all system-level results of Sections VIII and IX use. A 9.1 ms latency at power-up is negligible for a sensor that then runs continuously. This key now drives the keystream block of step 4; first, step 3 produces the bits it will encrypt.

### D. Step 3, transistor level in the loop: two chips' modulators

**Goal.** Run the victim's and the replica's second-order modulators with each chip's post-layout StrongARM comparator inside the loop, and test whether the behavioural comparator model of Section VIII predicts every decision the real circuit makes.

**Theory.** Points 1 to 4 of the Theory above apply here. The test is decision by decision: at each clock $k$ the threshold model, given the input $\Delta V_k$ that the transistor-level comparator actually saw and the chip's offset $V_{os}$, predicts the decision $[\Delta V_k > V_{os}]$, and it can be wrong only through noise. The comparator offset must be known for this test, and it is measured on its own (below).

*Prediction and pass criterion.* For each chip, the number of decisions that differ from the threshold model is consistent with $\mathbb{E}[N_{\neq}]$ computed from that chip's own $\Delta V_k$, $V_{os}$ and $\sigma_n$, and every differing decision lies within a few $\sigma_n$ of the threshold (the cell marks the run as failed if any lies beyond 6 $\sigma_n$). The receiver's decoded reading of the transistor-level bits equals that of the behavioural model of the same chip, and the input, within the decimator's resolution.

**Setup.** Transistor level in the loop: each chip's extracted StrongARM (Monte Carlo seeds 1000 and 1004, transient noise at the chosen corner and temperature) inside behavioural integrators, DAC and dither in ngspice; 250-clock segments with one warm-up decision; `reltol` = 10<sup>−6</sup>; each chip with its own dither and first-integrator noise; the two chips run in parallel on two cores. Before the loop, each chip's offset is measured in SPICE by the successive-approximation search of Section VII-B. The behavioural reference is the model of Section V-C with the same chip's offset and $\sigma_n$. The receiver's reading uses its CIC decimator only: the 31-tap compensation FIR runs at the output rate and needs 31 output samples (1,550 clocks) to fill, more than this short run.

> **Next cell.** 1. Measures each chip's comparator offset in SPICE; 2. runs both modulators in ngspice in parallel, with each chip's StrongARM in the loop (about two and a half minutes for 1,000 clocks on two cores; the time grows in proportion to the number of clocks); 3. tests every decision against the threshold model on the input the comparator saw and counts the disagreements against $\mathbb{E}[N_{\neq}]$; 4. runs the behavioural model of the same chip and decodes both bitstreams; 5. draws the comparator's waveforms in the loop, the integrator states, every decision's distance from the threshold and the decoded readings.


```python
#@title Fig.: mixed level, step 3: modulators with the transistor-level comparator
# Step 3, transistor level in the loop: each chip's second-order modulator in ngspice, with behavioural integrators, DAC
# and dither around its post-layout StrongARM comparator (its own Monte Carlo mismatch and transient noise). The two chips
# run in parallel. Then the decision-by-decision test of the behavioural comparator model of Section VIII
t0 = time.time()
def ccfg_m(tag):
    c = cs.default_config(str(SKY130_LIB), str(NGSPICE), str(MIX / f"cmp_{tag}"), quick=True)
    c = dict(c, layout=LAY_CMP, corner=CORNER, vdd=VDD_M, vcm=VDD_M / 2, temp_c=float(TEMP_C))
    os.makedirs(c["workdir"], exist_ok=True); return c
CM = [ccfg_m("victim"), ccfg_m("replica")]
S_M = cs.channel_noise_psd(CM[0], cs.reference_trajectory(CM[0]))     # the devices' noise PSD at this corner and T
u_m = (np.full(N_CLOCKS, s2d(tia(0.5e-6, P_sys["rtia"]), P_sys["buffer"])) if INPUT == "constant" else
       s2d(tia(sensor_current({**P_sys, "sig": "sine", "bin": 100}, N_CLOCKS), P_sys["rtia"]), P_sys["buffer"]))
d_m = [dsm2(u_m, P_sys)["DI"].astype(float), dsm2(u_m, P_sys, seeds=REPLICA_DITHER)["DI"].astype(float)]   # each chip's dither
n1_m = [P_sys["int_noise"] * np.random.default_rng(31 + i).standard_normal(N_CLOCKS) for i in range(2)]
def vos_of(c, seed):                                   # this chip's comparator offset, by the SAR search of Section VII-B
    net, te = cs.run_offset_job(c, 1, seed, "vos"); cs.run_ngspice(c["ngspice_bin"], net, c["workdir"], "vos")
    return cs.read_offsets(c, "vos", 1, te)[0][0]
with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
    VOS_M = [f.result() for f in [ex.submit(vos_of, CM[i], CHIPS[i]) for i in range(2)]]
    MOD = [f.result() for f in [ex.submit(MS.modulator, cs, CM[i], u_m, d_m[i], n1_m[i], CHIPS[i], S_M, 250, None, 4 if i == 0 else 0)
                                for i in range(2)]]
TIM_M["mod"] = time.time() - t0
VU_M = VDD_M / 4
chk = []
for m, d, vo in zip(MOD, d_m, VOS_M):                   # decision by decision: the threshold model on the input the circuit saw
    dv = VU_M * (m["x2"] * (1 + d) + d)
    dis = m["D"] != (dv >= vo).astype(np.uint8)
    chk.append(dict(dv=dv, dis=dis, exp=float(ndtr(-np.abs(dv - vo) / SIG_N_M).sum()),
                    worst=float(np.abs(dv - vo)[dis].max() / SIG_N_M) if dis.any() else 0.0))
D_A, D_B = MOD[0]["D"], MOD[1]["D"]
y_true = float(u_m.mean())
# the receiver's CIC stage alone: its 31-tap compensation FIR runs at the output rate and needs 31 output samples (1,550
# clocks) to fill, most of a short run, so the full decoder would still be settling here
dec_m = lambda D: cic(D)
reading = lambda D: float(dec_m(D)[3:].mean())
D_beh = dsm2(u_m, {**P_sys, "comp_noise": SIG_N_M / VU_M}, offset=-VOS_M[0] / VU_M)["D"]       # the behavioural model, same chip
card("Step 3, transistor level in the loop: the two chips' modulators",
     [("comparator offsets (SPICE, this corner and T)", f"victim {1e3 * VOS_M[0]:+.3f} mV, replica {1e3 * VOS_M[1]:+.3f} mV"),
      ("decisions equal to the threshold model [ΔV > V<sub>os</sub>]", "; ".join(
          f"{nm}: <b>{100 * (1 - c['dis'].mean()):.2f} %</b> ({int(c['dis'].sum())} differ, theory expects {c['exp']:.1f} from noise; "
          + (f"largest at |ΔV − V<sub>os</sub>| = {c['worst']:.1f} σ<sub>n</sub>)" if c["dis"].any() else "none differs)")
          for nm, c in zip(("victim", "replica"), chk))),
      ("both chips: observed against expected", (lambda n, lam: f"{n} differ, {lam:.1f} expected; a Poisson count of mean {lam:.1f} is "
       + (f"≤ {n} with probability {sum(np.exp(-lam) * lam**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(n + 1)):.0%}" if n <= lam else
          f"≥ {n} with probability {1 - sum(np.exp(-lam) * lam**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(n)):.0%}"))(
       int(sum(c['dis'].sum() for c in chk)), sum(c['exp'] for c in chk))),
      ("decoded reading of the victim's bits", f"transistor-level loop {reading(D_A):+.4f}, behavioural model {reading(D_beh):+.4f}, "
       f"input {y_true:+.4f} (full scale ±1)" if INPUT == "constant" else "see the figure"),
      ("run time (ngspice, two chips in parallel)", f"{TIM_M['mod']:.0f} s for {N_CLOCKS:,} clocks per chip "
       f"({1e3 * TIM_M['mod'] / N_CLOCKS:.0f} ms per clock)")],
     tone="ok" if all(c["worst"] < 6 for c in chk) else "bad")
# (a) the victim's StrongARM in the loop, (b) the integrator states from ngspice, (c) the decision-by-decision test: where
# every decision's input lay relative to the threshold and which ones differ from the model, (d) what the receiver decodes
n_dis, n_exp = int(sum(c["dis"].sum() for c in chk)), sum(c["exp"] for c in chk)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(W2, 5.8))
w = MOD[0]["waves"]; tw = 1e9 * (w["time"] - w["te"][0])
ax = axs[0, 0]                                                                  # a timing diagram: one row per node (names as in
ROWS_A = [(r"clock $\phi$", "v(clk)", COL["faint"]), (r"$\mathrm{out}_p$", "v(c0_outp)", COL["ok"]),   # the schematic), each row
          (r"$\mathrm{out}_n$", "v(c0_outn)", COL["bad"]), (r"SR latch $q$", "v(c0_q)", COL["ink"])]   # from 0 to 1.8 V
for k, (lab, node, col) in enumerate(ROWS_A):
    y0 = 1.3 * (len(ROWS_A) - 1 - k)
    ax.axhline(y0, color=COL["faint"], lw=0.4, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(tw, y0 + w[node] / 1.8, color=col, lw=1.2)
ax.set_yticks([1.3 * (len(ROWS_A) - 1 - k) + 0.5 for k in range(len(ROWS_A))], [r[0] for r in ROWS_A])
ax.tick_params(axis="y", left=False, right=False); ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 1.3 * (len(ROWS_A) - 1) + 1.25); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ns)")
panel(ax, "a", "the victim's StrongARM in the loop (4 clocks)")
ax = axs[0, 1]; kk = np.arange(min(200, N_CLOCKS))
ax.step(kk, MOD[0]["x2"][kk], where="post", color=COL["ink"], lw=1.2, label="$x_2$ (ngspice)")
ax.step(kk, MOD[0]["x1"][kk], where="post", color=COL["aqua"], lw=1.0, label="$x_1$ (ngspice)")
ax.set_xlabel("Clock"); ax.set_ylabel("Integrator output (model units)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")
panel(ax, "b", "integrator states")
ax = axs[1, 0]
xs_m = [np.log10(np.maximum(np.abs(c["dv"] - vo) / SIG_N_M, 1e-3)) for c, vo in zip(chk, VOS_M)]
lo_m = min(-1.25, min(x.min() for x in xs_m) - 0.15)
ax.axvspan(lo_m, np.log10(3), color=COL["faint"], alpha=0.15, lw=0, label=r"within $3\sigma_\mathrm{n}$")
for x, c, col, nm in zip(xs_m, chk, (COL["ok"], COL["bad"]), ("victim", "replica")):
    ax.hist(x, bins=60, color=col, alpha=0.35, label=f"{nm}: all decisions")
top_m = 1.45 * ax.get_ylim()[1]; ax.set_ylim(0, top_m)
for k, (x, c, col, nm) in enumerate(zip(xs_m, chk, (COL["ok"], COL["bad"]), ("victim", "replica"))):
    ax.plot(x[c["dis"]], np.full(int(c["dis"].sum()), top_m * (0.93 - 0.06 * k)), "v", color=col, ms=7, mec=COL["ink"], mew=0.5,
            label=f"{nm}: differs ({int(c['dis'].sum())})")
ax.set_xlim(lo_m, None)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_{10}(|\Delta V - V_\mathrm{os}|/\sigma_\mathrm{n})$"); ax.set_ylabel("Decisions")
ax.legend(fontsize=6.3, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.5), handlelength=1.2)
panel(ax, "c", f"decision test: {n_dis} of {2 * N_CLOCKS:,} differ, noise predicts {n_exp:.1f}")
ax = axs[1, 1]; yA, yB = dec_m(D_A), dec_m(D_beh)
ax.plot(yA, "o-", color=COL["ok"], ms=3, lw=1.2, label="transistor-level loop")
ax.plot(yB, "s--", color=COL["key"], ms=3, lw=1.0, label="behavioural model")
ax.plot(u_m[::OSR][:len(yA)], ":", color=COL["ink"], lw=1.2, label="input")
ax.set_xlabel("Output sample (OSR = 50)"); ax.set_ylabel("CIC output (full scale ±1)"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="best")
panel(ax, "d", "what the receiver's filters make of the bits")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```


<div style="font-family:'STIX Two Text','Times New Roman',Times,serif;font-size:15px;line-height:1.45;border:1px solid rgba(128,128,128,.45);border-left:4px solid #2a78d6;padding:8px 14px;margin:8px 0;max-width:860px"><div style="font-weight:bold;margin-bottom:3px">Step 3, transistor level in the loop: the two chips' modulators</div><table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px"><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">comparator offsets (SPICE, this corner and T)</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">victim +3.282 mV, replica -3.180 mV</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">decisions equal to the threshold model [ΔV > V<sub>os</sub>]</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">victim: <b>100.00 %</b> (0 differ, theory expects 0.3 from noise; none differs); replica: <b>100.00 %</b> (0 differ, theory expects 0.9 from noise; none differs)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">both chips: observed against expected</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">0 differ, 1.2 expected; a Poisson count of mean 1.2 is ≤ 0 with probability 30%</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">decoded reading of the victim's bits</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">transistor-level loop +0.1341, behavioural model +0.1341, input +0.1341 (full scale ±1)</td></tr><tr><td style="padding:2px 18px 2px 0;opacity:.8;vertical-align:top">run time (ngspice, two chips in parallel)</td><td style="padding:2px 0;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">114 s for 1,000 clocks per chip (114 ms per clock)</td></tr></table></div>
