<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 63.</b> Mixed level, step 3: modulators with the transistor-level comparator. (a) Victim's post-layout StrongARM in the loop, four clocks; each row from 0 to 1.8 V. (b) Integrator states from ngspice, first 200 clocks. (c) Distance of each decision's input from the threshold, log<sub>10</sub> |ΔV − V<sub>os</sub>|/σ<sub>n</sub>; grey: within 3 σ<sub>n</sub>; triangles: decisions that differ from the threshold model. (d) CIC decimator output: transistor-level loop, behavioural model, input.</p>

**Result.** The offsets found by the SPICE search are +3.282 mV (victim) and −3.180 mV (replica), against σ<sub>n</sub> = 0.594 mV. Fig. 63 shows the step from the circuit to the bits the receiver decodes, one panel per level. In panel (a), the post-layout StrongARM works inside the loop as it did on its own in Fig. 20: after each decision the outputs out<sub>p</sub> and out<sub>n</sub> settle at complementary levels, and the SR latch q follows the decision and holds it until the next one, so the feedback DAC sees one stable bit per clock (the waveforms are saved at the loop's 5 ns time step, so the regeneration and reset transients at the clock edges appear as short spikes). Panel (b) shows that the ngspice integrators behave as a second-order loop should: x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> stay bounded over the 200 clocks, with no drift or overload. Panel (c) places every decision by the distance of its input from the threshold: almost all lie tens to hundreds of σ<sub>n</sub> away, where noise cannot change them, and only a few lie within 3 σ<sub>n</sub> (grey band). Because the comparator noise is a random transient in ngspice, the number of decisions that differ from the threshold model varies from run to run; the card gives it for each chip together with the number the noise explains and the Poisson probability of the observed total, and the title of panel (c) gives the total. In the runs of this notebook made during its development and in the run saved here, 0 to 3 of the 2,000 decisions differed, against 0.8 to 2.5 expected from the noise, each count consistent with noise alone; a differing decision lies close to the threshold (the card gives the largest distance in σ<sub>n</sub>), where the comparator's own noise decides. The decoded reading of the victim's transistor-level bits is +0.1341 of full scale, equal to the behavioural model of the same chip (+0.1341) and to the input (+0.1341) at the four decimals the card prints. This agreement is weak evidence: any stable loop decodes a constant input correctly, whatever its individual decisions, so the decision-by-decision comparison above is the actual test; in panel (d) the decoded samples of the transistor-level loop and of the behavioural model lie on each other and on the input. The card gives this run's ngspice time (the two chips run in parallel).

**Interpretation.** In closed loop at tt, 37 °C and 1.8 V, **the post-layout StrongARM decides as the threshold model predicts**: its 2,000 decisions depart from the model only where the input lies within the comparator's noise of the threshold, as often as that noise explains, and no memory, kickback or metastability effect appears. The behavioural comparator behind the thousands of system runs of Section VIII therefore agrees with the post-layout circuit at this condition (tt, 37 °C, 1.8 V). The limit of the test is its length: 2,000 decisions at one corner cannot reveal an effect rarer than about one decision in a thousand. The victim's bitstream now goes to the encryption hardware, and the replica's to the attacker of step 5.

### E. Step 4, RTL: encryption and MAC

**Goal.** Encrypt and authenticate the victim's transistor-level bitstream of step 3 in the RTL of the proposal's keystream block, keyed by the key of step 2, and check the frame against the model.

**Theory.** Grain-128a is a deterministic stream cipher: from the 128-bit key and an initialisation vector built from the session nonce, the frame counter and the chip nonce, IV = 1 ‖ N ‖ ctr ‖ N<sub>c</sub>, it produces a keystream $z_0, z_1, \dots$. The frame carries the chip ID encrypted with the first 16 keystream bits, the ciphertext $C_j = D_j \oplus z_{16+j}$ of the modulator bits $D_j$, and a 32-bit tag computed by Grain-128a's authentication mode over the counter, the encrypted ID and $C$. The model's Grain-128a matches the published test vectors (Section V-B). Because every output is a deterministic function of the same inputs, any difference between RTL and model would be an error in the hardware's bit order, counter or MAC timing.

*Prediction and pass criterion.* The RTL's ciphertext, encrypted chip ID and tag equal the model's bit for bit.

**Setup.** RTL level: the proposal's keystream block in its form written for one bit per clock (`secure_ks_top`; the block placed and routed in Section X is its low-power form, bit-exact with it), simulated in Icarus Verilog with the key of step 2, nonce 0x3A94C1E7, frame counter 1, the 31-bit chip nonce N<sub>c</sub> that the model derives from the raw field read of step 1 (printed on the card), the 16-bit chip ID and the victim's 1,000 transistor-level bits; the model computes the same frame in Python.

> **Next cell.** 1. Simulates the keystream block in Icarus Verilog with the key of step 2 and the victim's bits of step 3; 2. computes the same frame with the model's Grain-128a; 3. compares the ciphertext, the encrypted chip ID and the MAC tag. Under a second.


```python
#@title Mixed level, step 4: Grain-128a and MAC in RTL
# Step 4, RTL: the proposal's keystream block (Grain-128a, MAC, frame counter, chip nonce; the block placed and routed in
# Section X) driven by the victim's transistor-level bitstream and the key of step 2, in Icarus Verilog; checked
# against the model's Grain-128a, which matches the published test vectors (Section V-B). The chip nonce N_c is
# the model's, from the raw field read of step 1 (IV = 1 | N | ctr | N_c)
t0 = time.time()
CN_M = chip_nonce(W_RD, 0)
RTL_M = MS.keystream_rtl(R, KEY_M, NONCE, CTR, P_sys["chip_id"], D_A, str(MIX / "rtl"), str(PNR_BIN / "iverilog"), str(PNR_BIN / "vvp"),
                         cn=CN_M)
KS_M = keystream_nl(KEY_M, iv_bits(NONCE, CTR, CN_M), ID_BITS + N_CLOCKS)
ID_M = int_to_bits(P_sys["chip_id"], ID_BITS)
C_ref = D_A ^ KS_M["enc"][ID_BITS:]; EID_ref = ID_M ^ KS_M["enc"][:ID_BITS]
TAG_ref = grain_tag(mac_msg(int_to_bits(CTR, 32), EID_ref, C_ref), KS_M)
TIM_M["rtl"] = time.time() - t0
card("Step 4, RTL: encryption and MAC in the generated hardware",
     [("IV = 1 ‖ N ‖ ctr ‖ N<sub>c</sub>", f"N = {NONCE:08x}, ctr = {CTR}, chip nonce N<sub>c</sub> = {CN_M:08x} (31 bits, from the step-1 read)"),
      ("ciphertext C = D ⊕ keystream", f"{N_CLOCKS:,} bits; equal to the model bit for bit: <b>{np.array_equal(RTL_M['C'], C_ref)}</b>"),
      ("encrypted chip ID", f"equal to the model: <b>{np.array_equal(RTL_M['enc_id'], EID_ref)}</b>"),
      ("MAC tag over counter | encrypted ID | C", f"RTL {RTL_M['tag']:08x}, model {TAG_ref:08x}: <b>{RTL_M['tag'] == TAG_ref}</b>"),
      ("run time (Icarus Verilog)", f"{TIM_M['rtl']:.1f} s")], tone="ok" if RTL_M["tag"] == TAG_ref else "bad")
```

**Result.** The 1,000-bit ciphertext and the encrypted chip ID equal the model's bit for bit, and the two tags agree (the card prints both; the tag changes from run to run with the transistor-level bits it authenticates).

**Interpretation.** **The RTL of the block that Section X prices (in the form written for one bit per clock, bit-exact with its low-power form) computes the same frame as the model that Section IX attacks**, here for one 1,000-bit frame, one key and one counter value. The security results of that section, which rest on the model's frames, therefore carry over to the hardware to the extent that this test and the test vectors of Section X cover its behaviour. The frame now goes over the air to the server and to the attackers of step 5.

### F. Step 5: the server, an eavesdropper and the replica attacker

**Goal.** Receive the frame of step 4 as the server does, and attack it three ways: a forger who changes the reading, an eavesdropper with a wrong key, and the replica attacker of Section VIII-B with the transistor-level bits of its own chip.

**Theory.**

* *Server.* The server holds the key it stored at enrolment. Since step 2 regenerated the same key, the tag verifies, and decryption $D_j = C_j \oplus z_{16+j}$ recovers the victim's bits exactly; the decoded reading must equal step 3's.
* *Forger.* Without the key, a frame with one ciphertext bit changed carries the old tag, which matches the new frame only with probability $2^{-32}$ for a 32-bit tag; the server must reject it.
* *Eavesdropper.* A wrong key gives a keystream unrelated to the true one, so the eavesdropper's decrypted bits agree with the true bits with probability 1/2. Over 1,000 bits the standard deviation of that fraction is $\sqrt{0.25/1000} \approx 1.6$ %. The eavesdropper's MAC check fails.
* *Replica attacker.* The victim sends $C_A = D_A \oplus K$, with $D_A$ its modulator bits and $K$ the keystream. The attacker applies the same input to the replica chip and reads its unencrypted bits $D_B$. Then $C_A \oplus D_B = K \oplus (D_A \oplus D_B)$: in any *clean window*, 64 consecutive clocks on which the two chips decide alike, the attacker holds 64 true keystream bits. For the original design's 16-bit LFSR, Berlekamp-Massey recovers the register from 32 bits, so one clean window yields the key. Grain-128a has no short linear register: Berlekamp-Massey on 64 of its bits finds a register of about 32 stages that predicts the following bits only at chance, so a window of the proposal yields nothing to this attack even when it is clean.
* *Why the attack is only illustrative at 1,000 clocks.* The attack draws its 80 window starts at random from clock 200 to clock N − 777 (Simulation setup). For N = 1,000 that range holds only 24 start positions, 200 to 223. The 80 attempts therefore lie on at most 24 distinct, heavily overlapping windows, all within clocks 200 to 286: they test one stretch of the run, not 80 independent windows. The card reports the number of distinct windows. Below 2,000 clocks the card labels the result illustrative; step 6 is the actual test.

*Prediction and pass criterion.* The server accepts the frame and recovers the bits exactly; the forged frame is rejected; the eavesdropper's MAC check fails and the eavesdropper's bits agree with the true bits in about 50 % (±1.6 %); the replica attack on the proposal recovers nothing. The replica attack on the original succeeds if and only if the stretch near clock 200 is clean, which a single short run cannot predict statistically.

**Setup.** Behavioural (Python): the model's receiver and MAC check on the RTL frame of step 4; the eavesdropper's key is a random 128-bit key (seed 99); the forged frame flips the ciphertext bit in the middle of the frame; the replica attack uses the replica's transistor-level bits of step 3 against both designs, with the original design keyed by its 16-bit LFSR. The clean-window fraction is measured over clocks 200 to the end of the run.

> **Next cell.** 1. Verifies, decrypts and decodes the frame with the server's enrolled key; 2. does the same with an eavesdropper's random key; 3. checks a frame with one ciphertext bit changed; 4. runs the replica attack (80 windows) on both designs with the replica's bits, counts the distinct windows and labels the result illustrative below 2,000 clocks; 5. draws what the server and the eavesdropper read, and the replica attack's result for both designs.


```python
#@title Fig.: mixed level, step 5: receiver and attackers
# Step 5, behavioural: the server receives the frame, verifies the MAC with the key stored at enrolment, decrypts and
# decodes; an eavesdropper without the key; and the replica attack of Section VIII-B with the replica's
# transistor-level bits, against the original design (LFSR-16) and against the proposal (Grain-128a)
ok_rx, _, ks_rx = mac_verify(KEY_SRV, NONCE, CTR, RTL_M["enc_id"], RTL_M["C"], RTL_M["tag"], cn=CN_M)   # N_c read from the frame
D_rx = RTL_M["C"] ^ ks_rx["enc"][ID_BITS:]
key_eve = np.random.default_rng(99).integers(0, 2, 128).astype(np.uint8)
ok_eve, _, ks_eve = mac_verify(key_eve, NONCE, CTR, RTL_M["enc_id"], RTL_M["C"], RTL_M["tag"], cn=CN_M)
D_eve = RTL_M["C"] ^ ks_eve["enc"][ID_BITS:]
C_forged = RTL_M["C"].copy(); C_forged[N_CLOCKS // 2] ^= 1                     # one bit of a forged reading
ok_forged = mac_verify(KEY_SRV, NONCE, CTR, RTL_M["enc_id"], C_forged, RTL_M["tag"], cn=CN_M)[0]
K16_M = lfsr16_bits(DEFAULTS["key16"], ID_BITS + N_CLOCKS)[ID_BITS:]
# window_attack draws its 80 window starts from clocks 200 ... 199 + N_POS (it keeps 976 clocks for the 64-bit window, its
# 512-bit check and a margin): a short run offers few, overlapping windows, so the attack below is only illustrative there
N_POS = max(0, min(N_CLOCKS, 30000) - 976)
_rw = rng_for(100); WIN_M = len({int(_rw.integers(N_POS)) for _ in range(80)}) if N_POS else 0   # distinct windows of the 80
SHORT_M = N_CLOCKS < 2000
if N_POS:
    atk_orig = window_attack(D_A ^ K16_M ^ D_B, K16_M, 100)                    # original: C = D_A ^ K16; the attacker has D_B
    atk_prop = window_attack(RTL_M["C"] ^ D_B, KS_M["enc"][ID_BITS:], 100)    # proposal: C = D_A ^ Grain keystream
else:                                                                           # too short for one window and its check
    atk_orig = atk_prop = dict(broken=0, tries=0, first=-1)
atk_note = ("" if not SHORT_M else f" (illustrative: the {atk_orig['tries']} tries fall on {WIN_M} distinct, overlapping windows "
            f"starting at clocks 200 to {199 + N_POS}; step 6 is the test)" if N_POS else " (skipped: the run is shorter than 977 clocks)")
x_ = (D_A ^ D_B)[200:].astype(int); c_ = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(x_)]); f64_m = float(np.mean(c_[64:] - c_[:-64] == 0))
card("Step 5: the server, the eavesdropper and the replica attacker",
     [("server: MAC check with the enrolled key", f"<b>{'accepted' if ok_rx else 'REJECTED'}</b>; bits recovered exactly: {np.array_equal(D_rx, D_A)}; "
       f"decoded reading {reading(D_rx):+.4f} (input {y_true:+.4f})" if INPUT == "constant" else f"<b>{'accepted' if ok_rx else 'REJECTED'}</b>"),
      ("a forged frame (one ciphertext bit changed)", f"MAC {'accepted' if ok_forged else '<b>rejected</b>'}"),
      ("eavesdropper with a wrong key", f"MAC {'accepted' if ok_eve else 'rejected'}; the eavesdropper's bits agree with the true ones in {100 * np.mean(D_eve == D_A):.1f} %"),
      ("the two chips' transistor-level bitstreams", f"disagree on {100 * x_.mean():.1f} % of bits; clean 64-bit windows {100 * f64_m:.1f} %"),
      ("replica attack on the original design (LFSR-16)", f"<b>{atk_orig['broken']} of {atk_orig['tries']}</b> windows recover the key" + atk_note),
      ("replica attack on the proposal (Grain-128a)", f"<b>{atk_prop['broken']} of {atk_prop['tries']}</b> windows" + atk_note)],
     tone="ok" if ok_rx and not ok_forged and atk_prop["broken"] == 0 else "bad")
# (a) what the server and an eavesdropper read; (b) the replica attack with the transistor-level chips
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(W2, 3.0), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.35, 1]))
ax = axs[0]
ax.plot(dec_m(D_rx), "o-", color=COL["ok"], ms=3, lw=1.3, label=f"server, enrolled key: MAC {'accepted' if ok_rx else 'rejected'}")
ax.plot(dec_m(D_eve), "x-", color=COL["bad"], ms=3.5, lw=1.0,
        label=f"eavesdropper, wrong key: MAC {'accepted' if ok_eve else 'rejected'}, {100 * np.mean(D_eve == D_A):.1f} % of bits right")
ax.plot(u_m[::OSR][:len(dec_m(D_rx))], ":", color=COL["ink"], lw=1.3, label="sensor input")
ax.set_xlabel("Output sample (OSR = 50)"); ax.set_ylabel("CIC output (full scale ±1)")
lo_r, hi_r = ax.get_ylim(); ax.set_ylim(lo_r, hi_r + 0.55 * (hi_r - lo_r))
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left", handlelength=1.6)
panel(ax, "a", "what the server and an eavesdropper read")
ax = axs[1]
ax.bar([0, 1], [atk_orig["broken"], atk_prop["broken"]], color=[COL["bad"], COL["ok"]], width=0.55)
for x, a in ((0, atk_orig), (1, atk_prop)):
    ax.text(x, a["broken"] + 0.02 * max(1, atk_orig["tries"]), f"{a['broken']} of {a['tries']}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["original (LFSR-16)", "proposal (Grain-128a)"]); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15 * max(1, atk_orig["tries"]))
ax.set_ylabel(f"Windows that recover the key (of {atk_orig['tries']})"); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
panel(ax, "b", "replica attack" + (f" ({WIN_M} distinct windows)" if SHORT_M else ""))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 64.</b> Mixed level, step 5: receiver and attackers. (a) CIC output (OSR = 50) decoded by the server with the enrolled key (blue) and by an eavesdropper with a wrong key (orange); dotted: sensor input. (b) Replica attack on both designs with the replica's transistor-level bits: tries of 80 that recover the key (illustrative below 2,000 clocks).</p>

**Result.** The server accepts the frame, recovers the victim's bits exactly and decodes +0.1341 of full scale, equal to the input (Fig. 64(a), blue on the dotted input). The forged frame is rejected. The eavesdropper's MAC check fails, its decoded reading is noise (Fig. 64(a), orange), and its bits agree with the true bits in 47.6 % of the clocks (legend and card), within two standard deviations (1.6 % each) of 50 %. This fraction does not depend on the modulator bits: an eavesdropper's bit is right exactly where its keystream bit equals the true one. The replica attack's bit-level numbers vary from run to run with the comparator noise of step 3 and are read from the card: over clocks 200 to 999, the two chips' bitstreams disagree on 3 to 13 % of bits and 16 to 65 % of the 64-bit windows are clean in the development runs and in this one. The 80 attempts fall on 23 distinct windows. In every one of those runs the attack recovered the original design's key in **80 of 80** attempts and the proposal's in **0 of 80** (Fig. 64(b)). Panel (b) shows the same replica attack as Section VIII-B, now with bits from two transistor-level chips instead of the behavioural model: the original design falls because a stretch of 64 clocks in which the two chips agree gives Berlekamp-Massey the 32 correct keystream bits it needs to rebuild the 16-bit LFSR, whereas on the proposal's Grain-128a keystream Berlekamp-Massey finds no short register that predicts the following bits, and the best published cryptanalysis of Grain-128a [18] requires a computation far beyond practical reach.

**Interpretation.** The server, the forger and the eavesdropper behave exactly as predicted. The replica result must be read with the caveat above: the 80 attempts all start at one of 23 distinct positions between clocks 200 and 223, so "80 of 80" means only that this one stretch of the run was clean for both chips. The short run is also not representative of a long capture: this run's disagreement (at most 11 %, card) is well below the 24.8 % that the same two chips reach over 30,000 clocks (step 6). Whether clean windows still occur, and how often, once the chips have drifted apart is what step 6 measures.

### G. Step 6, transistor level: the replica attack over 30,000 clocks

**Goal.** Run the replica attack with transistor-level chips over a capture long enough to be meaningful, and compare its statistics with the behavioural model **on the same pair of chips**, so that any difference can be attributed to the abstraction of the comparator and not to different chips, seeds or settings. Step 5 cannot do this: its 1,000 clocks offer at most 24 overlapping windows near the start of the run, where the two chips are still largely in step.

**Theory.** Once the two chips have drifted apart (Theory, point 4), they disagree on a fraction $p$ of their bits, yet the disagreements come in bursts, so a fraction $f_{64}$ of all 64-bit windows remains clean, far more than the $(1-p)^{64}$ that independent errors would leave. One clean window yields the original design's key (step 5). With 80 windows drawn at random, the probability that at least one is clean is $1 - (1 - f_{64})^{80}$, and about $80 f_{64}$ clean windows are expected among them. This count is a lower bound on the windows that yield the key, because Berlekamp-Massey also succeeds on a window whose only wrong bits lie within its first $L + 1 = 17$ bits (Section VIII-B). The behavioural model differs from the circuit only in the comparator: a threshold with the chip's offset and Gaussian noise instead of the extracted StrongARM. On the same pair, with the same dither, input and integrator noise, it should therefore give the same $p$ and $f_{64}$ to within the spread caused by the comparator's noise realisation, which no two simulators can share.

*Prediction and pass criterion.* The transistor-level chips disagree on about a quarter of their bits with a clean-window fraction of a few per cent, within or near the spread of the behavioural model on the same pair; the original design's key is recovered from at least one of the 80 windows; the proposal's never is.

**Setup.** The same two chips as step 3 (comparator seeds 1000 and 1004, their own dither and noise), tt, 37 °C, constant 0.5 µA input, 30,000 clocks per chip, the same 250-clock segments and `reltol` = 10<sup>−6</sup>. At this length the 80 window starts are drawn from clock 200 to 29,223, so they are distinct and spread over the whole capture. The run takes over an hour on two cores, too long for a Colab session; the cell shows the recorded run of `dev/system/long_replica.py` (same code, same seeds, embedded in the notebook), and the form option `LONG_RUN = True` re-runs it in this session at the corner and temperature of the settings form. The recorded run was made before the correction of the first-integrator noise (Section VII-E): its chips carry twice the corrected integrator noise. It is not re-recorded.

*Behavioural run on the same pair (live).* The loop of `mixedsim.loop_reference`, in the netlist's order, with the same input, each chip's dither sequence, the same two first-integrator noise realisations at the recorded run's setting (twice the corrected value), each chip's comparator offset measured in step 3 (SPICE, this corner and temperature) and the comparator noise σ<sub>n</sub> of this corner. Only the comparator's noise realisation differs; the behavioural run is repeated with 20 comparator-noise seeds. Metrics for both: the disagreement p, the clean-window fraction f<sub>64</sub> (from clock 200), the number of the 80 windows that yield the key (the same window positions), and the number of windows over the whole capture that yield the key. The comparison holds only when the settings form selects the recorded run's corner and temperature (tt, 37 °C); the card says when it does not.

> **Next cell.** 1. Loads the 30,000-clock transistor-level bitstreams of the two chips from the recorded run, or simulates them with `LONG_RUN = True`; 2. measures their disagreement and clean-window fraction; 3. runs the replica attack (80 windows) on both designs; 4. runs the behavioural model on the same pair (same input, dither, integrator noise and offsets, 20 comparator-noise seeds) and compares the two levels, including the windows over the whole capture that yield the key; 5. marks the 80 windows and those that yield the key, and maps where the bits agree.


```python
#@title Fig.: mixed level, step 6: replica attack, 30,000 clocks
# Step 6, transistor level: the replica attack over 30,000 clocks, the length of the behavioural attack runs of Section
# VIII-B. The same two chips as step 3 (tt, 37 °C, constant input). Over an hour on two cores (72 min recorded), so the run of
# dev/system/long_replica.py (same code, same seeds) is shown; LONG_RUN re-runs it in this session
LONG_RUN = False                        #@param {type:"boolean"}
if LONG_RUN:
    t0 = time.time(); NL = 30000; CL = [ccfg_m("long_victim"), ccfg_m("long_replica")]
    S_L = cs.channel_noise_psd(CL[0], cs.reference_trajectory(CL[0]))
    u_l = np.full(NL, s2d(tia(0.5e-6, P_sys["rtia"]), P_sys["buffer"]))
    d_l = [dsm2(u_l, P_sys)["DI"].astype(float), dsm2(u_l, P_sys, seeds=REPLICA_DITHER)["DI"].astype(float)]
    n1_l = [P_sys["int_noise"] * np.random.default_rng(31 + i).standard_normal(NL) for i in range(2)]
    with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
        ML = [f.result() for f in [ex.submit(MS.modulator, cs, CL[i], u_l, d_l[i], n1_l[i], CHIPS[i], S_L, 250, None, 0) for i in range(2)]]
    TIM_M["long"] = time.time() - t0
    DLA, DLB, src_l = ML[0]["D"], ML[1]["D"], f"simulated in this session ({TIM_M['long']:.0f} s)"
else:
    LR = json.loads('{"clocks": 30000, "corner": "tt", "temp": 37.0, "chips": [1000, 1004], "seconds": 4315.439863204956, "disagree": 0.24835570469798657, "clean64": 0.05114840098194169, "first_clean": 200, "original": {"broken": 8, "tries": 80, "first": 6795}, "proposal": {"broken": 0, "tries": 80}, "D_victim": "", "D_replica": ""}')
    DLA, DLB = (np.frombuffer(LR[k].encode(), np.uint8) - 48 for k in ("D_victim", "D_replica"))
    TIM_M["long"] = LR["seconds"]
    src_l = f"recorded run of dev/system/long_replica.py ({LR['seconds'] / 60:.0f} min on two cores)"
    LR_NOISE = LR.get("int_noise", 1.798e-05)          # records before the noise correction carry no field: 2x the value of [1]
    if abs(LR_NOISE - P_sys["int_noise"]) > 0.01 * P_sys["int_noise"]:
        src_l += (f"; recorded with the earlier first-integrator noise setting ({LR_NOISE:.2e} at the integrator output, "
                  f"{LR_NOISE / P_sys['int_noise']:.1f}× the corrected {P_sys['int_noise']:.2e}); LONG_RUN = True re-runs it "
                  "with the corrected value")
NL = len(DLA)
K16_L = lfsr16_bits(DEFAULTS["key16"], ID_BITS + NL)[ID_BITS:]
ks_l = keystream_nl(KEY_M, iv_bits(NONCE, CTR), ID_BITS + NL)["enc"][ID_BITS:]
atk_lo = window_attack(DLA ^ K16_L ^ DLB, K16_L, 100)                          # original design
atk_lp = window_attack(DLA ^ ks_l ^ DLB, ks_l, 100)                            # proposal
xl = (DLA ^ DLB)[200:].astype(int); cl_ = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(xl)]); clean_l = (cl_[64:] - cl_[:-64]) == 0
# the behavioural model on the same pair: the same input, each chip's dither sequence, the same first-integrator noise
# realisations and setting as the transistor-level run (from LR_NOISE: the recorded run's own value), each chip's comparator
# offset from step 3 and the comparator noise of this corner. Only the comparator's noise realisation cannot be shared
# with ngspice, so the behavioural run is repeated with N_BEH comparator-noise seeds, which gives its spread
def key_windows(D1, D2, K):                                    # windows (start >= 200) whose Berlekamp-Massey register yields the key
    e = (D1 ^ D2).astype(np.int64); kg = D1 ^ K[:len(D1)] ^ D2; c = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(e)])
    s_ = np.arange(200, len(e) - 63 - 512); cand = s_[c[s_ + 64] == c[s_ + 24]]
    return int(sum(bm_attack(kg[s0:s0 + 64], K[s0 + 64:s0 + 576])["acc"] > 0.99 for s0 in cand))
t0_b, N_BEH = time.time(), 20
NI_L = P_sys["int_noise"] if LONG_RUN else LR_NOISE
same_l = LONG_RUN or (CORNER == LR["corner"] and float(TEMP_C) == float(LR["temp"]) and tuple(CHIPS) == tuple(LR["chips"]))
u_b = np.full(NL, s2d(tia(0.5e-6, P_sys["rtia"]), P_sys["buffer"]))
d_b = [dsm2(u_b, P_sys)["DI"].astype(float), dsm2(u_b, P_sys, seeds=REPLICA_DITHER)["DI"].astype(float)]
n1_b = [NI_L * np.random.default_rng(31 + i).standard_normal(NL) for i in range(2)]
BEH = []
for r_ in range(N_BEH):
    Db = [MS.loop_reference(u_b, d_b[i], n1_b[i], -VOS_M[i] / VU_M,
                            noise=SIG_N_M / VU_M * np.random.default_rng((900 + r_, i)).standard_normal(NL)) for i in range(2)]
    xb = (Db[0] ^ Db[1])[200:].astype(np.int64); cb = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(xb)])
    BEH.append(dict(p=float(xb.mean()), f64=float(np.mean(cb[64:] == cb[:-64])), b80=window_attack(Db[0] ^ K16_L ^ Db[1], K16_L, 100)["broken"],
                    kw=key_windows(Db[0], Db[1], K16X)))
BEH = {k: np.array([b[k] for b in BEH]) for k in BEH[0]}
KW_T = key_windows(DLA, DLB, K16X)                             # the same count for the transistor-level bits
TIM_M["long_beh"] = time.time() - t0_b
rank = lambda v, a: f"{int(np.sum(a < v))} below, {int(np.sum(a == v))} equal, {int(np.sum(a > v))} above"
card("Step 6, transistor level: the replica attack over 30,000 clocks",
     [("bitstreams", f"{NL:,} clocks per chip, {src_l}"),
      ("the two chips' bits", f"disagree on {100 * xl.mean():.1f} %; clean 64-bit windows {100 * clean_l.mean():.1f} % "
       f"(behavioural model of Section VIII-B at PVT, other pairs: {100 * SYS['f64_pvt']:.1f} %)"),
      ("replica attack on the original design (LFSR-16)", f"<b>{atk_lo['broken']} of {atk_lo['tries']}</b> windows recover the key"
       + (": the key is recovered" if atk_lo["broken"] else "")),
      ("replica attack on the proposal (Grain-128a)", f"<b>{atk_lp['broken']} of {atk_lp['tries']}</b> windows"),
      (f"behavioural model on the same pair ({N_BEH} comparator-noise seeds; " + ("same chips, corner, temperature, dither and "
       f"integrator noise, {NI_L:.2e} at the integrator output" if same_l else "<b>not the same pair</b>: the settings form differs from "
       "the recorded run") + ")",
       f"bits disagree on {100 * BEH['p'].mean():.1f} % ({100 * BEH['p'].min():.1f}–{100 * BEH['p'].max():.1f} %); clean 64-bit windows "
       f"{100 * BEH['f64'].mean():.1f} % ({100 * BEH['f64'].min():.1f}–{100 * BEH['f64'].max():.1f} %); the 80-window attack recovers the key "
       f"from {BEH['b80'].mean():.1f} windows ({BEH['b80'].min()}–{BEH['b80'].max()}); windows that yield the key over the whole capture "
       f"{BEH['kw'].mean():.0f} ({BEH['kw'].min()}–{BEH['kw'].max()})"),
      ("transistor level against the behavioural spread (seeds below / equal / above)",
       f"disagreement {rank(xl.mean(), BEH['p'])}; clean windows {rank(clean_l.mean(), BEH['f64'])}; 80-window successes "
       f"{atk_lo['broken']}: {rank(atk_lo['broken'], BEH['b80'])}; key windows {KW_T}: {rank(KW_T, BEH['kw'])}"),
      ("run time of the behavioural comparison", f"{TIM_M['long_beh']:.1f} s")],
     tone="ok" if atk_lp["broken"] == 0 else "bad")
# the 80 windows the attack tried on the original design (the same draws as window_attack), and which of them yield the key
_rl = rng_for(100); starts_l = [200 + int(_rl.integers(min(NL, 30000) - 64 - 512 - 400)) for _ in range(atk_lo["tries"])]
hit_l = np.array([bm_attack((DLA ^ K16_L ^ DLB)[s0:s0 + 64], K16_L[s0 + 64:s0 + 576])["acc"] > 0.99 for s0 in starts_l])
fig, (ax0, ax) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(W2, 2.9), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 3.2], hspace=0.38))
st_l = np.array(starts_l)
ax0.plot(st_l[~hit_l], np.zeros((~hit_l).sum()), "|", color=COL["faint"], ms=9, mew=1.0, label="no key")
ax0.plot(st_l[hit_l], np.zeros(hit_l.sum()), "v", color=COL["bad"], ms=7, mec=COL["ink"], mew=0.5, label="key recovered")
ax0.set_yticks([]); ax0.set_ylim(-1, 1); ax0.grid(False); ax0.tick_params(axis="x", bottom=False)
ax0.legend(fontsize=7, loc="lower right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.98), ncol=2, handlelength=1.0, borderpad=0.1, frameon=False)
ax0.set_title(f"(a) replica attack, {atk_lo['tries']} windows: the original design's key from {int(hit_l.sum())}, the proposal's from "
              f"{atk_lp['broken']}", loc="left", fontsize=9, pad=3)
cov = np.zeros(len(xl), bool)
for s0 in np.flatnonzero(clean_l):
    cov[s0:s0 + 64] = True
ax.fill_between(np.arange(len(xl)) + 200, 0, 1, where=cov, color=COL["ok"], alpha=0.4, lw=0, step="mid", label="clean 64-bit windows")
ax.plot(np.arange(len(xl)) + 200, np.convolve(xl, np.ones(64) / 64, "same"), color=COL["ink"], lw=0.8, label="disagreement (64-clock mean)")
ax.set_xlim(0, NL); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_xlabel("Clock"); ax.set_ylabel("Fraction"); ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right", ncol=2)
ax.set_title(f"(b) victim and replica, transistor level: bits disagree on {100 * xl.mean():.1f} %, {100 * clean_l.mean():.1f} % of 64-bit "
             "windows clean", loc="left", fontsize=9, pad=3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.07, right=0.97, top=0.9, bottom=0.17); plt.show()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 65.</b> Mixed level, step 6: replica attack over 30,000 clocks (recorded run, tt, 37 °C; <code>LONG_RUN = True</code> re-runs it). (a) Start clocks of the 80 windows tried (close starts overlap): grey ticks, no key; orange triangles, the original design's key. (b) Disagreement between the victim's and the replica's bits (64-clock running mean); blue: clean 64-bit windows.</p>

**Result.** In the recorded run (72 min on two cores) the two chips' transistor-level bits disagree on 24.8 % of the clocks from clock 200 on, and 5.1 % of the 64-bit windows are clean. Berlekamp-Massey recovers the original design's key from **8 of 80** windows; the proposal's from **0 of 80**. The windows that yield the key are spread over the whole capture (Fig. 65(a)), and each falls on one of the short clean stretches between bursts of disagreement (Fig. 65(b)). The behavioural model on the same pair, over 20 comparator-noise seeds, gives a disagreement of 23.4–23.6 % (mean 23.5 %), a clean-window fraction of 3.9–4.6 % (mean 4.2 %), 6 to 8 of the 80 windows that yield the key (mean 7.1), and 1,917–2,090 windows over the whole capture that yield it. The transistor-level pair lies at the top of or above this spread: its 8 of 80 equals the largest behavioural value, but its disagreement (24.8 %), its clean-window fraction (5.1 %) and its 2,304 key-yielding windows lie above all 20 behavioural seeds.

**Interpretation.** On the same pair, with the same dither, input and integrator noise, the transistor-level chips are slightly burstier than the behavioural model: they disagree on 1.3 percentage points more bits, yet leave about a fifth more clean windows (5.1 % against 4.2 %). The difference lies outside the spread of the comparator's noise realisation, so it reflects the abstraction itself (a threshold with Gaussian noise in place of the StrongARM, and ideal integrators in place of the netlist solved by ngspice), and it goes in the attacker's favour: the behavioural model, which Section VIII uses for its statistics, slightly underestimates the windows available to the attacker, and the protection points found there are not optimistic on this account. Both levels recover the original design's key, from thousands of windows over the capture; **the analog differences between these two simulated chips do not protect the original design**, and the proposal, whose keystream has no short linear register, resists the same attack on the same bits. The comparison covers one pair at one condition, with twice the corrected integrator noise; the statistics over chips and PVT conditions remain those of Section VIII-B.

### H. The complete sensor in one figure
**Goal.** Show every result of the mixed-level run together, in the order of the signal chain, from the SRAM cells to the attacker, and test the security of the frame that the mixed-level run actually produces: the transistor-level modulator bits, the RTL ciphertext and the RTL MAC tag.

**Setup.** The figure reuses the results of steps 1 to 6; nothing is re-simulated at transistor level. Four security tests are added on the same frame. (1) Key search on the original design: each of the 65,535 non-zero 16-bit LFSR keys decrypts the original design's ciphertext of the victim's step-3 bits, and is scored by the fraction of decrypted bits that agree with the replica's transistor-level bits, the attacker's prediction of the plaintext under the known input; the true key is the one that agrees best if the attack works. (2) The same search against the proposal: the attacker knows the session nonce, the counter and the chip nonce, which travel in clear, and scores 1,000 random 128-bit keys and the 128 keys that differ from the true key in one bit; the latter show whether a partly correct key is rewarded, which would allow a search bit by bit. (3) Forgery: every single-bit change of the RTL frame (32 counter bits, 16 encrypted-ID bits, every payload bit and the 32 tag bits) is presented to the receiver, which recomputes the MAC with the enrolled key; the original design checks only the decrypted chip ID. In addition, 100,000 random tags are presented with the genuine frame. (4) Randomness of the bits on the air: four tests of NIST SP 800-22 (frequency, block frequency with 128-bit blocks, runs, cumulative sums) on the 30,000 transistor-level bits of step 6 before (*D*) and after (*C*) encryption with the proposal's keystream; a sequence passes a test at *p* ≥ 0.01. The spectrum of panel (e) is a Welch average of 4,096-point Blackman-Harris segments of the step-6 victim bitstream, against one behavioural run of the same chip (step 6's behavioural loop, one comparator-noise seed).

> **Next cell.** 1. Collects the results of steps 1 to 6. 2. Runs the four security tests on the mixed-level frame: the search of all 65,535 keys of the original design, the same search against the proposal with 1,128 keys, every single-bit forgery of the RTL frame and 100,000 random tags, and four NIST SP 800-22 tests on the 30,000-clock bits before and after encryption. 3. Draws the figure (14 panels in signal-chain order) and prints the card. About 5 s.


```python
#@title Fig.: the complete sensor in one figure
# The complete sensor in one figure: every result of steps 1-6 in the order of the signal chain, from the SRAM cells to
# the attacker. Nothing is re-simulated except one behavioural loop of 30,000 clocks (about a second), the reference for
# the spectrum of the transistor-level bitstream of step 6. Names stay local to the function (the step cells' globals are
# only read)
def _mixed_overview():
    from scipy.signal import welch
    from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
    from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
    t0 = time.time()
    GREY1 = "#a3a3a3"
    from scipy.special import erfc, gammaincc
    # ---- security tests on the mixed-level frame (step 3's transistor-level bits, step 4's RTL ciphertext and tag)
    # 1. brute force of the original design's 16-bit key: every key scored by how well its decryption of the victim's frame
    #    agrees with the replica's transistor-level bits (the replica attacker's prediction of D); all 65,535 keys at once
    C_o = D_A ^ K16_M                                            # the original design's ciphertext of the same bits
    s_ = np.arange(1, 65536, dtype=np.uint32); agree_o = np.zeros(len(s_))
    for i in range(ID_BITS + N_CLOCKS):
        if i >= ID_BITS:
            agree_o += ((s_ & 1) ^ C_o[i - ID_BITS]) == D_B[i - ID_BITS]
        fb = (s_ ^ (s_ >> 2) ^ (s_ >> 3) ^ (s_ >> 5)) & 1
        s_ = (s_ >> 1) | (fb << 15)
    agree_o /= N_CLOCKS
    k_true = DEFAULTS["key16"] & 0xFFFF or 1
    rank_o = int(np.sum(agree_o > agree_o[k_true - 1])) + 1
    others = np.delete(agree_o, k_true - 1)
    # 2. the same search against the proposal: the 128 keys one bit from the true key and 1,000 random keys (the attacker
    #    knows N, ctr and N_c, which travel in clear); a correct key would stand out as for the original design
    iv_p = iv_bits(NONCE, CTR, CN_M)
    score = lambda k: float(np.mean((RTL_M["C"] ^ keystream_nl(k, iv_p, ID_BITS + N_CLOCKS)["enc"][ID_BITS:]) == D_B))
    near = np.array([score(KEY_M ^ np.eye(128, dtype=np.uint8)[j]) for j in range(128)])
    rk = np.random.default_rng(2027).integers(0, 2, (1000, 128)).astype(np.uint8)
    rand_ = np.array([score(k) for k in rk]); true_p = score(KEY_M)
    right_eve = np.array([np.mean((RTL_M["C"] ^ keystream_nl(k, iv_p, ID_BITS + N_CLOCKS)["enc"][ID_BITS:]) == D_A) for k in rk[:200]])
    # 3. forgery: every single-bit change of the frame (counter, encrypted ID, payload, tag) presented to the receiver, and
    #    100,000 random tags for the genuine frame; the original design checks only the decrypted chip ID
    ctr_b = int_to_bits(CTR, 32); eid, C0, tag0 = RTL_M["enc_id"], RTL_M["C"], RTL_M["tag"]
    acc_p = dict(counter=0, ID=0, payload=0, tag=0)
    for j in range(32):
        cb = ctr_b.copy(); cb[j] ^= 1
        acc_p["counter"] += mac_verify(KEY_SRV, NONCE, bits_to_int(cb), eid, C0, tag0, cn=CN_M)[0]
    for j in range(ID_BITS):
        e2 = eid.copy(); e2[j] ^= 1; acc_p["ID"] += grain_tag(mac_msg(ctr_b, e2, C0), ks_rx) == tag0
    for j in range(N_CLOCKS):
        c2 = C0.copy(); c2[j] ^= 1; acc_p["payload"] += grain_tag(mac_msg(ctr_b, eid, c2), ks_rx) == tag0
    acc_p["tag"] = sum(((tag0 ^ (1 << j)) == tag0) for j in range(32))
    n_fields = dict(counter=32, ID=ID_BITS, payload=N_CLOCKS, tag=32)
    acc_o = dict(counter=None, ID=0, payload=N_CLOCKS, tag=None)  # original: no counter, no tag; a changed ID fails its check
    rand_tags = int(np.sum(np.random.default_rng(7).integers(0, 2**32, 100000, dtype=np.uint64) == tag0))
    # 4. randomness of the bits on the air: NIST SP 800-22 frequency, block frequency (M = 128), runs and cumulative sums,
    #    on the 30,000-clock transistor-level bits before (D) and after (C) encryption
    def nist(x):
        x = np.asarray(x, np.int64); n = len(x); S = np.cumsum(2 * x - 1); p_ = {}
        p_["frequency"] = erfc(abs(S[-1]) / np.sqrt(2 * n))
        M = 128; Nb = n // M; pib = x[:Nb * M].reshape(Nb, M).mean(1)
        p_["block frequency"] = gammaincc(Nb / 2, 4 * M * np.sum((pib - 0.5) ** 2) / 2)
        pi = x.mean(); V = 1 + np.sum(x[1:] != x[:-1])
        p_["runs"] = 0.0 if abs(pi - 0.5) >= 2 / np.sqrt(n) else erfc(abs(V - 2 * n * pi * (1 - pi)) / (2 * np.sqrt(2 * n) * pi * (1 - pi)))
        z = np.max(np.abs(S)); from scipy.special import ndtr as _N
        k1 = np.arange(int((-n / z + 1) // 4), int((n / z - 1) // 4) + 1)
        k2 = np.arange(int((-n / z - 3) // 4), int((n / z - 1) // 4) + 1)
        p_["cumulative sums"] = float(1 - np.sum(_N((4 * k1 + 1) * z / np.sqrt(n)) - _N((4 * k1 - 1) * z / np.sqrt(n)))
                                      + np.sum(_N((4 * k2 + 3) * z / np.sqrt(n)) - _N((4 * k2 + 1) * z / np.sqrt(n))))
        return {k: float(np.clip(v, 0, 1)) for k, v in p_.items()}
    P_D, P_C = nist(DLA), nist(DLA ^ ks_l)
    t_sec = time.time() - t0
    Dbeh_l = MS.loop_reference(u_b, d_b[0], n1_b[0], -VOS_M[0] / VU_M,         # behavioural reference of the spectrum
                               noise=SIG_N_M / VU_M * np.random.default_rng((900, 0)).standard_normal(NL))

    # ---- the figure: one journal page (7.16 in wide), 3 columns x 5 rows of equal panels, the 30,000-clock trace over two
    # columns; 8 pt labels, 7 pt ticks; one meaning per colour: black the transistor level, grey dashed the behavioural model,
    # blue the proposal and the server, orange the original design and what the attacker gains. Outcomes are drawn as parts
    # of the whole (accepted and rejected, key and no key), so that a result of zero is visible
    from matplotlib.transforms import blended_transform_factory as _bt
    RC = {"font.size": 8, "axes.labelsize": 8, "axes.titlesize": 8.6, "xtick.labelsize": 7, "ytick.labelsize": 7,
          "legend.fontsize": 6.5, "legend.title_fontsize": 6.5, "axes.linewidth": 0.6, "lines.linewidth": 0.9,
          "xtick.major.size": 2.5, "ytick.major.size": 2.5, "xtick.minor.size": 1.4, "ytick.minor.size": 1.4,
          "xtick.major.width": 0.6, "ytick.major.width": 0.6, "legend.handlelength": 1.3, "legend.borderpad": 0.3,
          "legend.labelspacing": 0.2, "legend.handletextpad": 0.4, "legend.borderaxespad": 0.35, "legend.columnspacing": 0.8}
    TR, MO, PR, OR, LG = COL["ink"], COL["faint"], COL["ok"], COL["bad"], "#c3c8cf"
    with plt.rc_context(RC):
        FH, CW, AH = 9.05, W2 / 3, 1.12
        TOP = [0.24 + 1.8 * r for r in range(5)]
        fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W2, FH))
        def AX(col, row, span=1):
            x0, w = col * CW + 0.5, span * CW - 0.6
            return fig.add_axes([x0 / W2, 1 - (TOP[row] + AH) / FH, w / W2, AH / FH])
        def ttl(ax, lab, txt):
            ax.set_title(f"({lab}) {txt}", loc="center", pad=3.5)
        def headroom(ax, f):
            lo, hi = ax.get_ylim(); ax.set_ylim(lo, hi + f * (hi - lo))
        def two_level(ax, groups, xs):                     # O/P under each bar, the group's name below
            ax.set_xticks(xs, ["O", "P"] * len(groups), fontsize=6.5)
            for g, nm in enumerate(groups):
                ax.text(g, -0.2, nm, transform=_bt(ax.transData, ax.transAxes), ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7)

        # (a) key generation: fingerprint, the cells that flip in the field read, and the key
        ax = AX(0, 0)
        ax.imshow(W_EN.reshape(20, 30), cmap=ListedColormap(["white", LG]), vmin=0, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest")
        for k in np.flatnonzero(W_EN != W_RD):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k % 30 - 0.5, k // 30 - 0.5), 1, 1, fc=OR, ec=TR, lw=0.5))
        ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
        key_ok = np.array_equal(KEY_M, KEY_SRV) and np.array_equal(KG_M["bits"], REC_M["w"])
        ax.set_xlabel(f"{n_err} of {PUF_BITS} cells flip (BCH t = {t_m})\n"
                      + ("128-bit key equals the server's" if key_ok else "key NOT recovered"), fontsize=7, labelpad=3)
        ttl(ax, "a", f"SRAM-PUF fingerprint, {TEMP_C} °C")

        # (b) the victim's comparator in the loop, (c) the decision test
        ax = AX(1, 0); w = MOD[0]["waves"]; tw = 1e9 * (w["time"] - w["te"][0])
        rows = [(r"$\phi$", "v(clk)", MO), (r"$\mathrm{out}_p$", "v(c0_outp)", TR), (r"$\mathrm{out}_n$", "v(c0_outn)", TR),
                (r"$q$", "v(c0_q)", TR)]
        for k, (lab, node, c) in enumerate(rows):
            y0 = 1.3 * (len(rows) - 1 - k)
            ax.axhline(y0, color=MO, lw=0.35, alpha=0.5); ax.plot(tw, y0 + w[node] / VDD_M, color=c, lw=0.9)
        ax.set_yticks([1.3 * (len(rows) - 1 - k) + 0.5 for k in range(len(rows))], [r[0] for r in rows])
        ax.tick_params(axis="y", left=False, right=False); ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 1.3 * (len(rows) - 1) + 1.2)
        ax.set_xlim(tw[0], tw[-1]); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False); ax.set_xlabel("Time (ns)")
        ttl(ax, "b", "Comparator in the loop")
        ax = AX(2, 0)
        xs = [np.log10(np.maximum(np.abs(c["dv"] - vo) / SIG_N_M, 1e-3)) for c, vo in zip(chk, VOS_M)]
        lo_x = min(-1.25, min(x.min() for x in xs) - 0.15); bins_c = np.linspace(lo_x, max(x.max() for x in xs) + 0.05, 45)
        ax.axvspan(lo_x, np.log10(3), color=MO, alpha=0.18, lw=0, label=r"within $3\sigma_\mathrm{n}$")
        for x, c, col, nm in zip(xs, chk, (TR, OR), ("victim", "replica")):
            ax.hist(x, bins=bins_c, histtype="step", color=col, lw=0.9, label=f"{nm}, {int(c['dis'].sum())} differ")
        ax.set_xlim(lo_x, bins_c[-1]); headroom(ax, 0.75)
        ax.set_xlabel(r"$\log_{10}(|\Delta V - V_\mathrm{os}|/\sigma_\mathrm{n})$"); ax.set_ylabel("Decisions")
        ax.legend(loc="upper left", title=f"noise predicts {n_exp:.1f}")
        ttl(ax, "c", f"Decision test, {2 * N_CLOCKS:,} decisions")

        # (d) integrator states, (e) spectrum of the 30,000-clock bitstream, (f) decoded readings
        ax = AX(0, 1)
        for m, c, nm in ((MOD[1], OR, "replica"), (MOD[0], TR, "victim")):
            ax.plot(m["x1"], m["x2"], "o", ms=1.4, mew=0, color=c, alpha=0.6, label=nm)
        ax.set_xlabel(r"$x_1$ (model units)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$x_2$"); headroom(ax, 0.3)
        ax.legend(loc="upper left", markerscale=2.5, ncol=2)
        ttl(ax, "d", f"Integrator states, {N_CLOCKS:,} clocks")
        ax = AX(1, 1)
        for D_, c, lab, ls, lw in ((DLA, TR, "transistor level", "-", 0.7), (Dbeh_l, MO, "behavioural model", "--", 0.9)):
            f_, p_ = welch(2.0 * np.asarray(D_, float) - 1.0, fs=10e6, window="blackmanharris", nperseg=4096)
            ax.semilogx(f_[1:], 10 * np.log10(p_[1:] * (f_[1] - f_[0]) / 2 + 1e-30), color=c, ls=ls, lw=lw, label=lab)
        ax.axvline(100e3, color=MO, lw=0.6, ls=":")
        ax.set_xlim(f_[1], 5e6); ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)"); ax.set_ylabel("PSD (dBFS/bin)")
        ax.legend(loc="lower right"); ttl(ax, "e", f"Bitstream spectrum, {NL:,} clocks")
        ax = AX(2, 1); ys = dec_m(D_rx); n_o = len(ys); xo = np.arange(n_o)
        ax.plot(xo, u_m[::OSR][:n_o], ":", color=TR, lw=1.0, label="input")
        ax.plot(xo, ys, "o-", color=PR, ms=2.5, lw=1.0, label=f"server (MAC {'accepted' if ok_rx else 'rejected'})")
        ax.plot(xo, dec_m(D_beh)[:n_o], "s", color=TR, mfc="none", ms=3.6, mew=0.6, label="behavioural model")
        ax.plot(xo, dec_m(D_eve)[:n_o], "x-", color=OR, ms=2.8, lw=0.8, label=f"wrong key (MAC {'accepted' if ok_eve else 'rejected'})")
        headroom(ax, 1.0); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
        ax.set_xlabel("Output sample (OSR = 50)"); ax.set_ylabel("CIC output (FS)"); ttl(ax, "f", "Decoded reading")

        # (g) the bits of the link, (h) autocorrelation before and after encryption, (i) the replica attack's windows
        ax = AX(0, 2); s0, n_ = 200, 40; seg = slice(s0, s0 + n_)
        rows = [(r"$D$", D_A[seg], TR), (r"$K$", (RTL_M["C"] ^ D_A)[seg], COL["key"]), (r"$C$", RTL_M["C"][seg], PR),
                (r"$D_\mathrm{rx}$", D_rx[seg], TR), (r"$\hat{D}$", D_eve[seg], OR)]
        for j in np.flatnonzero(D_eve[seg] != D_A[seg]):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((s0 + j, -0.12), 1, 1.07, fc=OR, alpha=0.2, lw=0))
        t_ = np.arange(s0, s0 + n_ + 1)
        for k, (lab, b, c) in enumerate(rows):
            y0 = 1.3 * (len(rows) - 1 - k)
            ax.axhline(y0, color=MO, lw=0.35, alpha=0.5); ax.step(t_, y0 + 0.85 * np.r_[b, b[-1]], where="post", color=c, lw=0.8)
        ax.set_yticks([1.3 * (len(rows) - 1 - k) + 0.42 for k in range(len(rows))], [r[0] for r in rows])
        ax.tick_params(axis="y", left=False, right=False); ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 1.3 * (len(rows) - 1) + 1.1); ax.grid(False)
        ax.set_xlim(s0, s0 + n_); ax.set_xlabel("Clock"); ttl(ax, "g", "Bits of the link (RTL)")
        ax = AX(1, 2); Lg = np.arange(1, 33); C_l = DLA ^ ks_l
        def acf(x):
            x = 2.0 * np.asarray(x, float) - 1.0; x = x - x.mean()
            return np.array([np.dot(x[:-l], x[l:]) / np.dot(x, x) for l in Lg])
        ax.axhspan(-2 / np.sqrt(NL), 2 / np.sqrt(NL), color=MO, alpha=0.3, lw=0)
        ax.plot(Lg, acf(DLA), "o-", color=TR, ms=2.2, lw=0.8, label="$D$, modulator")
        ax.plot(Lg, acf(C_l), "s-", color=PR, ms=2.2, lw=0.8, label="$C$, on the air")
        headroom(ax, 0.45); ax.legend(loc="upper right", ncol=2)
        ax.set_xlabel("Lag (clocks)"); ax.set_ylabel("Autocorrelation"); ttl(ax, "h", "Before and after encryption")
        ax = AX(2, 2); xb = []
        for g, (ao, ap) in enumerate(((atk_orig, atk_prop), (atk_lo, atk_lp))):
            for j, (at, c) in enumerate(((ao, OR), (ap, PR))):
                x = g + (j - 0.5) * 0.44; xb.append(x)
                ax.bar(x, at["broken"], 0.38, color=OR, ec=TR, lw=0.5, label="key recovered" if (g, j) == (0, 0) else None)
                ax.bar(x, at["tries"] - at["broken"], 0.38, bottom=at["broken"], color=LG, ec=TR, lw=0.5,
                       label="no key" if (g, j) == (0, 0) else None)
                ax.text(x, at["tries"] + 2, f"{at['broken']}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.5)
        two_level(ax, (f"{N_CLOCKS:,} clocks", f"{NL:,} clocks"), xb)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1.45 * atk_orig["tries"]); ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 1.6); ax.set_ylabel(f"Windows (of {atk_orig['tries']})")
        ax.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=2); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False); ttl(ax, "i", "Replica attack")

        # (j) victim against replica over the 30,000-clock capture, (k) transistor level against the behavioural spread
        ax = AX(0, 3, span=2)
        cov = np.zeros(len(xl), bool)
        for s in np.flatnonzero(clean_l):
            cov[s:s + 64] = True
        ax.fill_between(np.arange(len(xl)) + 200, 0, 1, where=cov, color=OR, alpha=0.22, lw=0, step="mid", label="clean 64-bit window")
        ax.plot(np.arange(len(xl)) + 200, np.convolve(xl, np.ones(64) / 64, "same"), color=TR, lw=0.55, label="disagreement, 64-clock mean")
        ax.axhline(1.0, color=MO, lw=0.4)
        ax.plot(st_l[~hit_l], np.full((~hit_l).sum(), 1.07), "|", color=MO, ms=5.5, mew=0.8, label="window tried")
        ax.plot(st_l[hit_l], np.full(hit_l.sum(), 1.07), "v", color=OR, ms=4.5, mec=TR, mew=0.4, label="key recovered")
        ax.set_xlim(0, NL); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.13); ax.set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1.0]); ax.set_xlabel("Clock"); ax.set_ylabel("Fraction")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.92), ncol=2)
        ttl(ax, "j", f"Victim against replica over {NL:,} clocks (recorded)")
        ax = AX(2, 3); rj = np.random.default_rng(5)
        mets = [("bits differ", BEH["p"], xl.mean()), ("clean win.", BEH["f64"], clean_l.mean()), ("key win.", BEH["kw"], KW_T)]
        for k, (lab, beh, tl) in enumerate(mets):
            m_ = beh.mean()
            ax.plot(k + rj.uniform(-0.14, 0.14, len(beh)), beh / m_, "o", ms=2.3, mew=0, color=MO,
                    label=f"model, {N_BEH} seeds" if k == 0 else None)
            ax.plot(k, tl / m_, "D", ms=4.2, color=TR, label="transistor level" if k == 0 else None)
        ax.axhline(1, color=MO, lw=0.6, ls=":"); ax.set_xticks(range(3), [m[0] for m in mets], fontsize=6.8); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.5)
        headroom(ax, 0.5); ax.set_ylabel("Ratio to model mean"); ax.legend(loc="upper left"); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
        ttl(ax, "k", "Transistor level vs. model")

        # (l) key search on both designs, (m) single-bit forgeries, (n) randomness of the bits on the air
        ax = AX(0, 4); bins = np.linspace(0.40, 1.0, 121); allp = np.r_[rand_, near]
        ax.hist(others, bins=bins, weights=np.full(len(others), 1 / len(others)), color=LG, label=f"original, {len(others):,} keys")
        ax.hist(allp, bins=bins, weights=np.full(len(allp), 1 / len(allp)), histtype="step", color=PR, lw=1.0,
                label=f"proposal, {len(allp):,} keys")
        ax.axvline(agree_o[k_true - 1], color=OR, lw=1.2)
        ax.text(agree_o[k_true - 1] - 0.015, 2e-3, f"original's key,\nrank {rank_o} of 65,535", ha="right", va="center",
                fontsize=6.5, color=OR)
        ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlim(0.4, 1.0); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 8)
        ax.set_xlabel("Agreement with the replica's bits"); ax.set_ylabel("Fraction of keys"); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
        ttl(ax, "l", "Key search")
        ax = AX(1, 4); fl = list(n_fields); xb = []
        for k, f in enumerate(fl):
            for j, acc in enumerate((acc_o, acc_p)):
                x = k + (j - 0.5) * 0.44; xb.append(x); v = acc[f]
                if v is None:
                    ax.bar(x, 100, 0.38, color="white", ec=MO, lw=0.5, hatch="////", label="field absent" if k == 0 else None)
                    continue
                a_ = 100 * v / n_fields[f]
                ax.bar(x, a_, 0.38, color=OR, ec=TR, lw=0.5, label="accepted" if (k, j) == (2, 0) else None)
                ax.bar(x, 100 - a_, 0.38, bottom=a_, color=PR, ec=TR, lw=0.5, label="rejected" if (k, j) == (2, 1) else None)
        two_level(ax, fl, xb)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 138); ax.set_yticks([0, 50, 100]); ax.set_xlim(-0.6, len(fl) - 0.4); ax.set_ylabel("Forgeries (%)")
        h_, l_ = ax.get_legend_handles_labels(); o_ = [l_.index(n) for n in ("accepted", "rejected", "field absent")]
        ax.legend([h_[i] for i in o_], [l_[i] for i in o_], loc="upper center", ncol=3); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
        ttl(ax, "m", "Single-bit forgeries")
        ax = AX(2, 4); tests = list(P_D); xq = np.arange(len(tests)); FL = 1e-30
        ax.axhline(0.01, color=OR, lw=0.7, ls=":", label="$p$ = 0.01")
        ax.plot(xq - 0.13, [max(P_D[t], FL) for t in tests], "s", color=TR, ms=4, label="$D$, modulator bits")
        ax.plot(xq + 0.13, [max(P_C[t], FL) for t in tests], "o", color=PR, ms=4, label="$C$, on the air")
        ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(FL / 300, 3e4); ax.set_yticks([1e-30, 1e-20, 1e-10, 1e0])
        ax.set_xticks(xq, ["freq.", "block", "runs", "cusum"]); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(tests) - 0.5); ax.set_ylabel(r"$p$-value")
        ax.text(-0.45, 0.01 * 0.2, "fail", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=6.5, color=OR)
        ax.text(-0.45, 0.01 * 5, "pass", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=6.5, color=OR)
        ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.45)); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
        ttl(ax, "n", f"NIST SP 800-22, {NL:,} bits")
        plt.show()
    card("The complete sensor in one figure: security of the mixed-level frame",
         [("brute force of the original design's 16-bit key with the replica's transistor-level bits (" f"{N_CLOCKS:,} clocks)",
           f"true key agrees on <b>{100 * agree_o[k_true - 1]:.1f} %</b>, rank <b>{rank_o} of 65,535</b>; wrong keys "
           f"{100 * others.mean():.1f} ± {100 * others.std():.1f} % (highest {100 * others.max():.1f} %)"),
          ("the same search against the proposal (the attacker knows N, ctr and N<sub>c</sub>)",
           f"1,000 random keys {100 * rand_.mean():.1f} ± {100 * rand_.std():.1f} % (highest {100 * rand_.max():.1f} %); the 128 keys "
           f"one bit from the true key {100 * near.mean():.1f} ± {100 * near.std():.1f} % (highest {100 * near.max():.1f} %): "
           f"no partial key is rewarded; the true key itself would give {100 * true_p:.1f} %"),
          ("eavesdropper with a wrong 128-bit key (200 keys)", f"{100 * right_eve.mean():.1f} ± {100 * right_eve.std():.1f} % of the "
           "victim's bits right"),
          ("single-bit forgeries accepted, proposal (counter, ID, payload, tag)",
           f"<b>{sum(acc_p.values())} of {sum(n_fields.values()):,}</b> ({', '.join(f'{f} {acc_p[f]}/{n_fields[f]}' for f in fl)})"),
          ("single-bit forgeries accepted, original (ID, payload; it has no counter or tag)",
           f"<b>{acc_o['payload']} of {N_CLOCKS + ID_BITS:,}</b> (every payload change; an ID change fails its ID check)"),
          ("100,000 random tags for the genuine frame (proposal)", f"{rand_tags} accepted (2<sup>−32</sup> each)"),
          (f"NIST SP 800-22 tests on {NL:,} transistor-level bits: p for D | for C",
           "; ".join(f"{t} {P_D[t]:.1e} | {P_C[t]:.2f}" for t in tests)),
          ("run time of the tests and the figure", f"{t_sec:.1f} s tests, {time.time() - t0:.1f} s in total")],
         tone="ok" if sum(acc_p.values()) == 0 and rand_tags == 0 and rank_o == 1 else "bad")
    return time.time() - t0
TIM_M["overview"] = _mixed_overview()
```

<p align="center" style="text-align:center"><b>Fig. 66.</b> The complete sensor in one mixed-level simulation (tt, 37 °C; panels (e), (h), (j), (k) and (n) from the recorded 30,000-clock run of step 6). (a) Enrolled fingerprint (grey: 1, white: 0) and cells that differ in the field read (orange). (b) Victim's comparator over four clocks, each row 0 to 1.8 V. (c) Distance of each decision's input from the threshold, victim and replica; grey: within 3 σ<sub>n</sub>. (d) Integrator states x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub> of both chips. (e) Spectrum of the victim's bitstream, transistor level and behavioural model; dotted: 100 kHz band edge. (f) CIC output: input, server, behavioural model and a wrong key. (g) Bits of the link: modulator bits D, RTL keystream K and ciphertext C, the server's D<sub>rx</sub> and an eavesdropper's D̂; shaded: the eavesdropper's wrong bits. (h) Autocorrelation of D and C; band: ±2/√N. (i) Replica attack: windows that yield the key among the 80 tried (O: original, P: proposal), steps 5 and 6. (j) Disagreement of victim and replica (64-clock mean), clean 64-bit windows (orange) and the windows tried (top; triangles: key recovered). (k) Transistor-level values (diamonds) and 20 behavioural seeds (dots), each divided by the seeds' mean. (l) Agreement with the replica's bits of every 16-bit key of the original design and of 1,128 keys of the proposal (1,000 random, 128 one bit from the true key). (m) Single-bit forgeries accepted and rejected per frame field (counter 32, ID 16, payload 1,000, tag 32 bits; O: original, P: proposal). (n) NIST SP 800-22 p-values of D and C (frequency, block frequency, runs, cumulative sums); values below 10<sup>−30</sup> drawn at 10<sup>−30</sup>; dotted: p = 0.01.</p>

**Result.** Fig. 66 collects the run in signal-chain order, and the card above gives its numbers. Panels (a) to (k) bring the results of steps 1 to 6 together: the field read stays far inside the code's correction capability and the chip's 128-bit key equals the server's (a); the post-layout comparators decide inside the loop as the threshold model predicts (b, c), the integrator states stay bounded (d), and the transistor-level bitstream has the noise shape of the behavioural model (e); the server decodes the reading while a wrong key yields noise (f); encryption removes the structure of the modulator bits (g, h); and the replica attack recovers the original design's key but never the proposal's (i, j). Over the 30,000-clock capture of the recorded run (twice the corrected first-integrator noise), the transistor-level pair lies above all 20 behavioural seeds in disagreement (24.8 % against 23.4–23.6 %), in clean windows (5.1 % against 3.9–4.6 %) and in windows that yield the key (2,304 against 1,917–2,090) (k).

Panels (l) to (n) test the frame itself. Against the original design, a search of all 65,535 keys with the replica's transistor-level bits as the plaintext guess ranks the true key first: it agrees with the replica's bits on 91.2 %, against 50.0 ± 1.6 % for the wrong keys (at most 56.0 %) (l). Against the proposal, the same search finds nothing: 1,000 random keys agree on 50.0 ± 1.6 % (at most 55.1 %) and the 128 keys that differ from the true key in a single bit on 49.8 ± 1.7 % (at most 53.9 %), so a nearly correct key is no closer than a random one (l); an eavesdropper with a wrong key gets 49.8 ± 1.5 % of the bits right. The receiver rejects all 1,080 single-bit forgeries of the proposal's RTL frame and all 100,000 random tags, whereas the original design accepts every one of the 1,000 payload changes (m). The ciphertext on the air passes the four NIST tests (p = 0.06 to 0.93), which the modulator bits fail by far (p ≤ 3 × 10⁻²⁶) (n).

**Interpretation.** At the full-system level, with the comparators simulated as transistors and the cipher and MAC as RTL, the original design falls to the simplest attack, a search of its 16-bit key with the replica's bits as the plaintext guess. The proposal rewards neither random nor nearly correct keys, so its 128-bit key cannot be found bit by bit; it rejects every forgery tested; and the bits it puts on the air carry no detectable structure of the sensor signal. **The security of the proposal holds on the bits of the transistor-level and RTL simulation of the circuit**, not only in the behavioural model of Sections VIII and IX. These tests cover one chip pair at one condition and a 1,000-clock frame; the statistics over chips and conditions are those of Sections VIII and IX.

### I. Summary of the run
**Goal.** Collect, block by block, the level, simulator, run time and pass check of every step in one table, Table XXIII.

> **Next cell.** 1. Tabulates each step's block, level, simulator and run time; 2. states its check: bit errors against t, RTL against the model, decisions against the theory, MAC and replica-attack outcomes. Step 6's run time is the recorded one unless `LONG_RUN` was set.


```python
#@title Mixed-level simulation: summary
# The mixed-level run, block by block: level, simulator, run time and the check that each block passed
rows_m = [("1", "SRAM-PUF power-ups (640 cells, enrolment and field)", "transistor (post-layout)", "ngspice", f"{TIM_M['puf']:.0f} s",
           f"{n_err} bit errors at {TEMP_C} °C (t = {CAL['bch_t']})"),
          ("2", "key reconstruction (BCH decoder from the compiler)", "RTL", "Icarus Verilog", f"{TIM_M['bch']:.0f} s",
           f"key {'recovered' if np.array_equal(KEY_M, KEY_SRV) else 'NOT recovered'}; RTL = model: {np.array_equal(KG_M['bits'], REC_M['w'])}"),
          ("3", "modulator: two chips, StrongARM in the loop", "transistor (post-layout) + behavioural", "ngspice", f"{TIM_M['mod']:.0f} s",
           f"{int(sum(c['dis'].sum() for c in chk))} decisions differ from the model (theory: {sum(c['exp'] for c in chk):.1f})"),
          ("4", "Grain-128a keystream and MAC", "RTL", "Icarus Verilog", f"{TIM_M['rtl']:.1f} s", f"RTL = model: {RTL_M['tag'] == TAG_ref}"),
          ("5", "server, eavesdropper, replica attacker", "behavioural", "Python", "&lt; 1 s",
           f"MAC {'accepted' if ok_rx else 'rejected'}; forged frame {'accepted' if ok_forged else 'rejected'}; replica attack: original "
           f"{atk_orig['broken']}/{atk_orig['tries']}, proposal {atk_prop['broken']}/{atk_prop['tries']}"
           + (f" (illustrative: {WIN_M} distinct windows)" if SHORT_M and N_POS else ""))]
if "atk_lo" in globals():
    rows_m.append(("6", "replica attack over 30,000 clocks", "transistor (post-layout) + behavioural", "ngspice",
                   f"{TIM_M['long'] / 60:.0f} min" + (" (recorded)" if not LONG_RUN else ""),
                   f"original {atk_lo['broken']}/{atk_lo['tries']} windows recover the key, proposal {atk_lp['broken']}/{atk_lp['tries']}"))
table(["Step", "Block", "Level", "Simulator", "Run time", "Check"], rows_m,
```

#### Summary of Section XII

The section asked whether the complete sensor works, and whether the system-level results hold, when the comparator and the SRAM cells are transistor-level circuits and the key decoder and cipher are RTL. Table XXIII lists every block with its level, simulator, run time and check. At the default settings (tt, 37 °C, 1,000 clocks; step 6 a recorded 30,000-clock run):

1. **The behavioural comparator model agrees with the post-layout comparator in closed loop (tt, 37 °C, 2,000 decisions).** The post-layout StrongARM, with its own mismatch and transient noise inside the modulator, decides as the threshold model predicts: of the 2,000 decisions over the two chips, only those whose input lies close to the threshold can differ, as often as the comparator's noise explains (0 to 3 of the 2,000 decisions differed in the development runs and in the run saved here, against 0.8 to 2.5 expected; this run's count is in Table XXIII). No memory, kickback or metastability effect appears at this length, and the transistor-level loop decodes to the same reading as the behavioural model (+0.1341 of full scale for both), as any stable loop would; the decision-by-decision comparison is the actual test. This supports the abstraction behind the system runs of Section VIII, with the limit that 2,000 decisions cannot reveal an effect rarer than about one in a thousand.
2. **The key generator recovers the key from transistor-level cells (one chip, one power-up, tt, 37 °C).** The field power-up of 600 Monte Carlo instances of the extracted SRAM cell at 37 °C differs from the enrolment in 7 of 600 cells (BER 1.17 %, against 1.32 % from the recorded Monte Carlo). The RTL decoder generated by the compiler corrects them, bit-identical to the model, and the server's enrolled key is recovered, after 91,127 clock cycles (9.1 ms at 10 MHz).
3. **The complete chain is consistent across levels.** The RTL keystream block encrypts and authenticates the transistor-level bitstream exactly as the model does, down to the 32-bit tag, in the one 1,000-bit frame simulated. The server accepts the frame and recovers every bit; a frame with one changed bit is rejected; an eavesdropper with a wrong key fails the MAC check and its bits agree with the true ones in 47.3 %, within two standard deviations of the 50 % that chance predicts.
4. **The replica attack succeeds against the original design at transistor level, over a long run (one recorded chip pair).** In the default 1,000-clock run the attack is only illustrative: its 80 attempts lie on 23 distinct, overlapping windows starting between clocks 200 and 223, and in every development run all of them yielded the original design's key (80 of 80 attempts; 0 of 80 for the proposal). Over this short run the two chips disagree on only 4 to 11 % of bits, so it says nothing about a long capture. Over 30,000 clocks (step 6, a recorded run of the same code and seeds), the chips disagree on 24.8 % of bits and 5.1 % of the 64-bit windows are clean, against 23.4–23.6 % and 3.9–4.6 % for a behavioural run on the same pair (same dither, input, offsets and doubled integrator noise; 20 comparator-noise seeds); Berlekamp-Massey recovers the original design's key from 8 of 80 windows (6–8 behaviourally) and the proposal's from none. The transistor-level pair lies slightly above the behavioural spread, so, for this pair, the behavioural model slightly underestimates the windows available to the attacker.

The run covers one corner and one temperature. Others can be chosen in the settings form; for example, fs at 85 °C should show the key failure that Section VIII-F predicts for a 25 °C enrolment (not part of the published run).

**Next.** Section XIII makes the same model available as an interactive, animated system, so that a reader can vary the settings that this section and Section VIII evaluated and watch their effect on every block.

# **XIII. The interactive explorer**
---
The sections before this one compute their results in fixed cells, at one setting at a time. This section answers a practical question: how can a reader follow any block of the link, under any attack, while changing the settings? The answer is the interactive explorer, a web page that runs the model of Section V in the browser. It supports the notebook's claims by making every intermediate signal visible, but **it computes none of the numbers reported here**: every card, table and figure of this notebook comes from the Python cells. The animations of the proposed system (Fig. 15) and of the spoofing attack (Fig. 48) were recorded from it.

**What it contains.** The model of Section V ported to JavaScript, with:

1. a transistor-level drawing of the chip (the simulation behind it is the behavioural model) and a live scope on every block (front end, modulator, PUF, fuzzy extractor, keystream, MAC, channel, receiver);
2. the attack evaluation of Section IX-A, with per-block waveforms for both designs under each attack;
3. a helper-data and key workbench, in which any helper-data bit or PUF cell can be inverted and its effect on the key followed;
4. the PUF reliability curves, the parameter sweeps of Section IX and the cost analysis of Section X.

**Settings it starts from.** The link below opens the explorer with the post-layout SKY130 values of Section VII-E (Table VIII): `comp_noise` = 0.001279, `int_noise` = 8.99e-06, `puf_sigma` = 0.02253, `puf_tc` = 0.02051, `puf_bias` = 0.4928, `bch_t` = 45. Here `comp_noise` is the comparator's input-referred noise σ<sub>n</sub> divided by V<sub>DD</sub>/4 (the model's full scale); `int_noise` is the first integrator's thermal noise per clock, in full-scale units, derived from the 9.48 pA measured in [1]; `puf_sigma` and `puf_tc` are the SRAM-PUF cell's noise-to-mismatch ratio s<sub>25</sub> at 25 °C and its temperature coefficient a, in s(T) = s<sub>25</sub>(1 + a·|T − 25 °C|); `puf_bias` is the fraction of cells that power up to 1, P(1); and `bch_t` is the number of fingerprint errors the BCH code corrects, t. The link carries these values in its address, so the page needs no other input. Its PUF reliability curves use the cell model's linear temperature law, which underestimates the 85 °C error rate (Section IX-B); the code strength t = 45 is the working setting of the system simulations, chosen with the simulated error rates of Section VII-E.

**How to use it.**

1. **[Open the explorer with this notebook's SKY130-derived settings](https://nithinpuru.github.io/secure_sensor_with_puf/#eyJzIjp7ImNvbXBfbm9pc2UiOjAuMDAxMjc5LCJpbnRfbm9pc2UiOjguOTkwMzM5NDYzNzY4ODc0ZS0wNiwicHVmX3NpZ21hIjowLjAyMjUzMTYzODg5OTYxNDExMiwicHVmX3RjIjowLjAyMDUwOTk4OTc4Mjg0NjY4MywicHVmX2JpYXMiOjAuNDkyNzk3ODUxNTYyNSwiYmNoX3QiOjQ1fX0)** (an internet connection is required; nothing is installed). The page itself is [nithinpuru.github.io/secure_sensor_with_puf](https://nithinpuru.github.io/secure_sensor_with_puf/).
2. Select an attack from the *Attack* menu above the diagram: every block then shows its signal under that attack, for the original design and for the proposal.
3. Change a setting and follow its effect block by block; the *Share* button generates a link that reproduces the current configuration.

The comparison with prior art follows in Section XIV.

# **XIV. Comparison with prior art**
---
**Question.** Where does the proposal stand among the four lines of work reviewed in Section III: compact cryptographic engines, physical-layer and analog-domain security, silicon PUF key generators, and the S-DSM of [1]? The answer places the two results of this notebook, the attack verdicts of Section IX and the cost of Section X, against what other approaches provide and what they cost. Table XXIV collects the comparison; this section explains how to read it, notes why its figures of merit cross technology nodes, and states what it shows.

### A. How to read the table
1. **Columns.** One column per line of prior work, with its references, then this work (shaded). A column summarises a family of designs, so an icon gives the family's typical behaviour, not that of every member.
2. **Upper row groups: properties** (cost, confidentiality, key protection, link integrity, evaluation). Each row is a property that matters for a micro-watt sensor link; read it across, from left to right. A positive icon means the approach provides the property, a neutral icon that it provides it in part or depending on the design, a negative icon that it does not; a dash means that the property does not apply or is not reported.
3. **Where this work's icons come from.** The confidentiality, key-protection and link-integrity rows of this work are the verdicts of the 15 attacks in Section IX (Table XIII); the cost rows are the area, power, figure of merit and transmitted bits of Section X (Table XVIII). The prior works' icons are this work's reading of what their own papers report.
4. **Lower row group: figures of merit,** read down a column. Each is quoted as reported by its reference, except the FOM row, computed from the reported energy per bit and process, with its own basis (measured chip, FPGA or simulation) and technology given in the first two rows; this work's values are from Section X.

### B. A note on technology
The prior works were fabricated in 14 to 65 nm CMOS; this work is synthesised in the SkyWater SKY130 open PDK, a 130 nm process whose 1.8 V devices have L<sub>min</sub> = 150 nm: 2.3× the minimum length of 65 nm and 6.8× to 10.7× that of 22 and 14 nm, at a supply 1.5× that of the 1.2 V chip of [1]. The raw figures of merit are therefore not an apples-to-apples comparison, and the difference favours the prior works: L<sub>min</sub>V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup>, to which the switching energy of a gate is proportional to first order, is 486 nm·V² for SKY130 against 93.6 nm·V² for the 65 nm process of [1], 5.2× less (Section X-E). No number is scaled from one process to another. Instead, four choices keep the comparison fair. Area is given in gate equivalents (GE, the area of a two-input NAND gate) of each library, which removes most of the node dependence. The designs of [1] that this work compares with, the S-DSM and Trivium, are re-implemented in the same SKY130 flow, in the same two forms as the proposal (one bit per clock, and radix 16 with clock gating), so that their power ratios to the proposal involve no scaling between processes (Table XV). Every work's energy per bit, measured on silicon or simulated at gate level, never estimated from a model, is divided by L<sub>min</sub>V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> of its own process at its nominal supply, which removes the process to first order, and by the security it buys, its security level S in bits and the number K of the four security properties it provides: **FOM = E<sub>bit</sub>/(L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> S K)**, lower is better (the FOM row of Table XXIV). And every number states its basis, measured or simulated. The open PDK is what makes every number here reproducible; a tape-out in a smaller node is a next step (Section XV).
