Upper row groups: properties, read across a row; icons: positive, provided; neutral, provided in part or depending on the design; negative, not provided; –: not applicable or not reported. Lower group: figures of merit, read down a column. Figures of merit are from each reference; GE: gate equivalents (NAND2 of each library). <b>The nodes differ, so the figures of merit are not a like-for-like comparison:</b> the prior works are in 14–65 nm, 2.3–10.7× smaller than SKY130 (L<sub>min</sub> = 150 nm), which favours their area and power. This work's area is in GE, which removes most of the node dependence; its power is given in SKY130 (gate-level simulation at 1.8 V, in a low-power form given equally to every design compared in Section X) and is not scaled to another process; the FOM row compares across processes. Energy per bit: the security block's power over its throughput, from each reference's own figure (Gbps/W, nJ/byte). FOM: energy per bit E<sub>bit</sub> (measured, or gate-level simulated for this work) over L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup>, the minimum gate length and nominal supply squared of the work's process (SKY130 150 nm, 1.8 V; 65 nm, 1.2 V), the security level S in bits and the number K of the four security properties provided (confidentiality, authentication, freshness, no key in NVM); no number is scaled between processes and no modelled number enters it (Section X-E). †: criteria that follow from this work's choice of architecture (bit-level encryption, shared with the S-DSM) or of method; the other columns do not aim at them, so their negative icons are not deficiencies.</div></div>

### C. What the comparison shows
1. **The proposal is the only approach that provides every security property of the table.** Crypto engines provide strong confidentiality but store their key and encrypt words, so the sensor must decimate first; PUF key generators protect the key but do not secure a link; the S-DSM keeps the cheapest link but, as Section IX shows, its short, linear and stored key fails 11 of the 15 attacks (Table XIII). The proposal fails none of them.
2. **By the figure of merit, the proposal is the most efficient secure design of the table; in absolute power it costs more than the S-DSM.** With every design given the same low-power techniques (radix-16 parallel state update and clock gating), the proposal's keystream block dissipates 64.3 µW in gate-level simulation in SKY130 at 1.8 V (73.4 µW routed), 3.6× the S-DSM in the same flow and form, a ratio taken within one process. Its FOM, FOM = E<sub>bit</sub>/(L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> S K), is 29.1 aJ/(nm·V²) (33.2 routed), against 1,603 for [1]'s measured S-DSM and 3,142 for the DTLS engine [9] (Table XXIV): its process-normalised energy per bit is 13,230 aJ/(nm·V²) against 25,641 for [1]'s measured S-DSM, but 3.6× the 3,724 of the S-DSM's RTL in the same flow and form, since [1]'s measured block takes 2.9× the value of its RTL; and it buys 113.8 bits of security and all four security properties against 16 bits and one. Placed unscaled on the chip of [1], its SKY130 power takes 4.5 % of the chip's total, against 1.7 % for the S-DSM and 14.0 % for Trivium as measured (Table XIX).
3. **The transmitted bits stay at the S-DSM's level, but they are not the fewest possible.** For the same information at OSR 50 the proposal sends 50.04 bits per reading, the S-DSM 50 and the decimating ADC with Trivium of [1] 72–80: 1.44–1.60× fewer, as for the S-DSM. A design that decimates on the sensor and encrypts 16-bit words at the Nyquist rate with Grain-128a + MAC sends 16.04, **3.1× fewer than the proposal** (Table XVIII). No radio is designed in this work, so no radio energy is claimed.
4. **The area is larger than that of the smallest engines.** The keystream block is 9,869 GE in its low-power form, against 2,090 gates for NanoAES [8] and 548 for SIMON [10]; the key decoder compiled in Section XI (8,984 GE), a SHA-256 core (15,097 GE) and the PUF array bring the designed parts to 38,638 GE, but the decoder and the hash work only at power-up. Those engines, however, still need a decimator and a stored key and, except for the DTLS engine [9], provide no integrity by themselves.

Section XV draws the conclusions of the notebook from these results.

# **XV. Conclusion, limitations and next steps**
---
Section I-C asked four questions. This section answers them from the results of this run, in order (A to D), states the limitations of the evidence (E) and the next steps (F). The numbers are those of this run, from the tables and figures cited with them.

### A. Question 1: how secure is the S-DSM against a realistic attacker?
1. **It withstands the cryptanalyses of [1] only as [1] carries them out, and the model shows why.** The model is consistent with the two-channel test of [1]: 50.0 % and 48.2 % of bits differ (zero input, same message), against 50.05 % and 49.8 % measured (Table III). With its simplified dither, the model reaches the measured value with a small offset between the channels; [1] attributes the disagreement to its dither, and the model does not contradict that measurement. A competent attacker does not stop there: a scan of every position of the replica's keystream estimate with the public LFSR polynomial, a replica trimmed in input, multi-frame majority voting and an amplitude estimate turn the same three experiments into successful attacks (A4–A6).
2. **It fails 11 of the 15 attacks** (Table XIII): brute force of its 16-bit key, Berlekamp-Massey recovery of its linear keystream, the three attacks of [1] by a competent attacker, extraction of its stored key and keystream reuse through a replayed session nonce breach or leak the data; spoofing (the attack anticipated in [1]), a cloned sensor, replay and bit-flipping make the server accept fake data. Brute force needs nothing beyond eavesdropping; each of the others needs one further capability: learning a few keystream bits, obtaining a chip, or transmitting on the link. Six of the 11 (key extraction, keystream reuse, spoofing, cloning, replay and bit-flipping) lie beyond the eavesdropper that [1] evaluates, and the multi-frame saturation attack assumes that the LFSR restarts from the key in every frame, which [1] does not state.

**Answer.** No. Against the cryptanalyses as [1] evaluates them (a zero or DC input with a replica chip, the same key with the same message) the S-DSM is protected by the decorrelation between the victim's and the replica's bits (Table III, Fig. 53), and an attacker who scans the whole capture with the public LFSR polynomial and trims the replica removes that protection. It also falls to an attacker who brute-forces its 16-bit key, which needs nothing beyond eavesdropping, or who learns a few keystream bits, obtains a chip or transmits on the link: **11 of the 15 attacks succeed**, and no comparator or integrator property within the accuracy budget changes that.

### B. Question 2: can the stored key be eliminated and every frame authenticated, and at what cost?
1. **Security: none of the 15 attacks succeeds against the proposal in this evaluation** (Table XIII): 0 of 15 succeed and 5 are detected, with the frame rejected; 9 verdicts are simulated, 2 analytic and 4 rest on stated assumptions (key length, no key in non-volatile memory and no read-out path, unclonability). Brute force and Berlekamp-Massey fail against Grain-128a's 128-bit key and nonlinear state; extraction and cloning fail because no secret is held in non-volatile memory and a counterfeit chip's SRAM powers up differently; forged, replayed and bit-flipped frames are rejected by the counter and the MAC; a replayed session nonce no longer repeats the keystream, because the chip nonce enters the IV; and helper-data manipulation leaks nothing (0 bits in 200 tampered power-ups), because in the syndrome construction the decoder never sees the fingerprint.
2. **Cost: 3.6× the S-DSM's power under equal treatment, the best figure of merit of the designs compared, and the S-DSM's transmitted bits** (Section X, Table XV, Table XVIII, Table XIX). Every compared design is given the same low-power techniques, a radix-16 parallel state update and clock gating, and simulated at gate level under the same conditions. The proposal's keystream block is 9,869 GE, against 869 for the S-DSM and 2,931 for Trivium in the same form. Placed and routed (399 × 399 µm, 0 DRC violations, LVS match, +85.5 ns setup slack at the slow corner at 10 MHz with OpenRCX-extracted wires; 16 antenna violations not yet closed), its gate-level simulated power is 64.3 µW in SKY130 (73.4 µW routed), against 415 µW as written for one bit per clock, and 3.6× the S-DSM's 18.1 µW in the same flow; the ratio does not depend on the process. No number is scaled between processes: placed unscaled on the chip of [1], its SKY130 power takes 4.5 % of the chip's total, against 1.7 % for the S-DSM and 14.0 % for Trivium as measured, and its figure of merit, FOM = E<sub>bit</sub>/(L<sub>min</sub> V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup> S K), is **29.1 aJ/(nm·V²) against 1,603 for [1]'s measured S-DSM** and 233 for the S-DSM in the same flow and form (requirement R1). No radio is designed in this work, so no radio energy is claimed; what the architecture sets is the number of bits sent for the same information. At OSR 50 the proposal sends 50.04 bits per reading, as the S-DSM sends 50, against 72–80 for the decimate-then-Trivium design of [1] (1.44–1.60× fewer); an information-equivalent design that decimates on the sensor and sends 16-bit words at the Nyquist rate sends 16.04, 3.1× fewer than the proposal. The key generator adds the compiled decoder (8,984 GE) and a SHA-256 core (15,097 GE); with the PUF array, the designed parts total 38,638 GE (Table XXII).

**Answer.** Yes, at a cost in power. A key regenerated from SRAM cells at every power-up, used by Grain-128a with its MAC, a counter, a session nonce and a chip nonce, closes all 15 attacks of this evaluation (9 verdicts simulated, 2 analytic, 4 under stated assumptions) while keeping the S-DSM's front end and its number of transmitted bits, 1.44–1.60× fewer than the decimate-then-Trivium design of [1] at OSR 50. The cost is digital power: 3.6× the S-DSM under strictly equal treatment, and 4.5 % of the chip's power even with the block's unscaled SKY130 power; per unit of security and of process it is the most efficient design compared; and a conventional design that decimates to the Nyquist rate before encrypting sends 3.1× fewer bits.

### C. Question 3: do real circuits change these answers?
1. **Neither the comparator nor the integrators protect it within the accuracy budget** (Section VIII). With identical analog front ends, the replica attack succeeds in 100 % of simulated chip pairs at all 45 process, supply and temperature (PVT) conditions, because two chips' loops still agree over clean 64-bit windows (4.9 % of windows, although the chips disagree on 25 % of bits; Fig. 42). A replica that differs from the victim only in its SKY130 comparator offset compromises the original design in 24 of 24 chip pairs (Fig. 41; Fig. 42(b)). Against an attacker who scans every 64-bit window of up to four frames, comparator noise protects the design only from σ<sub>n</sub> = 160 mV (0 of 100 pairs broken), 197× its largest PVT value, at a cost of 7.5 dB of SNDR; no comparator offset protects it (24 of 100 pairs still broken at 3 V); integrator noise does not even at 1,000× the value of [1] (97 of 100 pairs broken), nor capacitor-ratio mismatch at σ = 50 % (16 of 100).
2. **With 600 cells and a 25 °C enrolment, reliability and secrecy cannot both be met** (Section VII-E, Table VIII). The extracted SKY130 cell has a noise-to-mismatch ratio s<sub>25</sub> = 0.0225 at 25 °C (0.0205 from the schematic), about 2.7× below the illustrative 0.06 the model started from. From the simulated error rates (1.37 %, 0.99 % and 3.14 % at −40, 25 and 85 °C) and a cell model that also represents the cells that flip with temperature, a key-failure probability below 10<sup>−6</sup> from 0 to 85 °C needs t = 39 for the 99th percentile of 1,000 simulated chips (33–46 over the 95 % interval of the 85 °C error rate), whereas the bounded entropy budget (192 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy, for a 128-bit key with the hash margin) allows at most t = 35. The system simulations keep t = 45, which every simulated chip meets at the point estimate but which leaves 94–137 secret bits: a working setting for the system simulations, while the key generators that meet both requirements are the two below; an enrolment at −40 and 85 °C meets both: t = 17 holds 10⁻⁶ for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips at every corner and leaves 284–352 secret bits (935 cells, 600 kept; Section VIII-F); the key-generator compiler of Section XI generates a decoder, verified in RTL simulation, for an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C (repetition-3 and BCH t = 4 code, 1,395 cells, 194 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound, the same 192-bit budget). The earlier noise-only sizing of one chip needed t = 48, the schematic values t = 41, and the linear temperature law t = 32, because it underestimates the 85 °C error rate (1.75 % against 3.14 %).
3. **Across process corners, the key needs an enrolment at both ends of the temperature range** (Sections VII-F and VIII-F). With a 25 °C enrolment and t = 45, all simulated chips meet the target at tt and ss, 72.9 % at sf and none at ff and fs; the 99th-percentile chip needs t = 33 at tt, 29 at ss, 55 at sf, 89 at ff and more than 120 at fs, whereas the bounded secret of 600 cells allows at most t = 27, so no corner meets both requirements. At the fast-nMOS corners most errors are reproducible flips, cells whose preferred state reverses with temperature (25.6 % of 27.8 % errors at fs, 85 °C; Table XI). Keeping only the cells that are stable and equal at both enrolment temperatures removes them, provided the two temperatures bracket the operating range: an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C leaves the cells that flip at −40 °C (held-out error rate up to 3.09 % at sf), whereas one at −40 and 85 °C keeps 68.9–95.3 % of the cells and holds the held-out error rate at or below 1.01 % at every corner and temperature. With it, t = 17 meets 10<sup>−6</sup> for at least 99.7 % of the simulated chips at every corner and leaves 284–352 secret bits, from 935 cells for 600 kept.
4. **In simulation, the SKY130 circuits leave the sensor's accuracy unchanged across PVT, and the abstractions behind these results hold at the condition tested.** The analog front end is that of [1]; across the 45 PVT conditions its SNDR stays at 60.3–60.4 dB, with 88× margin in comparator noise before it loses 3 dB, and the modulator needs an OTA gain of about 40 dB or more (Table XII).

**Answer.** The real circuits do not change the sensor's accuracy, and they do not secure the original design at any PVT condition: its resistance to the cryptanalyses of [1] comes from analog mismatch ahead of the quantiser, and every analog quantity that could stop the replica attack does so only at a direct cost in accuracy. They do change the key: the SRAM cell's process corner and temperature set its reliability, so that 600 cells enrolled at 25 °C cannot meet both the reliability target and the secrecy limit even at the typical corner, and the key generator must be sized and enrolled for its worst corner, as the two-temperature enrolment of Section VIII-F and the compiled codes of Section XI are.

### D. Question 4: can the key generator be derived from a specification, and do the models hold together?
1. **A compiler turns this specification into a decoder verified in RTL simulation, synthesised and laid out** (Section XI, Table XX). With a 25 °C enrolment, no design with a repetition factor r ≤ 7 and BCH length n ≤ 1023 meets the target at all five corners. With an enrolment at 25 and 85 °C (specification C, for 0 to 85 °C), the selected design (r = 3, 324 groups, t = 4, 1,395 cells) does, with 194 secret bits at the 95 % lower bound of the min-entropy, the same 192-bit budget as the hand design; its generated decoder, 8,984 GE, reproduces the model's reconstruction in 12/12 directed and 60/60 random tests, bit for bit and in the success flag, and is placed live and routed with 0 DRC violations in a recorded run, with 2 antenna violations left open. The BCH-only designs (r = 1) need t = 21 to 36 and, by the compiler's area estimate (they are not synthesised), about 1.5–2.2× the total area of the selected designs. The selected decoder (8,984 GE) is larger than the keystream block as written for one bit per clock (5,240 GE) and close to its low-power form (9,869 GE), and a round-per-clock SHA-256 core (15,097 GE) is larger still: with the array and the low-power keystream block, the designed parts total 38,638 GE, 39 % of it the hash (Table XXII). In this serial template the key generator, not the cipher, dominates the area.
2. **The abstractions hold in one mixed-level simulation of the complete sensor** (Section XII, Table XXIII). The transistor-level SRAM array differs from its enrolment in 7 of 600 bits at 37 °C (1.17 %, against 1.32 % in the recorded Monte Carlo), the RTL decoder recovers the enrolled key bit for bit, the RTL keystream block matches the model, and the transistor-level comparators differ from the threshold model only as often as their noise predicts (0 to 3 of 2,000 decisions across the runs, each count within what the noise predicts; the card of step 3 gives this run's) (Table XXIII).
3. **The replica attack succeeds at transistor level** (Section XII, step 6, a recorded run made with twice the corrected first-integrator noise). With the post-layout comparator in the loop of two simulated chips that differ in their comparators' mismatch and noise, over 30,000 clocks, their bits disagree on 24.8 % and 5.1 % of the 64-bit windows are clean (the behavioural model gives 4.9 % over the PVT pairs of Section VIII-B and 3.9–4.6 % for the same pair); Berlekamp-Massey recovers the original design's key from 8 of 80 windows, and the proposal's from none.

**Answer.** Yes. The compiler derives a key generator that meets the target at all five corners, verified bit for bit and placed; and the mixed-level simulation agrees, at one condition, with the behavioural comparator and SRAM models behind the system-level results, and that the replica attack recovers the original design's key, but not the proposal's, from transistor-level chips.

### E. Limitations
* **The SRAM noise is thermal only.** 1/f noise, random telegraph noise, supply noise and ageing of real silicon are not in the SPICE model, so s<sub>25</sub> = 0.0225 is a lower bound. With a conservative noise about 2.7× higher (s<sub>25</sub> = 0.06), the target would need t = 60, which leaves no secret bits with 600 cells; a product would require more cells and a concatenated code (repetition and BCH, as compiled in Section XI, or Reed-Muller or Golay), or dark-bit masking [15].
* **The two-temperature enrolment is evaluated on limited simulated statistics.** Its benefit rests on 512 cells and two held-out power-ups per corner, which resolve error rates of about 0.1 %; a product must also screen chips at the maximum operating temperature, because the corners at risk cannot be identified at room temperature.
* **The PUF model's temperature law is linear and does not follow the simulated cell.** The SRAM-PUF is characterised at −40, 25 and 85 °C (the specified range is 0–85 °C). The noise-only law s(T) = s<sub>25</sub>(1 + a·|T − 25 °C|) is symmetric about 25 °C and cannot follow both −40 °C and 85 °C: it underestimates the 85 °C error rate of the extracted cell (1.75 % against 3.14 %, Table VIII), so the code is sized from the simulated error rates, not from the law, and the reliability results of Section IX-B and C, which use the law, are optimistic at 85 °C. Sized in this way, the 600-cell design enrolled at 25 °C cannot meet both the 10<sup>−6</sup> target and the secrecy limit (item C-2); the two-temperature enrolment and the compiled codes meet both. At the process corners, whose error rates rise far more steeply, the key is evaluated with a cell model anchored to every simulated temperature as well. The SRAM-PUF corners have no supply axis (the cell resolves while V<sub>DD</sub> ramps), and the 94–137 secret bits are computed at the nominal bias P(1) = 0.493 only.
* **The dither of [1] is modelled in simplified form.** [1] attributes the disagreement between its channels to its dither and supports this with chip measurements. The model reads the dither ladder as ±0.022 of full scale at the comparator of a discrete-time loop, where the loop corrects most of its effect, and reproduces the measured disagreement with a small channel offset instead (Section VI). The verdicts that rest on analog decorrelation (the replica, same-message and saturation attacks A4 to A6, and the system-level studies of the original design's analog protection) therefore hold for the dither as modelled; in the sweep of Section IX-C no point with a dither of 0.2 or more is breached by the attacker of [1], so the margin of the chip of [1] may be larger than the model's. The verdicts of key search, Berlekamp-Massey, key extraction, keystream reuse and the frame attacks (A2, A3, A7 to A9, A13 to A15) do not depend on the dither.
* **The comparison with prior art crosses technology nodes.** The prior works are in 14–65 nm, 2.3–10.7× smaller than SKY130 (L<sub>min</sub> = 150 nm), so it is not like-for-like (Section XIV).
* **Parts of the link are behavioural, and power is estimated.** The modulator's integrators, the TIA and the buffer are behavioural, although non-ideal (comparator noise and offset from SPICE, integrator thermal noise from [1], integrator saturation, and swept OTA gain and capacitor mismatch). Digital power comes from gate-level simulation at the typical corner without glitches (zero-delay activity); the wires of the keystream block are extracted with OpenRCX, those of the other designs estimated on the placement. No power is scaled between processes: the comparison with the 65 nm blocks of [1] uses the figure of merit, which normalises the process to first order (L<sub>min</sub>V<sub>nom</sub><sup>2</sup>) and cannot remove what [1]'s measured blocks contain beyond their logic (2.9× and 5.1× the normalised energy per bit of their RTL in this flow).
* **Not all of the security subsystem is implemented.** The keystream block is placed and routed live; the compiled key-reconstruction unit is placed live, and its detailed routing and DRC are from a recorded run of the same flow; a SHA-256 core is verified and synthesised (15,097 GE) but not placed, and its padding and control, the array periphery and the downlink receiver are not designed. The power and energy of the key-reconstruction unit and the hash are not computed, and the 32-bit delay line that lets lock-step hardware MAC the counter and ID ahead of the data (about 170 GE) is estimated, not designed. The blocks are not integrated into one layout.
* **The mixed-level simulation runs at one corner and for a short time live.** The live run covers 1,000 clocks at tt and 37 °C (other corners are a form option); the 30,000-clock replica attack of step 6 took 72 minutes on two cores and is shown from a recorded run, made before the correction of the first-integrator noise (twice the corrected value, which, if anything, makes the attack harder). Its key decoder is the 600-cell, t = 45 design of Section VII-E, not the two-temperature design selected by the compiler.
* **The layouts are single cells drawn with the logic design rules.** The SRAM cell is several times larger than the foundry's SRAM bit cell and is not placed in an array; the comparator's output buffers and SR latch stay at schematic level; the extraction is Magic's, capacitance only (the li1 and met1 runs are a few squares, so wire resistance is negligible here).
* **Grain-128a has a published full-round fast correlation attack** in stream-cipher mode (2<sup>113.8</sup> data, 2<sup>115.4</sup> time) [18]: impractical, but below the nominal 2<sup>128</sup>; its authors note that the authenticated mode used here is much harder to attack.

### F. Next steps
1. **A transistor-level front end:** SKY130 integrators and TIA in place of the behavioural ones, in the mixed-level simulation of Section XII.
2. **A noisier cell model:** 1/f and random telegraph noise and ageing added to the SRAM-PUF cell, and the compiler of Section XI re-run against it, with dark-bit masking as an alternative to the two-temperature enrolment.
3. **The compiled key generator in the mixed-level simulation:** the two-temperature design of specification C, with its array, enrolled and reconstructed from transistor-level cells at the fast-nMOS corners where the 25 °C design fails.
4. **The complete security subsystem in one layout:** key-reconstruction unit, a synthesised lightweight hash, the MAC delay line and the keystream block placed and routed together, with RC extraction and the power of every block.
5. **A tape-out in a node comparable to the prior works** (65 nm or below), where the power can be measured rather than scaled.

# **Appendix: Source, licence and reuse**
---
This appendix states where the code behind every result lives, which results come from recorded runs and how to re-run them, and under which terms the work may be reused.

**Source.** The notebook is self-contained, and none of this work's code is hidden in an installed package. The bit-exact model of both designs and the 15 attacks are defined in the cells of Section V; the larger modules are written into the session by `%%writefile` cells, where they can be read: the comparator and SRAM-PUF SPICE testbenches and the layout generators (`comparator_spice.py`, `puf_spice.py`, `sky130_layout.py`, `puf_layout.py`, `comparator_layout.py`; Section VII), the RTL, synthesis and place-and-route flows (`rtl_flow.py`, `pnr_flow.py`; Section X), the key-generator compiler (`keygen.py`; Section XI) and the mixed-level engine (`mixedsim.py`; Section XII). The open-source tools are installed by the setup cell of Section VII-A.

**Recorded runs.** Seven simulations are too long for a Colab session. They are shown from recorded runs of the same code and seeds, and each can be re-run: the 1,024-cell SRAM-PUF Monte Carlo runs (`PUF_MODE = "full"`; the live 128-cell run is checked bit for bit against the record), the post-layout Monte Carlo checks of both cells (`PEX_LIVE = True`), the PVT grids of both cells (`dev/spice_comparator/demo_pvt.py` and `dev/spice_puf/demo_pvt.py` in the source repository), the SRAM-PUF mechanism checks with floating or grounded bit lines and the supply-ramp sweep (`dev/spice_puf/demo_mechanism.py`), the clock-gating study of the keystream block, two routings of the gated and ungated block (`CLOCK_GATING_LIVE = True`; recorded by `dev/rtl/record_signoff.py`), the detailed routing of the compiled key-reconstruction unit (`ROUTE_COMPILED = True`) and the 30,000-clock transistor-level replica attack (`LONG_RUN = True`). The recorded SRAM-PUF runs also contain power-ups at 125 °C, above the specified 0–85 °C range; they are not used, and the cell is characterised at −40, 25 and 85 °C (`dev/spice_puf/refit_0_85.py`). All other results are computed in the session.

**Explorer.** The explorer of Section XIII is the first author's own open-source tool ([nithinpuru.github.io/secure_sensor_with_puf](https://nithinpuru.github.io/secure_sensor_with_puf/)).

**Licence.** This notebook and all code in it are released under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE). The SKY130 PDK, ngspice, Yosys, KLayout, Magic, netgen, OpenROAD and Icarus Verilog are downloaded at run time under their own open-source licences and are not redistributed here.
